questions.explanation: Diverticular disease Etiology Diverticulosis: ↑ intraluminal pressure causing herniation through points of weakness (vasa recta penetration) Diverticular bleeding: injury to exposed vasa recta Diverticulitis: trapped food particles & ↑ intraluminal pressure causing microperforation Symptoms Diverticulosis: none Diverticular bleeding: painless hematochezia Diverticulitis: left lower quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, fever Risk factors Diet high in red meat & fat & low in fiber Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking Diverticula are outpouchings of the colonic wall that form at points of weakness, most commonly in the sigmoid colon. Diverticular diseases are strongly associated with chronic constipation; the increased colonic pressures in constipation may promote the formation of diverticula, and conversely, the altered motility seen in diverticulosis may contribute to constipation. Diets high in fruit and vegetable fiber help prevent further complications of diverticulosis by softening the stool and preventing constipation, whereas decreased fiber intake (eg, excessive meat consumption) is associated with increased risk (Choice B). Physical activity is also inversely correlated with the risk for complications. Therefore, vigorous physical activity (eg, jogging, running) is recommended. Other factors associated with an increased risk include obesity and smoking. (Choice A) In the past, patients with diverticulosis were advised to avoid nuts and seeds under the assumption that these hard objects may obstruct the diverticular lumen and precipitate acute diverticulitis. However, recent studies have found no link between the intake of these foods and the incidence of diverticulitis. (Choice C) Elective surgical resection (eg, sigmoid colectomy) is indicated for diverticulosis complicated by recurrent bleeding, perforation, peritonitis, or abscess that does not resolve with percutaneous drainage. It is also occasionally considered for those with recurrent attacks of acute diverticulitis. Uncomplicated diverticulosis can otherwise be managed nonoperatively. (Choice D) Frequent colonoscopy is indicated for patients at increased risk for colon cancer (eg, large or multiple adenomatous polyps, Lynch syndrome). In the absence of adenomas, patients with diverticulosis may return to a routine colon screening schedule. Educational objective: Diverticulosis is characterized by outpouchings of the colonic wall and is strongly associated with chronic constipation. Complications include hemorrhage and diverticulitis. The risk for complications is lower with vigorous activity and a high-fiber diet; the risk is higher with heavy meat consumption, obesity, and smoking.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up after a recent colonoscopy. Six weeks ago, the patient was hospitalized due to abdominal pain in the left lower quadrant; CT scan of the abdomen revealed focal thickening of the sigmoid wall. He has never had similar symptoms. The symptoms resolved with treatment, and the patient underwent outpatient colonoscopy a week ago, which revealed sigmoid colon findings as shown in the exhibit. He now feels well and reports no residual symptoms. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for preventing future complications from this patient's condition?

questions.explanation: ASCVD risk-enhancing factors Clinical history Family history of premature ASCVD Chronic inflammatory conditions (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV/AIDS) Metabolic syndrome (eg, central obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia) Chronic kidney disease High-risk ethnicity (eg, South Asian) Lipid panel subsets LDL >160 mg/dL Triglycerides ≥175 mg/dL Other laboratory results High-sensitivity C-reactive protein ≥2 mg/dL Lipoprotein(a) ≥50 mg/dL Imaging tests Positive coronary artery calcium test ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. This patient has well-controlled diabetes mellitus (DM). DM is a major risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD); statin therapy is effective in reducing this risk regardless of baseline lipid levels. ASCVD risk increases with age; therefore, most patients age ≥40 with DM should be offered statin therapy (eg, rosuvastatin) for primary prevention of ASCVD. In younger patients, statins are recommended for those who have additional risk factors (eg, hypertension, smoking) and can be considered for any patients with DM who desire aggressive risk factor management. Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil) are highly effective in lowering triglyceride levels and reduce the risk for acute pancreatitis in those with severe hypertriglyceridemia (eg, >1,000 mg/dL) but do not provide the ASCVD risk reduction that statins provide (Choice B). Statins also reduce triglycerides, albeit to a smaller degree than fibrates, and are the preferred first-line therapy for patients with mild hypertriglyceridemia (ie, 150-500 mg/dL). (Choices A and D) ACE inhibitors (eg, lisinopril) are the preferred first-line antihypertensive agents in patients with DM and are also recommended for normotensive patients who have moderately increased (urine albumin/creatinine ratio [UACR] 30-300 mg/g) or severely increased (UACR >300 mg/g) albuminuria. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, amlodipine) are appropriate for add-on therapy when needed. However, this patient's blood pressure is at target (recommended: <125-130/80 mm Hg) and UACR is normal, so antihypertensive medication is not needed. (Choice C) This patient's hemoglobin A1c is at goal (ie, <7%); an increase in therapy (eg, the addition of glimepiride) is not indicated and is likely to precipitate hypoglycemia. Educational objective: Statin therapy (eg, rosuvastatin) is indicated for the primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in all patients age ≥40 with diabetes mellitus, regardless of baseline lipid levels. Statins should also be considered for younger patients with diabetes mellitus who have additional cardiovascular risk factors.

Current management includes dietary modification, exercise, and metformin, which he takes as prescribed. The patient does not smoke and drinks 1 or 2 glasses of wine 3 times a week. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min. BMI is 29 kg/m2. questions.explanation: This patient from a resource-limited region has persistent gastrointestinal discomfort, features of malabsorption (eg, chronic diarrhea, weight loss), and eosinophilia, likely due to a parasitic infection. Various parasites can cause intestinal infection, including protozoa (eg, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia) and helminths (eg, Ascaris lumbricoides, Strongyloides stercoralis). This patient's preceding self-limited pulmonary symptoms (eg, cough, dyspnea, wheezing) raise suspicion specifically for hookworm infection (eg, Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus), which is common in the tropics (eg, Thailand). After penetrating the skin, hookworm larvae migrate through blood vessels to the lungs, where they enter the alveoli, ascend to the pharynx, and are swallowed. The pulmonary phase may be asymptomatic or cause mild, self-limiting respiratory symptoms, as seen in this patient. Once inside the intestines, mature hookworms attach to the mucosa and lacerate capillaries to ingest the extravasated blood, causing diarrhea and iron deficiency anemia. Persistent intestinal attachment contributes to eosinophilia and typical symptoms of abdominal pain and excessive flatulence. Parasitic intestinal infections are diagnosed by stool analysis for ova and parasites with specimens obtained on 3 separate days because shedding of parasites is intermittent. Treatment involves iron replacement and antihelminthic therapy (eg, albendazole). (Choices A and E) Celiac disease, which can be evaluted by antiendomysial antibody testing and upper endoscopy, presents with chronic abdominal discomfort and malabsorption. However, eosinophilia is not characteristic. In addition, this patient's recent emigration from Thailand and brief pulmonary symptoms make hookworm infection more likely. (Choice B) Bronchoalveolar lavage detects various pulmonary diseases (eg, interstitial lung disease, acute eosinophilic pneumonia), which may present with chronic cough or wheezing. This patient's brief, self-limited respiratory symptoms make ongoing lung disease unlikely. (Choice C) Abdominal CT scan with oral contrast may be considered for suspected inflammatory bowel disease. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, chronic (often bloody) diarrhea, malabsorption, and microcytic anemia. However, this patient's nonbloody diarrhea, in conjunction with recent emigration from a resource-limited country and eosinophilia, makes parasitic infection more likely. (Choice F) Carcinoid syndrome, characterized by elevated urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels, presents with intermittent flushing and bronchospasm, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. Malabsorption and eosinophilia are not characteristic. Educational objective: Parasitic intestinal infections typically present with chronic gastrointestinal discomfort, malabsorption (eg, chronic diarrhea, weight loss), and eosinophilia in individuals from resource-limited regions. Concern for hookworm infection is raised when mild, self-limiting respiratory symptoms precede the gastrointestinal symptoms. Serial stool analysis for ova and parasites is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy comes to the office due to intermittent nausea, watery diarrhea, and a bloating sensation for the past several months. The patient has also had episodic periumbilical pain, especially after a meal, and has lost 2.3 kg (5.1 lb) since the symptoms started. He emigrated from rural Thailand with his family approximately 8 months ago. Shortly after arriving in the United States, the patient developed dry cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing that spontaneously resolved after several days; otherwise, he has no medical conditions. The patient is afebrile, and other vital signs are within normal range. Bilateral breath sounds are normal. Heart sounds are normal with no murmur. The abdomen is soft and nontender, and bowel sounds are normal. Laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 72 fL Leukocytes 8,000/mm3 Neutrophils 60% Eosinophils 10% Lymphocytes 30% Serum albumin 3.4 g/dL Serum amylase 91 U/L Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study for this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with generalized muscle pain also has loss of enjoyment of activities ("work stopped being fun"), poor concentration (eg, forgetting orders), low energy, early-morning awakening, and psychomotor slowing (eg, speaking slowly, minimal movement) on mental status examination. This constellation is consistent with a somatic presentation of major depressive disorder (MDD). Nonspecific muscle pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbance are commonly reported symptoms of depression in the primary care setting, where patients may feel reluctant to discuss emotional issues and may focus on their physical symptoms instead. When physical examination and laboratory evaluation fail to identify a medical etiology, treatment of depression should be initiated. Treatment of MDD consists of antidepressant medication and/or psychotherapy. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, sertraline, paroxetine) are commonly used first line. Antidepressant therapy has been shown to improve painful physical symptoms in patients with depressive disorders. (Choices A and D) Clonazepam, a benzodiazepine, and buspirone are antianxiety agents that are not used as first-line treatments for MDD. They have a role in the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or as adjunctive medication in depressed patients with comorbid GAD. This patient has some worries about finding a job and finances, but these are not out of proportion for the situation and are not causing distress, unlike in GAD. (Choices B and E) Cyclobenzaprine is a muscle relaxant used for chronic pain and fibromyalgia. Glucocorticoids can result in improvement in cases of polymyalgia rheumatica or other rheumatologic conditions. However, given this patient's normal physical examination findings (vs soft tissue tenderness in fibromyalgia) and her other constellation of symptoms (eg, anhedonia, poor concentration, sleep disturbances) that would not be explained by rheumatologic conditions, her generalized pain is most likely a somatic symptom of depression, best targeted with antidepressant medication. Antidepressant treatment frequently results in improvement in depression-related pain. (Choice C) This patient's depressive symptoms are having significant impact on her functioning; therefore, reassurance and regular follow-up would be inappropriate. Educational objective: Patients with major depressive disorder in the primary care setting may have somatic symptoms such as pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbance. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor therapy can improve these symptoms in addition to providing their antidepressant effect.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the office due to "pain all over." The patient has had generalized muscle pain for 2 months and feels that her symptoms are due to "standing all day" as a waitress. She notes that her pain has continued despite being fired from her job a few weeks ago. She says, "I worked at that restaurant for years and loved being a waitress. At some point, work stopped being fun—probably because I kept forgetting things and mixing up orders." The patient is worried about finding a new job but feels that she has very little energy and is too tired to fill out applications. She used to have no sleeping difficulties but now regularly wakes up hours before her alarm clock rings and lies in bed unable to fall back asleep. She is anxious about her finances and has forgotten to pay a couple of bills, although she has been able to borrow money from her parents to pay rent. Medications include as-needed acetaminophen for pain. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination, including neurological, rheumatologic, and musculoskeletal examination, is unremarkable. The patient appears tired and speaks slowly with minimal movement; she has no suicidal ideation. A basic metabolic profile, complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and TSH are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with hypertension and a pulsatile abdominal mass suggestive of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) now has acute bilateral digital cyanosis, likely due to atheroembolization from the AAA. AAA can trigger embolization from either an aneurysmal thrombus (arterio-arterial embolization) or from disrupted cholesterol plaque (atheroembolization). This patient has cholesterol embolization syndrome (CES), resulting from the breaking off and distal embolization of fragments of atherosclerotic plaque. CES classically presents following abdominal aorta instrumentation (eg, coronary angiography) but may also occur spontaneously or in the setting of rapid AAA expansion. The shower of cholesterol microemboli leads to inflammation and distal tissue ischemia, manifesting as acute kidney injury (suprarenal AAA), mesenteric ischemia, lower extremity livedo reticularis, and/or digital cyanosis (blue toe syndrome) that is typically bilateral. Neurologic sequelae can occur with ascending aorta and/or carotid involvement. In contrast with CES (atheroembolism), a thrombotic (arterio-arterial) embolus classically presents as a single, relatively large infarct in a distal organ or tissue (eg, discrete, wedge-shaped renal infarct). AAA should be suspected in patients with appropriate risk factors (eg, age >60, smoking, male sex, atherosclerosis) and manifestations of atheroembolization. Management is primarily supportive and involves (1) improving cardiovascular risk factors and (2) evaluating for endovascular AAA repair to prevent future atheroembolization and possible impending rupture. (Choice B) Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome most commonly occurs in young women. It is less likely in this older man without a history of arterial or venous thrombosis or associated rheumatological conditions. (Choice C) Extensive aortoiliac atherosclerotic stenosis can lead to erectile dysfunction and claudication of the gluteal muscles and lower extremities (Leriche syndrome). The presence of normal femoral and popliteal pulses argues against this diagnosis. (Choice D) Inferior vena cava obstruction results in massive bilateral lower extremity edema and would not present as isolated blue toe syndrome. (Choice E) Raynaud phenomenon, involving nonocclusive ischemia due to cold-induced vasospasm, most commonly affects the upper extremities of young patients (age <30). It is less likely in this older man with no history of digital cyanosis and multiple risk factors for AAA. (Choice F) Thromboangiitis obliterans presents with digital ischemia in tobacco users; however, affected patients are typically younger (age <45) and lack other signs of an embolic source (eg, palpable epigastric mass suggesting AAA). Educational objective: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) may initially present with cholesterol embolization syndrome, often following instrumentation of the abdominal aorta or triggered by rapid AAA expansion. Patients may have acute kidney injury, mesenteric ischemia, livedo reticularis, and/or bilateral digital cyanosis (blue toe syndrome) from inflammation and tissue ischemia.

questions.explanation: Testicular cancer Epidemiology Age 15-35 Risk factors: family history, cryptorchidism Manifestations Unilateral, painless testicular nodule or swelling Sometimes presents with dull lower abdominal ache Metastatic symptoms (eg, dyspnea, neck mass, low back pain) Diagnosis Examination: firm, ovoid mass or unilateral swelling Scrotal ultrasonography Tumor markers (α-fetoprotein, β-hCG) Staging imaging (CT scan, chest x-ray) Treatment Radical orchiectomy Chemotherapy Cure rate ~95% This patient's painless, unilateral testicular swelling, dull ache (eg, dragging sensation) in the lower abdomen, and negative transillumination raise strong suspicion for testicular cancer, the most common solid-organ malignancy in men age 15-35. Although testicular cancer often presents with a palpable testicular nodule, many cases are marked by unilateral testicular swelling with no defined mass. A dull ache in the perineum, testis, or lower abdomen may be present. Failure of the affected testis to become smaller in the recumbent position (making varicocele less likely) and negative transillumination (consistent with a solid mass vs fluid collection) support the diagnosis and should prompt additional evaluation (Choice C). Bilateral scrotal ultrasonography is the initial test of choice for any patient with painless, unilateral testicular swelling. The presence of a solid hypoechoic mass (seminoma) or a mass with cystic and calcified areas (nonseminoma) supports the diagnosis of testicular cancer. Serum tumor markers (eg, β-hCG, alpha fetoprotein, lactate dehydrogenase) and a radical inguinal orchiectomy are then generally required to complete diagnosis and begin treatment. (Choice A) Unilateral testicular swelling can occur with Chlamydia trachomatis and/or Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection (ie, acute epididymoorchitis), and this patient has increased infection risk (eg, multiple sexual partners, inconsistent condom use). However, swelling associated with acute epididymoorchitis is painful (not painless) on palpation, with tenderness most prominent over the epididymis on the posterior aspect of the testis. (Choice B) Although CT scan of the abdomen is often part of the staging work-up for testicular cancer (to evaluate for metastases), bilateral scrotal ultrasonography is required first to further define the testicular swelling. (Choice E) Semen analysis is primarily indicated in patients with infertility concerns and may be particularly helpful in patients with varicoceles, which can reduce fertility by raising scrotal temperature and decreasing sperm production. Although varicoceles can cause unilateral testicular swelling, they classically decompress (ie, decrease in size) when the patient is in the recumbent position. In addition, this patient has not expressed infertility concerns. Educational objective: Painless, unilateral testicular swelling with no palpable mass is a common presentation of testicular cancer and requires further evaluation with bilateral scrotal ultrasonography.

questions.explanation: This patient's chronic groin pain that is worse with sudden movement is consistent with sports-related groin pain (SRGP). SRGP is a relatively common condition in competitive athletes and is thought to be due to repetitive stress to the musculotendinous portions of the lower abdomen and groin (most commonly the external oblique aponeurosis at the pubis). It is sometimes referred to as a "sports hernia," but it does not involve true herniation of abdominal organs. SRGP should be suspected in young, physically active individuals with unexplained unilateral groin pain. The pain is often reproduced with Valsalva or sit-ups and may be elicited during the examination by resisted adduction of the thigh with the hip externally rotated and the knee bent (ie, frog-leg position). Ultrasound and MRI can be considered to clarify the diagnosis. Initial management includes ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ibuprofen), and rest; patients may gradually return to activity as symptoms allow. Surgery can be considered for competitive athletes who have significant limitations on activity, but usually is not needed. (Choice A) Chronic epididymoorchitis (due to infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis) is an uncommon cause of persistent groin pain. The risk may be increased in individuals who frequently engage in strenuous exercise, but examination shows tenderness in the posterior testis rather than at the pubic symphysis. (Choice B) Intermittent hernias can cause groin discomfort, particularly with mechanisms that increase intraabdominal pressure (eg, weight lifting, Valsalva). However, in addition to pain, Valsalva would typically produce a palpable bulge or impulse on examination. (Choice C) Rectus abdominis diastasis is usually asymptomatic, although mild discomfort may be present. Examination shows an ovoid bulge at the midline of the upper abdomen during Valsalva or when lifting the head while supine. (Choice D) Testicular torsion is the result of inadequate fixation of the lower pole of the testis to the tunica vaginalis, allowing twisting of the testis about the spermatic cord. It presents with sudden, severe pain; nausea; a high-riding testis; and loss of the cremasteric reflex (elevation of testis on pinching of the skin at the upper thigh). Educational objective: Sports-related groin pain (sometimes inaccurately referred to as a "sports hernia") is a common condition in athletes. It is thought to be due to repetitive stress to the musculotendinous portions of the groin (most commonly the external oblique aponeurosis). Symptoms include chronic, intermittent groin pain that is reproduced on Valsalva or sit-ups.

questions.explanation: Clinical features of acute limb ischemia Viable limb (no tissue loss) Threatened limb (risk for tissue loss) Nonviable limb (permanent tissue damage) Pain Mild Severe Variable Sensory/motor deficit None Mild/partial Severe/complete Capillary refill Intact Delayed Absent Arterial Doppler Audible Inaudible Inaudible Venous Doppler Audible Audible Inaudible Management Urgent revascularization Emergency revascularization Amputation The clinical manifestations of acute limb ischemia can be summarized by the 6 P's: Pain (often at rest) Pallor Pulselessness Poikilothermia (cold tissue) Paresthesia (sensory deficits) Paralysis (motor deficits) Acute limb ischemia is most commonly caused by acute thrombosis in a preexisting atherosclerotic plaque, but it can also be due to thromboembolism (eg, due to atrial fibrillation), arterial dissection, or coagulation disorders (eg, antiphospholipid syndrome). Risk factors include increasing age, smoking, diabetes mellitus, and obesity. Because complete arterial occlusion can result in irreversible tissue damage within a matter of hours, management is dependent upon the severity of ischemia at presentation (see table). Nonviable limb: Complete sensorimotor deficits (eg, paralysis, complete sensation loss), absent capillary refill, and inaudible pulses on venous and arterial doppler (as in this patient) indicate that irreversible tissue damage has occurred. Necrotic tissue may appear stiff (rigor) and darkened due to dry gangrene. Limb salvage is not possible, and amputation is necessary. Viable or threatened limb: The presentation is less severe (eg, intact/delayed capillary refill, no/mild sensory/motor deficits), reflecting either no tissue loss or increased risk of tissue loss. These patients require urgent or emergency imaging and revascularization to improve perfusion and prevent limb loss. (Choices A and E) Balloon angioplasty of the posterior tibial artery and urgent vascular bypass are indicated in cases of threatened limb ischemia; candidate patients would have audible pulses on venous Doppler, and sensorimotor deficits, if present, would be mild. This patient's absence of sensation, motor function, and arterial and venous blood flow indicate permanent damage has occurred, and distal reperfusion would not restore viability. However, proximal revascularization may be appropriate to facilitate healing of the amputation or allow a lower amputation (eg, below rather than above the knee). (Choice B) Gradual warming of the extremity is indicated for frostbite, which can cause numbness and cyanosis. Severe cases may occasionally cause reduction in arterial and venous flow due to intravascular thrombosis. However, frostbite occurs after exposure to extreme cold; although application of ice packs may rarely cause mild frostbite, this patient's symptoms began before their application. (Choice C) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (ie, application of 100% oxygen at supra-atmospheric pressures) is useful for patients with chronic arterial insufficiency ulcers in an otherwise viable limb. This patient has a nonviable limb with extensive tissue necrosis, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy will not restore viability. Educational objective: Clinical manifestations of acute limb ischemia include pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, and paralysis (the 6 P's). Irreversible limb ischemia (nonviable) typically presents with absent arterial and venous pulses, severe motor and sensory deficits, and absent capillary refill. Revascularization procedures are considered for patients with a viable limb or reversible ischemia; for patients with irreversible ischemia, limb salvage is not possible and amputation is necessary.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to discoloration and decreased sensation in her left foot. Two weeks ago, she developed pain in her foot while walking. questions.explanation: This patient has a lateral ankle sprain. Lateral ankle sprains are typically caused by forceful inversion of the foot during running, walking on uneven surfaces (eg, descending stairs), or falling from a height. The anterior talofibular ligament is most commonly injured, but the calcaneofibular ligament can also be injured in more severe sprains. Examination of a lateral ankle sprain typically shows swelling over the lateral ankle and tenderness over the ligaments. If the ligaments are intact (grade I sprain), the ankle will be stable and weightbearing only minimally affected. However, partial (grade II) or complete (grade III) ligament tears may be associated with ecchymosis, anterior or inversion laxity, and impaired weightbearing. The Ottawa ankle rules are a clinical decision-making tool used to determine when imaging is indicated in ankle and midfoot injuries. If the patient has tenderness only over the ligaments distal to the lateral malleoli and can bear weight (as in this case), conservative management (eg, compression bandage or brace, ice packs, crutches to reduce weightbearing) without imaging is appropriate. However, if there is tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of the malleolus or if the patient cannot bear weight, x-ray of the ankle is indicated to rule out a distal fibular fracture. (Choice B) Surgical intervention for ankle sprains is rarely indicated. It is primarily considered for patients with severe (grade III) sprains who have occupations (eg, professional athlete) or other factors that increase the risk of repeat injury. It is not clear whether immediate surgery is superior to delayed surgery. (Choice C) Intraarticular corticosteroid injections are primarily performed for inflammatory arthritis (eg, gout, rheumatoid arthritis) and are not indicated for acute trauma. (Choices D and E) This patient can bear weight and has no malleolar tenderness; x-ray is not indicated for acute management. MRI is rarely needed for ankle sprains, although it may be considered to rule out a concomitant talar fracture in patients who do not improve as expected in 6-8 weeks. If there is tenderness only over the ligaments distal to the lateral malleoli and the patient can bear weight, conservative management (eg, compression bandage or brace, ice packs, crutches to reduce weightbearing) without imaging is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Psoas abscess Clinical presentation Subacute fever & abdominal/flank pain that may radiate to the groin or hip Anorexia, weight loss Abdominal pain with hip extension (psoas sign) Diagnosis CT scan of the abdomen & pelvis Leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers Blood & abscess cultures Treatment Drainage Broad-spectrum antibiotics This patient has fever and right-sided groin pain with a positive psoas sign. The psoas sign (ie, abdominal pain that worsens with hip extension) suggests inflammation of the iliopsoas muscle. Although it can occur with multiple pathologies in the iliopsoas region (eg, retrocecal appendicitis), the subacute onset in a patient with untreated Crohn disease suggests a psoas abscess. Psoas abscess is a purulent fluid collection in or along the iliopsoas muscle; it can occur due to the direct spread of infection from an adjacent structure (eg, bowel) or from hematogenous seeding. Patients with uncontrolled Crohn disease are at particularly high risk due to fistula formation. Other risk factors include intravenous drug use, surgical instrumentation, and immunosuppression. Manifestations include the subacute onset (weeks to months) of fever and flank or groin pain that may radiate to the hip; limping and anorexia are also common. Because hip extension worsens the pain, patients may lie with the hip in flexion or sit in a lordotic position. Because of the posterior location of the muscle, deep abdominal palpation is required to reproduce the pain. Laboratory studies commonly show leukocytosis, anemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard for diagnosis, and management includes blood and abscess culture, drainage, and antibiotics. (Choice B) Retrocecal appendicitis causes a positive psoas sign and fever, but the onset is typically more acute (hours). Regardless, CT scan is needed to clarify the diagnosis prior to surgical intervention. (Choices C and D) Musculoskeletal injury is often treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, activity modification, and possibly muscle relaxants (for muscle spasms) and physical therapy. Although groin strain can cause pain and limping, it would not cause a fever or psoas sign. (Choice E) Urinary tract infection can cause fever and groin pain, but the pain is usually nonlateralizing and associated with dysuria and frequency. It would not be expected to cause psoas sign. Hip extension results in worsening abdominal pain (psoas sign), and patients may lie with the hip in flexion or sit in a lordotic position; limping and anorexia are common. Patients with Crohn disease are at particularly high risk. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is diagnostic.

questions.explanation: Acute aortic dissection Risk factors Chronic hypertension (strongest overall risk factor) Underlying aortopathy (eg, Marfan syndrome) Cocaine use Clinical presentation Severe, tearing chest or back pain, maximal at onset ± Variation in SBP between arms >20 mm Hg Hypertension usually present* Diagnosis ECG: normal or nonspecific ST-segment & T-wave changes Chest x-ray: mediastinal widening CT angiography or TEE for definitive diagnosis Treatment Pain control (eg, morphine) Intravenous beta blockers (eg, esmolol) ± Sodium nitroprusside (if SBP >120 mm Hg despite beta blockers) Emergency surgical repair for ascending dissection *Hypotension on presentation suggests aortic rupture or other complication (eg, cardiac tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation). SBP = systolic blood pressure; TEE = transesophageal echocardiography. This patient experienced abrupt-onset unilateral weakness and slurred speech consistent with acute stroke. The right-sided weakness with expressive aphasia suggests left cerebral ischemia, and the left carotid bruit combined with a left radial pulse deficit suggests impaired blood flow to both the left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery. This clinical picture is best explained by acute aortic dissection. Acute aortic dissection classically presents with abrupt-onset, severe chest pain (suggested by this patient clutching his chest). Syncope may also occur due to a vasovagal response to severe pain. Chronic hypertension is the most common risk factor, and patients usually have substantially elevated blood pressure on presentation. Complications result from extension of the dissection into branches of the aorta and consequent obstruction of blood flow. This patient's dissection likely involves the aortic arch, where blood flow to the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries has become partially obstructed by the dissecting intimal flap or false aortic lumen. Prompt diagnostic confirmation is obtained using CT aortography (CT angiography of the aorta) or transesophageal echocardiography. Emergency surgical repair is indicated. (Choices A and D) Cardiac rhythm monitoring is used to investigate suspected cardioembolic stroke (eg, due to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation). Echocardiographic bubble study is used to diagnose an underlying patent foramen ovale, which can allow for paradoxical embolization of a venous thrombus to the arterial circulation to cause stroke. However, it would be unusual for a thrombus from the heart to embolize through both the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. In addition, syncope resulting from stroke alone is extremely uncommon. Complicated aortic dissection is more likely and of more acute concern and should be promptly evaluated. (Choice C) CT pulmonary angiography is used to evaluate for pulmonary embolism, which may cause chest pain and syncope but would not explain this patient's stroke symptoms. (Choice E) MR venography of the brain is indicated in suspected cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). CVST may present with headache, loss of consciousness, and/or focal neurologic deficits; however, it would not explain this patient's severe hypertension or pulse deficit. Educational objective: Extension of an aortic dissection into the carotid arteries can obstruct cerebral blood flow and cause stroke. Stroke accompanied by features such as chest pain, syncope, and/or upper extremity pulse deficit should prompt investigation for acute aortic dissection.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to right-sided weakness and slurred speech. His wife states that the patient was sitting in his recliner 30 minutes ago when he suddenly grasped his chest and "blacked out." The patient spontaneously regained consciousness within a minute, but when he began to speak his speech was garbled. He was also unable to stand or walk due to right-sided weakness. Medical history is significant for hypertension and medication nonadherence. Blood pressure is 180/105 mm Hg in the right arm and pulse is 110/min. On examination, the patient is awake, alert, and anxious appearing with expressive aphasia. There is weakness of the right upper and lower extremities. A left-sided carotid bruit is present. The left radial pulse is decreased. Noncontrast CT scan of the head reveals no hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of this patient?

questions.explanation: Acute HIV infection Epidemiology Typically presents 2-4 weeks after exposure Clinical features Mononucleosis-like syndrome (eg, fever, lymphadenopathy, sore throat, arthralgia) Generalized macular rash Gastrointestinal symptoms Diagnosis Viral load is markedly elevated (>100,000 copies/mL) HIV antibody testing may be negative (not yet seroconverted) CD4 count may be normal Management Combination antiretroviral therapy Partner notification; consider secondary prophylaxis This patient's subacute flulike symptoms, oral ulcerations, lymphadenopathy, and lymphopenia raise strong suspicion for acute HIV infection. Although nonspecific symptoms frequently develop 2-4 weeks after HIV transmission, manifestations are often mild and do not lead to engagement with the healthcare system. However, acute HIV should generally be suspected in those with a prolonged mononucleosislike syndrome (eg, fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, headache, myalgia/arthralgia), particularly in the setting of painful mucocutaneous ulcerations and/or generalized rash (usually within 48 hours of fever onset). Laboratory evaluation frequently reveals lymphopenia due to dramatic T-lymphocyte decline prior to the development of partial humoral immunity against circulating virus. HIV is primarily transmitted via needle sharing during injection drug use or unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected partner. The risk of sexual transmission is greatest when mucosal disruption is present. The risk of transmission with vaginal intercourse is lower than with receptive anal intercourse (virus passage through the thin rectal epithelium). Transmission can also occur between an infected mother and child during birth and via blood transfusion. (Choice A) Enterovirus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. This class of viruses causes herpangina, which presents with oral ulcerations and a flulike prodrome. However, most cases resolve within 5-7 days; 3 weeks of symptoms is atypical. In addition, lymphopenia is not commonly seen. (Choice B) Splenectomy dramatically increases the risk of fulminant sepsis with encapsulated bacterial pathogens (eg, pneumococcus, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae). Therefore, vaccination against these organisms is recommended. However, encapsulated bacterial infections usually cause progressive, severe symptoms within hours or a few days; pneumococcal infection manifestations include pneumonia, sinusitis, acute otitis media, meningitis, and bacteremia. Three weeks of flulike symptoms, oral ulcerations, and lymphadenopathy is atypical. (Choice C) Mosquitos can transmit the Dengue virus, which generally causes high fever, headache, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, and severe myalgias and arthralgias. Some patients develop leukopenia and hemorrhagic vasculitis. However, most symptoms generally last approximately 1 week (not 3), and oral ulcerations are uncommon. (Choice E) Behçet syndrome is thought to be a vasculitis of arteries and veins. Patients frequently have recurrent, painful mucocutaneous ulcerations that last 1-3 weeks. However, fever, lymphadenopathy, myalgias, and pharyngitis are atypical and suggest an alternate diagnosis. Educational objective: Acute HIV infection frequently manifests 2-4 weeks after transmission with a persistent mononucleosislike syndrome. Oral ulcerations and a generalized rash are often present. Laboratory studies frequently reveal lymphopenia. Risk of infection is greatest with shared needle use and unprotected sexual intercourse.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to "a cold that won't go away." Over the last 3 weeks, she has had fevers, sore throat, and myalgias. The patient had a splenectomy 12 years ago after a Jet Ski accident. She drinks alcohol socially and smokes a pack of cigarettes daily but does not use injection drugs. Temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and pulse is 102/min. Examination reveals pharyngeal erythema, buccal ulcers, and enlarged lymph nodes in the cervical, occipital, and posterior auricular chains. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. No organomegaly is present on abdominal examination. Laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Hemoglobin 13 g/dL Platelets 185,000/mm3 Leukocytes 3,600/mm3 Neutrophils 82% Lymphocytes 18% Serum chemistry Blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL Which of the following underlying factors most likely led to this patient's symptoms?

choiceHtml: "If you can get your diabetes under control with insulin, that will make losing weight easier."

questions.explanation: Stages of change model Stage Motivational interviewing Precontemplation Not ready to change: patient does not acknowledge negative consequences Encourage patient to evaluate consequences of current behavior Explain & personalize the risk Recommending action is premature Contemplation Thinking of changing: patient acknowledges consequences but is ambivalent Encourage evaluation of pros & cons of behavior change Promote new, positive behaviors Preparation Ready to change: patient decides to change Encourage small initial steps Reinforce positive outcome expectations Action Making change: patient makes specific, overt changes Help identify appropriate change strategies & enlist social support Promote self-efficacy for dealing with obstacles Maintenance Changes integrated into patient’s life; focus on relapse prevention Follow-up support; reinforce intrinsic rewards Develop relapse prevention strategies Identification Behavior is automatic: changes incorporated into sense of self Praise changes This patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus wants to avoid insulin therapy and is considering lifestyle interventions for weight loss and better diabetic control. He has not committed to any specific intervention but acknowledges the need for change and is actively searching for information regarding options. When counseling patients on lifestyle modification, it is helpful to consider their readiness using a stages of change model. This patient who previously tried diets unsuccessfully is now again in the contemplation phase: he understands the need to modify his diet and is considering options but is not yet ready to commit to a specific plan. In this situation, the patient will benefit from the clinician's medical expertise to make an informed choice regarding dietary modifications. The clinician should probe the patient's current understanding of diabetic diet requirements and the specific details of the diet he is considering and provide a scientifically valid assessment of the pros and cons of the proposed diet. Once the clinician and patient agree on an intervention, they can begin discussing implementation and appropriate follow-up. (Choice A) Initiating insulin therapy can improve glycemic control. In addition, many patients find that, after maintaining tight control for an extended period, they are able to reduce their insulin doses, especially if they have instituted lifestyle changes in the interim. However, insulin induces weight gain in most patients. (Choice C) Although obesity is associated with insulin resistance, this statement does not provide the patient with any new information to make an informed decision about his diet. (Choice D) Not every diet is effective for every individual; patients often require multiple trials to find a program that works for them. In addition, although many dietary programs are not appropriate for patients with diabetes, referring to a diet as a fad may be considered demeaning and discouraging to the patient. (Choice E) Although a specialty provider's opinion should be respected, this patient has expressed hesitance to initiate insulin therapy. The patient brought up a specific dietary intervention and it is appropriate to discuss it in more detail. Educational objective: Counseling patients using a stages of change model can increase the likelihood of successful lifestyle change. In the contemplation phase (ie, the patient understands the need for change but has not committed to a specific plan), the clinician should probe the patient's level of understanding and provide a scientifically valid assessment of the pros and cons of the proposed change.

questions.explanation: Premature and low birth weight infants are at high risk for growth impairment and nutritional deficiencies, and growth charts should be monitored closely. In contrast to term infants, who commonly track along a relatively stable growth percentile from birth, preterm infants typically undergo early, rapid growth (ie, catch-up or compensatory growth), characterized by height and weight measurements starting at low percentiles and crossing several major percentiles during infancy. It is typically accomplished by age 2, as seen in this 18-month-old patient whose height and weight are now normal for age and tracking along the 50th percentile. Parents should be reassured that this pattern of catch-up growth is normal and beneficial to the child's neurocognitive development. During periods of rapid growth, children may have episodes of frequent feeding yet appear hungry between these episodes. Subsequent growth parameters are expected to be similar to those of term infants, and routine follow-up with regularly scheduled well-child checks is recommended. Notably, expected developmental milestones are adjusted based on gestational age until age 2 and also warrant close monitoring in premature children. Early intervention therapies (eg, multidisciplinary services targeting the development of physical, social-emotional, cognitive, and other skills) are typically started early in premature children to help them achieve their milestones. This 18-month-old patient who was born >3 months early and has achieved 15-month milestones is developing appropriately with the help of early interventions services. (Choice A) Rapid weight gain may occur with hypothyroidism, which is characterized by low free thyroxine and elevated TSH. However, decreased height velocity and short stature would also be expected. (Choice B) Gigantism is rare disorder of excess growth hormone that presents with rapid linear growth followed by excess weight gain. Growth charts typically show tall stature (ie, >97th percentile) and height that continues to increase across percentiles. In contrast, this patient's height is now tracking normally. (Choice D) Obesity due to hyperphagia is common in toddlers with Prader-Willi syndrome (ie, loss of paternally inherited alleles on chromosome 15), but infants are more likely to have failure to thrive due to hypotonia and associated feeding difficulties. Moreover, patients with Prader-Willi syndrome typically have short stature and dysmorphic facies, both not seen in this patient. (Choice E) Switching from whole to low-fat cow's milk is recommended at age 2 in children with normal growth. An earlier transition may be considered in children at risk of becoming overweight, which is not the case in this child whose weight is now stable at the 50th percentile. Moreover, a diet of 3 meals with healthy snacks is appropriate in toddlers; decreasing meal frequency would put this patient at risk of losing weight. Educational objective: Catch-up growth is a normal pattern of early, rapid growth in premature infants. Growth typically stabilizes by age 2, and management is reassurance and routine follow-up.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the clinic for a well-child check. His parents say that he has been generally well but are concerned because he seems hungry despite frequent feedings. The patient eats portions of meals, as well as 2 or 3 small fruit snacks throughout the day and whole cow's milk from a cup. He has been voiding and stooling well. The patient was born at 27 weeks gestation and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for the first 9 weeks of life. His global developmental milestones are at the level expected for a 15-month-old child, and he continues to show steady improvement since starting early intervention therapies a year ago. Vitals are normal. On examination, the patient is alert, active, and without obvious deformities. His growth chart is below. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This young patient has sustained significant trauma to his head and neck. Although he currently has no neurologic symptoms, the mechanism of injury (hyperextension with contralateral rotation of his neck) and the carotid bruit are very concerning for a traumatic carotid artery dissection, a condition that, left untreated, can result in stroke. The diagnosis of carotid artery dissection is confirmed with MR or CT angiography of the neck. Patients with a traumatic carotid artery dissection may not have neurologic symptoms on presentation, but symptoms can develop later (eg, hours to days) due to progression of the intimal tear, aneurysm formation, or thrombosis leading to arterial obstruction or thromboembolism. Horner syndrome (eg, ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) may occur due to aneurysmal dilation and compression of the sympathetic nerves that travel along the carotid artery. Other nonspecific symptoms (eg neck pain, headache, facial pain) may occur but are often attributed to the underlying trauma. (Choice B) In some patients, a carotid bruit can be suggestive of large-vessel vasculitis (eg, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis), in which an erythrocyte sedimentation rate could be indicated. However, vasculitis typically also causes systemic symptoms (eg fever, malaise, weight loss), and this patient's trauma history is more concerning for a carotid artery dissection. (Choice C) Lipid-lowering therapy could be appropriate in patients with a carotid bruit due to atherosclerosis, but such findings in a healthy, young person would be very unlikely. (Choice D) Because of the risk of significant morbidity and mortality due to stroke from an unrecognized traumatic carotid artery dissection, urgent imaging should be performed on all patients with blunt trauma and a concerning mechanism of injury or on those age <50 with a cervical bruit. (Choice E) Although a carotid ultrasound might reveal a carotid dissection or thrombus, it cannot visualize intracranial segments of the vessels (where many injuries occur) and is not as sensitive as CT angiography. In addition, this patient should have urgent evaluation, not outpatient diagnostic testing, because a delay in diagnosis risks significant morbidity. Educational objective: Traumatic carotid artery dissection, which can lead to stroke, should be suspected in patients with high-risk mechanisms of injury (eg, hanging, neck hyperextension with contralateral rotation) or with concerning physical examination findings (eg, carotid bruit, focal neurologic deficits). CT angiography is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a severe lip laceration. During a recreational boxing match, the patient received a punch to the right side of the face that split his upper lip and threw his head backward so that he lost his balance and fell; he did not lose consciousness. He has generalized soreness from the fight, but the worst pain is in the right upper lip and right neck. Vital signs are normal. Multiple bruises are present on the face and upper body. On the right upper lip, there is a 3-cm, jagged laceration involving the orbicularis muscle. No bony tenderness exists in the face or the midline posterior cervical spine. The neck is supple; a right carotid bruit is present. Neurologic examination is normal. In addition to repair of the lip laceration, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choiceHtml: "Are you aware that, although marijuana is relatively safe, it can lead to using other drugs that are much more dangerous?"
"I need you to tell me exactly how much and how frequently you are using marijuana."
"I would like to discuss some of the health effects of smoking marijuana, especially because you have asthma."
"I'm glad you have had no bad effects, but sometimes marijuana can be laced with other drugs."
"Some teenage patients smoke marijuana to feel more accepted by their friends; have you had a similar experience?"

"Some teenage patients smoke marijuana to feel more accepted by their friends; have you had a similar experience?"
questions.explanation: Cannabis use is common in adolescence and frequently begins in a social context with peers. In this case, the patient is forthcoming about her use of marijuana and perceives it as harmless. She also sees it as a behavioral norm or even socially desirable within her peer group (eg, tells the physician, "all my friends do it"). When initiating a discussion of drug use with an adolescent, it is more productive to explore motivations for using and the social context rather than initially focusing on potential risks and adverse outcomes. Most teens have a relatively egocentric perspective and feel they are invincible. This patient has not personally experienced any adverse effects and is therefore unlikely to perceive the risks of exposure to more dangerous drugs or adverse health effects as relevant to her situation; it is also unclear that cannabis use specifically (vs environmental/genetic factors associated with substance use generally) increases risk of other drug use (Choices A, C, and D). Warning the patient about adverse health effects before establishing rapport may also be experienced as a fear tactic and is unlikely to engage the patient in further discussion. Instead, normalizing the patient's experience while exploring the influence of her peer group is more likely to make her feel safe and understood, setting the stage for a productive interaction. (Choice B) Immediately questioning the patient about the amount and frequency of cannabis use is likely to put the patient on the defensive and is unlikely to promote collaboration. This information can be acquired after rapport is established. Educational objective: Peer influence is an important factor in adolescent cannabis use. An initial approach that focuses on understanding the social context and motivations for using cannabis, rather than the potential risks, is preferable.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for a health maintenance evaluation. The mother asks to first speak with the physician privately and expresses concern that her daughter is smoking marijuana. The mother says, "Although my daughter says she's only tried it once or twice, I frequently smell it in her clothes and hair." The patient has a history of asthma, managed with an albuterol inhaler as needed. She has no other medical problems. When questioned about drug use during the examination, the patient admits to smoking marijuana and says, "All my friends do it and I've never had a bad effect." Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best response to this patient?

questions.explanation: Factitious disorder (imposed on self) Behavioral characteristics Intentional falsification of illness: Feigning illness Self-induced illness Exacerbation of preexisting illness Motivation by internal factors rather than external gain (eg, financial compensation) Clinical presentation Overt/dramatic symptoms Frequent visits for medical care Patient possibly refusing consent to release records or tampering with test samples More common in health care workers Diagnostic confirmation Direct observation or discovery of medical supplies (eg, medications, syringes) Confirmatory testing (eg, sulfonylurea screen, stool laxative screen) Medical record review This patient has recurrent hypoglycemia, which is confirmed with a low blood glucose level and resolution of symptoms with the administration of oral carbohydrates. Although she has a history of diabetes mellitus, brittle diabetic control (eg, frequent hypoglycemia) is uncommon in patients with type 2 diabetes who are not treated with insulin or sulfonylureas (eg, glipizide). In addition, true hypoglycemia is rare in the absence of exogenous insulin or other hypoglycemic medications. This patient's elevated insulin level with low C-peptide, which is cosecreted with endogenous insulin, confirms that she is surreptitiously using exogenous insulin to induce hypoglycemia. Factitious disorder is characterized by intentional falsification of illness in the absence of external reward (eg, financial compensation, disability benefits). Patients with factitious disorder appear to be motivated by internal factors, such as psychosocial stressors (eg, relationship problems) or desire for validation. Establishing the diagnosis is often difficult, although laboratory testing (eg, insulin/C-peptide levels, sulfonylurea screen) or close observation in a controlled environment (eg, hospital) may confirm the abnormal behaviors. Treatment includes psychotherapy. (Choices A and E) Dumping syndrome, a common complication of bariatric surgery, is characterized by rapid emptying of hypertonic gastric contents into the intestines, which causes fluid shifts from the intravascular space to the small intestine and leads to hypotension, autonomic activation, and the release of vasoactive polypeptides. Concurrently, rapid absorption of glucose following a heavy intake of sugar or simple carbohydrates can cause swings in blood glucose and stimulate insulin secretion, leading to possible reactive hypoglycemia (ie, postbariatric hypoglycemia syndrome). However, because the insulin is endogenous, C-peptide is elevated. (Choice C) Insulinoma is a rare pancreatic islet cell tumor characterized by unregulated insulin secretion and episodic hypoglycemia. However, proinsulin and C-peptide levels are elevated in insulinoma and other causes of endogenous hyperinsulinism. (Choice D) Panic attacks can cause a myriad of autonomic symptoms, including restlessness, sweating, and palpitation. However, symptoms are not relieved with the intake of sugar, and blood glucose is typically normal. Educational objective: Frequent hypoglycemia is uncommon in patients with type 2 diabetes who are not treated with insulin or sulfonylureas. It should raise suspicion for factitious disorder, which is characterized by intentional falsification of illness in the absence of external reward. Laboratory testing (eg, insulin/C-peptide levels, sulfonylurea screen) or close observation in a controlled environment (eg, hospital) may confirm the abnormal behaviors.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent episodes of restlessness, sweating, and palpitation. The symptoms occur at any time of the day and improve quickly after she drinks orange juice. The patient has a history of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus; her insulin therapy was discontinued 8 months ago after she lost a significant amount of weight following a Roux-en-Y bariatric procedure. Her most recent hemoglobin A1c level was 5.5%. The patient reports that she is under significant emotional stress because her husband has filed for divorce, and she has not been sleeping or eating well. A blood sample drawn during an episode of symptoms shows a blood glucose level of 50 mg/dL, elevated insulin, and low proinsulin and C-peptide. A serum sulfonylurea screen is negative. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient's symptoms?

questions.explanation: ECG effects of common electrolyte abnormalities Hyperkalemia Peaked T waves Shortened QT interval Prolonged PR interval & QRS duration Sine wave pattern (severe) Hypokalemia ST-segment depression T-wave flattening Prolonged QT interval U waves Hypermagnesemia Prolonged PR interval, QRS duration & QT interval Complete heart block (severe) Hypomagnesemia Prolonged PR interval, QRS duration & QT interval Peaked T waves (moderate), flat T waves (severe) Hypercalcemia Shortened QT interval Hypocalcemia Prolonged QT interval This patient with generalized weakness and ECG demonstrating a prolonged QT interval most likely has hypokalemia. Hypokalemia is a common adverse effect of loop diuretics (eg, furosemide) used to treat decompensated heart failure. Severe hypokalemia (eg, serum potassium <2.5 mEq/L) often causes generalized muscle weakness. This may be due to the role of potassium in stimulating vasodilation of arterioles that supply blood to active skeletal muscle. With significant hypokalemia, insufficient potassium is released from active muscle, causing less-than-adequate vasodilation and resulting muscle ischemia. In addition to muscle weakness, cramps commonly occur. In severe cases, rhabdomyolysis can develop. Prolongation of the QT interval results from inhibition of the voltage-gated potassium channels that control the delayed rectifier current responsible for repolarization of the cardiomyocyte action potential. Hypokalemia may reduce the activity of this current to prolong the QT interval. Hypomagnesemia, and to a lesser extent hypocalcemia, can also prolong the QT interval. Other ECG findings that may be present with hypokalemia are ST-segment depression (visible in leads V4 and V5 in this patient), T-wave flattening (present diffusely in this patient), and U waves (not present in this patient). Arrhythmias are common and include premature atrial contractions, premature ventricular contractions, and torsades de pointes (resulting from excessive prolongation of the QT interval). (Choice A) Hypercalcemia (eg, serum calcium >12 mg/dL) commonly causes psychiatric effects (eg, anxiety, confusion), constipation, nephrolithiasis, and muscle weakness and/or aches. It shortens the QT interval on ECG, but this effect does not appear to have clinical significance. (Choice B) Like hypokalemia, hyperkalemia (eg, serum potassium >6.5 mEq/L) also causes generalized muscle weakness. However, ECG changes include peaked T waves and shortening of the QT interval. With severe hyperkalemia, the PR interval and QRS duration lengthen and a sine wave pattern develops, eventually leading to cessation of electrical activity and cardiac arrest. (Choice C) Hypermagnesemia (eg, serum magnesium >4 mg/dL) can cause lethargy, confusion, muscle weakness, and decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes. ECG effects include prolongation of the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval. Severe hypermagnesemia can cause complete heart block. (Choice E) The effects of hypophosphatemia (eg, serum phosphate <1 mg/dL) mostly result from depletion of ATP and include encephalopathy, reduced contractility of cardiac and skeletal muscle (potentially leading to respiratory failure), and hemolysis. ECG changes are not typical. Educational objective: Hypokalemia is a common adverse effect of loop diuretic use. It can cause generalized muscle weakness and ECG changes, including ST-segment depression, T-wave flattening, U waves, and prolongation of the QT interval.

wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Hypermagnesemia (eg, serum magnesium >4 mg/dL) can cause lethargy, confusion, muscle weakness, and decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes.  ECG effects include prolongation of the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval.  Severe hypermagnesemia can cause complete heart block.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  The effects of hypophosphatemia (eg, serum phosphate <1 mg/dL) mostly result from depletion of ATP and include encephalopathy, reduced contractility of cardiac and skeletal muscle (potentially leading to respiratory failure), and hemolysis.  ECG changes are not typical.

questions.explanation: Type 1, type 2 & cystic fibrosis–related diabetes mellitus Type 1 Type 2 Cystic fibrosis– related Primary pathogenesis Insulin deficiency due to autoimmune destruction of beta islet cells Insulin resistance Insulin deficiency due to fibrosis & fatty infiltration of pancreas Onset Acute (ketosis common) Insidious Insidious Typical age of onset Children age <14 Older adolescents & adults Young adults (age 18-30) Treatment Insulin Dietary modification, oral agents, insulin Insulin This patient with cystic fibrosis has polyuria, increased appetite, and weight loss. These findings are concerning for cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) mellitus. CFRD is the most common nonrespiratory complication of CF and contributes to worsening pulmonary function and increased mortality. The pathogenesis of CFRD is due primarily to insulin deficiency. In contrast to type 1 diabetes mellitus, CFRD is not typically associated with autoantibodies; instead, thick, viscous secretions in the pancreatic duct lead to obstruction and later fibrosis and fatty infiltration of the pancreas. Destruction of islet cells over time causes decreased secretion of insulin. Insulin resistance plays a secondary role and is likely related to chronic hypercortisolemia in the setting of recurrent, acute pulmonary exacerbations in patients with CF; in contrast to type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is also associated with insulin resistance, serum C-peptide is low in CFRD, as seen in this patient, because of low insulin production. All patients age ≥10 with CF should be screened annually with an oral glucose tolerance test because postprandial hyperglycemia is the earliest and most sensitive finding in CFRD. However, those who are symptomatic typically have an insidious presentation in early adulthood; osmotic diuresis from glucosuria (ie, polyuria) can occur, and protein catabolism due to insulin deficiency may lead to weight loss with increased appetite. Because persistent hyperglycemia can enhance bacterial growth on airway mucosa and diminish the immunologic response to infection, all patients with CFRD should be prescribed insulin therapy (eg, basal-bolus regimen). Over time, insulin replacement results in improved lung function and nutritional status. (Choices B, C, D, and E) Some patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus can be treated initially with weight reduction and dietary modifications; if glycemic control is poor at diagnosis or lifestyle modifications are unsuccessful, oral agents (eg, metformin) can be used. In contrast, metformin and other noninsulin agents (eg, acarbose, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist) do not play a role in CFRD treatment. Educational objective: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes mellitus, a common complication of cystic fibrosis, is caused primarily by insulin deficiency due to fibrosis and fatty infiltration of the pancreas. Management is with insulin therapy, and appropriate glucose control contributes to improved overall lung function and nutritional status.

questions.explanation: Cannabis withdrawal Clinical features Cessation of heavy, prolonged cannabis use (daily, months) ≥3 signs/symptoms (must include at least 1 physical symptom) Psychologic Irritability, anger Depressed mood Anxiety, restlessness Decreased appetite/weight loss Sleep disturbance Physical Abdominal pain Headache Shakiness/tremors Fevers, chills Sweating This patient's 2-week history of decreased appetite, abdominal pain, sleep disturbance, and unexplained mood changes temporally associated with abrupt cessation of daily cannabis use is most likely due to cannabis withdrawal. Symptoms most commonly occur in patients with heavy and prolonged use (eg, daily, months) and begin within a week after discontinuation. Diagnosis requires ≥3 symptoms; at least one symptom must be physical. Adolescent girls may have a triad of poor appetite, weight loss, and gastrointestinal symptoms, a clinical presentation that may be confused with an eating disorder. Cannabis withdrawal typically last 1-2 weeks and subsequently resolve, although sleep disturbance may persist for several weeks. Cannabis withdrawal should be suspected in heavy users who experience mood changes, sleep disturbance, decreased appetite, and physical symptoms within a week of abrupt reduction or cessation of use. (Choice A) In adjustment disorder with anxious mood, symptoms develop in direct response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor. Although this patient experiences some athletic performance pressure, the temporal association of her symptoms with abrupt cessation of cannabis makes a withdrawal diagnosis more likely. (Choice B) Anorexia nervosa is characterized by abnormally low body weight (typically BMI <18.5 kg/m2 or <85% of expected body weight), intense fears of weight gain, and distorted perceptions of weight and shape. (Choice D) Depressed mood is common in cannabis withdrawal. This patient does not exhibit sufficient additional depressive symptoms (eg, anhedonia, low energy, impaired concentration, guilt, suicidal ideation) to diagnose a major depressive disorder. (Choice E) Somatic symptom disorder is characterized by one or more persistent (ie, >6 months) somatic symptoms associated with excessive health anxiety and behaviors related to the symptoms. This patient is not excessively concerned with her abdominal pain. The short duration of symptoms and temporal association with cannabis discontinuation makes a withdrawal diagnosis more likely. Educational objective: Cannabis withdrawal should be suspected in heavy users who experience mood changes, sleep disturbance, decreased appetite, and physical symptoms within a week of abrupt reduction or cessation of use.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the office for a high school sports physical. The patient has no chronic medical conditions but reports that she has had little appetite, intermittent abdominal pain, and difficulty sleeping for the past 2 weeks. She says, "I think I may have lost 3-4 pounds. I feel anxious and depressed for no reason and wake up several times a night." The patient does well in school. She has been looking forward to playing basketball but feels some pressure to play well to earn an athletic college scholarship next year. The patient has a history of depression at age 12 following her parent's divorce that was treated with psychotherapy. She takes no medications. The patient drinks alcohol at parties. She does not use tobacco. She smoked cannabis daily but quit 3 weeks ago in anticipation of the basketball season coming up soon. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 10/min. BMI is 18.5 kg/m2. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

questions.explanation: Counseling patients & families on Klinefelter syndrome General/parent discussion Staged information Focus on individual concerns & inquiries Etiology, sporadic occurrence Children & adolescents Social & intellectual development Androgen replacement Gender identity & sexual orientation Adults Fertility Ongoing/follow-up androgen replacement This patient has Klinefelter syndrome (KS) (47,XXY), presenting with delayed puberty and primary hypogonadism (ie, low testosterone, elevated FSH and LH). Besides abnormalities in body habitus, KS has significant implications for intellectual and emotional development, reproduction, and interpersonal relationships. Disclosure must therefore be done with sensitivity to the possible reactions of the patient and family. Because of the numerous possible manifestations of chromosomal disorders, information should usually be presented in a staged strategy, starting with the most urgent matters first and moving to lesser concerns as the patient and family gain understanding. For KS, androgen replacement is often initiated early and should be discussed soon after diagnosis, whereas fertility and extragonadal manifestations can be discussed later as the patient inquires. Psychosocial issues also require careful discussion. Parents of a child with a genetic disorder often unfairly blame themselves for "passing on" the condition; however, KS is usually sporadic, and the family should understand that there is nothing they could or should have done to prevent it. Although KS often affects intellectual function, the effect on individuals is highly variable. KS does not impact gender identity or sexual orientation. (Choices A and B) Treatment decisions for chromosomal disorders generally need not be made immediately; the conversation can start with the family members present. It is helpful to have this minor's mother involved but not necessary to include the father if he is not present. Further discussions can be scheduled later involving additional family members or alone with the patient as needed. (Choice C) KS typically has a sporadic occurrence. Family members are not at increased risk and family testing is not needed. (Choice E) Infertility due to KS is often not treatable, although advanced techniques (eg, testicular sperm extraction) are successful in some cases. Many other symptoms of KS (eg, low libido) respond readily to androgen replacement. Educational objective: Because of the numerous possible manifestations of chromosomal disorders, information should usually be presented in a staged strategy, starting with the most urgent matters first and moving to lesser concerns as the patient and family gain understanding. Klinefelter syndrome is typically sporadic, and it may be helpful to explain to the family that there is nothing they could or should have done to prevent it.

questions.explanation: Asthma risk factors Perinatal Family history of asthma* Prematurity Childhood Atopy* (eg, eczema, allergies) RSV in infancy Air pollution, secondhand smoke Adolescence/adulthood Obesity Active smoking Occupational exposures (eg, pesticides, cleaning products) *Significant risk factor. RSV = respiratory syncytial virus. This patient with fever, cough, and nasal discharge most likely has a viral respiratory tract infection, which can often trigger acute wheezing (particularly in infants and toddlers) due to viral inflammation of the lower airways (ie, bronchioles). Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most common cause of wheezing in children age <2, but other viruses (eg, influenza, rhinovirus) may also be implicated. Asthma is a chronic lung condition characterized by recurrent wheezing due to airway hyperresponsiveness. Most children with viral-induced wheezing during infancy do not develop asthma; however, those who also have other predisposing factors are at increased risk. Major risk factors for asthma include the following: A family history of wheezing (particularly in a parent, as in this case) is the strongest risk factor for asthma. Although genetics plays a role in the development of asthma, the interaction of multiple involved genes leads to varied expression among individuals. A personal history of atopy (eg, eczema, allergic rhinitis) increases the likelihood that a child with wheezing will develop asthma. Hypersensitivity to allergens, detected with a positive skin test or by elevated IgE levels, is common in children with asthma. The presence of peripheral eosinophilia is also a predictive factor. Environmental exposures (eg, secondhand smoke, air pollutants) may also contribute to the development of asthma in children. Parents should be advised to limit avoidable triggers of airway reactivity when possible. (Choices A and E) Infants in the first few months of life are at the highest risk for severe bronchiolitis leading to respiratory distress and hospitalization; however, age of first wheezing episode and need for oxygen support are not significant risk factors for asthma. (Choice C) While children with IgE-mediated food allergies are more likely to wheeze, milk protein–induced allergic proctocolitis (ie, milk protein intolerance) is neither an IgE-mediated food allergy nor a risk factor associated with asthma. (Choice D) Although severe bronchiolitis caused by RSV in infancy is associated with the development of recurrent wheezing in early childhood in up to 30% of patients, influenza-associated wheezing is not a major risk factor for the development of asthma. Educational objective: Viral infections are a common cause of wheezing in infants and toddlers. Although most of these patients do not develop asthma, those with a family history of wheezing or concomitant atopy (eg, eczema, allergic rhinitis) are at an increased risk for it.
