questions.explanation: This patient had symptomatic internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis that caused a small ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery, a branch of the ICA. He underwent carotid artery stenting (CAS), then developed worsening left-sided weakness and dysarthria (ie, disordered speech due to facial muscle weakness) 2 weeks later. This presentation is most consistent with a periprocedural stroke resulting from an in-stent thrombosis of the carotid stent. Compared with carotid endarterectomy (CEA), a high-risk neurosurgical procedure used in some cases of carotid artery stenosis, CAS is less invasive and may have similar long-term outcomes for stroke prevention. However, CAS is associated with a higher risk for periprocedural stroke and mortality than CEA, so it is typically reserved for patients who are poor surgical candidates. Periprocedural stroke is the most common complication following CAS. It can develop due to different etiologies, which can often be distinguished by the timing of symptom onset: Thromboembolism may occur at the time of stent placement, typically from atherosclerotic plaque breaking loose from the vessel wall during the procedure. In-stent thrombosis most often occurs within the first 30 days following stent placement. Nonadherence to postprocedure antiplatelet therapy and continued tobacco use increase the risk. Carotid intimal hyperplasia and restenosis may occur when there is ongoing vascular injury following stent placement (eg, due to imperfect stent positioning). This typically develops over a few months (vs 2 weeks). (Choice D) (Choice A) Carotid artery dissection has a variable presentation, including stroke, although classic symptoms include neck pain, headache, and facial/eye pain. This complication can occur during carotid stent placement if the guidewire is aggressively manipulated and therefore typically occurs intraoperatively (vs 2 weeks later). It is treated with additional stent placements. (Choice B) Carotid baroreceptor stimulation may occur during stent placement from angioplasty balloon inflation. The resulting baroreceptor reflex can cause transient bradycardia and hypotension, leading to decreased cerebral perfusion; however, ensuing symptoms are typically more consistent with a watershed infarction (eg, proximal muscle weakness, cortical visual deficits). In addition, symptoms usually occur during or immediately after the procedure (vs 2 weeks later). (Choice E) Chronic carotid vascular bed ischemia can lead to impaired autoregulation (eg, chronic vasodilation with inability to vasoconstrict) and cerebral hyperperfusion once stenting restores blood flow. Although hyperperfusion (and the resulting edema or hemorrhage) can cause focal neurologic deficits, ipsilateral headache, hypertension, and/or seizures are also typically present. Educational objective: Periprocedural stroke is the most common complication following carotid stent placement. In-stent thrombosis is often the mechanism of stroke in the first 30 days.

This patient had symptomatic internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis that caused a small ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery, a branch of the ICA.  He underwent carotid artery stenting (CAS), then developed worsening left-sided weakness and dysarthria (ie, disordered speech due to facial muscle weakness) 2 weeks later.  This presentation is most consistent with a periprocedural stroke resulting from an in-stent thrombosis of the carotid stent.

Compared with carotid endarterectomy (CEA), a high-risk neurosurgical procedure used in some cases of carotid artery stenosis, CAS is less invasive and may have similar long-term outcomes for stroke prevention.  However, CAS is associated with a higher risk for periprocedural stroke and mortality than CEA, so it is typically reserved for patients who are poor surgical candidates.

Periprocedural stroke is the most common complication following CAS.  It can develop due to different etiologies, which can often be distinguished by the timing of symptom onset:

  • Thromboembolism may occur at the time of stent placement, typically from atherosclerotic plaque breaking loose from the vessel wall during the procedure.
  • In-stent thrombosis most often occurs within the first 30 days following stent placement.  Nonadherence to postprocedure antiplatelet therapy and continued tobacco use increase the risk.
  • Carotid intimal hyperplasia and restenosis may occur when there is ongoing vascular injury following stent placement (eg, due to imperfect stent positioning).  This typically develops over a few months (vs 2 weeks).

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Carotid artery dissection has a variable presentation, including stroke, although classic symptoms include neck pain, headache, and facial/eye pain.  This complication can occur during carotid stent placement if the guidewire is aggressively manipulated and therefore typically occurs intraoperatively (vs 2 weeks later).  It is treated with additional stent placements.
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Carotid baroreceptor stimulation may occur during stent placement from angioplasty balloon inflation.  The resulting baroreceptor reflex can cause transient bradycardia and hypotension, leading to decreased cerebral perfusion; however, ensuing symptoms are typically more consistent with a watershed infarction (eg, proximal muscle weakness, cortical visual deficits).  In addition, symptoms usually occur during or immediately after the procedure (vs 2 weeks later).
wrongAnswers.D: • (Choice D)
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Chronic carotid vascular bed ischemia can lead to impaired autoregulation (eg, chronic vasodilation with inability to vasoconstrict) and cerebral hyperperfusion once stenting restores blood flow.  Although hyperperfusion (and the resulting edema or hemorrhage) can cause focal neurologic deficits, ipsilateral headache, hypertension, and/or seizures are also typically present.

questions.explanation: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection Pathophysiology & epidemiology Intimal layer tear or vaso vasorum bleed → intramural hematoma → coronary artery occlusion Predominantly in women age <55 Risk factors: postpartum status, multiparity, connective tissue disorder (particularly fibromuscular dysplasia) Manifestations Chest pain: symptoms similar to myocardial infarction Elevated troponin level Diagnosis Coronary angiography (eg, dissection plane without atherosclerosis) Treatment Conservative management: ꞵ blockers, aspirin Percutaneous coronary intervention: complicated, less successful Coronary artery bypass grafting This young, postpartum woman with chest pain and troponin level elevation consistent with acute coronary syndrome likely has a spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD). SCADs are due to a nontraumatic separation in the coronary artery walls, resulting from either an intimal layer tear or vaso vasorum bleeding. These can lead to a false lumen or an intramural hematoma and potentially cause coronary artery occlusion, ischemia, myocardial infarction (MI). Risk factors include female sex, connective tissue disorders (particularly fibromuscular dysplasia), hormone therapy, multiparity (≥4 births), and postpartum status (possibly from hormonal effects on the artery wall or hemodynamic stresses). Symptoms of SCAD are similar to those of MI, including chest pain radiating to the left arm and neck, substernal pressure, diaphoresis, and nausea. Elevated troponin (from intramural separation and myocardial ischemia) and D-dimer (possibly from the hematoma) levels are common. ECG can be consistent with ST-segment elevation MI (up to 50% of cases) or non-ST segment MI, although lack of ECG changes (as in this patient) does not exclude dissection. Diagnosis can be made during coronary artery angiography (eg, visualizing the dissection) but is frequently missed and may require additional work-up. Treatment ranges from conservative management (beta blockers and aspirin) to coronary artery bypass grafting. Percutaneous coronary intervention is sometimes performed, but the risk of complications is high because the dissections can be extensive. (Choice A) Although acute cardiac tamponade can cause chest pain, the classic triad (ie, hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds) is absent in this patient. In addition, cardiac tamponade classically causes low voltage on ECG. (Choice B) Complete heart block manifests on ECG as atrioventricular electrical dissociation. It usually causes dizziness or syncope rather than chest pain. (Choice D) Pericarditis symptoms include sharp chest pain relieved with leaning forward or sitting up. ECG findings include widespread ST-segment elevation or PR-interval depression. (Choice E) This patient has findings concerning for pulmonary embolism (postpartum state, chest pain, tachycardia, elevated D-dimer), which can cause troponin elevation (reflecting right ventricle dysfunction). However, the normal oxygen saturation, lack of pleuritic chest pain, and radiation of pain to the left arm and neck all make SCAD more likely. In addition, such a significant degree of troponin elevation is less likely to be seen with pulmonary embolism. Educational objective: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is an infrequent cause of acute coronary syndrome, and the diagnosis is often missed. Risk factors include female sex, peripartum status, multiparity, connective tissue disorder, and hormone therapy. Troponin levels are almost always elevated. Diagnosis is made using coronary angiography.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to chest pain that started 8 hours ago while she was changing her 4-day-old baby's diaper. The pain, which has been unrelenting and has prevented her from caring for the baby and her 3 other children, is substernal and very uncomfortable, radiating to her neck and left arm. The patient reports no shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, or sweating. The pain does not worsen with exertion or deep breaths. The patient has no medical history. She is afebrile. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 106/min, and respirations are 18/min. Pulse oximetry reading is 100% on room air. On examination, the patient appears uncomfortable. The lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally, and heart sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender with a normal postpartum uterus. There is no lower extremity edema or swelling. Chest x-ray is normal. ECG is shown in the exhibit. Laboratory results are as follows: D-dimer, plasma 2.67 µg/mL (normal: <0.5) Troponin T, serum >80 ng/mL (normal: <0.04) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Culture-negative endocarditis Definition Endocarditis with ≥3 sets of negative blood cultures at 7 days incubation Common pathogens Highly fastidious bacteria (eg, Coxiella, Brucella, Bartonella, mycobacteria) Fungi (eg, Aspergillus) History clues Recent antibiotics (Streptococcus) Exposure to farm animals or unpasteurized milk (Brucella, Coxiella, Tropheryma) Contact with human body louse/homeless shelter (Bartonella quintana) Contact with cats (Bartonella henselae) Immunosuppression/HIV (fungi, Coxiella) This patient with a history of mitral valve prolapse has subacute nonspecific symptoms, mitral valve vegetations, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and negative blood cultures, indicating likely culture-negative infective endocarditis (IE). This condition, which occurs in 2%-7% of patients with IE, is defined as endocarditis with ≥3 sets of negative blood cultures after 7 days of incubation. Most cases of culture-negative IE arise: in the setting of recent exposure to antibiotics, which limits detection of common IE pathogens (eg, streptococci) due to infection with highly fastidious bacteria (eg, Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella, mycobacteria) or fungal organisms (eg, Aspergillus). HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella) organisms are no longer considered a common cause of culture negative IE because modern blood culture techniques can isolate these organisms after 3-5 days of incubation. Coxiella burnetii is a fastidious bacterium transmitted to humans primarily from infected farm animals (eg, cattle, sheep). Chronic infection (Q fever) is often associated with IE, particularly in those with structural heart disease (eg, mitral valve prolapse). Manifestations include weeks of constitutional symptoms (eg, myalgia, malaise) and waxing/waning fever; splenomegaly, digital clubbing, and purpuric rash are often present. Laboratory evaluation typically shows elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Echocardiography is frequently normal but may reveal small vegetations on the mitral or aortic valves. Diagnosis typically requires serologic testing and/or PCR testing of valve samples. Prolonged treatment (eg, doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine) is usually curative. (Choices A, C, D, and E) Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus viridans are the most common causes of IE. However, 3 sets of blood cultures can identify IE caused by one of these pathogens in >98% of cases; negative cultures are unlikely in the absence of recent antibiotic use. Furthermore, this patient who works on a dairy farm is at high risk for exposure to fastidious zoonotic pathogens such as C burnetii. Educational objective: Culture-negative endocarditis usually occurs due to recent antibiotic administration (eg, streptococci) or infection with highly fastidious bacteria (eg, Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella, mycobacteria) or fungal organisms (eg, Aspergillus). Coxiella burnetii is a common cause of culture-negative endocarditis in those who come into contact with farm animals, particularly in the setting of existing structural heart disease (eg, mitral valve prolapse).

Echocardiography reveals small vegetations over the mitral valve leaflets. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is markedly elevated. questions.explanation: This patient had longstanding, classic endometriosis symptoms (eg, dysmenorrhea, dyschezia, menorrhagia), but her diagnosis was delayed until she experienced an acute complication (ie, ovarian torsion). Delayed diagnosis occurred because the provider did not explore and work up (ie, with diagnostic laparoscopy) the possibility of endometriosis. This care pattern likely reflects cognitive bias (ie, mental patterns that incorrectly influence clinical reasoning and differential diagnosis), a leading cause of diagnostic errors: Anchoring bias, also known as premature closure, occurs when fixation on one aspect of the clinical presentation overly influences the diagnosis. This provider likely anchored on abdominal symptoms, leading to premature diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), which is normally a diagnosis of exclusion, at the expense of other diagnoses. Confirmation bias causes distorted interpretation of clinical findings to favor a presumptive diagnosis. This provider likely favored findings supporting IBS (eg, abdominal cramping, diarrhea) while overlooking findings suggesting alternate diagnoses (eg, minimally improving menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea despite oral contraceptive therapy; dyschezia). (Choice A) Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) may be appropriate therapy for mild endometriosis; however, this patient's only minimal improvement with OCPs and longstanding symptoms warranted further, earlier workup to assess for endometriosis. (Choice C) High-value medical care describes optimization of patient health outcomes and quality with efficient resource use (eg, avoiding overtreatment and unnecessary care). Although colonoscopy is not typically part of endometriosis workup, this patient's outcomes were suboptimal. (Choice D) Knowledge deficiency refers to insufficient didactic or theoretical medical knowledge (eg, inability to answer recall-based examination questions). In practice, it only rarely causes diagnostic errors, especially in common conditions (eg, endometriosis) manifesting with classic, rather than atypical, presentations, as seen in this patient. More often, providers have sufficient theoretical foundations but commit diagnostic errors from incorrect application of knowledge and biased clinical interpretations, due to cognitive distortions. (Choice E) Earlier workup for endometriosis could have prompted earlier discovery and treatment (eg, surgical excision), preventing unnecessary morbidity and suffering and acute oophorectomy. Educational objective: Cognitive bias (ie, mental shortcuts, patterns incorrectly influencing clinical reasoning) is a leading cause of diagnostic errors. Anchoring and confirmation biases lead to premature diagnoses based on initial impressions and failure to consider alternate diagnoses despite contradictory information.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes into the emergency department with severe, right-sided lower abdominal pain. Medical history includes an 8-year history of gradually worsening, intermittent diarrhea and crampy, severe lower abdominal pain during defecation. She recently saw a primary care provider and requested a colonoscopy but was told it was unnecessary because her symptoms were likely due to irritable bowel syndrome. The patient also has a history of heavy, painful menses for 8 years, which has only mildly improved with oral contraceptives. She is not sexually active. On physical examination, the patient has marked right-sided abdominal tenderness and guarding. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a complex right-sided adnexal mass with absent Doppler flow. The patient is taken to the operating room and is found to have ovarian torsion and necrosis due to large, right-sided endometrioma. Endometriosis lesions are also observed in the posterior cul-de-sac of the pelvis. Which of the following most accurately characterizes the pattern of care this patient received from the primary care provider?

questions.explanation: This patient has a tender, lobulated neck mass due to cervical lymphadenitis. Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus species; subacute and chronic cases are more likely due to atypical pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Toxoplasma gondii, Francisella tularensis, and Bartonella henselae. This patient who works as a pet groomer is at high risk for B henselae, a small pleomorphic bacterium that causes cat scratch disease. Transmission occurs via feline scratch, saliva, or flea bite. Within a few days, a vesicular lesion typically forms at the inoculation site and soon becomes erythematous and papular. Because the initial lesion may be subtle, it sometimes goes unnoticed and may not be included in the patient's history (as is likely in this case). Approximately 2 weeks after transmission, most patients develop tender, erythematous lymphadenopathy proximal to the inoculation site; affected lymph nodes may grow to >5 cm in diameter and form a lobulated mass. Fever is frequently present. Although most cases resolve spontaneously within 4 months, approximately 15% of patients develop disseminated disease. Therefore, antimicrobial treatment with a 5-day course of azithromycin is recommended. (Choice B) Nasopharyngeal endoscopy is part of the work-up for upper airway malignancy, which often metastasizes to unilateral lymph nodes. However, nasopharyngeal malignancy is uncommon in 19-year-olds; most cases occur in older adults with risk factors (eg, smoking). In addition, fever, lymph node tenderness, and a history of working as a pet groomer make cat scratch disease more likely. (Choice C) Group A streptococci often causes tender bilateral cervical lymphadenitis in the setting of tonsillitis or pharyngitis. This patient's lack of oropharyngeal symptoms and employment as a pet groomer make cat scratch disease more likely. (Choice D) Symptomatic treatment is warranted for infectious mononucleosis, which can cause fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. However, patients typically have pharyngitis and bilateral, generalized lymphadenopathy. (Choice E) Unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common manifestation of tuberculosis lymphadenitis. However, most cases arise in those who live in or travel to endemic areas or have underlying HIV infection. This patient's employment as a pet groomer makes cat scratch disease more likely. Educational objective: Cat scratch disease is caused by the small pleomorphic bacterium Bartonella henselae. Transmission occurs via feline scratch, saliva, or flea bite. An erythematous papule forms at the inoculation site; a few weeks later, exquisitely tender regional lymphadenitis develops. Nodes may grow to >5 cm. Treatment with azithromycin is recommended to prevent disseminated disease.

questions.explanation: Tuberculous pericardial effusion Etiology Spread of pulmonary tuberculosis to the pericardium Clinical presentation Insidious symptom development (eg, cough, dyspnea, weight loss) ± Chest pressure, orthopnea & signs of subacute tamponade Globally enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray Diagnosis Pericardial fluid showing lymphocytosis & ↑ protein, LDH & ADA* Positive acid-fast bacillus stain &/or culture** Treatment RIPE antibiotic therapy for 6 months Complications Constrictive pericarditis *Sensitive but not specific. **Specific but not sensitive. ADA = adenosine deaminase; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; RIPE = rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol. This patient's enlarged cardiac silhouette, history of lung infection, and recent emigration from an endemic region raise strong suspicion for tuberculous pericardial effusion, a potential complication of pulmonary tuberculosis. Pericardial involvement usually presents insidiously (ie, over several weeks or more) with symptoms similar to those of pulmonary tuberculosis (eg, cough, dyspnea, weight loss, fatigue, intermittent fever, hemoptysis). If a large pericardial effusion is present, the patient may also have chest pressure and orthopnea. Because pericardial fluid accumulates gradually, the normally noncompliant pericardium can stretch and prevent a rapid increase in pericardial pressure. Therefore, up to 2 L may collect in the pericardial space, causing global enlargement of the cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray and sometimes leading to subacute tamponade. Diagnosis is made using pericardiocentesis, with fluid analysis showing lymphocyte predominance, and elevated levels of protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and adenosine deaminase (produced during lymphocyte proliferation). Positive acid-fast bacillus smear and/or culture confirms the diagnosis. Despite long-term treatment with antibiotics, some patients develop constrictive pericarditis as a complication. (Choice A) Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) typically leads to decompensated heart failure with dilation of all 4 cardiac chambers and global enlargement of the cardiac silhouette, similar to that seen with large pericardial effusion. However, DCM is less likely in this patient with weight loss (weight gain is usually expected due to fluid accumulation) and without lung crackles or peripheral edema to suggest heart failure. (Choice B) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy involves thickening of the left ventricular septum that can obstruct left ventricular outflow during periods of exertion. Heart failure is rare, and the cardiac silhouette is mostly unchanged. (Choice C) Mitral valve stenosis (eg, due to rheumatic heart disease) classically presents with exertional dyspnea, with chest pain, cough, and hemoptysis occurring less commonly. The resultant left atrial enlargement may elevate the left main bronchus and straighten the left heart border; however, the majority of the cardiac silhouette is unaffected, unlike in this patient. Classic auscultatory findings include an opening snap and a diastolic murmur (which may be difficult to discern). (Choice E) Tricuspid valve endocarditis can cause severe tricuspid regurgitation with right-sided heart failure. Fever is typically present. The right cardiac border may be enlarged on chest x-ray due to right ventricular and right atrial enlargement, but the left cardiac border is generally unaffected. Educational objective: Tuberculous pericardial effusion is a complication of pulmonary tuberculosis that typically presents after several weeks of symptoms (eg, cough, dyspnea, weight loss). Because the fluid accumulates gradually, a large pericardial effusion often develops, with global cardiac silhouette enlargement on chest x-ray, and sometimes leads to subacute tamponade.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the office due to cough, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath for the past 4 weeks. The patient has been taking ibuprofen without improvement in his symptoms. He also has had profound fatigue, weight loss, and occasional hemoptysis. The patient recently emigrated from Eastern Europe; he says he was treated for a lung infection a year ago in his home country. Temperature is 37.5 C (99.5 F), blood pressure is 115/75 mm Hg, and pulse is 95/min and regular. On examination, the patient appears comfortable at rest. Both lung bases are clear to auscultation. There is no peripheral edema. Chest x-ray reveals an enlarged cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of this imaging finding?

questions.explanation: Neurosyphilis Early Meningitis Ocular: uveitis & optic neuritis Otologic: hearing loss & tinnitus Meningovascular: meningitis + ischemic stroke Late General paresis: progressive dementia Tabes dorsalis: sensory ataxia & lancinating pains Although this patient presents with a wide range of symptoms and physical examination findings, many features suggest syphilis, including the following: Recent diffuse scaly rash, a manifestation of secondary syphilis Posterior uveitis and possible optic neuritis, manifestations of ocular syphilis Previous sexually transmitted infection, suggesting a history of high-risk sexual behavior Ocular syphilis is a form of neurosyphilis that may occur at any stage of the infection. Although it can occur in nonimmunocompromised patients, cases are far more common in those with HIV (which may be present in this patient with oropharyngeal Candida [white mucosal patches]). Common findings include bilateral anterior or posterior uveitis (eg, floaters, reduced visual acuity) and optic neuritis (eg, flashing lights, photosensitivity), which may lead to vision loss and permanent blindness. Concurrent infection of cranial nerve VIII (eg, tinnitus, vertigo) and/or meninges (eg, headache, neck stiffness) frequently occurs. Syphilis is diagnosed with nontreponemal (eg, rapid plasma reagin) and treponemal-specific (eg, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) serology. Many patients with suspected neurosyphilis also undergo lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis. Treatment for ocular syphilis is the same as for neurosyphilis, which is 10-14 days of intravenous penicillin. (Choice A) CSF analysis for oligoclonal bands is sometimes part of the workup for multiple sclerosis, which often presents with optic neuritis. However, rash and oropharyngeal plaques would be atypical. (Choice B) Chest x-ray can help identify features (eg, hilar lymphadenopathy) of sarcoidosis, which can cause uveitis but is less likely to be associated with optic neuritis. Although a rash is common with sarcoid, it is usually nodular, papular, or plaque-like; a transient diffuse rash is less common. (Choice C) HLA-B27 testing helps diagnose ankylosing spondylitis, which is associated with anterior (not posterior) uveitis. In addition, most patients have low back pain, arthritis, and other joint/tendon symptoms. (Choice E) Salivary gland biopsy can help diagnose Sjögren syndrome, which often has ocular symptoms such as dry eye, sensation of grittiness, itching, and blurry vision. However, it does not cause optic neuritis or posterior uveitis. Educational objective: Ocular syphilis is a form of neurosyphilis that can occur at any stage of infection. Common manifestations include uveitis and optic neuritis. Patients with HIV are far more likely to have ocular syphilis as a primary manifestation of syphilis infection than are those who do not have HIV.

questions.explanation: This cyanotic newborn has a persistently low partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) despite receiving 100% fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2). These findings suggest a cyanotic congenital heart defect (CCHD) in which a right-to-left shunt forces most of the blood volume to bypass the pulmonary circulation. The degree of cyanosis and hypoxemia is variable and depends on the amount of mixing between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood (eg, presence of a patent ductus arteriosus). Examples of CCHD include D-transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, and hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Although CCHDs are often identified on prenatal ultrasound, they may present initially with cyanosis in the immediate newborn period, as the site of oxygenation abruptly changes from the placenta to the lungs after birth. The hyperoxia test, as seen here, helps to differentiate CCHD from pulmonary pathologies (eg, meconium aspiration, pulmonary hypoplasia), which typically cause hypoxemia due to ventilation-perfusion mismatching and therefore usually demonstrate marked improvement in PaO2 with the administration of supplemental 100% FiO2. In hemodynamically stable patients with suspected CCHD, the next step in evaluation is an echocardiogram to determine the underlying anatomic abnormality. Hemodynamically unstable patients or those with severe cyanosis should receive prostaglandin E1 therapy to maintain the patency of the ductus arteriosus, which provides a left-to-right shunt of partially oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. (Choices A and E) Neonatal sepsis, which may cause cyanosis due to poor tissue perfusion, typically warrants blood cultures, antibiotic therapy, and fluid resuscitation. However, sepsis is unlikely in this hemodynamically stable infant with normal temperature and complete blood count (ie, no leukopenia or leukocytosis). The mild metabolic acidosis (ie, low pH and bicarbonate) is likely due to lactic acidosis in the setting of tissue hypoxia from right-to-left shunting. (Choice C) Intubation is typically reserved for neonates with respiratory failure (eg, severe distress, CO2 retention). This intervention would not improve cyanosis caused by right-to-left shunting. (Choice D) Congenital methemoglobinemia, a rare cause of neonatal cyanosis, causes impaired delivery of oxygen to the tissues. Pulse oximetry is inaccurate in methemoglobinemia and reads no less than 85%, even if true oxygenation is very low. Moreover, PaO2, which represents unbound arterial oxygen, is typically falsely elevated in methemoglobinemia. Educational objective: Cyanotic congenital heart disease should be suspected in cyanotic and hypoxic neonates whose partial pressure of oxygen does not improve with oxygen supplementation. The first step in evaluation is an echocardiogram.

questions.explanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), a condition that occurs when the neurovascular bundle (consisting of the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, and subclavian vein) is compressed within the confined space between the clavicle and first rib (ie, thoracic outlet). TOS can be venous, arterial, or neurogenic. Neurogenic TOS is responsible for >95% of cases. Symptoms of neurogenic TOS include numbness or dysesthesia; in more advanced cases, weakness may also be present. The medial hand and forearm (innervated by the C8 and T1 nerve roots) are often affected because the inferior portion of the brachial plexus is more easily compressed, particularly during activities that require sustained overhead arm use (eg, box stacking, brushing hair). Symptoms may resolve completely with rest. In nonsevere cases, such as this one, physical examination may be normal, but reproduction of symptoms with raising the arm overhead is classic. Initial management is typically TOS-specific physical therapy. (Choice A) The C5 and C6 nerve roots comprise the superior trunk of the brachial plexus and provide sensory innervation to the lateral upper arm, forearm, and hand (eg, lateral palm and thumb). Neither provides sensory innervation to the fifth digit. (Choices C and D) The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the thenar eminence and the palmar surface of the first 3½ digits; it can be compressed in the proximal forearm by the pronator teres (ie, pronator teres syndrome). The radial nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsal lateral hand; it is prone to injury (typically fracture rather than compression) at the humeral midshaft. Neither median nor radial nerve compression would be expected to produce this patient's symptoms because neither provides sensation to the fifth digit. (Choice E) Compression of the ulnar nerve at the wrist (eg, Guyon canal) can result in intermittent numbness in the fifth digit, but it should not cause symptoms proximal to the wrist (eg, forearm). Educational objective: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) occurs when the brachial plexus is compressed within the confined space of the thoracic outlet. Symptoms of neurogenic TOS (the most common TOS subtype) include poorly located numbness and dysesthesia (often in the C8 and T1 nerve root distribution), typically exacerbated by sustained overhead arm use.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old, previously healthy woman comes to the office due to worsening right hand numbness. The patient first noticed intermittent numbness of the right fifth digit 8 months ago with activities such as combing her hair. Since then, the symptoms have progressed to involve more of the right hand and forearm. She has had difficulty performing her job in which she has to stack boxes on high shelves. The symptoms resolve with rest. Physical examination shows normal strength, reflexes, and sensation in the right upper extremity. Distal pulses are normal and capillary refill is not delayed. There is no neck deformity or tenderness. The symptoms are reproduced when the patient is instructed to raise her right arm over her head. Compression of the neural structures at which of the following locations is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

questions.explanation: Hemodynamic effects of common congenital heart defects Overload produced Ventricle primarily affected Atrial septal defect Volume Right Ventricular septal defect Volume Left Patent ductus arteriosus Volume Left Aortic coarctation Pressure Left The clinical presentation of decompensated heart failure (DHF) in infants differs from that in older children and adults. Infants commonly have dyspnea, feeding difficulty, diaphoresis, and poor weight gain and may demonstrate retractions, tachycardia, and an S3 on examination. However, jugular venous distension and peripheral edema are rarely noted. The source of DHF in this newborn is most likely a large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), which leads to left-to-right shunting that results in overcirculation and left ventricular (LV) volume overload. PDA is recognized by a continuous murmur best heard in the left infraclavicular area; a large PDA shunt is indicated by a hyperdynamic precordium with a palpable thrill, bounding peripheral pulses, and a large pulse pressure, as well as an apical diastolic rumble and an S3 (related to the high volume of recirculated blood entering the left ventricle across the mitral valve). questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia Pathogenesis TDP-43 mutation Tau protein inclusions (eg, Pick bodies) Clinical features Early onset (age 50s-60s) Behavior &/or personality changes Disinhibition Apathy Loss of empathy Compulsions or rituals Hyperorality Executive dysfunction Diagnosis Primarily clinical Neuroimaging (CT scan, MRI) Asymmetric frontal/anterior temporal lobe atrophy Functional imaging (eg, FDG-PET) may show hypometabolism Management Nonpharmacologic: behavior modification Pharmacologic (symptomatic): SSRI, atypical antipsychotic agent Prognosis Progressive course; survival 8-10 years FDG-PET = fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TDP-43 = 43 kD transactive response (TAR) DNA-binding protein. Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a common cause of early-onset dementia, typically occurring in patients in their late 50s or early 60s. Pathological inclusions (eg, hyperphosphorylated tau, TDP-43) with frontal and temporal lobe atrophy are stereotypic. As in this patient, functional decline follows early behavioral and personality changes of: disinhibition (including aggressive sexual behaviors such as kissing and offering sex to strangers) apathy loss of empathy compulsive behaviors (eg, spending the day watching religious programming) hyperorality (eg, smoking) executive decline (eg, neglecting bills, household chores) Diagnosis is based on having ≥3 of the 6 behavioral and personality changes. FTD is a progressive disease with no definitive treatment. Therefore, management is aimed at improving behavioral symptoms and patient safety. First-line management is with behavioral interventions (eg, exercise, trigger avoidance, distraction, redirection). In patients with prominent sexual aggression symptoms, serotonin modulators such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, citalopram) or trazodone can be used because their adverse effect profile can decrease sexual desire and arousal. (Choices A, C and, E) Alzheimer disease typically does not initially present with behavioral and personality changes. Late-onset (eg, age >65) schizophrenia can lead to behavioral disturbances but would still present characteristic features such as delusions (often persecutory), hallucinations (often auditory), grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, apathy). Vascular dementia classically presents with a stepwise decline, often with prominent cognitive dysfunction and localizing findings. This patient's disinhibition (with aggressive sexual behaviors), hyperorality, and compulsive behaviors make FTD more likely. (Choice D) Meningosyphilis, a form of neurosyphilis, results in an inflammatory arteritis that typically presents as stroke or other focal neurologic deficits most commonly affecting the middle cerebral artery. Many patients have prodromal headache and dizziness likely reflecting meningitis. None of these findings are seen in this patient. Educational objective: Frontotemporal dementia is a neurodegenerative disorder with stereotypic early onset (age 50s-60s) of personality and social decline in the setting of progressive impairment of functioning. Serotonin-modifying agents are recommended for patients with sexual or physical aggression.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the office by her husband due to several behavioral changes for the past year. The patient has had difficulty remembering how to perform routine household chores, such as operating the washing machine, and has been neglecting bills, which the husband attributed to old age. She spends most of the day watching either religious television shows and cooking shows even though she previously did not enjoy cooking and was not particularly religious. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Medication nonadherence Patient/disease characteristics Asymptomatic or chronic condition Denial of illness/chronicity No immediate harm from stopping Psychiatric illness (eg, depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment) Illness/cultural beliefs against medication Inadequate understanding of illness/risks of nonadherence Treatment/management characteristics Adverse effects Incomplete medication efficacy Complicated regimen Medication cost Impaired physician-patient communication, lack of follow-up This patient with hypertension was prescribed a common 2-drug antihypertension regimen, but his blood pressure has not lowered significantly. In a young patient without notable comorbidity, the most likely cause is medication nonadherence. Nonadherence is common in patients with hypertension because the condition is generally asymptomatic, whereas medication has cost, inconvenience, and often symptomatic adverse effects (eg, headache, lightheadedness). Besides young age, other factors associated with adherence include insurance plan (ie, lower adherence with Medicaid coverage), pharmacy type (ie, higher adherence with mail-order pharmacies), and use of fixed-dose combination pills (ie, higher adherence). If nonadherence is suspected, additional information can be obtained via patient interview, standardized survey, or inspection of the patient's pill bottles (eg, pill count, refills remaining). (Choice A) Diffuse vascular calcification can cause a falsely elevated blood pressure due to decreased compressibility of the brachial artery. This can be erroneously interpreted as treatment-resistant hypertension. However, diffuse vascular calcification is typically seen in patients age >60 with chronic kidney disease or multiple atherosclerotic risk factors (eg, smoking, diabetes). (Choice B) First-line antihypertensive medications include ACE inhibitors (eg, lisinopril), angiotensin II receptor blockers, thiazide diuretics, and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) (eg, amlodipine). The combination of ACE inhibitor and CCB is an appropriate 2-drug regimen and is highly effective for most patients. (Choice D) Left ventricular hypertrophy is a complication of long-standing hypertension and warrants aggressive blood pressure control; however, it does not alter the effectiveness of antihypertensive medications. (Choice E) Common conditions causing treatment-resistant hypertension include primary aldosteronism, obstructive sleep apnea, and renovascular disease (eg, renal artery stenosis). Renal parenchymal disease also can cause resistant hypertension but is usually known at the time of diagnosis. Most patients with hypertension due to renal parenchymal disease respond to ACE inhibitors and CCBs. Educational objective: Medication nonadherence is common in young patients with hypertension and can lead to persistent blood pressure elevation despite an appropriate drug regimen.

questions.explanation: This patient with recurrent episodes of hematuria after recent upper respiratory infections (URI) most likely has IgA nephropathy, an immune complex–mediated nephritic syndrome. The pathogenesis is as follows: A mucosal infection (eg, URI) triggers production of pathogenic IgA, which then deposits in the mesangium. This causes complement activation; however, due to the weak complement-fixing activity of IgA, which lacks the residues in the Fc region that bind complement, serum complement levels are normal. The influx of cytokines and resultant inflammation cause endothelial and mesangial cell proliferation, which results in glomerular hypertension and decreased glomerular filtration (eg, elevated creatinine). Subsequent podocyte disruption leads to increased membrane permeability, resulting in hematuria and red blood cell (RBC) casts (ie, aggregated RBCs that are dysmorphic due to deformation from the passage through the glomerular basement membrane). Although IgA deposition is diffuse and global, the resultant glomerulosclerosis, hypercellularity, and tubular atrophy are focal and limited; therefore, patients typically have mild proteinuria (<5% of IgA nephropathy patients have nephrotic-range proteinuria) (Choices A and B). Patients typically experience symptoms within days of a URI (synpharyngitic), but episodes can be spontaneous (~20%). Presentation ranges from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to nephritic syndrome (eg, gross hematuria, hypertension, renal insufficiency) with flank pain. Diagnosis is frequently clinical. Most patients follow a benign clinical course; however, patients with hypertension, elevated creatinine, or persistent proteinuria are at risk for disease progression. (Choice D) Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) can present with nephritic syndrome (eg, hematuria, hypertension); complement is low due to the stronger complement-fixing ability of IgM/IgG. APSGN is rarely recurrent, and hematuria occurs weeks (rather than days) after a Group A Streptococcus infection (eg, pharyngitis). (Choices E and F) Cellular casts can help diagnose some renal diseases. Muddy brown casts are formed by sloughing of tubular epithelial cells in the setting of ischemic injury, characteristic of acute tubular necrosis. White blood cell casts are seen in pyelonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis, which is typically triggered by drugs and, unlike this case, accompanied by fever and rash. Educational objective: IgA nephropathy occurs due to mesangial deposition of IgA and subsequent glomerular damage, leading to hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. Serum complement is typically normal.

questions.explanation: Infertility Etiology Diagnostic test Male factor Semen analysis Ovulatory function Midluteal phase (day 21) progesterone level Ovarian reserve Day 3 FSH & estradiol levels Clomiphene citrate challenge test Antral follicle count Antimüllerian hormone Fallopian tube patency Hysterosalpingogram Uterine cavity evaluation Sonohysterogram Infertility is the lack of conception after 12 months of unprotected intercourse in women age <35 (or after 6 months in women age ≥35). A normal semen analysis suggests female factor infertility, which most commonly occurs due to anatomic disorders (eg, fallopian tube obstruction), ovulatory dysfunction (eg, anovulation), or diminished ovarian reserve. Therefore, the initial evaluation includes assessments of tubal patency, ovulation, and ovarian reserve (rather than observation and reassurance only) (Choice E). Ovarian reserve refers to the quantity and quality of a patient's remaining oocytes (ie, primordial follicle pool), which naturally diminish with age. A serum marker of ovarian reserve is antimüllerian hormone (AMH), which is released by small preantral ovarian follicles as they are recruited from the primordial pool and mature. Therefore, in patients with infertility, low AMH levels typically reflect a smaller primordial pool and diminished ovarian reserve. Infertility due to diminished ovarian reserve may be a presenting sign of primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), which is the accelerated depletion of ovarian follicles leading to elevated FSH and low estradiol before age 40. Because autoimmune oophoritis can cause POI, rates of POI are higher in patients with autoimmune disease, such as this patient with celiac disease. (Choice B) Antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune disorder characterized by venous or arterial thrombosis, is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss (eg, ≥3 spontaneous abortions prior to 10 weeks gestation). This patient does not have any of these characteristics. (Choice C) Diagnostic laparoscopy can be used to diagnose infertility caused by intraabdominal adhesions or endometriosis. However, there is usually a history of abdominal surgery or severe dysmenorrhea, none of which are seen in this patient. In addition, noninvasive testing (eg, AMH level) is performed prior to invasive testing. (Choice D) Karyotype analysis can diagnose Turner syndrome (45,X), which is a cause of primary ovarian insufficiency that can present with infertility and autoimmune disorders (eg, celiac disease). However, unlike this patient with regular menses, patients with Turner syndrome typically have amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. Educational objective: Female factor infertility can occur due to anatomic disorders, ovulatory dysfunction, or diminished ovarian reserve. In patients with infertility, a low antimüllerian hormone level indicates diminished ovarian reserve (ie, diminished quantity and/or quality of remaining oocytes).

questions.explanation: This patient with pneumonia (fever, infiltrate on chest x-ray) has hypernatremia (serum sodium ≥145 mEq/L). Hypernatremia is caused by total body sodium content in excess of free water volume, leading to an elevated concentration. It is most often due to insensible losses of hypotonic fluid through transcutaneous (eg, sweat from fever and diaphoresis) and respiratory (eg, tachypnea from pneumonia) routes. Because the lost fluid is hypotonic (sodium < free water), the sodium left behind in plasma becomes hyperconcentrated (sodium > free water), producing hypernatremia. Normally, hypernatremia is an irresistible stimulant of thirst (ie, people seek water to maintain sodium homeostasis). Patients who cannot communicate thirst (eg, aphasic due to stroke or dementia) and depend on caregivers to provide free water are at high risk for hypernatremia. For this reason, free water replacement (eg, intravenous dextrose 5% water, frequent gastrostomy tube water flushes) must usually be increased during acute illness to compensate. Sodium is the primary determinant of intravascular volume, and the etiology of hypernatremia is often obvious from the clinical presentation. Assessing volume status along with urine sodium and osmolality provides additional clues. This patient receiving adequate sodium from tube feeds is euvolemic (good skin turgor, normal jugular venous pressure). His hypernatremia reflects an unreplaced free water deficit, with the elevated urine osmolality (UOsm ≥600 mOsm/kg H2O) reflecting the body's attempt to increase renal water reabsorption to compensate for nonrenal water loss (eg, insensible losses). (Choice A) Decreased mineralocorticoid release is associated with hyponatremia, rather than hypernatremia. Increased mineralocorticoid release from primary hyperaldosteronism can cause hypernatremia due to increased renal sodium resorption (in an excess of water) but would also cause secondary hypertension, metabolic alkalosis, and hypokalemia. (Choice B) Diabetes insipidus causes hypernatremia due to renal free water loss (hypotonic polyuria) attributable to insufficient vasopressin levels (central) or signaling (nephrogenic). However, UOsm should be very low because hypotonic polyuria dilutes urine. (Choice D) Osmotic diuresis (eg, hyperglycemia, mannitol therapy) can cause hypernatremia due to profound water excretion; UOsm is elevated. However, osmotic diuresis produces hypovolemia (hypotension, poor skin turgor) due to simultaneous sodium loss through osmotic drag. (Choice E) Iatrogenic sodium overload (eg, intravenous fluids) can cause hypernatremia, but patients have hypervolemia (eg, edema, elevated neck veins) and markedly elevated urine sodium. Educational objective: Hypernatremia (serum sodium ≥145 mEq/L) is due to sodium in excess of free water volume. Insensible loss of hypotonic fluid is accelerated during acute illness, leading to a free water deficit that must be replaced. Patients with impaired communication and mobility are most susceptible to hypernatremia.

questions.explanation: This patient with acute-onset, unilateral upper and lower facial drooping likely has Bell palsy, a peripheral neuropathy involving the facial nerve (CN VII). In classic cases of Bell palsy, no further diagnostic workup (eg, MRI, Lyme serologies) is required. Patients with Bell palsy often have incomplete eye closure and decreased tear production, which can lead to corneal dryness, abrasions, and, in severe cases, exposure keratitis that can cause blindness. Therefore, eyelid closure evaluation should be done in all patients who have facial nerve weakness. If closure is incomplete, corneal protection strategies should be instituted and may include: Lubricating eye drops Lubricating eye ointment (at night) Moisture chamber (ie, a clear patch worn over the affected eye to decrease evaporative moisture loss that is usually used during the day) Taping the eye closed (at night) High-dose corticosteroids should be started within 3 days to improve chances of complete recovery. Antivirals (eg, acyclovir) are sometimes added. (Choice A) A Dix-Hallpike maneuver, in which vertigo and nystagmus are triggered as the patient quickly lies back into a supine position with the head rotated 45 degrees, is used to support the diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. This condition causes brief (<1 min), often intense episodes of vertigo triggered by changes in head position. It does not cause facial weakness. (Choice C) Stroke patients are at risk for dysphagia and aspiration; assessment of swallowing safety may include bedside swallow evaluation or a fluoroscopic swallowing evaluation (ie, modified barium swallow). However, stroke often leads to facial weakness that spares the upper face because the upper face receives bicortical innervation. Bell palsy does not typically lead to dysphagia, although lip weakness can lead to food and fluids dripping out of the mouth. (Choice D) Bedside spirometry can be used to quickly assess pulmonary function and is often used to serially assess patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) who are at risk of respiratory failure. However, GBS typically presents with symmetric ascending weakness that usually includes limb weakness with decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes. (Choice E) The Weber and Rinne tuning fork tests can help distinguish between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. A tumor at the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic neuroma) can lead to sensorineural hearing loss and facial weakness. However, facial weakness would generally progress over weeks rather than hours. Educational objective: Bell palsy, an idiopathic peripheral neuropathy involving the facial nerve (CN VII), presents with acute, progressive, unilateral facial weakness. The eye is at risk for exposure keratitis, so eye closure should be assessed and corneal protection strategies employed in patients with incomplete eye closure.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to difficulty moving her face. The patient had no unusual symptoms this morning, but just before lunch she felt that the left side of her face was "melting." At lunchtime, she could not sip her iced tea out of a straw. The symptoms continued to worsen over the next few hours, so the patient came to the emergency department. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, the extraocular movements are intact, and the conjunctivae are clear. The external auditory canals are clear, and tympanic membranes are normal. Examination of the face is shown in the exhibit. Muscle strength is 5/5 in all 4 extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. There is no Babinski sign. Sensation over the face and body are normal. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: This patient's 2-week history of intermittent anxiety, restlessness, headache, and muscle aches coinciding with longer work hours and shift changes is most consistent with a mild antidepressant discontinuation syndrome (ADS). Onset of antidepressant discontinuation symptoms may occur in as little as 1 day following a missed dose of antidepressants that have shorter elimination half-lives (eg, <24 hours). The selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor paroxetine, in particular, is associated with more prominent discontinuation symptoms due to its short half-life. Common symptoms associated with abrupt discontinuation include headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness, and psychological symptoms (eg, dysphoria, anxiety, irritability). Other symptoms may include flu-like symptoms (eg, myalgias, chills, diaphoresis), insomnia, and neurosensory disturbances (eg, paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, vivid dreams). When ADS is a possible cause of new-onset symptoms, the next step is to ask how the patient is taking the medication to determine whether inconsistent dosing is occurring. Patients prescribed antidepressants with shorter elimination half-lives should be educated about the risk of ADS due to missed doses or abrupt discontinuation. (Choice A) Melatonin has been used to treat sleep-wake disturbances in shift workers. However, this patient does not describe difficulty falling or staying asleep, and her symptoms are more characteristic of ADS. (Choices B and C) Although stress can also cause a range of physical and psychological symptoms, monitoring the patient or suggesting time off from work (which may not be possible for her) will not target the likely underlying cause of the patient's symptoms; these can be readily addressed by educating her about the importance of taking medication on a regular basis. (Choice D) In some cases, ADS may be mistaken for other medical conditions due to prominent physical symptoms. In this patient, the onset of characteristic withdrawal symptoms coinciding with shift work and lack of other key signs of hyperthyroidism (eg, unintentional weight loss, tachycardia) make ADS more likely. Educational objective: Nonadherence to antidepressants can result in antidepressant discontinuation syndrome (eg, anxiety, headache, dizziness, flu-like symptoms, paresthesia). Patients prescribed antidepressants with shorter elimination half-lives should be educated about the risks of missing or skipping doses.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up regarding depression. She has been prescribed paroxetine for the past year. The patient reports doing well overall but has been more stressed by her job as a security guard. For the past 2 weeks, she has had to work longer hours due to a coworker quitting and frequently alternates between day and night shifts. During this time, the patient has had some periods of anxiety and restlessness, often accompanied by a headache and muscle aches, which she attributes to her sleep schedule and having to stand while working. She says, "I usually fall asleep right when I get home and wake up just in time for the next shift. Sometimes I forget which day it is because they've all started to blur together." Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?

questions.explanation: Across cultures and regions, diets typically consist of certain staples (eg, breads, grains, legumes) served with more variable accessory foods (eg, meats, flavorings, sauces). Physician counseling regarding dietary modification (eg, avoidance of excess calories and simple carbohydrates to promote glycemic control) should be tailored to the patient's cultural and social preferences: Elicit the patient's current dietary patterns, cultural influences, and preferences for specific staples and accessory foods. Understand the patient's environmental influences and constraints, including work and home schedules (eg, packing meals for work, dining with family). Provide specific recommendations for consuming high-quality foods, moderating the quantity of staples (eg, bread, tortillas), and substituting lower-calorie or less-processed alternatives (eg, quinoa instead of white bread or rice). (Choice A) A Mediterranean-style diet (ie, limited red meat; increased intake of vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats) is one dietary pattern associated with improved glycemic control. However, this recommendation, which may or may not align with the patient's preferences, is less effective than discussing specific staples based on the patient's current diet. (Choice C) Providing educational materials in the patient's preferred language is recommended as a complement to physician counseling. Although specific meal plans may benefit patients with complex dietary requirements or in need of drastic lifestyle change, interactive discussion of the patient's staple foods and healthful substitutions is a more tailored, effective approach. (Choice D) Although frequent snacking may lead to weight gain, this patient is obtaining most of her food intake at home; changing her midday snack is less likely to be helpful than reducing caloric intake in her main meals. (Choice E) Commercial meal preparation services (ie, pre-prepared frozen foods) can provide reduced-calorie meals for individuals attempting to lose weight. These programs can be effective but are typically expensive and may not be appropriate for a patient who is used to preparing her own meals. This alternative is not necessary if changes to her home meal preparation are effective. Educational objective: Across cultures and regions, diets typically consist of certain staples (eg, breads, grains, legumes) served with variable accessory foods. Patients with diabetes often do not appreciate the caloric content of the staple foods and may overeat, leading to weight gain and loss of glycemic control. This population can often lose weight and achieve better glycemic control by substituting high-calorie, processed staples with lower-calorie alternatives.

questions.explanation: Discussing code status Timing Initiate in outpatient setting & revisit upon hospital admission Incorporate into broader goals of care Language Use neutral & realistic language (eg, "attempt to resuscitate you if you die") Avoid positive (eg, "everything to keep you alive") & negative (eg, "artificial machine to help you breathe") phrases Scope includes DNR only pertains to moment of death (cardiac arrest) in hospital DNR = allow natural death (ie, no chest compressions, defibrillation, or intubation) Discuss as a package rather than separate components Scope excludes DNR does not preclude intubation & MV for prearrest respiratory failure DNR does not affect any other aspect of medical care DNR does not apply outside of the current hospital DNR = do not resuscitate; MV = mechanical ventilation. This patient is admitted with clinical deterioration potentially related to her underlying frailty and decompensation of serious chronic medical conditions (cardiopulmonary and renal disease). In all patients admitted to the hospital, code status should be discussed, documented, and formalized as a physician order as early as possible. The meaning of "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR) is often misunderstood by patients, surrogates, and health care providers alike. An organic definition of DNR is to "allow natural death" if the patient experiences cardiac arrest. Interventions to restore spontaneous circulation (eg, chest compressions, defibrillation, intubation and mechanical ventilation) should be withheld. DNR only applies to the moment of death (ie, cardiac arrest). It should be explicitly stated that electing DNR status does not impact any other aspect of medical treatment outside of how cardiac arrest is handled because many patients and families fear that DNR status may be interpreted as "giving up" and compromises quality of care. A DNR order still allows for maximal, life-prolonging treatment (eg, intensive care unit) (Choice E). It also does not preclude prearrest intubation and mechanical ventilation (Choice B); these procedures may be necessary to prevent progression to cardiac arrest (eg, from severe hypoxemia or hypercapnea). Similarly, a DNR order does not preclude invasive airway placement for patients requiring procedural anesthesia (eg, emergency surgery). However, patients' preferences regarding invasive respiratory support should be examined in the broader context of overall goals of care, ideally when clinically stable with the luxury of time. (Choices A and C) Patients and surrogates sometimes request specifically tailored code status designations, such as cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) but no intubation, or conversely, intubation but no CPR. This practice of partial DNR orders is generally discouraged. Splitting resuscitation into different components can create confusion among patients, families, and health care providers and set the stage for suboptimal resuscitation (eg, inability to intubate a patient who is apneic after successful CPR). Chest compressions, defibrillation, and invasive airway placement should be discussed together as a unified philosophy of care, rather than individually as separate interventions. Educational objective: A Do Not Resuscitate order is best interpreted as a directive to allow natural death when cardiac arrest occurs, withholding all life-sustaining interventions (eg, chest compressions, defibrillation, intubation, mechanical ventilation).

  • Avoid positive (eg, "everything to keep you alive") & negative (eg, "artificial machine to help you breathe") phrases
Scope includes
  • DNR only pertains to moment of death (cardiac arrest) in hospital
  • DNR = allow natural death (ie, no chest compressions, defibrillation, or intubation)
  • Discuss as a package rather than separate components
Scope excludes
  • DNR does not preclude intubation & MV for prearrest respiratory failure
  • DNR does not affect any other aspect of medical care
  • DNR does not apply outside of the current hospital
DNR = do not resuscitate; MV = mechanical ventilation.

This patient is admitted with clinical deterioration potentially related to her underlying frailty and decompensation of serious chronic medical conditions (cardiopulmonary and renal disease).  In all patients admitted to the hospital, code status should be discussed, documented, and formalized as a physician order as early as possible.

The meaning of "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR) is often misunderstood by patients, surrogates, and health care providers alike.  An organic definition of DNR is to "allow natural death" if the patient experiences cardiac arrest.  Interventions to restore spontaneous circulation (eg, chest compressions, defibrillation, intubation and mechanical ventilation) should be withheld.  DNR only applies to the moment of death (ie, cardiac arrest).  It should be explicitly stated that electing DNR status does not impact any other aspect of medical treatment outside of how cardiac arrest is handled because many patients and families fear that DNR status may be interpreted as "giving up" and compromises quality of care.

Similarly, a DNR order does not preclude invasive airway placement for patients requiring procedural anesthesia (eg, emergency surgery).  However, patients' preferences regarding invasive respiratory support should be examined in the broader context of overall goals of care, ideally when clinically stable with the luxury of time.

wrongAnswers.C: See the shared discussion for choice A.
wrongAnswers.E: A DNR order still allows for maximal, life-prolonging treatment (eg, intensive care unit) (Choice E).

Give the patient self-help pamphlets and audio recordings to use on an airplane

questions.explanation: Behavioral therapy approaches for smoking cessation Brief intervention Brief interaction with a physician in the office Individual counseling Formal in-person counseling at least once a week Group counseling Group teaching about behavioral techniques & coping skills Telephone counseling—proactive Counselor initiates calls to the patient at prearranged times Telephone counseling—reactive Patient initiates calls to the counselor when convenient for patient Text messaging Automated motivational text messages for support Self-help material Pamphlets, audio & video recordings This patient is highly motivated to quit smoking, but his job requirements limit behavioral intervention options. Although intensive in-office counseling is very effective for most patients, telephone counseling is likely more practical for this patient with a heavy travel schedule (Choice D). Proactive telephone counseling, in which a counselor initiates regular calls to the patient at prearranged times to check on the patient's progress, is effective at helping to reduce long-term smoking. It has a higher success rate than reactive telephone counseling, in which patients initiate a call when they want to talk (Choice A). Smoking cessation hotlines can be a useful adjunctive measure but would not be suitable as a replacement for regular counseling. Furthermore, calling a hotline right before lighting a cigarette would be ineffective because the intervention would likely be too late: it is much faster to light a cigarette than to dial and reach a hotline counselor (Choice E). The most effective approach is to set up regular calls from the counselor to the patient, as well as for the patient to call the hotline before cravings become severe and uncontrollable. (Choice B) Self-help materials (eg, pamphlets, audio guides) have some use as an introductory measure, but studies have shown that they are not effective in improving quit rates in patients already using nicotine replacement therapy. Educational objective: Proactive phone counseling, in which a counselor calls a patient at prearranged times, is an effective method for smoking cessation. It is more effective than reactive phone counseling, in which the patient calls the counselor when the patient feels like talking.

questions.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome Clinical features Hypotonia Weak suck/feeding problems in infancy Hyperphagia/obesity Short stature Hypogonadism Intellectual disability Dysmorphic facies Narrow forehead Almond-shaped eyes Downturned mouth Diagnosis Loss of expression on paternal chromosome 15 (q11-q13) Complications Sleep apnea (70%) Type 2 diabetes mellitus (25%) Gastric distension/rupture Death by choking (8%) This patient's obesity, developmental delay, dysmorphia (narrow forehead, almond-shaped eyes), small hands, and hypogonadism are characteristic of Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS). PWS results from the loss of expression of a critical region in the paternal copy of chromosome 15q11-q13, which occurs via deletion or receipt of 2 copies of the maternal chromosome (maternal uniparental disomy). It results in hypotonia, presenting with poor suck in infancy (which can lead to poor feeding and need for nutritional supplementation) and delayed onset of motor milestones (eg, sitting, walking). Subsequently, hyperphagia follows from age 1 to 6 and leads to obesity. Hypothalamic and pituitary dysfunction are common, resulting in short stature, hypogonadism, and osteoporosis. Other common features include skin-picking, behavioral difficulties (eg, irritability, tantrums especially if food is restricted), and autistic features such as poor eye contact and speech and social deficits, as seen in this patient. (Choice A) The most common chromosomal anomaly in live births is Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21. It could explain developmental delay, short stature, and autistic features. Although obesity is common, the pattern of feeding difficulty followed by the onset of weight gain in early childhood is typical of PWS. In addition, the characteristic dysmorphic features of Down syndrome (eg, up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge) are absent. (Choice B) Elevated phenylalanine levels are found in phenylketonuria caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. It results in intellectual disability, seizures, and microcephaly. (Choice C) Hypothyroidism can present with short stature and cognitive deficits; however, other symptoms would be expected, such as thyromegaly, lethargy, constipation, bradycardia, and delayed reflexes. (Choice D) Hyperuricemia is seen in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which results from a deficiency of the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase enzyme. It can result in hypotonia and developmental delay but would also present with more extreme self-mutilation (eg, biting, banging self) and extrapyramidal symptoms (eg, dystonia, choreoathetosis). (Choice F) Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene and mainly affects the female population. Key features include loss of speech, stereotypical hand movements, and gait abnormalities after an initial period of normal development. Educational objective: Developmental delay with skin-picking, dysmorphic features (eg, almond-shaped eyes), and early feeding difficulty followed by hyperphagia and obesity should prompt consideration of Prader-Willi syndrome, resulting from the loss of expression of the paternally active region on chromosome 15.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for assessment of anxiety. His mother says, "He has started rubbing and picking at his skin. Physical examination is significant for an overweight child with a narrow forehead, almond-shaped eyes, and red excoriations over the left hand and arm. The patient is noted to have small hands and genitalia. He makes little eye contact and begins to cry when the physician asks him questions. Which of the following is likely to be found on diagnostic testing?

questions.explanation: Meningiomas Risk factors Older age, female > male Radiation exposure NF-2 related schwannomatosis* Clinical manifestations Asymptomatic Headache Seizures Extremity weakness (parasagittal or spinal) Visual changes (optic) Loss of hearing or smell (cerebellopontine angle/olfactory groove) Obstructive hydrocephalus Diagnosis MRI with contrast: homogeneously contrast-enhancing, extraaxial dural mass ("dural tail") Management Observation/serial imaging: small, asymptomatic Surgery: large, symptomatic, or associated with edema Radiation: nonresectable tumors or poor surgical candidates *Previously known as neurofibromatosis type 2. This woman has a homogeneously contrast-enhancing, partially calcified, extraaxial tumor located at a dural reflection (falx), consistent with a meningioma. Meningiomas are benign, primary brain tumors most commonly found in middle-aged to elderly women. They may cause headaches, usually with a pattern consistent with increased intracranial pressure (eg, worsens during recumbency or straining, associated with nausea/vomiting). Meningiomas may also cause seizures or focal neurologic symptoms (eg, facial numbness) due to compression of neurovascular structures. On imaging, meningiomas classically appear as well-circumscribed, round masses attached to the dura and are commonly found at the lateral convexity or falcine (as in this patient) region of the brain. Because they have such a typical appearance on neuroimaging, usually no other diagnostic workup is required prior to definitive surgical treatment. In symptomatic patients, complete surgical excision is typically curative. In asymptomatic patients (especially elderly patients or those with significant comorbidities), observation with serial imaging may be appropriate. (Choice A) Interferon gamma release assay can be used to diagnose tuberculosis, which can cause a CNS tuberculoma and lead to headache without meningeal signs. However, MRI typically would reveal multiple ring-enhancing lesion(s) in the parenchyma (rather than dural-based by the falx), and patients are typically immunocompromised (eg, HIV). (Choice B) Meningiomas can occur in the spine, but these are much rarer than those in the brain. Therefore, patients with spinal meningiomas should have an MRI of the brain, but patients with brain meningiomas usually don't require an MRI of the spine. (Choice C) Spinal fluid analysis can be helpful to diagnose CNS infections that can lead to mass lesions (eg, tuberculoma, toxoplasma). Although spinal fluid analysis in patients with a meningioma may show elevated protein, this is not required for diagnosis of tumors with a classic appearance (as in this patient). (Choice E) Toxoplasmic encephalitis can lead to headaches and focal neurologic symptoms. However, MRI would show ring-enhancing lesion(s) with surrounding edema located in the brain parenchyma, rather than a dural-based, homogeneously enhancing lesion (as in this patient). Educational objective: Meningiomas appear as homogeneously contrast-enhancing, extraaxial tumors attached to the dura. For symptomatic tumors, surgical excision is curative.

questions.explanation: Neurocysticercosis Epidemiology Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) eggs Fecal-oral human transmission Central & South America, sub-Saharan Africa, Asia Manifestations Prolonged incubation (months to years) Seizures ICH (headache, vomiting, AMS) Diagnosis CT/MRI scans: cysts (hypodense, enhancement/edema, or calcified) T solium serology Treatment Seizure/ICH management Antiparasitic therapy (albendazole) Corticosteroids AMS = altered mental status; ICH = intracranial hypertension. This patient from Argentina with an adult-onset seizure has classical radiographic findings for neurocysticercosis (NCC), an infection caused by ingestion of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) eggs. Risk is greatest in those who have spent time in resource limited settings, particularly rural areas where the likelihood of poor sanitation and exposure to pigs increases. Cysticercosis is endemic in Central/South America, India, and sub-Saharan Africa. Most cases present months or years after transmission when viable cysts in the brain deteriorate due to a progressive host immune response. This generates inflammation and edema, which can trigger an adult-onset seizure. Notably, fever is absent, and physical examination and laboratory evaluation are typically normal (including no peripheral eosinophilia). Although serology should be sent, the diagnosis is considered sufficiently confirmed when neuroimaging (eg, MRI or CT scan of the head) shows ≥1 characteristic cyst. This patient's imaging reveals a scolex, the part of the worm that attaches with 4 suckers, along with an enhancing lesion with vasogenic edema (consistent with a degenerating cyst). Cysts can be seen in various stages of viability, including a round/hypodense/nonenhancing lesion (viable cyst) or a calcified nodule (nonviable cyst). Treatment includes corticosteroids (to limit inflammation as the organisms are destroyed) and albendazole; praziquantel is added when >2 viable or deteriorating cysts are present. Antiseizure medication (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine) is also typically required for several months. Ophthalmologic evaluation must be performed prior to antiparasitic therapy in order to limit loss of vision with treatment. (Choice A) Corticosteroids are administered with antiparasitic therapy to reduce brain inflammation as the parasite is destroyed, which limits additional seizures. (Choice C) Radiation therapy reduces intraparenchymal tumor burden and symptoms (eg, seizure, confusion, herniation) in those with brain malignancy or metastases. This young patient with a single cystic lesion that contains a scolex is far more likely to have NCC than cancer. (Choice D) Toxoplasmosis is treated with sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine. Although toxoplasmosis can cause seizure, imaging will show ring-enhancing lesions. Furthermore, it primarily occurs in those with severe immunocompromise due to AIDS. (Choice E) Some cases of brain abscess that do not respond to antimicrobial therapy are treated with neurosurgery; they would not cause a scolex. NCC sometimes presents with ventricular cysts, which can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid outflow and cause elevated intracranial pressure. Urgent neurosurgery may be required to divert cerebrospinal fluid or remove the cyst. However, intraparenchymal brain lesions (as in this case) are not typically treated with surgery. Educational objective: Neurocysticercosis is caused by ingestion of Taenia solium eggs and is endemic to rural regions of some developing countries. It generally presents with adult-onset seizure and imaging evidence of ≥1 cyst in the brain parenchyma. Treatment includes corticosteroids plus albendazole; an eye examination is required for all patients prior to treatment.
