questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the office after an episode of passing out. Over the past 6 months, the patient has had several short spells of feeling unsteady on his feet, almost as if he were on a boat, along with double vision and numbness of the bilateral limbs. He has not found a consistent trigger, but the events usually occur when he is fatigued. Today, the patient was working under his car in the garage and became severely dizzy when he went from kneeling to standing. He felt his knees giving away and he collapsed. The patient lost consciousness transiently; he was not confused after regaining consciousness but felt nauseated. Medical history is significant for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. Blood pressure is 144/92 mm Hg while supine and 140/88 mm Hg when upright and pulse is 70/min and regular. questions.explanation: Secondary causes of behavioral change in patients with intellectual disability Gastrointestinal disorders Constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, bowel obstruction Occult infection Cellulitis, cystitis, otitis media, pneumonia Unrecognized pain Dental caries, menstrual pain, unreported trauma/fracture Sensory impairment Cerumen impaction, visual problems Psychiatric disorders Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder Sleep disorders Obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia Behavioral disturbances (eg, headbanging, aggression toward caregivers) are common in patients with intellectual disability (ID) (eg, Down syndrome, fragile X syndrome). Although these behaviors may be consistent with developmental age, any acute change from baseline (as in this patient) should raise concern for a secondary medical cause, particularly given the communication barriers associated with worsening ID severity. Because these patients may be unable to describe symptoms of pain/distress, a thorough physical examination can be particularly useful. Constipation is a frequently missed secondary cause of behavioral change. This patient's distended abdomen, combined with his constipation history, warrants an abdominal x-ray to rule out stool retention. Even minor sources of discomfort (eg, cerumen impaction) can result in significant behavioral disruptions. Other easily missed secondary causes of behavioral disturbances that should also be considered include cystitis, gastroesophageal reflux, and occult trauma. (Choices A and C) In patients with ID who have behavioral disturbances, chronic use of antipsychotics or benzodiazepines may be indicated with longstanding behavioral diagnoses; these medications are sometimes used acutely to facilitate medical care or prevent extremely harmful behaviors. However, they are associated with adverse effects (eg, sedation, anticholinergic effects) that can mask or worsen secondary causes of behavioral changes. Acute changes from baseline behavior, as in this patient, should first be evaluated for a secondary cause and would not warrant medication adjustment unless there is a significantly increased danger to self or others (antipsychotic) or a new diagnosis of anxiety or spasticity (benzodiazepine). (Choice B) Behavioral modification strategies include rewarding appropriate behaviors and providing consequences for disruptive actions. These techniques can be useful for treating chronic behavioral disorders, but they would not address this patient's acute behavioral change, which may indicate an underlying medical condition that should be evaluated and treated. (Choice E) MRI of the brain is often used in the initial evaluation of ID when the etiology is in question or there are abnormal physical examination findings (eg, microcephaly). In this patient with Down syndrome and no evidence of seizure or focal neurologic deficit, MRI of the brain would not be indicated unless more common causes of behavioral abnormalities are not identified. Educational objective: Behavioral disorders are common in patients with intellectual disabilities, but an acute change from baseline may indicate an underlying medical condition that requires evaluation and treatment. Constipation is one of the most common secondary causes of behavioral change, and an abdominal x-ray to assess stool volume can help with diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with Down syndrome is brought to the office due to new-onset behavioral changes. At baseline, the patient has severe intellectual disability and difficulty communicating. He lives at home with his parents and a caregiver and attends a special school. His mother reports that the patient is usually quiet and social but has become aggressive recently. The patient occasionally bangs his head on a pillow and is verbally abusive to his caregiver. Review of systems is positive for constipation but negative for fever, vomiting, and appetite changes. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows normal dentition, tonsils and adenoids, and ear canals. Abdomen is distended but soft and nontender. Digital rectal examination shows normal tone and guaiac-negative stool in the rectal vault. The remainder of the examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormalities. Blood cell counts, serum chemistry studies, and urinalysis are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Secondary causes of behavioral change in patients with intellectual disability Gastrointestinal disorders Constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, bowel obstruction Occult infection Cellulitis, cystitis, otitis media, pneumonia Unrecognized pain Dental caries, menstrual pain, unreported trauma/fracture Sensory impairment Cerumen impaction, visual problems Psychiatric disorders Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder Sleep disorders Obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia This patient with intellectual disabilities from Down syndrome (DS) has new-onset behavioral disturbances (eg, irritability, impulsivity), which raise concern for an acute underlying condition. Careful investigation is negative for most secondary causes of behavioral change (eg, constipation, cystitis, dental caries). However, this patient's symptoms of daytime somnolence and worsening cognition (eg, loss of previously learned skills) point to possible obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Patients with DS are at high risk for OSA due to a combination of craniofacial abnormalities (eg, midfacial hypoplasia, relative macroglossia) and neuromuscular factors (eg, hypotonia) that can lead to upper airway obstruction, with the prevalence of OSA nearing 100% in adult patients with DS. Therefore, OSA requires careful surveillance in all patients with DS beginning in childhood, even in the absence of obesity or overt sleep-related symptoms (eg, snoring). This makes the STOP-bang survey unhelpful, and polysomnography is recommended for all children with DS (screening by age 4) as well for any DS patient with new, unexplained behavioral changes, as in this patient. Cognitive regression, which sometimes reflects nonspecific environmental stressors, can also be a sequela of OSA in patients with DS. (Choice A) Echocardiography is recommended for all newborns with DS to evaluate for congenital heart disease. However, patients with early repair of a ventricular septal defect rarely have long-term sequelae, and repeat echocardiogram is typically indicated only for signs of suspected heart failure (eg, crackles, edema), structural heart disease (eg, new/changed murmur, cyanosis), or endocarditis, none of which are seen in this patient. (Choice C) Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, fluoxetine) are useful for treating depression and anxiety, which are both very common in patients with DS. Although depression and anxiety in DS can present with irritable/impulsive behavior, cognitive decline, and increased somnolence, pharmacotherapy would be premature without first ruling out secondary medical causes. (Choice D) Modafinil is a stimulant used to promote wakefulness in patients with narcolepsy or rarely for residual sleepiness despite OSA treatment. Polysomnography would be indicated to establish a specific diagnosis before the initiation of stimulant medications. (Choice E) Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for a wide range of psychiatric and behavioral disorders (eg, depression, phobia). It requires problem-solving and high motivation and may be of somewhat limited use in certain patients with intellectual disability, depending on the degree of disability. In addition, it would not be indicated without first ruling out other underlying causes of behavioral change. Educational objective: Obstructive sleep apnea is common in patients with Down syndrome (DS) due to changes in airway structure and muscle tone. Polysomnography is indicated for all children with DS (screening) and for any DS patient with new, unexplained behavioral disturbances.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with Down syndrome is brought to the office due to behavioral changes over the past several months. She has moderate intellectual disability with limited verbal abilities and lives at a group home. The caregiver states that the patient has become irritable and impulsive. She does not participate in group activities like usual and pays no attention when she is there. The patient sleeps most days and has lost some of her previously learned vocational skills. She has had no constipation or urinary symptoms. Medical history is significant for repaired ventricular septal defect and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg and pulse is 74/min. BMI is 28 kg/m2. Physical examination shows craniofacial changes and generalized hypotonia consistent with Down syndrome. The remainder of the examination including dentition and ear canals shows no abnormalities. Blood cell counts, serum chemistry studies, TSH level, and urinalysis are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors: infection risk Screening Screen for & treat the following prior to initiation: Tuberculosis Hepatitis B & C viruses HIV Local endemic mycoses (eg, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus) High-prevalence infections Mycobacterial (tuberculous & nontuberculous) Bacterial pneumonia Disseminated Listeria monocytogenes Zoster Endemic fungi This patient takes a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Because TNF contributes to macrophage activation, phagolysosome function, neutrophil/macrophage recruitment, and the formation and maintenance of granulomas, patients on anti-TNF therapy are at much higher risk for infections, particularly bacterial pneumonia, herpes zoster, tuberculosis, and local endemic mycoses. This patient lives in an endemic area for Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus that grows in soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings. The organism is typically acquired via inhalation and may cause illness shortly after transmission or months or years later. Illness is uncommon (<5%) in those with intact immunity because H capsulatum is rapidly destroyed by phagolysosomes in macrophages. In contrast, those with impaired immunity are at much greater risk for pulmonary or disseminated disease. The most common clinical finding is bilateral, reticulonodular pulmonary infiltrates with hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Continued spread through the reticuloendothelial system (within macrophages) can lead to prolonged inflammatory symptoms (eg, fatigue, weight loss, fever, elevated ESR/CRP), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. Adrenal infiltration occurs in a minority of cases and can be an important diagnostic clue. Rapid diagnosis is most often made with serum or urine Histoplasma antigen testing. (Choice A) Autoimmune adrenalitis occurs when antibodies against steroidogenic enzymes destroy the adrenal cortex. Although this can cause adrenal insufficiency and adrenalitis, it would not explain the patient's pulmonary findings, hepatosplenomegaly, or pancytopenia. (Choice B) Chronic myeloid leukemia can cause hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and nonspecific systemic symptoms; those in blast crisis can also have diffuse lymphadenopathy. However, patients generally have significant leukocytosis with levels up to 100,000/mm3; thrombocytosis may also occur. The presence of pancytopenia makes this unlikely. (Choice D) Mixed connective tissue disease is due to high titer antibodies against anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein. Although patients frequently have pulmonary disease, anemia, nonspecific symptoms, and elevated inflammatory markers, the absence of joint findings and the presence of hepatosplenomegaly make this less likely. (Choice E) Patients with RA are at elevated risk for secondary amyloidosis, which can cause pulmonary infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. However, almost all cases occur in the setting of poorly controlled RA; this patient with no joint swelling/tenderness and normal range of motion is unlikely to develop secondary amyloidosis. Educational objective: Patients on anti-tumor necrosis factor therapy for rheumatoid arthritis who live in endemic areas for histoplasmosis are at high risk for disseminated infection. They usually present with nonspecific symptoms, pulmonary infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Infection risk is also particularly increased for bacterial pneumonia, zoster, and tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the office due to 2 months of worsening fatigue, a 10-kg (22-lb) unintentional weight loss, and recurrent low-grade fevers. She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 5 years ago and has been on anti–tumor necrosis factor (TNF) therapy for a year. The patient was ruled out for tuberculosis prior to starting the TNF inhibitor, and she has not traveled recently from her home state of Indiana. Temperature is 37.9 C (100.2 F), blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. On physical examination, the patient is thin and ill appearing. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender with hepatosplenomegaly. There is generalized muscle weakness, normal range of motion, and no active joint swelling or tenderness. Laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit 22% Platelets 80,000/mm3 Leukocytes 2,600/mm3 Cortisol, serum 5 µg/dL (normal: 8-20) C-reactive protein (CRP) 32 mg/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/h High-resolution CT scan of the chest and abdomen reveals a diffuse reticulonodular infiltrate of both lung fields with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral adrenal gland enlargement. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?

questions.explanation: This patient with allergic rhinitis has respiratory symptoms (ie, chest tightness, night-predominant cough) and reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry (ie, significant bronchodilator response after albuterol: ≥12% increase in FEV1). This combination of symptoms and spirometry confirms the diagnosis of asthma. Improvement with caffeine intake is commonly reported in asthma, likely due to its bronchodilator effect as a methylxanthine (analogous to theophylline). Because the patient's symptoms occur less than daily and never awaken him and because FEV1 is fully restored after albuterol administration, he is classified as having intermittent asthma. Asthma treatment guidelines target the underlying pathophysiology of leukocyte-induced bronchoconstriction. Therefore, a combination of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) (target leukocytes) and beta agonists (target bronchoconstriction) is recommended. ICS should be used at every step of asthma treatment. For intermittent asthma, low-dose ICS are taken as needed (ie, whenever a beta agonist reliever is used). For persistent asthma, ICS are scheduled (usually twice daily) and a higher dose is selected (Choice C). In addition to ICS, a fast-onset (<5 min), long-acting beta agonist (LABA) (eg, formoterol) is recommended as an acute reliever. Short-acting beta agonists (SABA) (eg, albuterol) may also be used for intermittent symptoms. This strategy, which aims to extinguish airway inflammation as early as possible, has been shown to reduce the risk of acute asthma exacerbations, progression to persistent asthma, and long-term lung function decline. (Choice A) LABA monotherapy is linked to increased respiratory-related mortality. The mechanism is likely due to increased airway inflammation that occurs with chronic beta-2 receptor stimulation of the bronchial epithelium and leukocytes. The addition of ICS neutralizes the harm. (Choice D) Long-acting antimuscarinic agents (LAMA) (eg, tiotropium) are indicated for patients with uncontrolled asthma despite scheduled high-dose ICS and LABA. LAMAs are also recommended for most patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Although this patient has a 5-pack-year history, the presence of full bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry supports a diagnosis of asthma. (Choice E) Leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) (eg, montelukast) are used as adjunctive controller therapies, taken in addition to ICS-formoterol. They are especially helpful for patients with aspirin- and NSAID-exacerbated asthma due to the higher abundance of leukotrienes in these conditions. However, LTRAs are not used as acute relievers. Educational objective: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are recommended at every step of asthma treatment. Intermittent asthma is treated with ICS and beta agonists as needed. Formoterol is a fast-onset, long-acting beta agonist that can be used as an acute reliever.

questions.explanation: Urinary tract obstruction Common etiologies Bladder: prostate disease, stones, tumors, neurogenic Ureters: tumors/adenopathy, stones, retroperitoneal fibrosis Urethra: posterior valves (in children) Clinical presentation Site of obstruction Bladder: bilateral hydronephrosis; high postvoid residual Ureter: unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis; low/no postvoid residual if bilateral Complications Renal function: AKI progressing to CKD (atrophy) if untreated Other: infection & urosepsis (due to stasis) Management Decompression: PCNT/stenting (ureteral); urethral Foley catheterization (bladder) Postobstructive polyuria: careful fluid & electrolyte management Address underlying cause AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; PCNT = percutaneous nephrostomy tube. This patient has acute kidney injury (AKI). Bladder catheterization recovers a small amount of urine (eg, 40 mL/24 hr), which is consistent with oliguria, and imaging reveals bilateral hydronephrosis. This presentation suggests ureteral obstruction, likely from extrinsic compression by an abdominopelvic mass (most common: lymphoma, cervical cancer). This patient's B symptoms (anorexia, weight loss, fevers), hepatosplenomegaly, and bulky lymphadenopathy are concerning for a malignancy causing ureteral obstruction. Urine cannot drain distally to the obstruction, leading to renal pelvis dilation and increased upstream pressure in the collecting system, which opposes glomerular filtration. This causes postrenal AKI (ie, obstructive uropathy) and oliguria (if bilateral blockage). Management involves urinary system decompression upstream of the obstruction. This patient with likely bilateral ureteral blockages (given oliguria) requires bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement. Small tubes are inserted into the dilated renal pelvis, allowing external urinary drainage. Alternately, internal ureteral stents can bypass the obstructed segment, allowing urine passage. If untreated, obstruction leads to renal atrophy (thin, clubbed renal cortices), scarring, and permanent loss of kidney function. (Choice A) Spontaneous necrosis of aggressive malignancies (eg, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) can release potassium, phosphate, and purines (uric acid); precipitation within the kidney causes AKI. However, tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) typically causes significant electrolyte abnormalities (eg, potassium: ≥6 mEq/L, calcium: ≤7 mg/dL, uric acid: ≥8 mg/dL) and does not cause postrenal AKI with hydronephrosis. Although urinary alkalization improves uric acid solubility, it is not a first-line therapy for TLS and is generally unnecessary. (Choice B) AKI sometimes requires dialysis, but this patient has no indications, including uremic encephalopathy (eg, confusion) or pericarditis (eg, friction rub), life-threatening hyperkalemia (eg, peaked T waves), volume overload (eg, crackles), or severe acidosis (eg, markedly decreased bicarbonate). (Choice C) Bladder obstruction (eg, prostate disease) can cause bilateral hydronephrosis and hydroureter. However, postvoid urinary volumes, assessed by 1-time straight catherization or ultrasonography, would be elevated. A urethrally inserted indwelling catheter decompresses the bladder while the underlying cause of obstruction is treated. (Choice D) A nuclear renal excretion study quantifies residual kidney function. It can evaluate differential kidney function in unilateral/asymmetric hydronephrosis or determine whether permanent loss of kidney function has occurred in chronic obstruction. This patient's lack of cortical atrophy and normal-sized kidneys makes chronic obstruction unlikely. Educational objective: Bilateral hydronephrosis is a common complication of abdominopelvic malignancy. Acute hydronephrosis due to ureteral obstruction is treated with percutaneous nephrostomy placement to decompress the collecting system.

questions.explanation: Actinic keratosis Clinical features Erythematous, scaly papules; rough plaques Sun-exposed areas Diagnosis Clinical appearance Biopsy if features of possible SCC (eg, size ≥1 cm, rapid growth, ulceration, tenderness) Prognosis Chronic/persistent Progression to SCC Spontaneous resolution Treatment Isolated lesions: cryotherapy Diffuse lesions: topical fluorouracil, imiquimod, tirbanibulin SCC = squamous cell carcinoma. This patient's skin changes are concerning for actinic keratosis (AK) and advanced, chronic photodamage. AK presents as erythematous, scaly papules or plaques. Most AKs are asymptomatic but some may produce a stinging sensation. AK is caused by ultraviolet radiation and is most common in sun-exposed areas (eg, face, scalp, dorsal hands). It often occurs with a history of chronically photodamaged skin (eg, wrinkling, xerosis). In particular, dyspigmentation, rough texture, atrophy, and telangiectasia indicate cellular carcinogenic changes; this diffuse surface involvement is termed field cancerization. AK in the setting of field cancerization has a higher likelihood of transforming to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Such lesions should be treated promptly with topical therapy (eg, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod) that can cover the entire area. In contrast, isolated AKs without field cancerization can be effectively treated with spot cryotherapy. (Choice A) Field radiation therapy is sometimes used for patients with SCC; however, even with SCC, surgical excision is typically first-line. Distinguishing AK from SCC can sometimes be difficult; however, SCC lesions may be tender, rapidly growing, or ulcerated and sometimes manifest as nodules with ulceration. (Choice C) Topical clotrimazole is used to treat tinea faciei, which presents as an erythematous, scaly, annular patch or plaque, features absent in this patient. (Choice D) Topical hydrocortisone is used to treat a variety of inflammatory skin lesions (eg, contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis); most of these disorders are associated with significant pruritus and other inflammatory features (eg, erythema, papule/vesicle formation). This patient's scaly, nonpruritic lesions are more characteristic of AK, which does not respond to topical corticosteroids. (Choice E) Topical metronidazole is used to treat rosacea, which is most common on the cheeks and central face and presents as chronic erythema with papules, pustules, flushing, or telangiectasia. A rough texture is not characteristic. Educational objective: Actinic keratosis occurring with field cancerization, as well as advanced photodamage indicative of carcinogenesis, has a higher risk of transforming to squamous cell carcinoma. Because treatment of the entire area is needed, topical therapy (eg, 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod) is recommended.

questions.explanation: The fishbone diagram (cause-and-effect diagram) is a tool used in root-causes analysis to organize information collected during team discussions. It visually categorizes the potential factors contributing to a quality-of-care problem. The diagram is analogous to a fish skeleton, displaying the following: The problem of concern (eg, prolonged wait times) is placed at the far right of the diagram, representing the "head" of the fish (Choice A). Categories of factors (eg, staffing, organizational, patient) that may be contributing to the problem are placed in diagonal spokes coming off the central spine, representing the "ribs" (Choices B and D). Individual specific causes are listed under each main category, representing the "scales." In this case, the medical assistant's observation that patients are frequently double-booked describes a specific cause, and this information is best placed under a pertinent category heading (eg, scheduling factors). (Choice E) This position (the tail) is not typically used in the diagram. Educational objective: The fishbone diagram (cause-and-effect diagram) is a tool used in root-causes analysis to visually organize specific causes of a quality-of-care problem. Components include the problem being analyzed, categories of contributing factors, and specific causes pertaining to each category.

questions.explanation: Salmonella Nontyphoidal Typhoidal Epidemiology Major cause of gastroenteritis worldwide (including United States) Associated with undercooked poultry/eggs Most common in resource-limited regions with poor sanitation (eg, unvaccinated travelers) Associated with contaminated food or water Clinical Vomiting Diarrhea ± blood Fever Invasive disease rare Fever & bacteremia Abdominal pain & rose spots Late findings: HSM, intestinal perforation Diagnosis Stool culture Blood culture Outcome & treatment Usually self-limited Antibiotics rarely needed Potentially fatal Antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone) Drug resistance common HSM = hepatosplenomegaly. This patient has Salmonella gastroenteritis, a common cause of acute diarrhea due to nontyphoidal Salmonella. Transmission is via consumption of undercooked poultry/eggs, and infection causes fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea that is typically watery but can be mucoid or bloody. Unlike typhoidal Salmonella, invasive disease (eg, bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis) due to nontyphoidal Salmonella is rare. Salmonella gastroenteritis is usually a self-limited infection, and management focuses on fluid and electrolyte repletion. Although most patients have asymptomatic carriage for weeks to months after symptom resolution, antimicrobial therapy is not warranted in most cases because treatment is paradoxically associated with an extended time of asymptomatic carriage. This is likely due to disruption of nonpathogenic gut microbiota, which normally limits colonization of pathogenic organisms. In addition to an increased likelihood of Salmonella transmission due to extended carriage, antibiotic therapy increases the risk of antibiotic resistance. Patients at higher risk of invasive disease do warrant antibiotic therapy and include the following: Extremes of age (eg, age <1) Immunocompromised state Sickle cell disease Cardiovascular or significant joint disease Severe disease requiring hospitalization (eg, >10 diarrheal episodes a day, severe dehydration) Bloody diarrhea alone due to nontyphoidal Salmonella does not increase the risk for invasive disease and does not warrant antimicrobial therapy in the absence of established risk factors. Antibiotics are not indicated in this otherwise healthy child with mild dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes, normal capillary refill) and mild abdominal pain. (Choices A and B) In contrast to nontyphoidal Salmonella infection, disease caused by typhoidal Salmonella strains is more commonly seen in resource-limited regions and causes prolonged fever (due to bacteremia), with patients classically developing abdominal pain and truncal macules ("rose spots"). Due to bacteremia and potentially severe complications (eg, intestinal perforation, encephalopathy), patients with typhoidal Salmonella warrant antibiotic therapy, which decreases the duration and severity of infection and risk of organ dysfunction and sepsis. (Choice C) Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a potential complication of gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea due to Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli (particularly strain O157:H7) or Shigella (not Salmonella) infections. HUS risk is increased after antibiotic use for E coli but not Shigella. Educational objective: Antimicrobial therapy is not typically warranted for healthy immunocompetent patients with mild nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis because infection is usually self-limited and antibiotics paradoxically increase the risk of prolonged asymptomatic bacterial carriage.

This patient has Salmonella gastroenteritis, a common cause of acute diarrhea due to nontyphoidal Salmonella.  Transmission is via consumption of undercooked poultry/eggs, and infection causes fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea that is typically watery but can be mucoid or bloody.  Unlike typhoidal Salmonella, invasive disease (eg, bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis) due to nontyphoidal Salmonella is rare.

Salmonella gastroenteritis is usually a self-limited infection, and management focuses on fluid and electrolyte repletion.  Although most patients have asymptomatic carriage for weeks to months after symptom resolution, antimicrobial therapy is not warranted in most cases because treatment is paradoxically associated with an extended time of asymptomatic carriage.  This is likely due to disruption of nonpathogenic gut microbiota, which normally limits colonization of pathogenic organisms.  In addition to an increased likelihood of Salmonella transmission due to extended carriage, antibiotic therapy increases the risk of antibiotic resistance.

Patients at higher risk of invasive disease do warrant antibiotic therapy and include the following:

  • Extremes of age (eg, age <1)
  • Immunocompromised state
  • Sickle cell disease
  • Cardiovascular or significant joint disease
  • Severe disease requiring hospitalization (eg, >10 diarrheal episodes a day, severe dehydration)

Bloody diarrhea alone due to nontyphoidal Salmonella does not increase the risk for invasive disease and does not warrant antimicrobial therapy in the absence of established risk factors.  Antibiotics are not indicated in this otherwise healthy child with mild dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes, normal capillary refill) and mild abdominal pain.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the hospital due to fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea for 3 days. questions.explanation: Cryptosporidiosis Epidemiology Fecal-oral transmission (eg, contaminated water, animal contact) Risk factors: immunosuppression (eg, AIDS, transplant recipient) Clinical manifestations Immunocompetent: self-resolving, watery (noninflammatory) diarrhea <2 weeks Immunosuppressed: Prolonged, severe diarrhea with weight loss/malabsorption Biliary disease (eg, cholecystitis, cholangitis) Diagnosis Stool PCR testing Stool microscopy: acid-fast staining oocysts or immunofluorescent assay Intestinal biopsy: organisms on mucosal brush border Treatment Immunocompetent: supportive care only Immunocompromised*: nitazoxanide *Patients with HIV should be prescribed antiretroviral therapy first & treated with antimicrobial therapy only if symptoms persist. This immunosuppressed patient has developed watery diarrhea that is noninflammatory (ie, no fecal leukocytes and/or blood). In contrast to the inflammatory diarrhea seen with certain pathogens (eg, cytomegalovirus), Cryptosporidium parvum typically causes prolonged, noninflammatory diarrhea in immunosuppressed patients, making it the most likely cause of the given choices. This protozoan is spread fecal-orally and most commonly via ingestion of contaminated water (eg, drinking supply, pools); individuals in close contact with animals (eg, veterinarians) are also at risk. Immunocompetent individuals infected with Cryptosporidium usually have self-limited (10-14 days) watery diarrhea, whereas the disease course in immunocompromised patients (eg, AIDS, organ transplant recipients) is often prolonged. Watery stools may be mild, but some patients develop severe diarrhea with fluid loss >20 L per day. Associated nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain are typical. Diagnosis can be made by stool microscopy that reveals acid-fast staining oocytes; stool PCR testing also has high sensitivity and specificity. Most immunosuppressed patients infected with Cryptosporidium require antimicrobial therapy (eg, nitazoxanide) due to an increased risk of protracted illness and complications (eg, ascending biliary infection). In patients with AIDS, diarrhea may improve with initiation of HIV antiretroviral therapy alone due to immune reconstitution. (Choice A) Clostridioides difficile infection is increased in those who are immunosuppressed or who have had recent antibiotic use or hospitalization. Although watery diarrhea is typical, most patients also have fever, leukocytosis, and positive fecal leukocytes and/or occult blood. (Choice C) Tissue-invasive cytomegalovirus disease causing gastrointestinal manifestations is seen with kidney transplant, but it would typically cause inflammatory diarrhea (eg, bloody stools, fecal leukocytes, occult blood). (Choice D) Listeria gastroenteritis can present with diarrhea, but symptoms are typically self-limited to a few days and associated with fever and muscle aches, features not seen in this patient. In addition, although immunosuppressed patients are at risk for invasive disease from L monocytogenes (eg, sepsis, meningitis), this patient's lack of fever and normal white blood cell count make this an unlikely cause. (Choice E) Nontyphoidal Salmonella (eg, S Enteritidis) causes diarrhea that typically resolves within a few days; prolonged symptoms are not typical. Moreover, Salmonella causes inflammatory diarrhea so fecal leukocytes and/or blood would be seen. Educational objective: Cryptosporidium can cause prolonged, watery (noninflammatory) diarrhea in immunosuppressed patients (eg, AIDS, organ transplant recipients).

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a 3-week history of watery diarrhea. She also has had nausea, vomiting, and crampy upper abdominal pain. questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes mellitus Pathophysiology Human placental lactogen secretion Screening 24-28 weeks gestation 1-hr 50-g GCT 3-hr 100-g GTT Management 1st line: diet 2nd line: insulin, glyburide, metformin Target blood glucose goals Fasting: ≤95 mg/dL 1-hr postprandial: ≤140 mg/dL 2-hr postprandial: ≤120 mg/dL Postpartum management Fasting glucose at 24-72 hr 2-hr 75-g GTT at 6- to 12-week visit GCT = glucose challenge test; GTT = glucose tolerance test. During the second and third trimesters, placental hormones (eg, human placental lactogen) cause increased maternal insulin resistance to raise maternal glucose levels to promote fetal growth. Patients with risk factors (eg, older maternal age, excessive gestational weight gain) may develop gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), which is associated with obstetric (eg, preeclampsia) and neonatal (eg, macrosomia, hypoglycemia) complications. Treatment decreases the risk; first-line treatment to achieve euglycemia is with dietary modifications and exercise. Patients are also instructed to self-monitor blood glucose levels throughout the day. Self-monitoring involves taking a fasting and either a 1- or a 2-hour postprandial level following each meal. Fasting levels are highly specific but not as sensitive for identifying persistent hyperglycemia that may necessitate additional pharmacotherapy; therefore, additional diabetic monitoring is indicated (Choice D). The addition of 1- or 2-hour postprandial levels improves the sensitivity because these values reflect exactly how well and how quickly a patient can metabolize glucose following a meal. Target blood glucose levels, which differ from those of nonpregnant patients with diabetes mellitus, are as follows: Fasting ≤95 mg/dL 1-hour postprandial ≤140 mg/dL or 2-hour postprandial ≤120 mg/dL Patients who remain hyperglycemic (>50% of blood glucose readings above target levels) despite diet and exercise require pharmacotherapy (eg, insulin). (Choice B) A 24-hour urine collection for total protein can be used to diagnose preeclampsia in patients with new-onset hypertension at ≥20 weeks gestation. This patient's vital signs are normal, and trace protein on urinalysis is normal in pregnancy. Patients at high-risk for preeclampsia (eg, type 1 diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, multiple gestation) also require 24-hour urine collection for total protein at the initial prenatal visit to establish a proteinuria assessment; GDM by itself is not an indication for a 24-hour urine collection. (Choice C) Hemoglobin A1c levels decrease as pregnancy progresses due to physiologic increases in red blood cell mass and cell turnover. Therefore, A1c levels are less reliable than daily self-monitoring of fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels. Serial hemoglobin A1c levels are an option for monitoring in patients who cannot or will not self-monitor blood glucose levels. Educational objective: First-line treatment of gestational diabetes mellitus is dietary modification. Patients are also instructed to self-monitor their blood glucose levels by obtaining daily fasting and either a 1- or a 2-hour postprandial level following each meal. These readings are used to determine the need for pharmacotherapy.

questions.explanation: This elderly woman has acute back pain and spinal tenderness, findings consistent with osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (VCF). VCF commonly occurs following minimal trauma (eg, lifting, twisting, ground-level fall). The pain is usually sharp or achy; it may be worse with the Valsalva maneuver, position changes, or spinal extension. The pain and spinal tenderness of VCF are classically localized to the midline, but referred or radicular pain in the flank or upper abdomen may also occur. Although diagnostic testing is not needed for uncomplicated lumbar strain (eg, pain and tenderness in lumbar paraspinal muscles), patients with suspected VCF require imaging for confirmation (Choice C). X-ray can be obtained easily and is a good initial study; MRI is recommended if the patient has significant neurologic deficits. If VCF is confirmed, patients generally also warrant DXA to assess the severity of bone loss and guide chronic management (eg, antiresorptive therapy). (Choices A and B) Abdominal ultrasound and CT scan can be used to evaluate abdominal aortic aneurysm, which can present with acute back pain. These imaging tests can also identify ureteral obstruction in patients with back or flank pain due to renal colic. However, these conditions would not cause spinal tenderness, which is more consistent with VCF. (Choice E) Technetium 99m skeletal scintigraphy (ie, bone scan) is used to identify skeletal metastasis, especially from cancers (eg, prostate, small cell lung) that form osteoblastic/sclerotic bone metastases. Although spinal metastasis can cause midline spinal pain and tenderness, this patient has no history of malignancy or systemic symptoms (eg, weight loss) to raise suspicion. Also, if spinal metastasis is suspected, MRI has a higher sensitivity. Educational objective: Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (VCF) presents with acute back pain and spinal tenderness following minimal trauma. The diagnosis is confirmed with x-ray. If VCF is diagnosed, patients also warrant DXA to assess the severity of bone loss.

questions.explanation: Peritoneal dialysis–related peritonitis Pathophysiology Touch contamination of catheter lumen Extension of catheter site skin infection Clinical presentation Abdominal pain ± fever & nausea Diffuse abdominal tenderness ± rebound Cloudy peritoneal fluid Microbiology Gram-positive bacteria (~65%) Gram-negative bacteria (~30%) Fungal organism (~5%) Diagnosis Clinical presentation (ie, abdominal pain, cloudy fluid) Relative neutrophilia on fluid analysis Positive fluid Gram stain or culture Treatment Intraperitoneal antibiotics (eg, vancomycin + gentamicin)* *Empiric therapy should cover both gram-positive & gram-negative organisms. This patient with a history of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) has abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and peripheral leukocytosis concerning for acute infection. Although there are many causes of intraabdominal infections in adults, this patient's peritoneal dialysis (PD) and diffuse abdominal pain and tenderness raise suspicion for PD-related peritonitis. The diagnosis is made via peritoneal fluid analysis. Cell count showing >50% neutrophils (usually with >100/mm3 total leukocytes) is highly suggestive of PD-related peritonitis, and positive Gram stain or culture is confirmatory. Although Gram stain has low sensitivity due to relatively low bacterial concentration in infected peritoneal fluid, it is sometimes helpful in guiding early antibiotic management. Peritoneal fluid culture is highly sensitive. Gram-positive bacteria account for approximately 65% of infections (Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus are most common), gram-negative bacteria for approximately 30%, and fungal organisms for approximately 5%. Given the significant morbidity and mortality associated with PD-related peritonitis, intraperitoneal antibiotics should be initiated as soon as the infection is suspected based on consistent clinical presentation or fluid cell count. Empiric therapy should cover both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria (eg, vancomycin + gentamicin) until antibiotics can be tailored based on culture results. (Choice A) CT scan of the abdomen is indicated in patients with suspected secondary peritonitis due to enteric pathology (eg, appendicitis, ruptured diverticula), but this is less likely with only mild peripheral leukocytosis. PD should raise suspicion for PD-related peritonitis. (Choice C) MR angiography can be used to evaluate for mesenteric ischemia, which would not explain this patient's diffuse abdominal tenderness on physical examination (eg, pain out of proportion to the examination). In addition, the gadolinium contrast used with MR angiography is contraindicated in patients with ESRD due to the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. (Choice D) Blood cultures are appropriate in patients with signs of sepsis (eg, fever, tachycardia), but they are rarely positive in patients with PD-related peritonitis (ie, bacteremia is often not present). Peritoneal fluid culture has far greater sensitivity. (Choice E) Urinary tract infections can occur in patients with ESRD whose kidneys still make urine. They can cause suprapubic abdominal tenderness, but this would not explain this patient's diffuse abdominal tenderness, so a urine culture would not be helpful. Educational objective: Peritoneal dialysis–related peritonitis presents with diffuse abdominal pain/tenderness and, sometimes, fever and nausea. The diagnosis is confirmed with peritoneal fluid analysis and Gram stain with culture; patients should be treated empirically with intraperitoneal antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to abdominal pain and nausea for a day. choiceHtml: Administer an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent then proceed with surgery
Complete an extended hemodialysis session then proceed with surgery
Delay surgery until normalization of serum potassium with medical management

questions.explanation: This patient with groin pain, vomiting, a tender inguinal mass, and clinical signs of sepsis (eg, fever, leukocytosis, hypotension) most likely has a strangulated inguinal hernia, a condition that typically requires emergency surgery. However, she also has hyperkalemia (ie, >5.5 mEq/L), a concerning finding in the perioperative setting because serum potassium can become further elevated during surgery (eg, released from muscle tissue) and increase the risk for intraoperative cardiovascular events (eg, arrhythmias). When surgery is elective, preoperative hyperkalemia is typically treated before surgery. However, when emergency surgery is required (eg, this patient's strangulated hernia), the decision about whether to delay surgery for the treatment of hyperkalemia is largely dependent on whether ECG changes (eg, peaked T waves, widened QRS complex) are present: Absent ECG changes: Proceed with surgery immediately. The anesthesia team can perform intraoperative monitoring of potassium and provide medical management (eg, insulin, calcium), if needed; surgery should not be delayed for normalization of serum potassium (Choice C). Present ECG changes: Perform a short hemodialysis session (eg, 1 hr), if feasible (eg, dialysis access available). If surgery is needed sooner than this (eg, hemorrhaging patient), it should occur regardless of potassium level with intraoperative monitoring and management of hyperkalemia. This patient has hyperkalemia but no ECG abnormalities, likely due to increased tolerance for hyperkalemia in end-stage kidney disease. She should proceed to surgery immediately to treat her incarcerated hernia. (Choice A) Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are not appropriate in the acute setting because they increase hemoglobin slowly over time (ie, weeks). If significant anemia (eg, 7-8 g/dL) is present, red blood cell transfusion can rapidly increase hemoglobin levels. (Choice B) A short and expedited preoperative hemodialysis session (eg, 1 hr) can be considered in hemodynamically stable patients with hyperkalemia who have existing dialysis access. However, an extended hemodialysis session (eg, >4 hr) would delay care and likely result in a worse clinical outcome than immediate surgery. (Choice E) Hospice care would not be an appropriate next step in this patient because prompt antibiotics and abdominal surgery may maintain her good functional status (eg, lives alone, manages activities of daily living). Educational objective: The decision of whether to treat preoperative hyperkalemia in patients needing emergency surgery is largely dependent on the presence or absence of ECG changes. Patients without ECG changes should have immediate surgery with intraoperative monitoring of potassium and medical management.

questions.explanation: Absolute & functional iron deficiency Cause Ferritin* Iron responsiveness Absolute Depleted iron stores Low (<100 ng/mL) High Functional from ESA use Insufficient iron to accommodate accelerated erythropoiesis Normal or high High Functional from anemia of chronic disease Iron sequestered in macrophages and cannot be mobilized Normal or high Low *Transferrin saturation (iron/total iron-binding capacity) <20% for all types. ESA = erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. This patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) has anemia with normal vitamin B12 and folate levels but abnormal iron studies. CKD predisposes to anemia due to several factors, primarily renal erythropoietin hypoproduction and possible iron deficiency. Renal erythropoetin hypoproduction is often managed with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) (eg, darbepoetin). Iron deficiency in CKD is diagnosed by a low (eg, ≤20%) transferrin saturation (TSAT; aka "iron saturation"). This represents the ratio of serum iron to serum transferrin (aka "total iron-binding capacity"), an iron transport protein increased in iron deficiency. Iron deficiency can be functional (ie, normal/high iron stores that cannot be used effectively for erythropoiesis) or absolute (ie, severely decreased iron stores in bone marrow). Functional iron deficiency in CKD can be due to: Anemia of chronic disease: Systemic inflammation upregulates hepcidin, which prevents iron release from macrophages into the plasma, making it unavailable for erythropoiesis. ESA use: Iron stores are adequate for low-grade erythropoiesis but insufficient to meet the sudden increased erythropoietic demand when an ESA is administered. Functional iron deficiency is typically reflected in normal (to high) ferritin levels. In contrast, absolute iron deficiency in CKD would cause a relatively low ferritin (reflecting iron storage); it can be due to decreased iron absorption (also from systemic inflammation), multiple blood draws, bleeding (eg, platelet dysfunction), or dialysis itself (eg, blood in the tubing) in hemodialysis patients. (Cutoffs for abnormal transferrin saturation and ferritin levels differ in CKD.) This patient with CKD and anemia has low transferrin saturation and ferritin values, suggesting absolute iron deficiency anemia; he should receive iron replacement therapy. Iron repletion increases hemoglobin concentration and helps optimize the erythropoietic response to an ESA and reduce the amount of ESA needed (important because of ESA adverse effects). In practice, even some patients with CKD and functional iron deficiency may receive iron replacement to help tailor ESA management. (Choices A and B) Serum hepcidin and erythropoietin levels are rarely useful in patients with anemia of CKD; the levels are likely high (due to inflammation) and low (due to decreased production), respectively. (Choice C) A bone marrow biopsy showing reduced or absent iron stores is the gold standard for diagnosing absolute iron deficiency. However, bone marrow biopsy is rarely needed for the diagnosis of any type of iron deficiency because iron stores can be accurately estimated with iron studies. (Choice E) Slow blood loss from the lower gastrointestinal tract (eg, due to polyps or colorectal carcinoma) is a common cause of absolute iron deficiency, but it is unlikely in this patient with a negative stool occult blood test and colonoscopy 5 years ago showing only mild diverticulosis. Educational objective: Chronic kidney disease can cause iron deficiency (typically diagnosed by low transferrin saturation) that can be either absolute (ie, reduced total iron stores) or functional. Functional iron deficiency is characterized by adequate iron stores (ie, normal to high ferritin) that cannot be effectively used for erythropoiesis; the main causes are anemia of chronic disease and erythropoiesis-stimulating agent use. Treatment of iron deficiency is with iron replacement.

questions.explanation: This patient has run out of his opioid prescription prematurely; furthermore, he threatens to leave the practice if he does not obtain a specific dosage of fentanyl. His actions raise concerns for drug-seeking behavior (ie, false report or exaggeration of pain to obtain an opioid medication to satisfy craving). Drug-seeking behavior, which suggests potential opioid use disorder (OUD), is characterized by the following: Asking for a specific opioid and dosage Aggressively demanding opioid therapy Reporting allergies to alternate pain medications Requesting early refills Using/stealing opioid medication from others Refusing diagnostic evaluation When patients exhibit these behaviors, further questions should be asked to determine whether they have OUD, which is characterized by uncontrolled opioid craving and intake despite harmful consequences (eg, legal trouble, job loss, overdose). These questions include whether patients take opioid medications for reasons other than pain control (eg, euphoria), how much opioid do patients take from nonprescribed sources, or if opioid intake has caused occupational or relational consequences. When OUD is diagnosed, patients should undergo medication-assisted treatment (eg, buprenorphine, methadone) and counseling. (Choice B) Taking opioid medication from someone else is a violation of the controlled substance agreement; however, a patient's pain can still be managed with nonopioid therapy. Discharging the patient from care is a loss of opportunity for potentially lifesaving interventions. (Choice C) A true worsening of pain in a patient with chronic pancreatitis is concerning for serious complications (eg, pseudocysts, pancreatic adenocarcinoma); gastroenterology evaluation is recommended. However, the physician may continue to manage the patient's pain with nonopioid therapy even when OUD is suspected. (Choice D) Although this patient's escalating dose of opioids is consistent with tolerance, an expected and normal outcome of chronic opioid therapy, his most recent actions (eg, using a friend's fentanyl, refusing gastroenterology evaluation, threatening the physician) are concerning for drug-seeking behavior. Further questions should be asked about his opioid use patterns before referral to addiction medicine. Educational objective: Drug-seeking behavior, as suggested by the patient aggressively demanding a specific opioid and dosage, requesting early refills, taking someone else's medications, and refusing diagnostic work-up, is concerning for opioid use disorder. If further questioning confirms this concern, the patient should undergo medication-assisted treatment programs (eg, buprenorphine) with counseling.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man comes to the office to discuss his pain medication. Over the past 2 years, he has required an escalating dose of extended-release oxycodone to control abdominal pain from chronic pancreatitis, with the most recent dose increase being 3 months ago. The next scheduled prescription renewal is in 3 weeks, but the patient has run out of the medication because he has been taking it more frequently than prescribed due to worsening pain. He also used a fentanyl patch from a friend and requests a prescription for fentanyl 200 mcg/hr transdermal patches, which is equivalent to a dose escalation from his current dose of oxycodone. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the patient is alert and has mild epigastric tenderness. Previous urine drug tests have all been appropriately positive for oxycodone and negative for other substances. The state prescription drug monitoring database reveals no irregularities. A signed controlled substance agreement is on file. The physician recommends evaluation by the patient's gastroenterologist, but the patient refuses, saying "All I need is the fentanyl patch. If you won't prescribe it, I'll find another doctor." Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the patient?

questions.explanation: Autoimmune conditions* associated with T1DM Condition Common pediatric manifestations Evaluation Autoimmune thyroiditis (up to 30%) Declining growth velocity/short stature Delayed puberty Screen with TSH & anti-TPO & anti-TG at diagnosis Retest if symptomatic Celiac disease (up to 5%) Erratic glucose levels & growth failure (malabsoprtion) Often no gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, diarrhea) Screen with anti-TTG IgA at diagnosis Retest if symptomatic *Less common associations include Addison disease, autoimmune gastritis & vitiligo. T1DM = type 1 diabetes mellitus; TG = thyroglobulin; TPO = thyroid peroxidase; TTG = tissue transglutaminase. This patient with hair loss and fatigue has type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). Patients with T1DM, characterized by autoimmune (T-cell–mediated) pancreatic islet cell destruction, are at increased risk for other autoimmune diseases, which is likely due to joint susceptibility genes and loci shared between various conditions. The most commonly associated conditions are autoimmune thyroiditis and celiac disease. Routine screening in asymptomatic patients begins on diagnosis of T1DM, but a low threshold for repeat testing should be maintained for symptomatic disease: Autoimmune thyroiditis: Up to 30% of patients develop hypothyroidism (less commonly, hyperthyroidism). In this case, the patient's fatigue and hair loss are classic features of hypothyroidism; declining linear velocity and low heart rate are also common. Therefore, these findings warrant evaluation with a TSH level. Celiac disease: Approximately 5% of patients with T1DM develop celiac disease. Presentation may include growth failure (as seen here) or unpredictable glucose levels due to variable degrees of malabsorption, often without gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, diarrhea). Malabsorption may also result in iron deficiency anemia, causing fatigue (and rarely hair loss). Therefore, testing with antitissue transglutaminase antibodies (± serum iron and ferritin) is also warranted. (Choice A) The goal hemoglobin A1c in T1DM is <7%, making stricter glycemic control (which is associated with an increased risk of hypoglycemia) unnecessary in this patient who is at goal. (Choice B) ACTH stimulation test helps diagnose autoimmune adrenalitis (adrenal insufficiency), the risk of which is increased in T1DM. Decreased pubic/axillary hair can occur in older patients, but diffuse hair loss and thinning does not; in addition, weight loss due to poor appetite (not seen here) is characteristic. (Choice C) Systemic lupus erythematosus (eg, positive antinuclear antibodies) is rarely associated with T1DM. Growth failure and hair loss occasionally occur due to chronic, systemic inflammation. However, this patient does not have any common manifestations (eg, joint pain, malar rash, arthritis) of this condition. (Choice E) Microscopic examination of shed hair, which identifies the phase of the hair follicle and structural abnormalities, is sometimes used when the initial evaluation of hair loss is unrevealing. However, results are often nonspecific (eg, prolonged telogen related to telogen effluvium). Definitive laboratory testing is preferred in this patient with manifestations (eg, fatigue, growth failure) of treatable diseases leading to hair loss. Educational objective: Type 1 diabetes mellitus increases the risk of other autoimmune conditions, most commonly thyroiditis and celiac disease. Testing for these conditions (eg, TSH) should be performed for characteristic symptoms (eg, fatigue, poor growth); hair loss is more common with hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 11-year-old girl is brought to the office due to fatigue and excessive hair loss for the past 4 weeks. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 5 years ago and uses insulin glargine plus premeal lispro insulin. The patient has no changes in appetite. Vital signs show a temperature of 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure of 104/70 mm Hg, pulse of 64/min, and respirations of 16/min. Her height has dropped from the 40th percentile to the 15th percentile over the past year. Examination shows dry, thinning hair but is otherwise unremarkable. Hemoglobin A1c level is 6.6%. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.explanation: In children, the most common cause of neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] <1,500/mm3) is an acquired, transient, postinfectious etiology. An alternate diagnosis should be considered in patients with a previously low ANC, a history of recurrent infections, or symptomatic neutropenia (eg, mucositis). Postinfectious neutropenia is the most likely diagnosis in this otherwise healthy patient with confirmed influenza. Postinfectious neutropenia is most commonly due to viruses, such as human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis viruses, enterovirus, influenza virus, and Epstein Barr virus. Pathogenesis often involves transient bone marrow suppression likely related to indirect suppression of progenitor cell proliferation from prolonged exposure to inflammatory cytokines and rarely from direct infection of progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Peripheral neutrophil destruction also plays a role in postinfectious neutropenia and occurs due to antineutrophil antibodies (possibly from molecular mimicry between viral and cellular proteins). Low ANC in postinfectious neutropenia may be noted during or following symptomatic illness. It is typically mild to moderate (500-1,500/mm3), and patients generally do not have complications from the neutropenia itself because the bone marrow still has an adequate reserve of neutrophils to rapidly mobilize to a site of infection if necessary. Management is to repeat the complete blood count in 3-4 weeks because the ANC begins to rise within a week and typically normalizes within a month. (Choice A) Bone marrow evaluation is warranted for suspicion of disorders such as aplastic anemia or leukemia. In contrast to this patient's isolated neutropenia, bone marrow disorders usually present with multiple cytopenias. (Choice B) Genetic testing can identify mutations associated with congenital causes of neutropenia; cyclic neutropenia results in predictable nadirs (every 3 weeks) of ANCs associated with fever and mucositis whereas severe congenital neutropenia causes recurrent infections starting in early infancy due to persistent, severe neutropenia. In contrast, this patient has an identified infectious source and is otherwise healthy. (Choice C) Some automated tests identify neutrophils based on myeloperoxidase positivity, and patients with myeloperoxidase deficiency are sometimes falsely identified as neutropenic. This patient had a manual peripheral smear confirming neutropenia. (Choice E) B12 deficiency is associated with neutropenia, but hypersegmented (≥6 lobes) neutrophils and a macrocytic anemia (as opposed to this patient's normal-appearing erythrocytes on smear) would also be expected. Educational objective: The most common cause of neutropenia is postinfectious and usually due to transient bone marrow suppression and/or peripheral neutrophil destruction. The neutropenia is typically mild-to-moderate neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] 500-1,500/mm3) and resolves within a month. An alternate diagnosis should be considered in patients with recurrent infections, a prior low ANC, or symptomatic neutropenia (eg, mucositis).

questions.stem: A 15-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for evaluation of persistent fevers. Her symptoms began 4 days ago with fever and fussiness. The patient vomited once but has had no diarrhea or cough. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications aside from acetaminophen for the fever. Weight is stable at the 15th percentile. Temperature is 39 C (102.2 F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 20/min. The patient is alert. Bilateral conjunctivae are clear, and tympanic membranes appear normal. The oropharynx is clear without ulcerations. The neck is supple, and there is no lymphadenopathy. Cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable. Abdominal examination shows no palpable liver or spleen, and there are no skin lesions. Laboratory results are as follows: Complete blood count Hemoglobin 12 g/dL Platelets 205,000/mm3 Leukocytes 3,000/mm3 Neutrophils 30% Lymphocytes 70% Urinalysis Leukocyte esterase negative Nitrites negative Influenza A positive Influenza B negative A manual peripheral smear reveals a normal morphologic appearance of erythrocytes and platelets. Granulocytes are decreased, and the few segmented neutrophils visualized contain 4-5 nuclear lobes. Which of the following is the best next step in evaluation of this patient's neutropenia?

questions.explanation: Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy Pathophysiology & causes Repetitive bone & joint trauma due to impaired sensation/ proprioception Diabetes mellitus (most common) Posterior column disease (eg, B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis) Clinical manifestations Acute Inflammatory erythema, warmth & edema of the foot Minimal bone involvement (x-rays often normal) Chronic Bone deformities (eg, subluxation, collapsed arch, stress fracture) Neuropathic ulcers, cellulitis, osteomyelitis Management Acute Foot cast to reduce edema & offload weight bearing Chronic Orthotic footwear, infection management, surgical realignment Foot erythema, warmth, and edema, nonspecific findings suggesting inflammation, can reflect multiple conditions including: infection (eg, cellulitis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) crystal-induced arthropathy (eg, gout) deep vein thrombosis (DVT) trauma (eg, ligamentous sprain, neuropathic arthropathy). Differentiating between these conditions is sometimes difficult, and a process of elimination may be helpful. In this patient, swelling limited to the foot is unlikely to be due to DVT. A normal leukocyte count and lack of fever (as seen here) can sometimes occur with chronic infection and arthropathy; however, acute (eg, 3 days of symptoms in this patient) infection and arthropathy (eg, gout flare) would more typically be associated with leukocytosis, fever, and significant pain and inflammation (eg, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]). In addition, cellulitis (which sometimes develops after minor trauma) is often associated with a bacterial entry portal (eg, skin breakdown, ulcer), not seen here. Therefore, in the absence of suspected infection, crystal-induced arthropathy, DVT, and significant trauma (eg, ligamentous sprain), this patient's inflammatory changes shortly after mild trauma in the setting of diabetic peripheral neuropathy (eg, abnormal monofilament testing) should raise suspicion for acute neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy. Acute neuropathic arthropathy is commonly elicited by minor trauma (eg, slight twisting of the foot) leading to an exaggerated inflammatory response. X-ray during the acute phase can show mild edema but typically no bony changes. If untreated, rapid and progressive resorption can lead to bone destruction (ie, chronic neuropathic arthropathy). Therefore, early recognition is critical to limit progression to chronic disease. Treatment is with a foot cast to avoid weight bearing, reduce edema, and protect from further injury. (Choices A and C) Mild pain, accompanied by a normal leukocyte count and ESR, makes acute infection (eg, cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis) and acute gout flare unlikely. In addition, gram-positive coverage alone is typically sufficient in cellulitis, including in patients with diabetes mellitus. Serum uric acid levels are variable during an acute gout flare and therefore have little diagnostic value; arthrocentesis should be obtained if suspicion is high. (Choice D) This patient has no evidence of a fluid collection requiring surgical incision and drainage. In patients with diabetes mellitus, surgical incision should be performed only if absolutely necessary (eg, risk of infection, poor wound healing). Educational objective: Patients with diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy who develop foot erythema, warmth, and edema should be suspected of having acute neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy. Avoiding weight bearing (eg, use of cast) reduces edema and protects from further injury.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man comes to the office due to a 3-day history of worsening redness and swelling of his left foot. The patient reports only minimal pain and has had no fever, chills, or malaise. One day prior to the onset of these symptoms, the patient slightly twisted his foot while getting out of the bathtub, but he recalls no major injury. Medical history is significant for type 1 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min. On examination, the entire left foot is edematous, erythematous, and warm compared to the right foot, with moderately restricted range of motion. Monofilament testing reveals significant impairment of sensation of both feet. No skin ulcers or gross bony abnormalities are noted. Dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL Leukocytes 9,800/mm3 Platelets 240,000/mm3 Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 15 mm/hr Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL X-rays of the left foot show mild soft tissue edema but no fracture or dislocation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Gastroparesis Causes Diabetes mellitus (autonomic neuropathy) Medications (eg, opioids, anticholinergic drugs) Traumatic/postsurgical injury (ie, vagus nerve injury) Neurologic (eg, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury) Idiopathic/postviral Clinical features Nausea & vomiting, epigastric abdominal pain Early satiety, bloating, weight loss Labile glucose (diabetes mellitus) Epigastric distension & succussion splash Diagnosis Exclude obstruction: upper endoscopy ± CT/MR enterography Assess motility: nuclear gastric emptying study Treatment Frequent small meals (low fat, soluble fiber only) Promotility drugs (eg, metoclopramide, erythromycin) Gastric electrical stimulation &/or jejunal feeding tube (refractory symptoms) This patient has evidence of stomach dysmotility (as demonstrated by gastric-emptying scan) in the absence of mechanical obstruction (eg, negative upper endoscopy and CT enterography). This is consistent with a diagnosis of gastroparesis. Gastroparesis commonly results from uncontrolled diabetes, medication effects (eg, opioids), post-surgery complications (eg, vagal nerve injury), and certain viral infections (eg, postviral gastroparesis). Patients typically vomit undigested food, sometimes several hours after eating; other symptoms include abdominal pain, early satiety, and unintentional weight loss due to decreased oral intake. Physical examination may show mild epigastric tenderness or a succussion splash. Given this patient's recent viral illness and lack of other risk factors (eg, no metabolic/laboratory abnormalities to suggest diabetes, not on opioids, no recent surgery), she most likely has postviral gastroparesis, which typically improves over time. The first step in management of gastroparesis is dietary modification. Foods high in fat and insoluble fiber pass slowly through the stomach and should be avoided (Choice C). Frequent small meals are advisable, and homogenized food can help in severe cases. Prokinetic drugs (eg, metoclopramide) are used when symptoms fail to improve with dietary measures alone; more invasive options such as a percutaneous jejunal feeding tube or an implantable gastric stimulator are reserved for treatment-refractory patients (Choice E). (Choice A) Although anticholinergic medications (eg, tricyclic antidepressants) and opioids may exacerbate gastroparesis, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, sertraline) do not slow gastric motility and may be continued. (Choice D) Proton pump inhibitors are commonly used to treat peptic ulcer disease and dyspepsia, but they are less helpful in the management of gastroparesis and would not be preferred over dietary modification. Educational objective: Gastroparesis is diagnosed by a gastric-emptying scan in the absence of mechanical (eg, gastric outlet) obstruction. Patients should be advised to consume a low-fat and low-insoluble fiber diet as well as frequent small meals. Prokinetic drugs (eg, metoclopramide) are used when dietary modification fails to improve symptoms.

Gastroparesis
Causes
  • Diabetes mellitus (autonomic neuropathy)
  • Medications (eg, opioids, anticholinergic drugs)
  • Traumatic/postsurgical injury (ie, vagus nerve injury)
  • Neurologic (eg, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury)
  • Idiopathic/postviral

  • Nausea & vomiting, epigastric abdominal pain
  • Early satiety, bloating, weight loss
  • Labile glucose (diabetes mellitus)
  • Epigastric distension & succussion splash
Diagnosis
  • Exclude obstruction: upper endoscopy ± CT/MR enterography
  • Assess motility: nuclear gastric emptying study
Treatment
  • Frequent small meals (low fat, soluble fiber only)
  • Promotility drugs (eg, metoclopramide, erythromycin)
  • Gastric electrical stimulation &/or jejunal feeding tube (refractory symptoms)

Given this patient's recent viral illness and lack of other risk factors (eg, no metabolic/laboratory abnormalities to suggest diabetes, not on opioids, no recent surgery), she most likely has postviral gastroparesis, which typically improves over time.  The first step in management of gastroparesis is dietary modification. 

Frequent small meals are advisable, and homogenized food can help in severe cases.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a 4-week history of progressively worsening nausea, vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, and an unintentional 2.3-kg (5.1-lb) weight loss. The patient has no abdominal pain. The symptoms started after a recent flu-like illness that included fever, generalized body aches, nausea, and malaise. Her only other medical concern is major depression, for which she takes sertraline. Vital signs are normal. Examination discloses mild epigastric tenderness to palpation and is otherwise normal. Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel are normal. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals retained gastric contents but no obstruction. CT enterography shows a distended stomach with no obstruction. A gastric emptying study using a solid meal reveals significant delay in stomach emptying at 4 hours. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Temper tantrums Characteristics Treatment Normal Brief (<10 min) Unpleasant or aggressive behavior in response to frustration Normalization of mood/behavior between episodes Ensure child is safe Withdraw attention, stay calm Avoid: Giving in Physical punishment Explaining/reasoning Pathologic Duration >25 min >5 tantrums per day Self-injurious behavior Age >4 Medical or psychiatric evaluation This healthy toddler has temper tantrums, a type of developmentally normal behavior in this age group. Toddlers have a desire for independence, control, and caregiver attention but lack mature coping skills and often become frustrated when they do not get what they want. Because toddlers are unable to verbally communicate effectively, they instead externalize their frustrations through temper tantrums, or outbursts of unpleasant or aggressive behaviors (eg, crying, screaming, rolling on the floor, kicking, hitting). Additional stressors (eg, new sibling, hunger, sleepiness, illness) lower the threshold for temper tantrums. As in this patient, temper tantrums are brief (eg, 5-10 min) and may be fueled by the attention of a loved one. Validating the child's feelings (eg, "you're angry because I didn't give you another cookie") sometimes helps regulate emotions but may not always be successful. In such situations, parents should stay calm and withdraw attention from the tantrum until the child calms down. Depending on the age of the child, examples include placing the child in a safe, quiet space or standing nearby without talking. Compromise of rules (eg, giving the child another cookie) should be avoided because it legitimizes misbehaviors and empowers these outbursts. (Choice A) Medical or psychological evaluation is needed when tantrums are prolonged (eg, hours), persist past age 4, endanger the patient (eg, headbanging) or others, or are accompanied by other physical findings (eg, pallor). (Choice B) Providing positive attention (eg, hugs) to the child during a temper tantrum prolongs the outburst and may encourage future tantrums because the child learns that tantrums are an effective means to get parental attention. (Choice D) Attempting to reason with toddlers who are throwing a temper tantrum is generally difficult because their frontal cortices are unable to simultaneously calm down and process complex explanations; this action may prolong the tantrum by providing unnecessary attention. Children usually develop these reasoning skills by age 5 or 6. (Choice E) Although the stress of decreased parental attention associated with a new sibling often exacerbates temper tantrums, simple reassurance is not adequate. Parents should be encouraged to include the older child (eg, this patient) when they spend time with the new sibling and also provide him or her with dedicated parental time. Management of tantrums should not change. Educational objective: A temper tantrum is a developmentally normal outburst of unpleasant or aggressive behavior seen in toddlers in response to frustration. When a temper tantrum occurs, withdrawing attention to the outburst (eg, placing the child in a separate room) reduces the duration. Physical punishment, prolonged explanations, and compromise of rules should be avoided.

questions.explanation: Candiduria Risk factors Chronic colonization Urinary tract drainage device (eg, Foley catheter) Prior antibiotic use Diabetes mellitus Clinical features Asymptomatic UTI (most common) Cystitis: suprapubic pain Pyelonephritis: flank pain, CVA tenderness Disseminated candidemia Treatment Asymptomatic: none indicated Symptomatic UTI & disseminated infection: antifungal therapy* Complications Perinephric abscess Fungus ball *Fluconazole (amphotericin B if fluconazole resistant). CVA = costovertebral angle; UTI = urinary tract infection. This patient with numerous yeasts on urinalysis has candiduria. Fungal species, most commonly Candida, can enter the urinary tract via hematogenous spread (less common) or genitourinary spread by ascending from the perineum and urethra (most common). Risk factors include chronic urinary catheter use (due to chronic colonization) and diabetes mellitus. Most cases of candiduria are benign and due to asymptomatic colonization rather than active infection. However, treatment is recommended if patients are symptomatic or at risk for disseminated candidiasis: Patients with symptomatic candiduria (cystitis) or those at risk for disseminated candidiasis (eg, neutropenia, anticipated urologic procedure) require empiric therapy (prior to sensitivity results) with an azole such as fluconazole (Choice D). If symptoms or urinalysis results do not resolve with empiric azole therapy, additional sensitivity testing is performed (Choice A). In contrast, patients with no associated urinary symptoms (eg, dysuria, frequency, urgency) or signs of upper urinary tract involvement (eg, flank pain) and a urinalysis with no signs of inflammation (ie, no leukocyte esterase or white blood cells) do not require antifungal therapy. This is because these cases represent colonization rather than active infection. Although this patient has diabetes mellitus and candiduria, she is asymptomatic with a normal physical examination and is not at high risk for disseminated candidiasis; therefore, she may receive reassurance. (Choice B) Patients with persistent symptomatic candiduria require renal imaging to assess for upper urinary tract involvement (eg, hydronephrosis, perinephric abscess) or fungus ball formation. This patient is asymptomatic. (Choice C) Vaginal swab microscopy is indicated in patients with vulvovaginitis (eg, vulvovaginal pruritus and erythema, vaginal discharge) to determine the responsible pathogen (eg, candidiasis, trichomoniasis). However, vaginal swab microscopy is not indicated in asymptomatic patients because Candida is present in the normal vaginal microbiome. Educational objective: In most patients, asymptomatic candiduria represents colonization and does not require additional evaluation (eg, renal imaging) or empiric antifungal therapy.
