questions.explanation: Clinical features of hypothyroidism Mood symptoms Depression Apathy Social withdrawal Cognitive symptoms Impaired concentration & memory Psychomotor slowing Executive dysfunction Severe symptoms Delirium Psychosis (myxedema madness) Physical symptoms Bradycardia Cold intolerance Fatigue Muscle weakness & myalgia Hyporeflexia This patient's cognitive impairment, associated with excessive tiredness and physical examination findings of slow speech and movements, decreased deep tendon reflexes, muscle weakness, and bradycardia, is consistent with hypothyroidism. Cognitive dysfunction is common in overt hypothyroidism and is characterized by slowed mentation and speech (due to slowed processing speed and resultant delayed responses), decreased concentration, short-term memory impairment, and executive dysfunction. Other neuropsychiatric findings in hypothyroidism include depressed mood and apathy and psychosis (sometimes called myxedema madness). Delirium can occur in severe cases. A screening TSH test is indicated in all dementia workups to rule out hypothyroidism because it is a potentially reversible cause of cognitive impairment. An elevated TSH level with a decreased serum-free thyroxine confirms the diagnosis. (Choice A) 14-3-3 protein in cerebrospinal fluid is a supportive finding in the diagnosis of prion diseases (eg, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). Clinical features include rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus, with death usually occurring within a year of symptom onset. Upper motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia, spasticity, rigidity) are more likely instead of this patient's hyporeflexia. (Choice C) Vitamin B12 deficiency is another potentially reversible cause of dementia, presenting with cognitive slowing and forgetfulness. However, it is characterized by ataxia and sensory abnormalities with the deficiency developing over the course of years. (Choice D) A positive serum treponemal test is consistent with a diagnosis of syphilis. Although late neurosyphilis can cause dementia, this is expected to occur over the course of years with locomotor ataxia and sharp pains characteristically developing progressively. In contrast, this patient's quicker decline with decreased reflexes, bradycardia, and slowed but intact movements is more characteristic of thyroid dysfunction. (Choice E) Enlarged brain ventricles on CT scan or MRI are a feature of normal pressure hydrocephalus with a triad of urinary incontinence, gait disturbance, and dementia. Gait is slow with small steps, a wide base, and an appearance of feet being stuck to the floor (magnetic gait). This patient's slow but otherwise normal gait, generalized muscle weakness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and bradycardia are more consistent with hypothyroidism. Educational objective: Hypothyroidism should be considered in patients with slowed mentation, impaired short-term memory, and executive dysfunction, particularly when accompanied by suggestive physical manifestations such as slowed reflexes and bradycardia. An elevated serum TSH level and low free thyroxine concentration confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the office by her son due to memory impairment over the past 6 months. The son reports that she has had increasing forgetfulness and difficulty performing daily activities such as dressing. He has also observed periods of inappropriate irritability and paranoia. In addition, the patient has been excessively tired and rarely leaves the house. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg, and pulse is 58/min. On physical examination, the patient has poor eye contact and a flat affect. She talks slowly with low volume, and responses are markedly delayed, even to simple yes-no questions. Neurologic examination shows generalized muscle weakness with decreased deep tendon reflexes. Sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Gait and general movements are slow but otherwise normal. Short-term memory is impaired. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?

questions.explanation: Infection control: isolation precautions Type Pathogen* Key requirements Airborne Bacterial: tuberculosis Viral: primary VZV (chickenpox), disseminated VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster), dermatomal VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster) in immunocompromised patients, SARS-CoV-2, measles Negative pressure room N95 respirator Contact Multidrug-resistant organism (eg, MRSA, VRE, ESBL producing) Bacterial: Clostridioides difficile, Escherichia coli O157:H7 Viral: RSV, primary VZV (chickenpox), disseminated VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster), dermatomal VZV reactivation (shingles/zoster) in immunocompromised patients Gloves & gowns Single-use equipment (eg, stethoscope) Droplet Bacterial: Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type B, Mycoplasma pneumoniae Viral: influenza virus, adenovirus Mask within 1-2 m (3-6 ft) of patient Standard Followed for all patients even when no infection is apparent Hand hygiene Gowns/gloves/masks when appropriate (eg, during procedures) *Precaution is started immediately when infection with pathogen is suspected. ESBL = extended-spectrum beta-lactamase; MRSA = methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; RSV = respiratory syncytial virus; SARS-CoV-2 = severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2; VRE = vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus; VZV = varicella-zoster virus. Clostridioides difficile is a rising cause of outbreaks and morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients. C difficile infection is highly likely in this patient who has developed profuse watery diarrhea in the setting of relevant risk factors including hospitalization and recent antibiotic therapy (eg, treatment for community-acquired pneumonia). Confirmatory stool testing (eg, stool enzyme immunoassay for C difficile toxin, stool PCR for toxigenic C difficile genes) should be performed (Choice E). In addition, infection control measures should be initiated because they are essential to limiting outbreaks of C difficile in health care and community settings. C difficile is transmitted primarily through direct contact with infectious spores, which can survive on environmental surfaces for extended time periods and be carried room to room by hospital staff. As a result, any patient suspected to have C difficile infection (such as this man) should preemptively be placed on contact precautions while stool studies are pending (Choice B). These precautions include: Use of gowns and gloves upon entry into the patient's room Employment of single-use equipment if available (eg, dedicated stethoscope for patient) Placement of the patient in a private room or cohort with other patients known to have C difficile infection Contact precautions should be continued until after resolution of diarrhea. (Choices C and D) Standard precautions are followed for all patients; they include hand hygiene before and after each patient interaction and use of gowns and gloves when contact with bodily fluids is expected. Standard precautions alone are insufficient to promote adequate infection control given this patient's suspected C difficile infection; contact precautions are also required. Educational objective: The diagnosis of Clostridioides difficile infection should be suspected when patients with relevant risk factors (eg, hospitalization, exposure to antibiotics) develop acute diarrhea (especially profuse watery diarrhea). Patients suspected to have C difficile infection should preemptively be placed on contact precautions (ie, use of gowns, gloves, and single-use equipment) while stool testing is pending.

This patient has symptoms of gas-bloat syndrome (eg, bloating, inability to belch) after Nissen fundoplication, a surgical procedure used to treat resistant gastroesophageal reflux disease. During this procedure, the fundus is folded and sewn around the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to decrease the amount of gastric acid that refluxes into the esophagus. Gas-bloat syndrome is thought to be the result of gastric air trapping due to the tightened LES. Symptoms typically develop postprandially and are often precipitated by the consumption of carbonated beverages. Patients can generally be reassured that the condition is benign and usually improves over time with simethicone (which facilitates gas bubble expulsion by decreasing their surface tension) and avoidance of carbonated beverages. Persistent cases may require pyloroplasty or conversion from a full to a partial fundoplication (Choice B). (Choices A and E) Dysphagia (eg, difficulty swallowing) is common within 12 weeks of Nissen fundoplication and usually self-resolves. For patients with long-standing dysphagia after surgery (ie, >12 weeks), barium esophagography (ie, barium swallow) can identify narrowing of the distal esophagus. These patients benefit from esophageal dilation, a procedure usually performed during upper endoscopy. Because this patient does not have dysphagia, neither procedure is indicated. (Choice C) Rifaximin is used to treat bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine commonly associated with chronic pancreatitis or intestinal motility disorders (eg, irritable bowel syndrome, diabetic neuropathy). Patients have abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and/or chronic diarrhea; inability to belch is not a feature. Educational objective: Gas-bloat syndrome presents with bloating and inability to belch following Nissen fundoplication. The condition is benign and usually improves over time. Treatment includes simethicone and avoidance of carbonated beverages.

questions.explanation: This patient has signs of gastrointestinal perforation (ie, free air under the diaphragm) with findings of diffuse peritonitis (eg, guarding, rebound) and needs emergency laparotomy. He is also at increased risk for perioperative cardiac complications due to ischemic heart disease (eg, stable angina at 2 blocks) and heart failure, which typically require preoperative assessment. However, patients with conditions requiring emergency surgery (life/limb threatened <6 hr) should proceed to surgery without further testing because there is insufficient time for test results, and the potential benefit of immediate operative intervention outweighs the risk of delay for cardiac evaluation. In the absence of emergent/urgent surgical indications, the presence of an acute coronary syndrome (ie, unstable angina, recent myocardial infarction [≤60 days]) should prompt delay of surgery for cardiac evaluation/management. All other patients being considered for noncardiac surgery should undergo preoperative assessment of their perioperative cardiovascular risk using a validated patient- and procedure-specific prediction model such as the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI). Patients with low perioperative risk (≤1%), as well as those who can perform ≥4 METs on functional assessment despite increased risk (>1%), can proceed to surgery without further evaluation. Patients with moderate or high RCRI (>1%) and poor (or unknown) functional status (<4 METs) can typically also proceed with surgery unless preoperative cardiac evaluation will impact surgical decision-making. If cardiac evaluation may impact decision-making, stress testing is performed followed by coronary angiography/revascularization, if indicated (Choices C and E). (Choice A) Baseline troponin I and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels are sometimes obtained preoperatively to help interpret postoperative levels (eg, for screening of myocardial injury after surgery). However, serial troponin I levels (used to exclude acute coronary syndrome) are not indicated prior to emergency surgery because they would not change management, particularly in a patient without active chest pain. Similarly, BNP levels (which are elevated in acute decompensated heart failure) would not impact decision-making for emergency surgery, particularly in a patient without dyspnea or crackles to suggest volume overload. (Choice B) Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is most often used for patients with intermediate pretest probability (10%-90%) to exclude significant coronary artery disease while avoiding invasive angiography. CCTA does not allow for coronary intervention and would not affect emergency surgical management. Educational objective: Patients with emergent/urgent surgical conditions should be taken to surgery without further cardiac testing because the potential benefit of surgery outweighs the risk of delay for cardiac evaluation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for sudden-onset severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Medical conditions include hypertension, dyslipidemia, and coronary artery disease. His coronary artery disease is being medically managed. The most recent echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 40%. Review of symptoms is notable for substernal chest pain upon walking 2-3 blocks that resolves with rest, but the patient has no active chest pain. Temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 96/64 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, and respirations are 24/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable. The abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender to palpation with rebound and guarding. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST-T wave abnormalities. Upright x-ray of the chest shows free air under the diaphragm. After an intravenous fluid bolus, the patient's blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. Antibiotics are administered. Which of the following is the next best step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Chronic mercury toxicity Exposures Incidental (eg, broken lightbulbs or thermometers) Ingestion (eg, shark, swordfish) Occupational Clinical features* Neuropsychiatric: tremor, insomnia, personality changes (eg, irritability) Cardiovascular: hypertension, tachycardia Mucocutaneous: gingivitis; diaphoresis; swelling, redness, desquamation of hands/feet Renal: tubular damage/proteinuria *Some features may mimic pheochromocytoma, including elevated urinary catecholamines. This patient has neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, anxiety, insomnia), tachycardia, and diaphoresis in the setting of elevated urinary catecholamines, findings often seen in those with pheochromocytoma. However, this patient has an unrevealing work-up and now warrants evaluation for mimics of pheochromocytoma. Mercury inactivates catechol O-methyltransferase (COMT), an enzyme responsible for catecholamine breakdown; therefore, chronic mercury toxicity can mimic pheochromocytoma. Exposure to mercury is usually occupational (eg, gold miner), but children may inadvertently be exposed via broken thermometers or lightbulbs or by playing with quicksilver, a silver liquid that vaporizes easily at room temperature. Manifestations of mercury poisoning include the following: Cardiovascular/sympathetic nervous systems: Because mercury impairs catecholamine breakdown, mercury toxicity leads to increased serum and urinary epinephrine and norepinephrine, as seen in this patient. Excess stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system causes diaphoresis, tachycardia, and anxiety (may be episodic, as seen in this patient). Neuropsychiatric: Mercury can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in the CNS, specifically the cerebral cortex, leading to a range of psychiatric and motor symptoms (eg, personality changes, insomnia, tremor). Dermatologic: Mercury toxicity, particularly in children, can lead to a hypersensitivity rash (acrodynia). A diffuse, pruritic body rash or a desquamating, pink rash on the palms and soles is characteristic. (Choice A) Aluminum toxicity leads to progressive dementia, muscle weakness, and bone pain/fractures, none of which are seen in this patient. Moreover, this diagnosis typically occurs only in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis. (Choice B) Chronic copper toxicity (similar to Wilson disease) can cause neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as personality changes. However, elevated urinary catecholamines and their associated cardiovascular effects (eg, tachycardia, diaphoresis) would not be seen. (Choice C) Acute iron toxicity initially causes vomiting and diarrhea followed by shock (eg, tachycardia, hypotension) and hepatotoxicity. Chronic iron overload (eg, hereditary hemochromatosis, recurrent transfusions) is often asymptomatic but may cause heart failure, skin hyperpigmentation, or arthropathy. This otherwise healthy patient's desquamating rash and elevated urinary catecholamines are inconsistent with iron toxicity. (Choice E) Zinc toxicity (eg, contaminated food items) is rare because humans are tolerant of high doses. It typically manifests as gastrointestinal disturbance (eg, nausea, diarrhea); catecholaminergic manifestations (eg, diaphoresis, tachycardia) are not expected. High zinc intake may lead to copper deficiency (interfence with copper absorption). Educational objective: Mercury impairs the breakdown of catecholamines, and toxicity may lead to a clinical presentation similar to that of pheochromocytoma, including episodic diaphoresis, anxiety, and tachycardia. Other common findings include neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, personality changes, insomnia, tremor) and a desquamating rash.

questions.explanation: This patient with acute kidney injury (AKI) following chemotherapy has characteristic electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypocalcemia) suggestive of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). TLS is caused by the rapid destruction of malignant cells, which release intracellular potassium, purine nucleic acids (metabolized to uric acid [ie, urate]), and phosphate into the bloodstream. Hyperphosphatemia leads to hypocalcemia (ie, binding of phosphate to free calcium), which can cause symptoms such as perioral numbness and muscle cramps. In addition, calcium phosphate stone formation can cause AKI due to renal tubular obstruction and direct cellular injury. A serum phosphate level should therefore be included in the laboratory evaluation of patients with suspected TLS. The risk for calcium phosphate stone formation can be reduced by maximizing the glomerular filtration rate and urine output with prophylactic intravenous fluids. Specific agents (eg, phosphate binders) can also be used depending on phosphate levels. (Choice B) Xanthine is metabolized to urate by xanthine oxidase. Patients receiving a xanthine oxidase inhibitor are at risk for elevated serum and urine xanthine levels, which can result in xanthine stone formation and AKI. However, this patient received rasburicase, which does not affect xanthine oxidase and therefore would not increase the serum xanthine level. (Choice C) Urinary allantoin is expected to be elevated in this patient receiving rasburicase, which metabolizes urate to allantoin, but allantoin is an inert compound and does not cause stone formation or AKI. (Choice D) Measurement of urinary creatinine with serum creatinine can be helpful in calculating the creatinine clearance to provide the most precise measure of renal function. However, this would not help determine the etiology of this patient's AKI. (Choice E) Increased urinary urate, which can cause AKI due to urate stone formation, typically results from hyperuricemia, but this patient's serum urate is normal due to the intended effect of rasburicase. Educational objective: Patients receiving chemotherapy are at risk for tumor lysis syndrome, which can cause acute kidney injury due to the renal precipitation of uric acid (ie, urate) or calcium phosphates stones. The risk for stone formation can be reduced by maximizing glomerular filtration and urine output with prophylactic intravenous fluids.

questions.explanation: The number needed to harm (NNH) represents the mean number of patients who must be exposed to a specific treatment (eg, new-umab) for a particular period of time (eg, 12 weeks) to cause harm (eg, serious adverse event [SAE]) to 1 patient who otherwise would not have been harmed if treated with a different treatment or control (eg, standard-umab). In other words, the NNH compares the harm of 2 treatments in a specific group of patients, on a specific outcome, during a predetermined time. Therefore, the NNH will vary depending on the population under consideration, the treatments being compared, the outcomes of interest, and the length of time the outcomes were observed. This trial compared the effectiveness of a new drug (ie, new-umab) for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis against the standard drug (ie, standard-umab). Based on the table in the question, the new drug has an NNH of 6. This means that 6 patients (on average) must be exposed to new-umab to cause an SAE to 1 patient who otherwise would not have been harmed if treated with standard-umab (Choice B). In other words, on average, for every 6 patients treated for 12 weeks with new-umab instead of standard-umab, 1 will experience an SAE. In this case, new-umab (ie, new drug) is as effective as standard-umab (ie, standard drug) (p = 0.294 >0.05) to treat moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, but the new drug seems to cause more harm than the standard drug (p = 0.007 <0.05). (Choice A) The results show that 22% (11 of 50), not 6%, of patients treated for 12 weeks with new-umab had SAEs. (Choice D) The risk of SAEs in patients treated for 12 weeks with new-umab compared to patients treated with standard-umab is the relative risk (RR) of SAEs. Based on the results, the correct RR = 0.22 / 0.04 = 5.5 (not 6). Educational objective: The number needed to harm represents the mean number of patients who must be exposed to a specific treatment for a particular time to cause harm to 1 patient who otherwise would not have been harmed if treated with a different treatment or placebo.

questions.explanation: Elements of medical malpractice Duty Physician provides care for the patient in the context of an established patient-physician relationship Deviation from standard (or breach of care) Physician fails to follow standard of care for similar specialty/setting or acts negligently Direct causation Physician's actions directly & proximately cause patient harm Damages Patient suffers harm (emotional or physical), injury, or death Medical malpractice is characterized by failure to practice according to accepted standards of care, either due to lack of attention and care (ie, negligence, dereliction of duty) or due to deficits in knowledge or skill. Establishing malpractice also requires that the physician's action directly caused patient harm (eg, injury, death). This surgeon declined to offer an emergency surgery (ie, repair of perforated gallbladder) primarily due to the patient's advanced age and comorbid conditions. A physician may decline to provide an intervention that is medically futile (ie, clearly offering no benefit to the patient and unlikely to accomplish its intended goals). However, standard management of acute cholecystitis with gallbladder perforation includes surgical intervention and, as determined by the surgeon himself, would have reduced the patient's mortality risk compared to withholding surgery (Choice F). Therefore, the surgeon could be found liable for malpractice due to failure to provide beneficial care in accordance with standard practice. (Choice B) Although physicians should consider recommendations of referring providers, failure to follow their recommendations is not sufficient basis for a malpractice claim. Rather, liability is ultimately determined by whether the physician provided care according to established standards of care. (Choices C, D, and E) This patient has dementia with multiple comorbidities and limited life expectancy, which could make him a medically vulnerable person (eg, elderly with multiple comorbodities and/or inability to self-care); in addition, consent cannot be immediately obtained due to the patient's dementia and the daughter's unavailability. However, the patient does not have an advance directive refusing life-sustaining care (and in fact has documented full code status), and surgical intervention represents life-sustaining treatment that will lower the patient's mortality risk. Therefore, in this emergency situation, neither the inability to obtain consent nor the patient's low life expectancy is a valid reason to withhold life-sustaining care. Educational objective: Medical malpractice is characterized by a physician's failure to practice according to accepted standards, which directly causes patient harm. Although a physician may decline to offer care that is medically futile (ie, offers no benefit to the patient and is unlikely to accomplish its intended goals), failure to provide beneficial care may constitute malpractice.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old man is brought to the emergency department from an assisted living facility due to abdominal pain and fever. Medical history is notable for advanced Alzheimer disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Initial evaluation indicates acute cholecystitis with gallbladder perforation and septic shock. Antibiotics and vasopressor therapy are started. The emergency department staff consult the on-call surgeon for emergency surgery. The patient's records indicate he is full code. The surgeon estimates the perioperative mortality risk for this patient to be very high but lower than for nonsurgical management. However, he chooses to not operate because the patient's premorbid life expectancy is low and because he has been unable to reach the patient's daughter, who is the patient's designated decision maker, to obtain consent, despite repeated phone calls. If the patient subsequently experiences an adverse outcome, which of the following best describes the surgeon's malpractice liability in this case?

questions.explanation: Full-thickness burns, which injure the entire epidermis and dermis, result in leathery, noncompliant eschars that can constrict affected body parts when the burns are circumferential. This patient sustained full-thickness burns throughout his chest and back, likely resulting in areas of circumferential eschar. When coupled with soft tissue edema resulting from fluid resuscitation and increased capillary permeability (from the postburn inflammatory response), this can cause impaired chest wall excursion. In patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, such as this one, the inability of the chest wall to expand in response to the forceful injection of air causes increased intrathoracic pressure, leading to high peak pressures and hypotension (due to decreased cardiac preload). If the condition is left untreated, cardiac arrest results. Thoracic escharotomy should be performed immediately to release the constrictive effect of the circumferential eschar, allow adequate chest wall excursion, and improve ventilation. Escharotomy creates an incision through the burned skin until subcutaneous fat is observed and skin tension is released. (Choice A) Burn patients can develop myocardial dysfunction due to the postburn inflammatory response; when coupled with massive volume loading, this can result in cardiogenic pulmonary edema (often treated with furosemide). In extreme cases, pulmonary edema can decrease lung compliance and cause high ventilator peak pressures; however, chest x-ray would be abnormal, and crackles/wheezing would be present. (Choice B) Nebulized albuterol can improve ventilation and decrease peak pressures in patients with bronchospasm. However, this patient has no evidence of bronchospasm (auscultation shows clear lungs); high peak pressures are more likely due to the inability of the chest wall to expand. (Choices C and D) Increasing positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) can increase ventilation and decrease peak pressure by recruiting underdistended alveoli when the chest wall and lungs still have some compliance. However, this patient's chest wall is no longer compliant due to a circumferential, constrictive eschar. Increasing PEEP would only increase peak pressure, causing more barotrauma, and exacerbate hypotension (by decreasing preload) while leaving the underlying cause (constrictive eschar) unaddressed. Similar negative effects would be expected if the tidal volume were increased in the setting of a noncompliant chest wall. Educational objective: In patients with circumferential full-thickness burns to the thorax, increased peak pressures, difficulty with ventilation, and hypotension are consistent with impaired chest wall excursion due to constrictive eschar. Thoracic escharotomy can release the eschar and restore appropriate chest wall excursion.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an attacker soaked him with gasoline and set him on fire. The patient has burns to >65% of his body. He was intubated at the scene. Medical history is unknown. Temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), blood pressure is 117/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 135/min. Oxygen saturation is 96% on 40% FiO2 with volume-controlled mechanical ventilation. On examination, the patient is intubated and sedated. He has deep partial- and full-thickness burns to his face, neck, chest, and upper and lower back. There are also deep and superficial partial-thickness burns to his extremities. He is administered intravenous fluids and admitted to the burn intensive care unit. Some 24 hours later, the high peak pressure alarm sounds multiple times on his ventilator, the patient's lungs become difficult to ventilate, and he is increasingly hypotensive. Auscultation demonstrates clear lungs. Heart sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. Chest x-ray reveals no significant infiltrates or consolidations. What is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with advanced cancer and limited life expectancy has decided to forgo antineoplastic therapy and wishes to optimize comfort. He prefers to be home as much as possible and has a family member who is available to provide basic assistance. Therefore, home hospice should be recommended. Although most patients receiving home hospice services die at home, patients may perceive that as a "burden" on their family, and some family members may feel uncomfortable having their loved ones die in the home. In these situations, arrangements can be made to transfer the patient elsewhere (eg, inpatient hospice facility) when death becomes imminent (eg, worsening vital signs, significantly increased need for medications) (Choice A). (Choice B) Although hospice provides spiritual support for the family, offering such support after the patient's death does not address the daughter's concern that the patient will die at home. (Choice C) Even though the patient currently does not have significant symptoms (eg, pain, shortness of breath) to necessitate palliative therapy, worsening symptoms are inevitable due to cancer progression. The physician should place a hospice referral as soon as possible in anticipation of these needs. Educational objective: Family members of patients who are in home hospice may not feel comfortable having the patient die at home. In these situations, arrangements can be made to transfer the patient elsewhere (eg, inpatient hospice facility) when death is imminent.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with stage IV squamous cell carcinoma of the lung comes to the office with his daughter to discuss end-of-life care. The patient understands that chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation therapy are options that may prolong his life, but a cure at this stage is unlikely and his life expectancy is <6 months. His sister died from metastatic lung cancer 5 years ago. Having watched her experience significant adverse effects from cancer therapy, the patient wishes to forgo cancer treatment and spend as much time as possible at home but does not want to be a "burden" on his family. The patient does not have significant pain or shortness of breath and can independently perform activities of daily living. He lives with his daughter, who is willing to take care of him; however, she is uncomfortable with the thought that he may die at home one day. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation from the physician?

questions.explanation: This patient's fever, dysphagia, neck stiffness, anterior cervical adenopathy, muffled voice, and trismus (restriction in mouth opening) are concerning for retropharyngeal abscess (RPA). RPA is a soft tissue infection of the neck due to polymicrobial bacterial infection (eg, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, oral anaerobes) of the potential space between the pharynx and the vertebral fascia. It is most often preceded by upper respiratory infection, as in this patient, but can also result from the direct spread of local bacterial infection (eg, pharyngitis, tonsillitis). RPA occurs most commonly in children age 2-4. The incidence decreases after age 4 due to retropharyngeal lymph node regression and fewer viral upper respiratory infections. The most important step in management is assessment of the airway. If the patient has signs of severe airway obstruction (eg, tripod position, inability to lie flat, nasal flaring, stridor, retractions), securing the airway with emergency laryngoscopy (performed by otolaryngology and/or anesthesia) is essential (Choice D). This should be done without delay before other diagnostic procedures. However, in patients such as this one with no signs of severe airway obstruction, CT scan of the neck (with contrast) is very helpful for confirming the diagnosis of RPA and defining the extent of spread. A small RPA (<2.5 cm) or a retropharyngeal phlegmon can be treated with a trial of empiric antibiotics; large RPAs require drainage in the operating room. (Choice A) Diphtheria presents with cervical adenopathy, fever, and sore throat. However, it is unlikely in a child who has received normal childhood vaccinations (which include diphtheria) and classically has a gray, adherent, posterior pharyngeal pseudomembrane. (Choice B) A barium swallow test can be helpful in evaluating chronic dysphagia. However, this patient's dysphagia is due to an acute infection compressing the pharynx and will likely resolve after recovery from the RPA. (Choice E) Lumbar puncture can be used to diagnose meningitis, which can also present with fever and neck stiffness. In contrast to patients with RPA, patients with meningitis have pain with neck flexion; neck extension usually brings relief. This child's muffled voice, trismus, and oropharyngeal erythema with a notable absence of headache and photophobia make RPA much more likely. Educational objective: Retropharyngeal abscess in children presents with fever, dysphagia, muffled voice, and pain with neck extension. After assessment of the airway, CT scan of the neck can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office due to a progressively increasing sore throat, difficulty eating solid foods, neck pain, and fever with chills for 2 days. The patient has had a cough and runny nose for a week. He has no chronic medical conditions, and immunizations are up to date. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg, pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 28/min. Oxygen saturation is 98% by pulse oximetry. On examination, the voice is muffled. The patient has tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. He sits upright, holding his neck stiff and straight, and has difficulty opening his mouth. The posterior oropharynx appears erythematous. The uvula is in the midline. Lung fields are clear with good air entry. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. What is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient has systemic sclerosis (SS) (ie, scleroderma), an autoimmune disease characterized by abnormal deposition of collagen in multiple organ systems. The development of acute kidney injury associated with severe hypertension and signs of end-organ dysfunction (eg, flame-shaped retinal hemorrhage, blurred vision) is consistent with scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). SRC is a life-threatening complication of SS that likely occurs due to collagen deposition and endothelial injury in the renal vasculature, which leads to intimal proliferation and narrowing of the vascular lumen. The resultant hypoperfusion causes renal failure and promotes hyperactivity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in the abrupt onset of severe hypertension. End-organ dysfunction (eg, retinal hemorrhage, encephalopathy) is common. Because the renal dysfunction in SRC occurs from vascular injury, rather than a glomerular or tubulointerstitial etiology (eg, glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis), the urinary sediment is typically normal; red blood cells, white blood cells, and casts are unexpected. Urinalysis may show mild proteinuria, but nephrotic range protein is atypical. Risk factors for SRC include extensive skin involvement (as seen in this patient with scleroderma extending to the chest) and the presence of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Glucocorticoids, which increase fluid retention and blood pressure, may also precipitate SRC. (Choice A) Dysmorphic red blood cells are typically seen in glomerulonephritis, which can also cause hypertension. Although glomerulonephritis is associated with multiple autoimmune diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus), it is not typical in SS. The acute onset of hypertension and renal dysfunction is more consistent with SRC. (Choice B) Numerous red blood cells may be seen with injury (eg, nephrolithiasis), malignancy (eg, renal cell carcinoma, bladder cancer), or infection throughout the genitourinary system, and may occur in association with dysmorphic RBCs as a result of glomerular bleeding. However, they do not typically occur with SRC. (Choices D and E) Urinary eosinophilia and white blood cell casts are typical of acute interstitial nephritis, which also causes renal dysfunction. However, it typically occurs after the initiation of a new drug (eg, antibiotic, proton pump inhibitor) and is associated with fever and rash; severe hypertension and end-organ dysfunction is unexpected. Educational objective: Scleroderma renal crisis is a life-threatening complication of systemic sclerosis that occurs due to narrowing and obliteration of the renal vasculature lumen, leading to abrupt-onset renal failure and severe hypertension. Urinary sediment is typically normal; hematuria or cellular casts are unexpected.

This patient has systemic sclerosis (SS) (ie, scleroderma), an autoimmune disease characterized by abnormal deposition of collagen in multiple organ systems.  The development of acute kidney injury associated with severe hypertension and signs of end-organ dysfunction (eg, flame-shaped retinal hemorrhage, blurred vision) is consistent with scleroderma renal crisis (SRC).

Because the renal dysfunction in SRC occurs from vascular injury, rather than a glomerular or tubulointerstitial etiology (eg, glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis), the urinary sediment is typically normal; red blood cells, white blood cells, and casts are unexpected.  Urinalysis may show mild proteinuria, but nephrotic range protein is atypical.  Risk factors for SRC include extensive skin involvement (as seen in this patient with scleroderma extending to the chest) and the presence of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies.  Glucocorticoids, which increase fluid retention and blood pressure, may also precipitate SRC.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Dysmorphic red blood cells are typically seen in glomerulonephritis, which can also cause hypertension.  Although glomerulonephritis is associated with multiple autoimmune diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus), it is not typical in SS.  The acute onset of hypertension and renal dysfunction is more consistent with SRC.
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Numerous red blood cells may be seen with injury (eg, nephrolithiasis), malignancy (eg, renal cell carcinoma, bladder cancer), or infection throughout the genitourinary system, and may occur in association with dysmorphic RBCs as a result of glomerular bleeding.  However, they do not typically occur with SRC.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choices D and E)  Urinary eosinophilia and white blood cell casts are typical of acute interstitial nephritis, which also causes renal dysfunction.  However, it typically occurs after the initiation of a new drug (eg, antibiotic, proton pump inhibitor) and is associated with fever and rash; severe hypertension and end-organ dysfunction is unexpected.
wrongAnswers.E: See the shared discussion for choice D.

questions.explanation: This patient with complex baseline disability requires intubation for influenza pneumonia; intubation should not be withheld based on her disability. The decision to withhold aggressive resuscitation (eg, intubation) is often considered for patients with limited life expectancy, such as those with comorbid terminal illnesses (eg, metastatic cancer). In such patients, the harms of aggressive resuscitation (eg, discomfort, ventilator-associated pneumonia) likely outweigh the benefit of temporary life extension. If resuscitation is withheld, the overall prognosis remains largely unchanged. However, developmental and intellectual disability is not a terminal illness, and patients with these disabilities often have life expectancies comparable to that of the general population. They also typically have fulfilling and meaningful lives, albeit requiring certain adaptations and dependence on others for assistance with activities of daily living (eg, feeding, dressing, toileting). Therefore, in this otherwise healthy patient with complex baseline disability, resuscitative efforts should be initiated for her acute, recoverable illness and should not be withheld based on her disability (Choices A, B, and D). Educational objective: Many patients with intellectual and developmental disability live meaningful and fulfilling lives and have life expectancies comparable to that of the general population. Such disability is not a terminal illness, and premature withdrawal of resuscitative measures should be avoided.

questions.explanation: This physician is considering termination of the patient-physician relationship due to the patient's deceptiveness and pattern of inappropriate behavior. Aside from nonpayment for services, physicians most commonly dismiss patients when patient behavior compromises the therapeutic relationship (eg, falsification of information, nonadherence to treatment recommendations), interferes with normal operations or the care of other patients (eg, habitual tardiness for appointments), or causes significant hardship to the physician and/or office staff (eg, hostile or demeaning behavior). Abrupt termination of care in a manner that does not allow adequate time for the patient to obtain care elsewhere is considered abandonment and is unethical. Therefore, the following guidelines should be followed when dismissing a patient from the practice: Notify the patient in writing of the termination. Offer to provide care for a reasonable, finite period (eg, 60 days) to allow the patient time to find another provider. Provide instructions for the patient to obtain a copy of the medical record or to have a copy sent to the new provider. Avoid termination of care during a medical crisis (eg, acute illness, postoperative recovery, complicated pregnancy). (Choice B) A corrective action plan (eg, payment plan for accrued debt) can be considered in specific circumstances for otherwise conscientious patients. However, this patient's deceptive behavior has already compromised the therapeutic relationship and will make it difficult for the physician to make objective treatment recommendations. In addition, instituting an action plan for the deceptive and demeaning behavior may be seen by the patient as insulting and may lead to additional hostility. (Choice C) In addition to her long-standing pattern of inappropriate behavior, the patient's deceptive actions have compromised the therapeutic relationship and are likely to affect future care decisions. Dismissal should be initiated now and not deferred until the patient chooses to leave the practice. (Choice D) Providing the patient with general information (eg, medical society directory, hospital referral line) on finding a new physician is appropriate. However, directing a patient to a specific provider may lead to mistrust by the patient of the new provider. (Choice E) Immediate termination of care should be considered only in certain unusual circumstances, such as violent or threatening behavior, severely inappropriate behavior (eg, sexual misconduct), or criminal activity (eg, theft) that involves the practice. Educational objective: Abrupt termination of care in a manner that does not allow the patient time to obtain care elsewhere (ie, abandonment) is unethical. When dismissing a patient from care, the physician should notify the patient in writing; offer to provide care for a reasonable, finite time period; and provide instructions for the patient to obtain a copy of the medical record.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the office to request amphetamine stimulants for a reported diagnosis of attention deficit disorder. questions.explanation: This patient has a chronic cough, defined as a cough >4 weeks in children (>8 weeks in adults). The cough may be characterized by specific features or examination findings that suggest a particular diagnosis (eg, paroxysmal cough in patients with pertussis) or underlying illness (eg, failure to thrive in patients with cystic fibrosis). In the absence of such findings, as in this case, a common cause of chronic cough in children is asthma. Many children with asthma have associated cough triggers (eg, sleep, exercise), but these are generally considered nonspecific features because different causes of cough may present similarly (eg, postinfectious cough). Wheeze is characteristic but may be absent on examination. Therefore, the first step in evaluation of chronic cough in children is spirometry. Spirometry is a measure of the expiratory flow rate, and in patients with asthma, the flow-volume loop demonstrates an obstructive pattern due to diffuse bronchial inflammation and smooth muscle contraction. Findings that further support asthma include reversible obstruction with a short-acting beta agonist (SABA), such as albuterol, that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Improvement of the cough following a 2-week trial of a SABA and low-dose inhaled corticosteroid confirms the diagnosis. Lack of reversible airway obstruction on spirometry warrants further evaluation with chest x-ray. (Choice A) Chronic cough may warrant evaluation with a CT scan of the sinuses if there is concern for chronic sinusitis. However, this diagnosis is rare in immunocompetent children and is associated with chronic mucopurulent drainage, not seen in this patient. (Choice B) Chronic cough in children may be a presenting symptom of underlying congestive heart failure, for which an echocardiogram is indicated. Patients can present with easy fatiguability; however, they typically have associated abnormal examination findings (eg, tachycardia, a gallop rhythm)—this patient has a normal cardiopulmonary examination. Moreover, most with chronic symptoms have failure to thrive. (Choices C and D) Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a common cause of chronic cough in adults and often treated empirically. Similarly, adults with obstructive sleep apnea, diagnosed by polysomnography, can have a chronic cough (possibly related to GERD or upper airway inflammation). In contrast, these conditions are very rare causes of chronic cough in children, and evaluation for asthma should be performed first. Educational objective: The first step in management of children with nonspecific chronic cough (>4 weeks) is spirometry to evaluate for underlying asthma. Supportive findings include reversible obstruction with a short-acting beta-agonist.

questions.explanation: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder beginning in childhood, with many experiencing impairments into adulthood. However, symptoms may be overlooked until adulthood, when patients are first diagnosed after repeated struggles in adult-specific roles and responsibilities. In these instances, obtaining a childhood history (eg, forgetting chores, missing assignments), ideally with the help of collateral informants (eg, parents, significant others, friends), should be combined with assessment of common adult manifestations of ADHD. Typically, adults with ADHD have more prominent inattention and impulsivity with less obvious hyperactivity symptoms. This patient's symptoms include the following: Inattention (eg, distracted driving, quality-control issues, missing quotas, forgetting questions) Impulsivity (eg, speeding, abruptly quitting job with failure to anticipate consequences [losing health insurance]) Hyperactivity (eg, preferring active jobs, circumstantial thought) ADHD is diagnosed clinically with ≥6 inattention symptoms and/or ≥6 hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms in ≥2 settings for ≥6 months. Medication options for adults include stimulants (eg, methylphenidate, amphetamines) or selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (eg, atomoxetine), which can be augmented with behavioral strategies (eg, to-do lists, scheduling). (Choice A) Antisocial personality disorder can present with impulsivity (eg, quitting job, speeding), failure to plan ahead (eg, lost health insurance), and irresponsibility (eg, inconsistent work); however, it presents within a context of significant disregard for societal norms and/or violations of personal rights of others with evidence of similar behaviors in adolescence, findings not seen in this patient. (Choice C) Borderline personality disorder may include impulsivity (eg, quitting job, speeding), unstable relationships (eg, girlfriend breaking up with him), and emotional reactivity (eg, felt "unstable"); however, it presents with a pattern of extreme relational instability and fears of abandonment that often trigger severe emotional lability and reactive self-destructive behaviors (eg, suicidal behavior, self-harm, substance use) not found in this patient. (Choice D) Generalized anxiety disorder can present with restlessness and inattention due to excessive worry. In contrast, inattention in ADHD is driven by distraction with internal (eg, daydreaming) or external (eg, noises outside, peers talking) stimuli, which often leads to mistakes (eg, quality-control issues, missing of quotas). (Choice E) Intermittent explosive disorder involves impulsive, agitated behavior; however, it does not involve inattention symptoms and presents with an excessive level of aggression not characteristic of ADHD. Educational objective: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder can first present clinically as repeated struggles in adult-specific roles and responsibilities. Assessment should involve consideration of alternate causes (eg, personality disorders, anxiety disorders) of inattention or impulsivity/hyperactivity symptoms.

questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism Risk factors Advanced maternal age Gravida ≥5 (live births or stillbirths) Cesarean or instrumental delivery Placenta previa or abruption Preeclampsia Clinical presentation Shock Hypoxemic respiratory failure Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy Coma or seizures Treatment Respiratory & hemodynamic support ± Transfusion Following artificial rupture of membranes, this patient developed increasing pain and anxiety with rapid-onset hypotension, tachycardia, and fetal heart rate decelerations. This constellation of findings is concerning for amniotic fluid embolism syndrome (AFES), a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency that typically occurs during labor or immediately postpartum. When amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation, it can initiate a massive anaphylactoid reaction that results in the classic triad of hypoxemia (eg, respiratory failure, pulmonary edema), hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC). This inflammatory reaction generates pulmonary vasoconstrictors (increased respirations and decreased oxygen saturation) and prostaglandins (tense uterus with increasing pain), leading to fetal acidosis (fetal decelerations). DIC, a hallmark of AFES, occurs when amniotic fluid activates both factor VII and platelets, triggering the coagulation cascade. Persistent bleeding at line sites (ie, intravenous lines, epidural catheter) is often the earliest clue to a developing coagulopathy. Urgent coagulation studies are required to confirm the coagulopathy; abnormal studies are part of the diagnostic criteria for AFES. This allows for early and aggressive treatment with massive blood product transfusion to reverse the consumptive coagulopathy to prevent devastating hemorrhage. Additional management focuses on supportive care of the mother to correct the hypoxemia (eg, oxygen, intubation, mechanical ventilation) and hypotension (eg, vasopressors), with prompt delivery of the infant. Despite early recognition, few women survive, and those who do have a high incidence of neurologic damage. (Choices A and C) Increased abdominal pain despite epidural analgesia can occur with labor progression as the fetal head descends through the pelvis and stimulates sacral pain fibers. However, increased respiratory rate and hypoxemia are not part of normal labor. Increasing the epidural infusion rate may help alleviate the increasing pain; however, it does not address the pain's underlying cause, which needs to be investigated. (Choice B) This patient's tense uterus with palpable, frequent contractions and new fetal decelerations is concerning for placental abruption, which can be evaluated with abdominal ultrasound. Although severe abruption can lead to DIC and hypotension, it is not typically associated with hypoxemia. AFES evaluation should be prioritized as delays could be fatal. (Choice D) Removing and replacing the epidural catheter during a coagulopathic state are contraindicated because they increase the risk for epidural hematoma, which can cause severe neurologic damage. Educational objective: Amniotic fluid embolus syndrome is a rare, catastrophic complication that results from amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. Common signs include hypoxia, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Urgent coagulation studies can be used to diagnose early coagulopathy.

Following artificial rupture of membranes, this patient developed increasing pain and anxiety with rapid-onset hypotension, tachycardia, and fetal heart rate decelerations.  This constellation of findings is concerning for amniotic fluid embolism syndrome (AFES), a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency that typically occurs during labor or immediately postpartum.

When amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation, it can initiate a massive anaphylactoid reaction that results in the classic triad of hypoxemia (eg, respiratory failure, pulmonary edema), hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC).  This inflammatory reaction generates pulmonary vasoconstrictors (increased respirations and decreased oxygen saturation) and prostaglandins (tense uterus with increasing pain), leading to fetal acidosis (fetal decelerations).

DIC, a hallmark of AFES, occurs when amniotic fluid activates both factor VII and platelets, triggering the coagulation cascade.  Persistent bleeding at line sites (ie, intravenous lines, epidural catheter) is often the earliest clue to a developing coagulopathy.  Urgent coagulation studies are required to confirm the coagulopathy; abnormal studies are part of the diagnostic criteria for AFES.  This allows for early and aggressive treatment with massive blood product transfusion to reverse the consumptive coagulopathy to prevent devastating hemorrhage.

Additional management focuses on supportive care of the mother to correct the hypoxemia (eg, oxygen, intubation, mechanical ventilation) and hypotension (eg, vasopressors), with prompt delivery of the infant.  Despite early recognition, few women survive, and those who do have a high incidence of neurologic damage.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  This patient's tense uterus with palpable, frequent contractions and new fetal decelerations is concerning for placental abruption, which can be evaluated with abdominal ultrasound.  Although severe abruption can lead to DIC and hypotension, it is not typically associated with hypoxemia.  AFES evaluation should be prioritized as delays could be fatal.
wrongAnswers.C: See the shared discussion for choice A.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Removing and replacing the epidural catheter during a coagulopathic state are contraindicated because they increase the risk for epidural hematoma, which can cause severe neurologic damage.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old healthy woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 41 weeks gestation is undergoing induction of labor with an oxytocin infusion. After several hours, the patient has painful contractions and receives epidural analgesia for pain management. After placement of the epidural, she no longer has contraction pains, and artificial rupture of membranes is performed, during which a large amount of clear fluid returns. Several minutes later, the patient has increasingly intense lower back and abdominal pain and begins to feel anxious. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 24/min. Oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. Fetal heart rate tracing shows a baseline of 160/min and multiple decelerations. The epidural catheter has bleeding around the insertion site. The uterus has palpable contractions and is tense. There is no abdominal rebound or guarding. On cervical examination, the patient's cervix has dilated to 6 cm and 100% effacement. questions.explanation: During pregnancy, nausea and vomiting can be physiologic or pathologic; differentiating between the two determines the potential for additional obstetric complications and guides patient management. Distinguishing features are as follows: Physiologic nausea and vomiting of pregnancy typically begin in the early first trimester and gradually peak at 9 weeks gestation. Symptoms are usually mild, self-limited, and there is no associated abdominal pain, diarrhea, or constipation. Laboratory results are normal. First-line treatment is with dietary modification and pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation (Choice B). In contrast, pathologic nausea and vomiting should be suspected if symptoms develop or worsen after 10 weeks gestation. Other findings that warrant additional evaluation include acute-onset severe symptoms (as in this patient), abdominal pain, biliary colic (eg, intermittent, postprandial abdominal pain), fever, and bilious or bloody emesis. Laboratory abnormalities (eg, leukocytosis, electrolyte abnormalities, elevated aminotransferases) vary, depending on the underlying pathology. In this patient at 12 weeks gestation with biliary colic and right upper quadrant (RUQ) discomfort, the most likely diagnosis is symptomatic cholelithiasis. Diagnosis is confirmed with RUQ abdominal ultrasound. (Choice A) A 24-hour urine total protein collection is used to evaluate for preeclampsia in patients with new-onset hypertension (ie, ≥140 mm Hg systolic or ≥90 mm Hg diastolic) at ≥20 weeks gestation. This patient's blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg, but she has no proteinuria (normal urinalysis) or signs of end-organ damage (eg, aminotransferases not >2× normal). Her hypertension is likely pain-related, and it can be reevaluated after administering antiemetics and an analgesic. (Choice C) Reassurance is inappropriate in this patient with multiple features that warrant additional evaluation for pathologic nausea and vomiting. (Choice D) Elevated β-hCG levels (eg, twin gestation, hydatidiform mole) may contribute to hyperemesis gravidarum, a type of pathologic nausea/vomiting in pregnancy that can cause epigastric or RUQ discomfort due to persistent vomiting. However, patients typically have electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypokalemia, hypochloremia) and ketonuria. In addition, this patient with a single fetal heart tone is unlikely to have a twin gestation or hydatidiform mole; therefore, a β-hCG level would not change management. Educational objective: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy associated with recurrent, postprandial upper abdominal pain and right upper quadrant (RUQ) discomfort suggest symptomatic cholelithiasis (ie, biliary colic). Diagnosis is with RUQ abdominal ultrasonography.

questions.explanation: Individuals who enroll in a clinical trial face risks related to the investigational treatment, which may not be fully known at the time the trial is conducted. In addition, participants may receive treatment, whether in the intervention or control arm of the study, that is ultimately found to be inferior for the condition being studied. Participants in resource-limited settings may not have ready access to assistance (eg, emergency department care) in the event of a serious adverse outcome. Although research in resource-limited countries is often necessary to help validate treatment effects in diverse populations, study design should include protections for participants. In particular, studies that use inactive placebo arms pose ethical concerns because they withhold treatment from participants who may not otherwise have access to care. A placebo arm is inappropriate for this study because effective antiviral medications are currently available. The study should use a control arm that includes an antiviral treatment in accordance with the current standard of care. (Choice B) Experimental treatments are not generally used in control arms because comparative effectiveness with respect to standard treatment is often unknown. The uncertainty can lead to over- or underestimation of treatment effects of the investigational intervention. (Choice C) Participant selection (eg, sample size, demographic diversity) must be carefully planned to reduce bias and improve external validity. However, enrolling a large and diverse subject population does not guarantee the safety of individual participants if a potentially harmful treatment is administered or a standard treatment is withheld. (Choice D) Research subjects commonly receive reimbursement commensurate with the time and requirements of the study. Excessive payment should be avoided because it may induce individuals to accept risks they might otherwise not agree to, undermining informed consent and patient autonomy. In this study, ensuring that potentially effective treatments are not withheld from participants during the trial is more important than paying individuals to participate. (Choice E) The study protocol should address adverse event monitoring among all participants, not just those in the active intervention arm. Participants should be protected by ensuring they receive treatment equivalent to the standard of care. Educational objective: Research participants in resource-limited settings may not have ready access to standard treatment or to assistance in the event of a serious adverse outcome. Therefore, study design should include protections for the participants; control arm participants should receive treatment equivalent to the current standard of care rather than placebo.

questions.explanation: Foreign body aspiration Clinical features ± History of choking event with sudden-onset cough Symptoms depend on location Trachea/main bronchus: acute respiratory distress, cyanosis, stridor (trachea), hemoptysis (bronchial) Lower airway: chronic/recurrent cough Examination findings Focal, unilateral &/or monophonic wheeze Focal area of diminished breath sounds X-ray findings Hyperinflation of affected side ± mediastinal shift toward unaffected side Atelectasis if complete obstruction ± Foreign body Complications Recurrent pneumonia Bronchiectasis Management Bronchoscopic removal This patient has a chronic cough and recurrent pneumonia, findings that raise suspicion for an underlying systemic disorder or a local anatomic abnormality. Systemic disorders (eg, immunodeficiency, cystic fibrosis) usually cause recurrent infections affecting different regions of the lung and are often associated with poor growth, findings not seen in this patient (Choice A). In contrast, recurrent pneumonia of the same region (particularly the right middle/lower lobes) in an otherwise healthy, young child should raise concern for a retained foreign body. Foreign body aspiration is most common in children age 1-3 and typically involves food or a small toy. In cases where the choking event is unwitnessed, the diagnosis is often delayed. The aspirated object obstructs the bronchus, preventing clearance of secretions and allowing for bacterial colonization and infection. Children may have chronic cough and/or wheezing or experience complications of a retained foreign body, such as recurrent pneumonia (as seen here) or bronchiectasis (due to destruction of the bronchial walls from chronic inflammation). The right lower lobe is most commonly implicated due to the vertical orientation of the right mainstem bronchus. Although antibiotics may resolve the fever, the infection is likely to recur without extraction of the foreign body. Definitive treatment involves rigid bronchoscopy to remove the obstruction and prevent further complications. (Choice B) In patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), microaspiration of gastric contents into the trachea can cause recurrent cough and wheeze, but symptoms would be associated with eating rather than activity. In addition, aspiration pneumonia from GERD typically occurs in patients with neurologic conditions (eg, neuromuscular disease) and would not be expected in an otherwise healthy child due to a protective cough reflex. (Choice C) Moderate persistent asthma is characterized by daily cough that is classically worse with activity, but nonfocal wheezing (in contrast to this child's localized wheezing) would be expected on examination in a patient with uncontrolled asthma. Moreover, although patients with asthma are prone to more severe manifestations and complications of respiratory infections, asthma does not cause recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia. (Choice D) Paradoxical vocal cord motion presents with episodic cough, dyspnea, and stridor/wheezing that can mimic an asthma exacerbation. This diagnosis would not explain recurrent pneumonia. Educational objective: Foreign body aspiration should be suspected in a young child with recurrent pneumonia, particularly when the right lower lobe is involved.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents due to worsening cough and fever for 5 days. He has had 2 episodes of right lower lobe pneumonia in the past 4 months. The patient had fever with each episode that resolved with antibiotics; however, his cough has persisted for the past 4 months. The cough is worse with activity. He lives at home with his mother and father and does not attend day care. Immunizations are up to date. Height and weight are tracking at the 70th percentile. Temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 38/min. Examination shows crackles and expiratory wheezes over the right lower lobe. Heart sounds are normal, and the abdomen is soft and nontender. Chest radiograph reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following underlying conditions is most likely responsible for this patient's findings?

questions.explanation: Occupational HIV exposure High-risk contact (postexposure prophylaxis* recommended) Exposure of: Mucous membranes, nonintact skin, percutaneous exposure & Exposure to: Blood, semen, vaginal secretions, body fluid with visible blood (uncertain risk: cerebrospinal fluid, pleural/pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, amniotic fluid) Low-risk contact (postexposure prophylaxis not recommended) Exposure of: Intact skin OR exposure to: Urine, feces, nasal secretions, saliva, tears (without visible blood) *Three-drug regimen: 2 nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (eg, tenofovir, emtricitabine) plus integrase strand transfer inhibitor (eg, raltegravir) or protease inhibitor. HIV seroconversion following occupational exposure is rare and occurs primarily with percutaneous injury (eg, needlestick). HIV postexposure prophylactic antiretroviral therapy (PEP) is recommended following percutaneous exposure or exposure of mucous membranes or nonintact skin to blood or other potentially infectious body fluids (eg, semen, vaginal secretions, other fluids with visible blood) from a source patient who is HIV positive. In contrast, this health care worker had a low-risk exposure (ie, superficial exposure to intact skin) to blood from a patient with chronic HIV infection. The risk for transdermal infection via intact skin is minimal; the potential benefit of PEP, if any, will likely be outweighed by the risk from treatment. Therefore, all visible contamination should be cleaned with soap and water, but no testing or treatment is required (Choices D and E). (Choices B and C) CD4 cell count and HIV viral load are commonly used in the management of patients with chronic HIV infection (eg, estimation of risk for opportunistic infection). Although the risk for transmission is greater from a source patient with a high viral load, the decision to initiate occupational PEP is based on the nature of the exposure (ie, type of exposure and body fluid) rather than the current status of HIV infection in the source patient. Educational objective: HIV postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended following occupational exposure to blood or potentially infectious body fluids from a source patient who is HIV-positive via percutaneous exposure or exposure to mucous membranes or nonintact skin. The risk for HIV transmission following occupational exposure via intact skin is low, so PEP is not indicated.

questions.explanation: This pregnant patient with heavy vaginal bleeding and passage of tan-colored tissue likely had a spontaneous abortion (SAB), or fetal loss at <20 weeks gestation. Patients with SABs are evaluated for the following: Hemodynamic status and bleeding on pelvic examination. Patients with active, heavy vaginal bleeding, a dilated cervix, and hemodynamic instability require emergency suction curettage (Choice E). Signs of infection, which may indicate a septic abortion requiring suction curettage and broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (Choice B). Patients with a septic abortion typically have fever, purulent discharge, and severe uterine tenderness, none of which are present in this patient. Type of abortion based on the location of the products of conception (POCs) on pelvic ultrasound. Patients with retained POCs (eg, intrauterine vascular mass, fetal parts) can receive misoprostol and mifepristone to promote tissue passage (Choice D). This patient's decrease in bleeding and 2-cm heterogenous endometrium (a normal finding) indicate complete passage of all POCs. The mild uterine enlargement (6-week-size) will resolve as the uterus involutes. Maternal blood typing is performed because obstetric bleeding, including SABs at later gestational ages (13 weeks in this patient), can result in maternal-fetal hemorrhage. This introduces the risk for Rh(D) alloimmunization in patients who are Rh(D) negative. This hemodynamically stable patient with no retained POCs and no signs of infection has an uncomplicated, complete SAB, which is usually managed expectantly. Anti-D immune globulin is also required because the patient is Rh(D) negative and the fetal blood type is unknown. (Choice C) Diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated for a suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which can present with first-trimester bleeding and a closed cervix. However, patients typically have acute abdominal pain, a complex adnexal mass, and hemoperitoneum. questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, comes to the emergency department due to vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 13 weeks ago, and 2 weeks ago the patient had a positive home urine pregnancy test. Yesterday, she began having intense lower abdominal cramps along with vaginal bleeding. The patient reports soaking 8 pads overnight, and she noticed some tan-colored tissue intermixed with large blood clots. Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 108/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 102/min. The abdomen is soft and nontender to palpation. On pelvic examination, there is a small amount of bright red blood coming from the cervix. The cervix is closed, and the uterus is 6-week-sized, retroverted, and slightly tender to palpation. A pelvic ultrasound reveals a heterogenous endometrium measuring 2 cm, a simple cyst in the right adnexa, and a small amount of free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac. Hemoglobin is 10.9 mg/dL and maternal blood type is O, Rh negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This case-control study evaluated the association between severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use and brain cancer in 50 adults with brain cancer and 200 adults without brain cancer. The study estimated the odds ratio (OR) of exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use among adults with brain cancer compared to adults without brain cancer at OR of 1.2 with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.64-2.23. The OR is a measure of association between an exposure to a risk factor and an outcome, usually defined as the odds of an exposure in cases divided by the odds of the same exposure in controls. OR = (odds of exposure in cases) / (odds of exposure in controls) An OR greater than 1.0 indicates that the odds of exposure are greater in cases than in controls. The CI of an OR indicates, with a certain confidence level, whether a given OR is statistically different from the null value (OR = 1.0). A CI that excludes the null value is statistically significant at that confidence level. In this study, the 95% CI (0.64-2.23) includes the null value (OR = 1.0). This means that, although the estimated OR (ie, OR = 1.2) indicates that severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use was 1.2 times more common in adults with brain cancer than in adults without brain cancer, there is no statistical evidence of a significant association. Therefore, the students are incorrect because the findings are not statistically significant. (Choice A) A CI that excludes the null value reflects statistical significance. However, the null value for the OR is 1.0 (ie, odds in cases are the same as in controls). The null value for a risk difference would be 0 (ie, no difference in risk). (Choice B) An OR greater than 1.0 indicates that the odds of exposure are greater in cases than in controls; however, given the lack of statistical significance, the students' conclusion is not correct. (Choice C) In a case-control study, if the prevalence of the disease is low (ie, <10%), then the OR approaches the relative risk. Brain cancer is very uncommon, so the OR from this case-control study is an estimate of the risk of disease. Educational objective: An odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.0 indicates that the exposure is associated with an increase in the odds of an outcome. A confidence interval that excludes the null value (OR = 1.0) is statistically significant.

questions.stem: A group of students conducted a case-control study to evaluate the association between severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use and brain cancer. Cases (n = 50) were adults age 21-45 with brain cancer, and controls (n = 200) were adults age 21-45 without brain cancer. All participants completed a structured questionnaire to collect data on demographics, general health, and level of exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use. A total of 27 cases and 99 controls had a severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use (odds ratio of 1.2 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.64-2.23). The students reported that severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use was 1.2 times more common in adults with brain cancer than in adults without brain cancer, and that severe exposure to electromagnetic fields from cell phone use is significantly associated with brain cancer. Based on this information, which of the following is true about the students' conclusion?

questions.explanation: Osteoporotic hip fractures are common, and typically occur at the femoral neck or intertrochanteric region following minor trauma (eg, ground level fall). In contrast, this patient has no traumatic injury and has insidious, dull, aching pain; imaging confirms a subtrochanteric stress fracture, which is an atypical location for an osteoporotic fracture. Atypical femur fractures are a recognized complication of prolonged bisphosphonate use. Bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate) increase bone density (or slow the rate of bone loss) by suppressing osteoclast activity. However, with prolonged use (ie, >5 years), bisphosphonates prevent appropriate bone turnover (ie, "frozen bone"), leading to skeletal fragility and increased risk for atypical fracture. To prevent this complication, a 3- to 5-year drug holiday is recommended after 5 years of bisphosphonate treatment. (Choice A) X-ray findings consistent with age-related degeneration (eg, osteoarthritis) include joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and periarticular osteophyte formation, findings not seen in this patient. Age-related osteoporosis typically presents with femoral neck or intertrochanteric fractures, not subtrochanteric fractures. Moreover, this patient's bone density increased with therapy, making osteoporosis less likely. (Choice B) Heavy alcohol use (eg, >2 drinks/day) is associated with bone loss and increased risk of osteoporotic fracture; this patient's alcohol consumption is not expected to increase her fracture risk. (Choice C) The risk of osteoporotic fractures and stress fractures is increased in patients with a low BMI. Although having higher BMI may slightly increase the risk of atypical stress fracture in patients who take bisphosphonates, it is not the underlying cause. (Choice E) Bone metastasis can cause pathologic fractures due to localized loss of bone. However, MRI is very sensitive for metastatic lesions, which were not noted on this patient's study. Educational objective: Prolonged bisphosphonate treatment lasting >5 years is associated with an increased risk of atypical stress fractures in the subtrochanteric region of the femur.
