questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressively worsening dull, aching pain in the right groin for the past 2 weeks. Walking for longer than 2 minutes or going up more than 2 flights of stairs exacerbates the discomfort. She reports no trauma or overuse. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoporosis. She has been taking alendronate for the past 7 years; other medications include metformin and lisinopril. The patient drinks a shot of vodka daily. Vital signs are normal. BMI is 32 kg/m2. Physical examination reveals pain localized to the right groin that is worse with internal and external rotation of the hip. X-ray of the right hip is normal. MRI reveals a stress fracture of the lateral aspect of the subtrochanteric region of right femur and no other significant abnormalities. DEXA scan shows that bone density has increased compared to 5 years ago. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the fracture in this patient?

questions.explanation: Antepartum fetal surveillance Test Description Normal result Abnormal result Nonstress test External fetal heart rate monitoring for 20-40 minutes Reactive: ≥2 accelerations 2 points Nonreactive: <2 accelerations Recurrent variable or late decelerations 0 points Biophysical profile Nonstress test plus ultrasound assessment of the following: Amniotic fluid volume Fetal breathing movement Fetal movement Fetal tone 2 points per category if normal (maximum 10/10) 0 points per category if abnormal 8 or 10 points Equivocal: 6 points Abnormal: 0, 2, or 4 points Oligohydramnios Contraction stress test External fetal heart rate monitoring during spontaneous or induced (eg, oxytocin, nipple stimulation) uterine contractions No late or recurrent variable decelerations Late decelerations with >50% of contractions Doppler sonography of the umbilical artery Evaluation of umbilical artery flow in fetal intrauterine growth restriction only High-velocity diastolic flow in umbilical artery Decreased, absent, or reversed end-diastolic flow This patient presents with decreased fetal movement, a symptom that may be benign (eg, normal fetal sleep cycle) or life-threatening (eg, fetal hypoxemia, acidosis, stillbirth). A nonstress test (NST) is a form of antenatal fetal surveillance used to monitor fetal heart rate in order to assess fetal status and identify compromised (eg, hypoxemic) fetuses at risk of adverse outcomes. During an NST, the heart rate of a well-oxygenated fetus rises with fetal movement (accelerations). A reactive NST (≥2 accelerations) has a high negative predictive value for fetal compromise. In contrast, a nonreactive NST has a high false-positive rate and low positive predictive value for fetal compromise; it requires further evaluation with either a biophysical profile (BPP) or contraction stress test (CST). These tests are equivalent in assessing fetal status, and selection is based on available resources and relevant contraindications. A BPP includes an NST plus an ultrasound for amniotic fluid volume, fetal movement, tone, and breathing within 30 minutes. A CST is similar to an NST, but contractions are first induced with oxytocin or nipple stimulation. Patients with contraindications to uterine contractions (eg, placenta previa [as in this patient], history of uterine rupture) should not undergo a CST (Choice D). Therefore, the most appropriate next test for this patient is a BPP. (Choice B) Although nonreactive NSTs lack the reassurance of a reactive NST, they are not diagnostic for fetal compromise (ie, high false-positive rate). A follow-up test is required. If the BPP is also abnormal, cesarean delivery may be warranted for this patient with placenta previa. (Choice C) Fetal sleep cycles are a common cause of nonreactive NSTs. Therefore, monitoring can last ≥40 minutes (average length of a fetal sleep cycle). However, continuing this patient's NST would not be helpful because vibroacoustic stimulation, which typically wakes the fetus and induces movement, did not produce accelerations. Further testing is needed to determine if there is underlying pathology. (Choice E) Umbilical artery flow velocimetry is used to monitor growth-restricted fetuses (estimated fetal weight <10th percentile). This fetus has normal growth. Educational objective: Patients with decreased fetal movement require a nonstress test (NST) followed by a biophysical profile (BPP) or a contraction stress test (CST) if the NST is nonreactive. A BPP rather than a CST is performed if uterine contractions are contraindicated (eg, placenta previa).

questions.explanation: Recommended treatment for latent tuberculosis infection Rifamycin-based therapy (preferred) Rifampin daily for 4 months Rifampin plus isoniazid daily for 3 months Rifapentine plus isoniazid weekly for 3 months Isoniazid monotherapy for 6-9 months* *Used primarily for patients who cannot tolerate rifamycin due to drug interactions or hypersensitivity reactions. This patient with a positive interferon gamma release assay has negative tuberculosis symptom screening and chest x-ray indicating latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). LTBI is treated with either a rifamycin-based regimen (eg, rifampin daily for 4 months) or isoniazid monotherapy. Although both provide excellent cure rates (>90%), rifamycin-based regimens are generally preferred due to shorter treatment duration and less serious adverse effects. However, rifamycin medications have a large number of drug interactions because they are a major inducer of the cytochrome P-450 system (eg, CYP3A4). This can reduce the bioavailability and potency of several medications, most notably warfarin, antiepileptics, antiarrhythmics, methadone, and oral hormonal contraceptive pills. Therefore, patients taking oral hormonal contraceptive pills require an alternate form of contraception while taking rifamycin. (Choice A) LTBI is considered noninfectious because acid-fast bacilli are walled off in a cavity and not freely shed in respiratory droplets or secretions. Therefore, patients with LTBI do not generally need to avoid contact with immunosuppressed individuals. (Choice B) Because rifampin increases the metabolism of hormonal contraception, this patient will not be adequately protected from pregnancy with hormonal contraception alone during treatment. She should be advised to use a nonhormonal form of contraception while on rifampin. (Choice C) Ethambutol is used as part of conventional four-drug therapy for active tuberculosis. A major adverse effect is the development of optic neuritis, which should prompt ophthalmologic consultation. This typically resolves over weeks with the cessation of the medication. Rifamycin medications do not typically trigger ophthalmologic adverse effects. (Choice D) Isoniazid is frequently associated with hepatotoxicity. Although isoniazid-induced hepatitis is often mild and does not necessitate alteration in treatment, it may be severe or fulminant in a small minority of patients. To limit hepatotoxicity, all patients on isoniazid therapy should be advised to strictly avoid alcohol use. This is not required for those on rifampin monotherapy. Educational objective: Rifamycin-based therapy for latent tuberculosis infection has fewer adverse effects and shorter treatment duration compared to isoniazid monotherapy. However, rifamycins are potent inducers of the cytochrome P-450 system and may reduce bioavailability of several medications (eg, warfarin, methadone, hormonal contraceptive pills). Patients taking hormonal contraception who require rifamycin treatment should be advised to use a nonhormonal form of contraception to prevent pregnancy.

questions.explanation: This patient has double vision due to unilateral lateral rectus palsy (CN VI dysfunction). Although she had preeclampsia, which can be associated with neurologic findings and have postpartum manifestations, it has now resolved (normal blood pressure without antihypertensives, lack of other preeclamptic signs such as edema and right upper quadrant pain). The patient's prior episodes of neurologic dysfunction disseminated in space (blurry vision of left eye, numbness and tingling of left hand) and time (months to years) are most consistent with multiple sclerosis, which often worsens in the postpartum period. Imaging findings are also disseminated in space (multiple CNS locations) and time (present then resolve). MRI lesions can often be correlated directly to the clinical presentation (ie, enhancement of optic nerve in a patient with blurry vision). Lesions are due to inflammatory plaques that are hyperintense on MRI. Typically, multiple, scattered, ovoid lesions are in the periventricular regions and spinal cord. (Choice A) Lateral ventricle enlargement occurs with noncommunicating hydrocephalus (due to cerebrospinal fluid flow obstruction), which often presents with signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, vomiting). Normal pressure hydrocephalus (associated with ventriculomegaly) typically presents with a wide-based gait, urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment. (Choice B) Pregnancy and postpartum states increase the risk for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can be seen on MR venography as a flow deficit in the cavernous venous sinus. Usually, headache and signs of increased intracranial pressure occur, findings absent in this patient. Seizures and stroke symptoms (localizing to venous drainage territories) are also common. (Choice C) Brainstem strokes (showing ischemic changes on MRI) classically lead to synchronous crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral motor and/or sensory deficits). This patient has no crossed signs (left eye symptoms, left hand numbness), and dissemination in time and space makes multiple sclerosis more likely. (Choice D) Visual changes (eg, blurred vision, photopsia), common in preeclampsia with severe features, are a manifestation of posterior cerebral edema (ie, posterior reversible encephalopathy). However, this patient's visual disturbances developed following the resolution of preeclampsia (normotensive without antihypertensives with a normal neurologic examination), making this diagnosis less likely. Educational objective: Multiple sclerosis often worsens, or initially presents, in the postpartum period. It is defined by neurologic lesions disseminated in time and space. MRI typically shows multiple, scattered, ovoid plaques in the periventricular white matter.

choices: Reassurance that amenorrhea is normal after IUD removal
questions.explanation: This patient has secondary amenorrhea (ie, no menses for >3 months in women with previously regular menses or >6 months with previously irregular menses). Dysfunction at any level of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis can cause amenorrhea. Initial evaluation is with pregnancy testing and FSH, prolactin, and TSH levels. In patients (such as this one) with normal initial laboratory results, a progesterone withdrawal test can be used to assess the effect of estrogen on the uterine endometrium. In this test, progesterone is administered for several days and then discontinued. Bleeding after progesterone withdrawal confirms ovarian estrogen production. This is because estrogen normally stimulates endometrial proliferation and thickening, and progesterone normally maintains the endometrium (eg, supporting implantation). Therefore, withdrawal of oral progesterone leads to shedding of the endometrium (mimicking the menstrual bleeding following ovulation). Secondary amenorrhea despite the presence of estrogen is most commonly due to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), in which elevated estrogen levels cause a relatively normal FSH level but do not allow for ovulation due to an imbalanced FSH/LH ratio. Absence of withdrawal bleeding suggests either no endometrial proliferation due to hypoestrogenism (with an inappropriately normal FSH [eg, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea]) or structural abnormalities (eg, intrauterine adhesions, cervical stenosis). In addition to secondary amenorrhea, this patient also has features of hyperandrogenism (eg, chest acne); therefore, withdrawal bleeding confirms PCOS as the etiology of this patient's amenorrhea. (Choice A) Dexamethasone suppression testing can be used to assess for Cushing syndrome, which can also present with signs of hyperandrogenism (eg, irregular menstrual cycles, acne). However, patients typically have low FSH levels because the elevated androgen levels suppress GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus. (Choice B) Endometrial biopsy is indicated for patients with risk factors for endometrial malignancy and abnormal uterine bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding. This young patient with amenorrhea is unlikely to have endometrial cancer. In addition, her recent use of a progestin-releasing IUD is a protective factor against endometrial cancer. (Choice D) Progestin-releasing IUDs induce amenorrhea by thinning the endometrium; however, menses typically resume within 1 or 2 months of IUD removal. (Choice E) TSH is more sensitive than either T3 or T4 for diagnosing hypothyroidism; therefore, a serum TSH level is sufficient to exclude thyroid dysfunction as the cause of secondary amenorrhea. Educational objective: Progesterone withdrawal testing is performed in patients with secondary amenorrhea to assess the effect of estrogen on the endometrium. Withdrawal bleeding confirms ovarian estrogen production; in contrast, the lack of withdrawal bleeding indicates either hypoestrogenism or structural abnormalities (eg, intrauterine adhesions, cervical stenosis).

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 aborta 1, comes to the office for evaluation of amenorrhea. The patient desires another child, so she had her progestin-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) removed 6 months ago. There was some spotting immediately following removal, but she has not had a menstrual cycle since. The IUD was placed for contraception following her second pregnancy, which ended in a spontaneous abortion that was complicated by a retained placenta requiring suction dilation and curettage. The first pregnancy resulted in a term vaginal delivery. Menarche was at age 12, and she has always had heavy and irregular periods. Vital signs are normal. BMI is 24 kg/m2. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Acne is noted on the cheeks and upper chest. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Pelvic examination shows a normal-appearing cervix. The uterus is mobile, and the adnexa are nonpalpable on bimanual examination. Urine pregnancy test is negative. FSH, prolactin, and TSH hormone levels are normal. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Pathogenesis Premature arrest of pulmonary development Alveolar hypoplasia with ↓ septation Impaired vasculogenesis Clinical diagnosis Premature infant with continued supplemental oxygen requirement ≥28 days from birth* Chest x-ray Mild: diffuse hazy infiltrates, low/normal lung volumes Severe: fibrocystic changes, hyperinflation Treatment Supportive (eg, oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction/diuretics) Complications Pulmonary artery hypertension Cardiovascular disease (eg, hypertension) Recurrent respiratory infections *Some definitions include an oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (ie, gestational + chronologic age). This preterm infant with a persistent oxygen requirement for ≥28 days after birth now has hypertension. Elevated blood pressure in infants is usually due to renal parenchymal disease or chronic lung disease; in this case, the most likely cause is bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), or chronic lung disease of prematurity. BPD is due to the premature arrest of fetal lung development (ie, impaired alveolarization), and the incidence is inversely correlated with gestational age. As new alveoli are formed over the first few months of life, most infants experience symptomatic improvement. However, complications of BPD can include: Systemic hypertension: Elevated blood pressure is detected in about half of infants with BPD and is in part due to increased circulating catecholamines causing vasoconstriction; the use of postnatal corticosteroids to treat BPD may also contribute. Hypertension usually spontaneously resolves within a few months. Pulmonary artery hypertension: Disrupted vasculogenesis in premature infants can result in thickening of the muscular layer of the pulmonary arteries. In addition, prolonged alveolar hypoxia in patients with BPD can cause vasoconstriction and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. Pulmonary hypertension may improve with lung growth but is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in infants with BPD. (Choice A) Maternal antenatal corticosteroid administration may be correlated with increased blood pressure in a neonate in the days immediately following birth but would not cause new-onset hypertension in a 3-month-old infant. (Choice B) Aortic coarctation presents with blood pressure that is elevated in the upper extremities but low (eg, >20 mm Hg difference) in the legs; diminished/delayed femoral pulses are also expected. This infant's strong pulses, similar blood pressures in the upper and lower extremities, and 3/6 holosystolic murmur are most consistent with an isolated ventricular septal defect. (Choice D) Intracranial hemorrhage can lead to increased intracranial and systemic pressures, and premature infants are at increased risk due to fragile germinal matrix vessels. However, behavioral changes (eg, lethargy, irritability) and a bulging fontanelle would be expected and are not seen in this alert, well-appearing infant. (Choice E) Umbilical artery catheterization is a risk factor for renal artery embolism and, in turn, ischemic kidney injury causing hypertension. However, this complication is unlikely 3 months after short-term catheter placement. In addition, this patient has no decreased urine output to suggest renal injury. Educational objective: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is characterized by a prolonged oxygen requirement in infants born prematurely. Patients often have systemic hypertension due to increased catecholamines.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old female is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for new-onset hypertension. She was born at 26 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. The mother received betamethasone prior to delivery due to preterm labor. The patient was apneic at birth and required intubation. Umbilical venous and arterial catheters were placed for resuscitation and removed the following day. After one week, she was extubated to continuous positive airway pressure and continues to require supplemental oxygen. The patient receives breastmilk via orogastric tube and has had 10 wet diapers and 2 yellow, seedy stools in the past 24 hours. Temperature is 37 C (99 F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 45/min. Blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg in the right arm and 115/75 mm Hg in the right leg. Physical examination shows a well-appearing, alert infant. The anterior fontanelle is flat. Auscultation reveals a normal S1 and S2 with a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border. Breath sounds are coarse bilaterally. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. Brachial and femoral pulses are 2+. Which of the following is the most likely cause of elevated blood pressure in this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient with a significant cigarette smoking history has expiratory wheezing suggestive of airflow obstruction. On pulmonary function testing, flow-volume loop (FVL) shape helps distinguish the nature (fixed vs variable) and location (intrathoracic vs extrathoracic) of airflow obstruction: Fixed obstruction (intrathoracic or extrathoracic): In patients with fixed (immobile) obstruction, airflow is blocked by immobile narrowing of the intrathoracic (eg, bronchogenic carcinoma) or extrathoracic (eg, thyroid carcinoma) upper airway (Choice C). Both inspiratory and expiratory airflow are equally reduced throughout; therefore, the FVL would be flattened throughout the respiratory cycle. Variable extrathoracic obstruction: During inspiration, extrathoracic airway pressure drops below atmospheric pressure, which favors airway collapse but is normally counteracted by vocal cord abduction; conversely, during expiration, the upper airway is propped open. Vocal cord paralysis would cause variable extrathoracic obstruction with inspiratory airflow reduction (eg, flat floor of lower half of FVL), but expiratory airflow is preserved; moreover, it would be accompanied by inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheezing (Choice E). Variable intrathoracic obstruction: In patients with variable (mobile) intrathoracic obstruction, positive pleural pressure generated during expiration causes intrathoracic airways to dynamically collapse and (mobile) tissue to be pulled into the airway. This manifests as expiratory flow reduction (eg, flat ceiling of upper half of FVL) with inspiratory flow preservation, as seen in this patient. Uniform expiratory flattening reflects immediate collapse, signifying flaccidity of the large airways (eg, trachea, mainstem bronchi). Tracheobronchomalacia (TBM) represents weakness of the anterior tracheobronchial cartilage caused by chronic irritation (eg, smoking, acid reflux) or prior injury (eg, prolonged intubation). Patients commonly have dyspnea and turbulent expiratory sounds (grossly audible "noisy breathing"). The dynamic airway collapse can be directly visualized on bronchoscopy or expiratory-inspiratory chest CT images, confirming the diagnosis. Like TBM, asthma may also present with dyspnea and expiratory airflow obstruction. However, asthma involves bronchospasm of smaller airways, producing worse obstruction toward the end of expiration (vs uniform throughout), leading to a scalloped appearance of the FVL. In addition, beta agonists (ie, smooth muscle relaxants) relieve asthmatic small airway bronchoconstriction, but they can worsen TBM (as in this patient) because they also relax tracheal tone (Choice A). (Choice B) Pulmonary fibrosis produces a restrictive pattern characterized by supranormal early expiratory airflow (stiff lungs increase recoil) with lower lung volumes. Therefore, the FVL of restriction appears peaked and narrow ("witch's hat"). In addition, inspiratory crackles would be heard on lung auscultation. Educational objective: Tracheobronchomalacia involves flaccidity of the large airways and is often the sequela of chronic irritation (eg, smoking, acid reflux) or injury (eg, prolonged intubation). Flow-volume loop testing demonstrates isolated flattening of the upper half of the loop. Diagnosis is confirmed by direct visualization of luminal collapse on bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of exertional dyspnea and "noisy breathing" that worsen with exercise. She has no sputum production or hoarseness. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes a day since age 20. A trial of bronchodilators has worsened her symptoms. Temperature is 36.1 C (97 F), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 18/min. BMI is 33.5 kg/m2. Pulse oximetry is 97% on room air. On examination, the patient has audible noises on expiration that can be heard without a stethoscope. Lung auscultation demonstrates expiratory wheezes. This patient is alert, oriented, and able to understand and communicate a preferred treatment option (ie, she does not want to undergo surgery and instead prefers to go home with antibiotics). It is less clear to what extent she appreciates the consequences of her decision and whether current psychotic symptoms (eg, commentary auditory hallucinations) may be influencing her ability to weigh the risks and benefits rationally. Medication nonadherence and psychosis (eg, delusions, hallucinations), if present, are relevant to the assessment only if they interfere with the patient's decision-making abilities (eg, the patient is taking direction from command hallucinations). When there is a possibility that psychiatric symptoms are impairing medical decision-making, the next step is to perform a formal, decision-specific capacity assessment, wherein the patient's ability to understand and weigh the risks of going home should be explored. However, if she meets the requisite criteria for decisional capacity, her decision must be respected (Choice D). (Choice A) This patient's brother may be involved as a surrogate decision maker if the patient is assessed as lacking decision-making capacity. However, prematurely involving him before performing a capacity evaluation undermines her autonomy. (Choice B) Coordination of care and confirmation of aftercare follow-up with the patient's treating psychiatrist is necessary; however, the next step is a capacity assessment that should be completed by the treating hospital physician. (Choice E) A patient cannot be hospitalized involuntarily on the basis of a diagnosis of schizophrenia. Criteria for involuntary hospitalization include dangerousness to self or others and grave disability/inability to care for self. (Choice F) The right to refuse treatment requires intact decision-making capacity. A decision-specific capacity assessment (eg, refusing a cholecystectomy) should be performed before accepting the patient's refusal of surgery. Educational objective: A diagnosis of schizophrenia in itself is not a reason to assume a patient lacks decision-making capacity. A capacity assessment should be performed prior to treatment and includes the ability to understand information, appreciate potential consequences, communicate a choice, and offer a rationale.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia is hospitalized for right upper quadrant abdominal pain and diagnosed with cholecystitis. The patient is initially treated with antibiotics, and a scheduled cholecystectomy is planned. On day 2 of hospitalization, she reports that she feels much better. The patient does not want to undergo surgery and instead prefers to go home with oral antibiotics. She says, "I know that God is on my side and will take care of me." The patient lives in a group home and is prescribed risperidone daily, although she states that she missed 2 doses in the past week due to abdominal pain. Her brother lives nearby and helps with errands and transportation to appointments. On examination, the patient is alert and fully oriented. She reports hearing voices commenting on her behaviors "all the time" and states she is "used to them now." The patient has no suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: Malaria Epidemiology Vector: female Anopheles mosquito 4 major species of Plasmodium: P falciparum, P vivax, P ovale, P malariae Highest burden of disease is in Africa but is found in most tropical/subtropical areas worldwide Manifestations Periodic febrile paroxysms Nonspecific malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, myalgia Complications Cerebral (eg, delirium, seizure), hypoglycemia, ARDS, acidosis, renal/hepatic failure, coagulopathy Diagnosis Thin & thick peripheral blood smears Rapid testing ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome. This patient has intermittent high-grade fevers following a trip to Vietnam, with marked anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bilateral flank pain. The differential for fever in the returning traveler is broad. Viral infections can cause fever and thrombocytopenia, but few febrile viral infections cause marked anemia. Bacterial infections (eg, pyelonephritis) can cause sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (eg, thrombocytopenia, anemia). However, intermittent fevers, normal leukocyte count, and absence of localizing findings (eg, normal physical examination) are unusual for bacterial infection; bilateral (vs unilateral) flank pain is atypical for pyelonephritis (ascending infection into one kidney). Similar to hemolytic transfusion reactions, hemolysis should be considered when anemia is associated with bilateral flank pain (likely from cytokine inflammation in the setting of hemolysis). Because Vietnam is a malaria-endemic region, this patient most likely has malaria. Manifestations typically arise 2-6 weeks after transmission, when schizonts lyse erythrocytes, leading to cytokine release. A classic feature includes paroxysmal fevers, with variable patterns (intermittent lysis) based on the species (eg, every 48h with Plasmodium falciparum); common findings include vomiting, headache, arthralgia/myalgia, and/or fatigue. Evaluation typically shows anemia (intravascular hemolysis) and thrombocytopenia (platelet activation from increased adhesion molecules on infected erythrocytes). Malaria is diagnosed by Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smears, which quantify parasitemia and identify the infecting species. Rapid diagnostic tests are also available in resource-limited countries. (Choice A) Heterophile antibody can diagnose infectious mononucleosis, which may also cause fever and thrombocytopenia. However, common associations are generalized lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, and splenomegaly; paroxysms of high fever are rare. (Choice B) Blood cultures should be obtained to exclude bacteremia; however, many features of this presentation make bacterial infection less likely (eg, normal examination, normal leukocyte count). Typhoid fever (eg, Salmonella bacteremia) can cause fever, but the classic presentation is stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, and abdominal pain. (Choice D) CT scan of the abdomen can diagnose pyelonephritis and nephrolithiasis, which frequently cause unilateral (vs bilateral) flank pain and are not associated with anemia and thrombocytopenia. (Choice E) Stool culture can diagnose several illnesses associated with travel (eg, amebiasis, infectious bacterial diarrhea). Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (eg, due to Escherichia coli O157:H7) infection can cause hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. This patient's lack of diarrhea make these conditions less likely and stool cultures less useful. Educational objective: Malaria should be suspected in any patient returning from an endemic area with fever. Classic features include intermittent fever, vomiting, headache, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis is most often made using blood smears.

questions.explanation: In this example, the study must determine whether there is an association between long-term treatment with an immunosuppressive medication used to treat plaque psoriasis in adults and the development of a very rare but serious progressive neurologic disease. This means that the study should have an analytic design (ie, able to test a hypothesis about associations between exposure and disease) rather than a descriptive design (Choice A). A case-control study is an analytic design in which potential participants are initially identified based on disease status as cases (ie, have the disease) or controls (ie, do not have the disease). Once cases and controls are identified, the presence of past exposure to ≥1 risk factors of interest can be determined in each group. Because participants have been deliberately chosen based on disease status, the case-control study design is particularly efficient and cost effective for studying an uncommon (rare) disease with a long latent period (ie, time between exposure and disease occurrence), such as a very rare neurologic disease. (Choices C, D, and E) Study designs that require follow-up time are inefficient for studying an uncommon disease or a disease with a long latent period because a considerable amount of time must pass (in this example, years) before the disease develops. In addition, the likelihood that a sufficiently large number of participants will develop the disease to allow the researcher to draw valid conclusions is very low. Educational objective: The case-control study is the most appropriate analytic design for studying uncommon (rare) diseases and diseases with long latent periods.

questions.explanation: This cross-sectional study compared insulin sensitivity in patients with HIV-1 infection treated with protease inhibitors (PIs), therapy-naive patients, and HIV-1–negative controls. The box plots show the distribution of insulin sensitivity in the 3 groups of study participants. A box plot is a graph of a distribution of data based on a 5-number summary: Minimum First quartile (Q1) Median/second quartile (Q2) Third quartile (Q3) Maximum Quartiles divide a distribution into 4 quarters, each holding ~25% of the data. In the figure, the dotted line indicates the cutoff (~90 µmol/L/min) between normal and pathologic insulin sensitivity. Based on the box plots, in patients with HIV-1 infection treated with PIs, the median insulin sensitivity (~75 µmol/L/min) is below the cutoff, but the third quartile of insulin sensitivity (~125 µmol/L/min) is above the cutoff. This result indicates that more than 50% but fewer than 75% of patients with HIV-1 infection treated with PIs had insulin sensitivity below the cutoff. (Choices A, B, C, and E) Boxplots describe the distribution of data. The median insulin sensitivity (Q2) of ~75 µmol/L/min means that 50% of patients have insulin sensitivity levels below (and 50% above) this value; given that the cutoff for pathologic insulin sensitivity is higher than the median, this further justifies that more than 50% of patients have insulin sensitivity levels below the cutoff. Other conclusions are that: fewer than 25% of patients have insulin sensitivity levels below Q1 (eg, below ~40 µmol/L/min); more than 25% but fewer than 50% of patients have insulin sensitivity levels below Q2 but above Q1 (eg, below ~75 µmol/L/min but above ~40 µmol/L/min); and more than 75% of patients have insulin sensitivity levels below Q3 (eg, below ~125 µmol/L/min). Educational objective: A box plot is a graph of a distribution of data based on a 5-number summary: minimum, first quartile (Q1), median/second quartile (Q2), third quartile (Q3), and maximum. Quartiles divide a distribution into 4 quarters, each holding about 25% of the data.

questions.explanation: Dependent variable Qualitative (categorical) Quantitative Independent variable Qualitative (categorical) Chi-square, logistic regression* t test, ANOVA, linear regression Quantitative Logistic regression* Correlation, linear regression *Dependent variable must be dichotomous. ANOVA = analysis of variance. Variables are broadly classified as qualitative (ie, categorical) or quantitative (eg, continuous) based on the scale of measurement. Qualitative variables (eg, type of treatment, blood type) represent categories or groups, whereas quantitative variables (eg, temperature, glucose level) represent numeric values. The scale of measurement of the dependent (eg, outcome) and independent (eg, exposure, risk factor) variables in a study determines the correct statistical test for any given situation. The analysis of variance (ANOVA) test compares the means of ≥3 groups. It requires a categorical independent variable (eg, exposure) used to divide study participants into ≥3 groups and a quantitative dependent variable (eg, outcome) for which an average (eg, mean) is calculated. In this study: the categorical independent variable is type of patient divided into 3 different groups: patients with HIV-1 infection treated with protease inhibitors (PIs), therapy-naive patients, and HIV-1–negative controls. the quantitative dependent variable is insulin sensitivity, for which a mean can be calculated. An ANOVA test can determine whether a statistically significant difference in mean insulin sensitivity exists among the 3 groups of study participants. A large, statistically significant difference among groups indicates that at least 1 group has a different mean insulin sensitivity. (Choice B) The chi-square test evaluates the association between 2 categorical variables, as in a study evaluating the association between sex (eg, male, female) and presence of myocardial infarction (eg, present, absent). (Choice C) A correlation analysis uses the correlation coefficient to describe the linear relationship between 2 quantitative variables, as in a study evaluating the linear relationship between hours of sleep and irritability score. (Choice D) The 2-sample t test compares the mean of a quantitative variable between 2 groups, as in a study comparing mean insulin sensitivity (quantitative variable) between a group of patients with HIV-1 infection treated with PIs and a second group of patients with HIV-1 infection not treated with PIs. (Choice E) The 2-sample z test compares the proportion of a categorical variable between 2 groups, as in a study comparing the proportion of patients with pathologic insulin sensitivity (considered as a categorical [yes, no] variable) between a group of patients with HIV-1 infection treated with PIs and a second group of patients with HIV-1 infection not treated with PIs. The test requires a quantitative dependent variable (eg, outcome) and a categorical independent variable (eg, exposure, risk factor).

questions.explanation: This patient with a history of severe malnutrition has symptoms of bowel obstruction (eg, postprandial epigastric pain and fullness relieved with emesis) following reintroduction of nutrition (ie, refeeding). Imaging demonstrates narrowing of the angle between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and the aorta. This presentation is consistent with SMA syndrome. At the origin of the SMA is a mesenteric fat pad that separates the aorta from the SMA (forming the aortomesenteric angle) and acts as a conduit for the third duodenal segment. Patients with severe malnourishment (eg, anorexia nervosa) metabolize fat stores, narrowing the aortomesenteric angle with potential duodenal compression/obstruction. Refeeding precipitates a compensatory hypermetabolic state, which risks further fat metabolism, aortomesenteric angle reduction, and worsening of obstruction symptoms. The obstruction can be partial (delayed contrast passage on imaging, as in this patient) or complete (absent contrast passage). Because this patient has a partial obstruction, management can be focused on relieving the obstruction without an operation. Slowed nutritional rehabilitation targeted toward the patient's increased calorie requirements (from the starvation/hypermetabolic state) can rebuild the mesenteric fat pad and relieve duodenal compression. (Choices A, B, C, and D) If conservative management fails (or if a patient has complete obstruction), surgical management may be required. Educational objective: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome results from depletion of the fat pad separating the SMA from the aorta (eg, due to severe malnourishment or hypermetabolic state). This can lead to compression of the duodenal segment traveling through the fat pad, causing small bowel obstruction. Initial management is often conservative (eg, slow nutritional rehabilitation).

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is evaluated in the office for abdominal pain. The patient has a prolonged history of restricting subtype anorexia nervosa and recently started a nutritional rehabilitation program. As his oral intake has increased, the patient has experienced worsening postprandial fullness and epigastric pain. The symptoms are often relieved by emesis. The patient prefers liquid rather than solid food. His weight is 51% of the ideal body weight with a BMI of 14 kg/m2. Physical examination is notable for cachexia and epigastric fullness. There is no rebound tenderness. CT scan of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast reveals distension of the stomach and proximal duodenum with abrupt delay in contrast passage at the third portion of the duodenum. There is abnormal narrowing of the angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's abdominal symptoms?

questions.explanation: Cardiovascular manifestations of anorexia nervosa Structural Myocardial atrophy ± fibrosis Decreased wall thickness & chamber volume Mitral valve prolapse* Conduction Increased vagal tone leading to bradycardia Impaired chronotropic response Vascular Decreased sympathetic tone Impaired vasoconstrictive response Functional Reduced cardiac output & blood pressure Diminished exertional & orthostatic response *Occurs secondary to reduced chamber volume. Although eating disorders are more common in women, they are an important cause of morbidity and mortality in men. BMI can be useful in determining the diagnosis and severity of anorexia nervosa (AN), but in men, BMI may be higher than expected, given their larger bone density and mass. This patient who experienced syncope in the setting of thinness, bradycardia, prolonged QT interval (likely from electrolyte abnormalities), and echocardiographic findings of decreased ventricular wall thickness and reduced chamber volumes should be evaluated for AN. The primary cardiovascular manifestation of AN is myocardial atrophy, resulting in decreased ventricular mass and small chamber volumes. The small ventricular volumes cause a fixed, small stroke volume that impairs cardiac output. Increased vagal tone with bradycardia and impaired chronotropic response are also typical, increasing susceptibility to hypotension, orthostasis, and syncope. The myocardial changes (which sometimes progress to fibrosis) also increase the risk for ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Other cardiac manifestations of AN include small pericardial effusion, elevated HDL, and mitral valve prolapse (because the decreased left ventricular size creates a relative excess of valve tissue that can prolapse into the left atrium). Most of these manifestations of AN are reversible with treatment but are a common cause of mortality. (Choice A) Androgenic steroid use causes concentric ventricular hypertrophy and increased myocardial mass rather than decreased wall thickness and reduced myocardial mass. (Choices B and E) Chagas cardiomyopathy is caused by infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and is usually seen in Latin America. It typically produces dilated cardiomyopathy with ventricular cavity enlargement and increased myocardial mass. Cardiac sarcoidosis can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy, typically with thickening of the ventricular walls and no change in cavity size. (Choice D) Hypothyroidism can cause bradycardia and pericardial effusion, but a decrease in myocardial mass and ventricular chamber size is not expected. Educational objective: The primary cardiovascular manifestation of anorexia nervosa is myocardial atrophy with a resultant decrease in ventricular wall thickness and chamber volume. Increased vagal tone also occurs, leading to bradycardia and an impaired chronotropic response. These changes result in a small, fixed stroke volume and reduced cardiac output.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after passing out in a gym. Before the patient started his workout, he collapsed. There was no seizure-like activity, and he spontaneously regained consciousness within a minute. The patient reports no chronic medical conditions. Blood pressure is 106/60 mm Hg and pulse is 58/min. On physical examination, the patient appears thin and younger than the stated age. Heart sounds are normal. ECG shows sinus bradycardia and a QTc of 500 msec. Echocardiography reveals decreased left ventricular wall thickness, reduced cardiac chamber volumes, and small pericardial effusion. Ventricular systolic function is normal. Based on the findings, this patient should be further evaluated for which of the following conditions?

questions.explanation: Features of anterior cruciate ligament injury Injury mechanisms Rapid deceleration or direction changes Pivoting on lower extremity with foot planted Symptoms Pain: sudden onset, severe Popping sensation at the time of injury Significant swelling (effusion/hemarthrosis) Joint instability Examination findings Anterior laxity of the tibia relative to the femur (anterior drawer test, Lachman test) Imaging Plain x-rays usually normal, but fracture of tibial spine or anterolateral tibial plateau suggests ACL tear MRI provides definitive diagnosis Treatment RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) measures ± Surgery depending on age & activity level ACL = anterior cruciate ligament. This patient sustained knee trauma during the motorcycle collision, as evidenced by severe knee pain and swelling immediately afterward. His description of an unstable knee (eg, knee "giving out") and difficulty walking downstairs is particularly concerning for a ligamentous injury. In particular, this patient's clinical findings suggest an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury: Instability occurs because the ACL functions to maintain anterior-posterior stability (and some rotational stability) of the knee as it is flexed and extended. Instability is exacerbated when full weight is placed on the affected knee, as occurs when going down stairs. Avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibial plateau (Segond fracture) is classically associated with ACL injury. Although the mechanism is not completely understood, >75% of Segond fractures occur with ACL tears. Provocative maneuvers such as the Lachman and anterior drawer tests can reveal excessive anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur and are highly sensitive (>90%) for an ACL tear. MRI of the knee should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis. (Choice B) Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tears can occur with high-energy trauma and result in anterior-posterior instability but rarely cause avulsion fractures. If present, a PCL avulsion fracture typically occurs at the PCL's tibial insertion site, which is at the posterior aspect of the tibia. (Choices C and D) Medial and lateral meniscus injuries can occur due to a twisting mechanism during high-energy trauma. However, associated effusion is typically delayed (eg, over hours to days) rather than immediate, and knee locking/catching (vs instability) is usually described. (Choices E and F) Medial and lateral collateral ligament injuries result primarily in lateral instability (eg, during sidestepping movements) rather than anterior-posterior instability (eg, while going down stairs). They are also less likely to be associated with a Segond fracture than an ACL injury. Educational objective: Sudden, severe knee pain and swelling with knee instability after high-energy trauma are concerning for ligamentous injury. Anterior-posterior instability (eg, difficulty going down stairs) and avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibial plateau (ie, Segond fracture) are highly suggestive of anterior cruciate ligament injury.

questions.explanation: Exceptions to informed consent by parent/guardian in minors Emergency care Condition in which treatment delay can cause serious impairment or death Emancipated minor (adolescents) Parent Married Military service Financially independent High school graduate Homeless Specific medical care (adolescents) Sexually transmitted infection Substance use disorder (most states) Pregnancy care (most states) Contraception Parental consent is normally required for medical assessment and treatment of a minor; however, in emergencies, parents may not be readily available to provide consent. In situations with threat of serious impairment or death if a medical condition is left unaddressed, care should not be delayed because a guardian is not available to consent. The emergency exception rule provides a legal basis for providing emergency care and assumes that, if present, a reasonable parent would consent to medical intervention if aware of the severity of the emergency. Therefore, physicians may presume consent and proceed with evaluation and stabilizing treatment if: The child has an emergency condition placing life or health in danger A legal guardian is unavailable or unable to provide consent Care cannot be safely delayed until consent can be obtained Treatment is limited to the immediate threat In this situation, the patient has a diminished radial pulse and paresthesia following supracondylar fracture, raising significant concern for neurovascular compromise, a limb-threatening medical emergency. While reasonable efforts should be made to contact the parents for consent, delaying emergency treatment is inappropriate given the severe pain and high risk of irreversible disability (Choice A). (Choice B) Depending on jurisdiction, consent can be provided by non-parent adult relatives (eg, grandparents, siblings, aunts/uncles) when parents cannot be contacted. In this emergency, parental and non-parent adult relative consent is not required. (Choice D) In situations with injuries suspicious for child abuse (eg, rib fractures, metaphyseal corner fractures, multiple fractures in various stages of healing), child protective services or local law enforcement may be able to consent to treatment depending on jurisdiction. However, child abuse is unlikely as this patient's supracondylar fracture is consistent with the reported mechanism. The emergent nature of the injury is the basis for providing care without parental consent. (Choice E) Extended consent can be obtained in certain circumstances (eg, blood transfusions in oncology patients); however, consent for treatment is generally obtained for each new medical encounter and procedure. Educational objective: While consent for treatment is generally obtained from a parent prior to initiating medical treatment for a minor, emergency evaluation and treatment may be provided without consent to preserve life or prevent permanent disability.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his aunt with right arm pain and swelling. The aunt says that the patient fell off the monkey bars at the park and landed on his right hand. There was no head injury or vomiting. On physical examination, the patient cries in pain and feels tingling in his right fifth digit. The right elbow is swollen and deformed. The right radial pulse is diminished but sensation is intact. X-ray of the right elbow is shown in the exhibit. The patient is currently staying with his aunt while his parents are out of town. The aunt mentions that he was brought to this hospital by his mother 3 months ago and treated for an ankle fracture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.explanation: The first step in evaluation of a newborn immediately after birth is the assessment of respirations and muscle tone. Newborns who are crying or breathing without distress and have vigorous movement can be managed routinely (eg, skin-to-skin with the mother) without resuscitation. In this case, the newborn is not crying and has minimal spontaneous movements. Any newborn with poor tone and/or respiratory effort after birth requires initial resuscitation, which includes the following actions for the first 30 seconds of life: Provide warmth: The newborn should be dried of amniotic fluid to help maintain body temperature. Warmth should be provided by placing the newborn under a radiant warmer. Position and clear the airway: The newborn should be placed supine with the neck in a neutral or slightly extended position to maximize air entry. Obvious secretions in the oropharynx or nasopharynx should be suctioned with a bulb syringe. Deeper suctioning should be avoided due to risk for vagal stimulation and subsequent apnea or bradycardia. Provide tactile stimulation: Drying and suctioning often provides sufficient tactile stimulation to promote respiratory effort, but additional maneuvers include rubbing the back or flicking the soles of the feet. (Choices A, B, and E) After 30 seconds of initial resuscitation with providing warmth, clearing the airway, and using tactile stimulation, positive pressure ventilation (PPV) and supplemental oxygen are typically indicated for continued poor respiratory effort and/or pulse <100/min. If bradycardia persists despite PPV, advanced neonatal resuscitation with chest compressions should be performed. This patient should first receive tactile stimulation. (Choice D) Similar to chest compressions, intubation is typically reserved for persistent apnea despite PPV. Surfactant may be indicated for newborns with suspected respiratory distress syndrome, the risk of which is increased in this patient due to the association between poorly controlled maternal gestational diabetes mellitus and delayed fetal surfactant synthesis. However, routine resuscitation with tactile stimulation should be performed first. Educational objective: Newborns with poor tone and/or respiratory effort immediately after birth require brief (30 sec) initial resuscitation, including providing warmth, clearing the airway (eg, suctioning secretions), and providing tactile stimulation.

questions.explanation: This cohort study compared the incidence of pediatric hepatitis linked to a new adenovirus strain in a group of infants vaccinated against the new strain with that of a group of infants unvaccinated against the new strain. The results of the study show that: 10 of 200 vaccinated participants developed pediatric hepatitis, so the 2-year incidence in vaccinated infants is 10 / 200 = 0.05. 40 of 200 unvaccinated participants developed pediatric hepatitis, so the 2-year incidence in unvaccinated infants is 40 / 200 = 0.2. These results indicate the following relative risk (RR) for pediatric hepatitis linked to the new adenovirus strain in vaccinated infants compared to unvaccinated infants: RR vaccinated versus unvaccinated = 0.05 / 0.2 = 0.25 RR = 0.25 means that vaccinated infants are only 25% as likely to develop pediatric hepatitis as compared to unvaccinated infants, or, 75% less likely (1.0 − 0.25 = 1 − RR). This calculation is known as relative risk reduction (RRR = 1 − RR) (Choice C). questions.explanation: Chlamydia & gonorrhea in women Risk factors Age <25 High-risk sexual behavior Manifestations Asymptomatic (most common) Cervicitis Urethritis Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome) Diagnosis Nucleic acid amplification testing Treatment Empiric: ceftriaxone + doxycycline* Confirmed chlamydia: doxycycline* Confirmed gonorrhea: ceftriaxone Complications Pelvic inflammatory disease Ectopic pregnancy Infertility Pharyngitis *Azithromycin in pregnancy. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are common sexually transmitted infections with a high prevalence in women age <25. Because of high rates of asymptomatic infection (and subsequent lack of treatment), women are at risk for ascending infection (eg, pelvic inflammatory disease) that can lead to long-term complications (eg, infertility, ectopic pregnancy). Therefore, annual screening for N gonorrhoeae and C trachomatis is recommended in sexually active women age <25. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the gold standard for both screening and diagnosis due to high sensitivity (96%) and specificity (99%). Antibiotic therapy is indicated for a positive N gonorrhoeae NAAT result, even in asymptomatic patients, because treatment decreases the risk for worsening infection (eg, disseminated gonococcal infection) and reduces rates of transmission to sexual partners (Choice B). Confirmation testing, with either cervical cultures or repeat NAAT, is not required due to high specificity of NAAT results (Choices A and D). Patients with positive N gonorrhoeae but negative C trachomatis NAAT results are treated with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone). In nonpregnant patients, such as this one, follow-up pelvic examination and repeat NAAT testing (ie, test of cure) are not typically required (unless new symptoms develop) because antibiotic therapy is typically highly effective (Choice E). Educational objective: Sexually active women age <25 undergo annual screening for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis due to high rates of asymptomatic infection and risk for long-term complications (eg, infertility). questions.explanation: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease Definition Hepatic steatosis on imaging or biopsy Exclusion of other etiologies (eg, alcohol, hepatitis C, glucocorticoids) Clinical features Mostly asymptomatic Metabolic syndrome* AST/ALT ratio <1 Ultrasonographic findings: ↑ echogenicity (steatosis), coarse echotexture (fibrosis) Treatment Weight loss (eg, diet modification, exercise) Consider bariatric surgery if BMI ≥35 kg/m2 Prognosis Hepatic fibrosis associated with increased risk for cirrhosis & liver-related death *Obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension. ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase. This patient with obesity, elevated aminotransferases, and an otherwise negative work-up likely has metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. MASLD is defined as hepatic steatosis not due to a secondary cause (eg, alcohol use, chronic viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis). MASLD is the most common liver disease in countries with a high prevalence of metabolic syndrome (eg, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension) and is thought to occur as a result of insulin resistance. The diagnosis is confirmed by a finding of steatosis (eg, increased echogenicity of the liver parenchyma) on ultrasonography of the liver. Management of MASLD focuses on weight loss of 5%-10% of body weight, which reduces liver fat content and reverses inflammation (ie, steatohepatitis) and fibrosis seen in more advanced disease. Weight loss can be achieved by calorie reduction (eg, eliminating high-calorie foods such as soda and fried food) and exercise (eg, combination of regular cardiovascular activity and resistance training). If initial weight loss attempts are unsatisfactory, weight loss medications (for BMI ≥27 kg/m2) or bariatric surgery (for BMI ≥35 kg/m2) may be considered to prevent progression of MASLD to cirrhosis (Choice D). (Choice A) Liver function abnormalities associated with oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are relatively rare; when present, they typically follow a cholestatic pattern with bilirubin elevation (not seen in this patient). Although OCPs are contraindicated in patients with cirrhosis, they are safe for use in patients with MASLD without cirrhosis, as in this patient. (Choice B) Metformin is used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is common in patients with MASLD. However, this patient has a normal fasting glucose level. Furthermore, metformin has not been shown to improve histologic findings (eg, inflammation, fibrosis) in MASLD. Therefore, it should not be started in this patient. (Choice C) Screening for hepatocellular carcinoma (eg, alpha fetoprotein, hepatic ultrasonography) is recommended only in patients with cirrhosis. Patients with MASLD are at elevated risk for cirrhosis and possibly hepatocellular carcinoma; however, routine screening is not recommended in patients with MASLD who do not have cirrhosis. Educational objective: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease focuses on weight loss of 5%-10% of body weight, which can reduce hepatic fat content and reverse inflammatory damage and fibrosis. Patients should be advised to reduce dietary calories and engage in regular physical activity (combination of cardiovascular and resistance training).

questions.explanation: This cross-sectional study examined the differences in cardiometabolic risk factors between women and men with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The study evaluated the following cardiometabolic risk factors: BMI, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), total cholesterol (TC), LDL cholesterol (LDL-c), HDL cholesterol (HDL-c) sex standardized, triglycerides, and TC/HDL ratio. Study results for these risk factors are presented as mean sex differences (women − men) along with their respective 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Because the mean value for men is subtracted from the mean value for women, a positive difference indicates that women have a greater mean value compared with men. Conversely, a negative difference indicates that women have a lower mean value compared with men. If a CI includes 0 (ie, null value for a difference), there is no significant difference between the means for men and women (ie, no statistical significance). If a CI excludes 0, there is a significant difference between the means for men and women (ie, statistical significance). In this study, statistical significance can be evaluated by either the line representations or the numeric values for the difference in means and respective CIs. The results of the study indicate that, compared with men, women have: greater mean values for BMI, TC, LDL-c, and HDL-standardized because the line representation is completely contained on the positive end of the values for a difference and the corresponding CIs exclude 0 (Choices A, D, and E). lower mean values for DBP, log triglycerides, and TC/HDL ratio because the line representation is completely contained on the negative end of the values for a difference and the corresponding CIs exclude 0 (Choice C). similar mean values for HbA1c and SBP because the line representation goes through a difference of 0 and the corresponding CIs include 0. Therefore, the conclusion that is justified is that men and women have similar mean levels of HbA1c and SBP. Educational objective: A confidence interval (CI) for a difference between means that excludes 0 (ie, null value for a difference) is statistically significant, and a CI for a difference between means that includes 0 is not statistically significant.

questions.explanation: Major types of systemic amyloidosis Primary Secondary Age related Dialysis related Disease association Plasma cell dyscrasia Chronic infection/ inflammation Elderly men ESRD on dialysis Precursor protein ↓ Misfolding mechanism ↓ Amyloid fibril type Immunoglobulin light chains ↓ Increased production ↓ AL Serum amyloid A ↓ Increased production ↓ AA Transthyretin (prealbumin) ↓ Accumulation over time ↓ ATTR* β2-Microglobulin ↓ Decreased clearance ↓ Aβ2M Clinical manifestations Nephropathy, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiomyopathy (AL > AA), peripheral neuropathy, macroglossia, skin bruising Cardiomyopathy, CTS, other peripheral neuropathy Scapulohumeral arthritis, CTS Amyloid names begin with "A" followed by the precursor protein abbreviation. *ATTR also occurs in a hereditary form that affects younger patients. CTS = carpal tunnel syndrome; ESRD = end-stage renal disease. This patient's progressive fatigue, dyspnea, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), and edema are consistent with heart failure. Several features suggest an infiltrative cardiomyopathy: His echocardiography shows thickened ventricular walls with low voltage on ECG, suggesting that the thickening is not due to myocardial hypertrophy (which would cause high voltage) but rather due to infiltrative deposit. This initially causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy, with nondilated ventricular cavities (ie, normal ventricular cavity dimensions) and a rigid/stiff myocardium; the persistent pressure elevation leads to biatrial enlargement. Amyloidosis, a multisystemic condition due to amyloid fibril deposits, is a classic example of infiltrative cardiomyopathy. There are different types of amyloidosis, and the 2 types associated with cardiomyopathy include: Amyloidosis light chain (AL), which involves production of monoclonal proteins that can infiltrate multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, skin, and heart; and ATTR, which is caused by the abnormal deposition of transthyretin protein (produced in the liver) and can occur either with aging (wild type, mostly in men) or from a mutation in the TTR gene (hereditary). Wild-type ATTR (most likely in this elderly man) tends to cause peripheral nerve infiltration; carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), as seen in this patient, is common and can be a clue to the diagnosis. Autonomic nervous system and gastrointestinal tract involvement can also present with motility issues (eg, gastrointestinal reflux, diarrhea, constipation). Cardiac amyloidosis may progress from restrictive cardiomyopathy (with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]) early in the disease course to dilated cardiomyopathy (with reduced LVEF) late in the course. (Choice A) Constrictive pericarditis presents with heart failure (eg, fatigue, dyspnea, elevated JVP, peripheral edema), but it would not explain this patient's thickened ventricular walls and CTS. In addition, this patient has no apparent risk factors for constrictive pericarditis (eg, previous acute pericarditis, chest irradiation, heart surgery). (Choice B) Hemochromatosis can cause an infiltrative cardiomyopathy that presents similarly to cardiac amyloidosis. However, it usually involves excessive iron deposition in the liver and pancreas in addition to the heart and is less likely in this patient with normal liver enzymes and blood glucose. (Choice C) Hypertensive heart disease can present similarly to cardiac amyloidosis (eg, thickened ventricular walls, preserved LVEF), but high voltage is expected on ECG with the true concentric left ventricular hypertrophy that occurs with hypertensive heart disease. In addition, evidence of kidney disease (eg, elevated creatinine, proteinuria) is commonly present with advanced hypertension but is not expected with ATTR (although it is commonly seen with AL due to amyloid renal involvement). (Choice E) Heart failure due to viral myocarditis typically manifests as dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced LVEF. Educational objective: Thickened ventricular walls with low-voltage QRS complexes on ECG should raise suspicion for infiltrative myocardial disease. Cardiac amyloidosis due to age-related (wild-type) amyloid transthyretin (ATTR) is typically seen in elderly men and is often associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.explanation: Postpartum endometritis Risk factors Cesarean delivery Intraamniotic infection Group B Streptococcus colonization Prolonged rupture of membranes Operative vaginal delivery Clinical features Fever >24 hr postpartum Uterine fundal tenderness Purulent lochia Etiology Polymicrobial infection Treatment Clindamycin & gentamicin During normal postpartum recovery, a physiologic fever may occur in the first 24 hours after delivery (due to increased prostaglandin levels associated with uterine contractions) but usually resolves without treatment. However, fever at >24 hours postpartum is usually pathologic and requires evaluation (Choice D). In this patient with uterine tenderness and recent cesarean delivery, the most likely cause is postpartum endometritis, an infection of the uterine decidua due to direct bacterial inoculation of the uterine cavity during labor and delivery. Risk factors for postpartum endometritis include prolonged time of exposure to vaginal flora (ie, prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes) and cesarean delivery, particularly cesarean delivery performed after the onset of labor. Additional risk factors include intraamniotic infection and group B Streptococcus colonization. Other than fever and uterine tenderness, additional clinical findings may include purulent or malodorous lochia. The infected endometrium can also delay uterine involution, which may lead to a soft, tender uterus and increased postpartum bleeding. Treatment is empiric with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (eg, gentamicin and clindamycin) for polymicrobial coverage. (Choice B) Incisional cellulitis is a common cause of postoperative fever. Although this patient has induration and serosanguinous discharge on the right side of the surgical incision, there is no associated erythema, fluctuance, or purulent drainage to suggest cellulitis. (Choice C) Lactational mastitis can present with postpartum fever. However, patients typically have unilateral breast findings (eg, erythema, edema, tenderness). In contrast, this patient's bilateral breast engorgement and tenderness are more consistent with normal postpartum milk letdown. (Choice E) Postoperative ileus can be associated with hypoactive bowel sounds, but this is a nonspecific finding that can be normal following cesarean delivery (due to manipulation of adjacent bowel and residual intraperitoneal inflammation). Patients with postoperative ileus usually have nausea and/or vomiting and abdominal distension, which are not seen in this patient. In addition, uncomplicated postoperative ileus is not associated with fever. Educational objective: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial infection that presents with fever >24 hours postpartum, uterine tenderness, and malodorous or purulent lochia. Risk factors include prolonged labor and cesarean delivery.

questions.explanation: The prevalence of depression among outpatient psychiatric patients (50%) is much higher than the prevalence reported by the primary care physician (20%) (Choice D). Therefore, a measure that is independent of prevalence would be expected to be equal in value whether the short test is used on primary care patients or outpatient psychiatric care patients. The likelihood ratio (LR) is the probability of finding an event (eg, positive or negative test result) in patients with the disease divided by the probability of the same finding in patients without the disease. Unlike predictive values, LRs are independent of the prevalence of disease. The positive LR (LR+) and negative LR (LR−) can be calculated from sensitivity and specificity estimates, which are unaffected by changes in prevalence, with LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity. Of the given options, the LR+ is independent of prevalence and would be expected to be equal in value whether the short test is used on primary care patients or outpatient psychiatric care patients. The LR+ can answer the question, "If a patient has condition X (eg, depression), how likely is the patient to have a positive test result (eg, positive short test result) compared with a patient without the condition having a positive test result?" (Choice A) Contrary to LRs, the positive and negative predictive values depend on prevalence. (Choice C) Because disease prevalence is typically used as a surrogate for pretest probability of disease (ie, the probability before testing of having the disease) in a population of interest, the pretest probability of depression among outpatient psychiatric patients (50%, or 1/2) is expected to be greater than the pretest probability of depression among patients from a primary care physician (20%, or 1/5). Educational objective: Likelihood ratios are independent of the prevalence of disease and can be calculated from sensitivity and specificity estimates, which are unaffected by changes in prevalence.

questions.explanation: This patient has episodic vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, the classic triad of Ménière disease, a disorder of the inner ear characterized by increased volume and pressure of endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). Diet and lifestyle modifications are first-line therapy for Ménière disease and include: Dietary salt restriction (2-3 g maximum per day): Sodium may reduce endolymphatic fluid. Limitation of caffeine and nicotine: Vasoconstrictors may reduce blood flow to the inner ear. Limitation of alcohol: Alcohol may cause fluid shifts that impact the inner ear. Avoidance of allergy triggers: Both food and environmental allergies seem to trigger attacks in some patients, perhaps due to allergies leading to increased fluid extravasation into the endolymphatic sac. Improving sleep hygiene and stress management skills may also help. If lifestyle modifications fail to control symptoms, diuretics (eg, hydrochlorothiazide) and/or vasodilators (eg, betahistine) are often used. Vestibular suppressants (eg, benzodiazepines) and/or antiemetics (eg, promethazine) can be used during acute attacks, but are not helpful as daily preventive therapy (ie, unlikely to decrease frequency of episodes); in addition, daily benzodiazepine use is associated with a risk of dependence (Choice B). (Choice A) Canalith repositioning maneuvers are used to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), which causes brief (<1 min), episodes of vertigo triggered by changes in head position. In BPPV, vertigo is not associated with tinnitus, aural fullness, or hearing loss. (Choice C) Daily topiramate (an anticonvulsive) can be used to treat vestibular migraines, which can also present with episodes of vertigo of a similar length and frequency to those of Ménière disease. However, vestibular migraines do not cause hearing loss, which is seen in this patient. (Choice E) A short course of oral prednisone is often used to treat vestibular neuritis (termed labyrinthitis if associated with hearing loss). Prednisone is not first-line therapy for Ménière disease. Although vestibular neuritis also presents with vertigo, it occurs as a single episode of dizziness, usually lasting a few days, and often following an upper respiratory infection. It would not present as multiple discrete episodes as seen in this patient. Educational objective: Ménière disease presents with episodic vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Lifestyle modifications including a low-salt diet, limitation of alcohol and caffeine, and avoidance of allergy triggers are first-line therapy.

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome Etiology Complete or partial loss of X chromosome Presentation Infancy: Lymphedema, cystic hygroma Renal & heart defects (eg, horseshoe kidney, aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve) Childhood: Short stature Dysmorphic features (eg, webbed neck, broad chest, high-arched palate, cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals) Adolescence: Delayed thelarche Amenorrhea (primary or secondary) Diagnosis & management Karyotype (45,X) Comorbidity screening (eg, cardiac & renal imaging) Growth hormone & estrogen (± progestin) therapy This patient with primary amenorrhea, short stature, and a heart murmur most likely has Turner syndrome (TS), a genetic condition caused by complete or partial loss of an X chromosome. Short stature is a universal finding, and left-sided cardiac lesions (eg, aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve) are common, as seen in this patient with findings consistent with aortic stenosis (systolic murmur with ejection click) from a bicuspid aortic valve. Patients with TS have primary ovarian insufficiency caused by gonadal dysgenesis ("streak ovaries"). Due to low ovarian estrogen production, most patients have absent or minimal breast development and primary amenorrhea, as seen in this girl. Because adrenal androgens are in part responsible for pubic hair growth, pubarche may be normal or delayed, as seen by this patient's scant pubic hair. A minority of patients (particularly if mosaic 45X/46XX) may have only partial ovarian atrophy with normal pubertal progression and menarche initially followed later by secondary amenorrhea. The vast majority are infertile. Low-dose estrogen therapy should be started in preadolescence (eg, age 11-12) and gradually increased to induce puberty and breast growth (Choice D). Estrogen is continued throughout adulthood (age 40-50) to improve bone mineral density (ie, prevent osteoporotic fractures), reduce cardiovascular complications (eg, coronary heart disease), and maintain sexual health. Progestin therapy is added to prevent endometrial hyperplasia (from unopposed estrogen exposure) (Choice E). (Choice A) Dopamine agonists (eg, bromocriptine) suppress prolactin and treat hyperprolactinemia (eg, prolactinoma), which can cause amenorrhea due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. However, galactorrhea, headache, and visual field defects are other signs of a prolactinoma, whereas this patient's short stature and bicuspid aortic valve make TS more likely. (Choice C) A GnRH agonist (eg, leuprolide) is used as continuous therapy to treat central precocious puberty, not pubertal delay, by inhibiting gonadotropin release. It can also be used as pulsatile therapy in the treatment of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, but this condition is typically due to insufficient caloric intake to meet nutritional needs (eg, anorexia nervosa), which is unlikely in this patient with a normal BMI. Educational objective: Turner syndrome should be suspected in a patient with short stature and primary amenorrhea. Treatment is estrogen to induce puberty and breast growth, increase bone mineral density, and reduce cardiovascular complications as well as progestin to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.
