questions.explanation: Process of informed consentfor research Disclosure Disclosure of key information: medical condition, proposed intervention & risks/benefits of accepting/declining intervention Understanding Confirmation of decision-making capacity & understanding of disclosed information Voluntariness Process conducted without coercion or manipulation; consent must be freely given Authorization Documentation of accepting/declining intervention once fully informed Informed consent is a complex medicolegal process that varies slightly across jurisdiction and setting (eg, a clinical versus research setting). Informed consent for research is generally broken into 4 primary principles: Disclosure: participant receives easily understood information about the condition of interest, the proposed medical intervention (eg, experimental drug), and the potential risks and benefits of accepting or declining the proposed intervention Understanding: participant is allowed to ask questions and demonstrates an ability to accurately describe information provided in disclosure and integrate it into a decision Voluntariness: participant is able to make a decision free from coercion, undue influence, or manipulation Authorization: participant signs a document confirming decision In this scenario, the research coordinator expresses optimism that the medication will help the patient, suggests to the patient's wife that the study may fail (ie, the medication will not be available) without more participants, and then asks for her participation as well. Given the wife's investment in her husband's health and his possible benefit from the medication, she is being unduly influenced toward a decision of volunteering as a study participant. Rather than being provided an opportunity to make a deliberate uninfluenced choice, the fear of missing out on a potentially helpful medication for her husband is coercing her decision, violating the element of voluntariness. (Choices A and C) Beneficence (ie, the duty to promote good and act in the best interest of the patient) and nonmaleficence (ie, the duty to do no harm to the patient) are medical ethical principles that direct physicians' behaviors toward patients. Although the research coordinator would ideally also act in accordance with these principles, they are not explicit components of informed consent for research participation. (Choice B) Confidentiality is based on the guiding principles of nonmaleficence and respect for patient autonomy; it refers to safeguarding patient privacy to foster medical care and transparent discussion, as well as to prevent discrimination. No confidential information about the wife has been disclosed in attempting to obtain her consent to participate. (Choice D) Veracity (ie, truth-telling) is derived from the guiding ethical principle of respect for patient autonomy and refers to the need to communicate truthfully with patients. Educational objective: Informed consent for research participation comprises 4 major principles: disclosure, understanding, voluntariness, and authorization. For informed consent to be truly voluntary, it must be free from coercion or manipulation.

questions.explanation: Dyspepsia Symptoms Epigastric pain or burning Postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating ≥1 months Etiology Functional/idiopathic (75%) Malignancy (eg, gastric, esophageal) Peptic ulcer (eg, Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAIDs) Drug-induced (eg, NSAIDs, bisphosphonate) Work-up Low malignancy risk (eg, age <60 & no alarm symptoms*) Testing & treatment for H pylori High malignancy risk (eg, age >60 or alarm symptoms) Gastroenterology referral/upper endoscopy Treatment Treatment of underlying cause Trial of proton pump inhibitor if no cause found *GI bleeding, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, palpable mass, family history of upper GI cancer. GI = gastrointestinal; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. This patient has dyspepsia, which is characterized by epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness (bloating), and early satiety for ≥1 months. Most cases of dyspepsia are idiopathic (ie, functional dyspepsia); however, causes such as malignancy (eg, gastric adenocarcinoma), peptic ulcer disease (eg, caused by Helicobacter pylori), and drug-induced dyspepsia (eg, chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy) should also be considered. Management of dyspepsia is influenced by risk of malignancy. Older patients (eg, age ≥60) or those with alarm symptoms (eg, dysphagia, weight loss) are more concerning for malignancy. A esophagogastroduodenoscopy should be considered, which allows direct visualization and biopsy of masses or lesions (eg, ulcers) as well as biopsy testing for H pylori. Endoscopic findings can then guide further management (eg, cancer staging, treatment of H pylori, stopping nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy, if possible, for peptic ulcer disease). (Choice A) Abdominal ultrasound can assess for cholelithiasis, which is suspected in patients with biliary colic. Biliary colic is characterized by intense, episodic epigastric or upper right quadrant pain following a meal, rather than the constant epigastric discomfort, bloating, and early satiety seen in this patient. Abdominal ultrasonography is not routinely recommended for dyspepsia evaluation; there are no specific sonographic characteristics associated with dyspepsia, and incidental findings may be present (eg, gallstones that do not warrant cholecystectomy). (Choice B) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis do not visualize the esophageal and gastric lumens to assess for malignancy or peptic ulcers. After malignancy is detected, a CT scan is useful in cancer staging. (Choice D) A trial of proton pump inhibitor is appropriate for patients with classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (eg, substernal burning, regurgitation) and for those with dyspepsia whose work-up is negative for malignancy or H pylori infection. This patient has dyspepsia without symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux and first needs endoscopic evaluation (to rule out malignancy) and biopsy testing for H pylori. Educational objective: Dyspepsia is characterized by epigastric pain/burning, postprandial fullness, and early satiety. Management of dyspepsia is largely determined by malignancy risk. Older patients (ie, age ≥60) and those with alarm symptoms (eg, dysphagia) concerning for malignancy should be considered for esophagogastroduodenoscopy.

questions.explanation: Viral myocarditis Clinical presentation Commonly asymptomatic & resolves without detection Heart failure that may progress to DCM* Chest pain, ventricular arrhythmia with risk of SCD Relatively young adults usually affected (eg, age <55) ± Viral prodrome (eg, fever, malaise, myalgia) Diagnosis ECG: nonspecific findings Laboratory: mild to moderate serum troponin elevation Echocardiography: 4-chamber dilation with diffuse hypokinesis Cardiac MRI: epicardial or midwall enhancement Biopsy: lymphocytic infiltration, viral DNA or RNA** Treatment Supportive care to allow time for recovery HFrEF medications (eg, diuretic, ACE inhibitor, β blocker) Temporary ventricular assist device, if needed Heart transplant if no recovery *Most common symptomatic presentation. **Endomyocardial biopsy is rarely required for diagnosis. DCM = dilated cardiomyopathy; HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; SCD = sudden cardiac death. This young patient with a weeklong history of persistent chest pain, mild-to-moderate troponin elevation, and global left ventricular (LV) systolic function reduction most likely has acute myocarditis. Myocarditis involves myocardial inflammation resulting from various potential etiologies (infectious and noninfectious). Viral infection is the most common cause and is most likely in this patient; some patients will describe a viral prodrome (eg, preceding fever, myalgia), but many will not (eg, minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic). Clinical presentation of viral myocarditis is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic, self-limited illness to heart failure, arrhythmia, or chest pain. Myocarditis chest pain can mimic acute coronary syndrome (eg, elevated troponin, nonspecific ECG changes), but the pain is commonly persistent (eg, days) and sharp (vs pressure-like in ischemia). As in this patient, troponin elevation (myocardial inflammation rather than ischemia) and globally reduced LV systolic function (myocardial involvement) are consistent with myocarditis. Diffuse hypokinesis and chamber dilation is classically noted on echocardiography. Heart failure is the most common symptomatic presentation. Definitive diagnosis with endomyocardial biopsy is rarely required as the diagnosis is often sufficiently confirmed based on clinical presentation and noninvasive imaging (ie, echocardiography and cardiac MRI). The same viruses can lead to myocardial inflammation (myocarditis) and pericardial inflammation (pericarditis; eg, pericardial effusion, diffuse ST-segment elevation), so the 2 conditions can coexist. Unlike pericarditis chest pain (treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs] and colchicine), myocarditis chest pain should not be managed with NSAIDs, which may worsen myocarditis progression. (Choices A and C) Cardiac manifestations occur in a small percentage of patients with sarcoidosis and untreated Lyme disease. Acute myocarditis is possible in both conditions, but presentation with a disruption of cardiac conduction (eg, varying degrees of atrioventricular block) is more typical. Viral myocarditis is more likely in this patient with no significant medical history and no symptoms until only a week ago. (Choice B) Ischemic chest pain due to underlying coronary artery disease (eg, angina, myocardial infarction) is typically associated with segmental, rather than diffuse, LV dysfunction on echocardiography and is unlikely in this young patient with persistent, sharp pain. (Choice D) Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (takotsubo cardiomyopathy) is usually seen following a physically or emotionally stressful event, most commonly in postmenopausal women. It can present with chest pain and troponin elevation, but LV wall motion dysfunction is characteristically apical rather than diffuse. Educational objective: Acute myocarditis is most commonly caused by viral infection and can have variable presentation. Presentation with chest pain can mimic acute coronary syndrome (eg, troponin elevation, ECG changes), but relatively young patient age, persistent chest pain, and diffuse wall motion abnormalities favor myocarditis.

questions.explanation: Toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol or ethylene glycol) Typical sources Methanol: windshield wiper fluid, contaminated homemade liquor Ethylene glycol: automotive coolant/antifreeze, brake fluid Industrial solvents & deicing solutions may contain either toxic alcohol Clinical features Early: CNS sedation & inebriation, osmolar gap Late: anion gap metabolic acidosis, compensatory tachypnea Ocular toxicity (methanol) Urine oxalate crystals, hypocalcemia, AKI (ethylene glycol) Management Fomepizole (inhibits ADHase) is preferred therapy Ethanol solution (competes for ADHase) if fomepizole unavailable IV sodium bicarbonate for acidemia (eg, pH <7.3) Hemodialysis for severe cases (eg, acidosis, end-organ damage) ADHase = alcohol dehydrogenase; AKI = acute kidney injury; IV = intravenous. This patient has altered mental status, gastrointestinal irritation (abdominal pain and vomiting), and ocular involvement (visual impairment and abnormal ophthalmic examination). His laboratory findings (eg, pH of 7.15, bicarbonate of 6 mEq/L, and anion gap of 28 mEq/L) indicate anion gap metabolic acidosis (AGMA). Together, these findings are consistent with poisoning by methanol, a toxic alcohol that may be ingested unintentionally (eg, contaminated homemade alcohol) or deliberately (eg, self-harm attempt). Methanol is converted by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid. In addition to causing AGMA, formic acid causes retinal and optic nerve injury (eg, retinal edema, optic disc hyperemia); fixed mydriasis (due to an afferent pupillary defect) indicates advanced poisoning with high risk for permanent blindness. Treatment of methanol poisoning includes: Fomepizole to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing further formic acid formation. Ethanol, which competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase, can be used if fomepizole is unavailable. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct acidemia, which decreases tissue penetration of formic acid. Hemodialysis to rapidly remove toxic metabolites and the parent alcohol when AGMA and/or end-organ damage (eg, retinal injury) is present. Because definitive testing (eg, methanol level) is usually too slow to assist with clinical decision-making, empiric treatment is necessary to reduce morbidity and mortality. (Choice B) Severe carbon monoxide poisoning (treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy) commonly presents with AGMA due to profoundly elevated lactic acid (eg, >10 mg/dL). This patient's lactic acid is near normal. (Choice C) Intraabdominal pathology (eg, perforated viscus, ischemic bowel) is often diagnosed with abdominal CT scan and can present with abdominal pain, vomiting, altered mental status, and AGMA. However, intraabdominal pathology would not explain this patient's visual impairment and abnormal eye examination. (Choice D) CT scan of the head, rather than MRI, is generally more appropriate for rapid evaluation of patients with altered mental status because MRI is time-consuming. Although MRI could detect basal ganglia injury, a potential effect of methanol poisoning, it would not affect (and would adversely delay) definitive management (eg, hemodialysis), which is urgently needed to prevent permanent blindness. (Choice E) Urine ketones are present in diabetic and alcoholic ketoacidosis, common conditions associated with vomiting, abdominal pain, and AGMA. However, neither condition causes acute retinal injury with visual impairment, and patients with diabetic ketoacidosis typically have an elevated blood glucose. Educational objective: Methanol poisoning causes altered mental status, abdominal pain and vomiting, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and retinal/optic nerve injury. Treatment includes fomepizole, intravenous sodium bicarbonate, and hemodialysis.

questions.explanation: Dependent variable Qualitative (categorical) Quantitative Independent variable Qualitative (categorical) Chi-square, logistic regression* t test, ANOVA, linear regression Quantitative Logistic regression* Correlation, linear regression *Dependent variable must be dichotomous. ANOVA = analysis of variance. Variables are broadly classified as qualitative (ie, categorical) or quantitative (eg, continuous) based on their scale of measurement. Qualitative variables (eg, type of treatment, blood type) represent categories or groups whereas quantitative variables (eg, temperature, glucose level) represent numeric values. The scale of measurement of the dependent (eg, outcome) and independent (eg, explanatory) variables in a study determines the correct statistical test. Linear regression analysis is used to describe the linear relationship between 1 quantitative dependent (ie, outcome) variable; and ≥1 independent (ie, explanatory) variables, which may be quantitative or qualitative. In this study, prevalence of marijuana use is the quantitative outcome variable, and age is a quantitative explanatory variable. In general, many variables are studied as part of linear regression analysis. A regression analysis can determine whether age (an explanatory variable) is linearly related to the prevalence of marijuana use (an outcome variable). This means that a regression analysis can determine whether a positive linear trend (as age increases, the prevalence increases) or a negative linear trend (as age increases, the prevalence decreases) exists. A hypothesis test for the slope of the regression line determines whether the relationship (eg, linear trend) is statistically significant. (Choice A) Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the mean of a quantitative dependent variable in several independent groups. For example, ANOVA could be used to compare mean serum triglyceride level in patients with low, normal, or high serum uric acid levels (3 groups). (Choices B and C) The chi-square test and Fisher's exact test evaluate the association between 2 categorical variables, as in a study evaluating the association between sex (male or female) and myocardial infarction (presence of myocardial infarction or absence of myocardial infarction). Fisher's exact test is commonly used to analyze 2 × 2 contingency tables when the sample sizes are small. (Choice E) Survival analysis (also known as time-to-event analysis) estimates the time for ≥1 experimental groups to experience an event of interest. It considers the number of events in each experimental group (an indicator of incidence). However, the analysis focuses on the timing of events in each of the experimental groups throughout the follow-up period. Educational objective: A regression analysis is a statistical technique used to describe the effect of ≥1 quantitative or qualitative independent (ie, explanatory) variables on 1 quantitative dependent (ie, outcome) variable.

questions.stem: A mailed, anonymous, self-report survey was conducted to estimate the prevalence of substance use among US physicians. A national sample consisting of 10,200 physicians was randomly selected and asked about use of substances in their lifetime, the past year, and the past month; reasons for use; self-admitted dependence or substance use disorder; and whether treatment was received. Preliminary results showed that the demographic characteristics of responders closely reflected those of the US physician population. Results also showed that as the age of physicians increased, the prevalence of marijuana use seemed to decline. Which of the following statistical techniques would be appropriate to assess this trend?

questions.explanation: This patient has gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), characterized by substernal burning (ie, heartburn) and regurgitation (eg, sour taste in the mouth). He also has cough and hoarseness, which are caused by acidic irritation of the larynx and pharynx. Of concern is this patient's unexplained microcytic anemia, an alarm feature associated with GERD that suggests chronic gastrointestinal blood loss (resulting in iron deficiency). Associated conditions resulting in chronic blood loss include malignancy (eg, esophageal adenocarcinoma) or erosive disease (eg, erosive esophagitis). Therefore, patients with GERD and iron deficiency anemia should undergo upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess for these conditions, even if fecal occult blood testing is negative (given its low sensitivity for detecting upper gastrointestinal bleeding). Colonoscopy is also indicated for unexplained iron deficiency anemia (eg, rule out colon cancer). Since this patient had a recent and normal colonoscopy, upper endoscopy should be performed first. (Choice A) CT scan of the chest and abdomen is used in cancer staging, typically after a gastrointestinal malignancy is diagnosed endoscopically. CT scan does not visualize the gastrointestinal lumen; it is not useful in identifying sources of blood loss. (Choice B) Esophageal pH monitoring is typically done in patients with refractory GERD symptoms despite taking proton pump inhibitor therapy. It is used to assess whether persistent symptoms are caused by acid reflux. It is not an appropriate first step for patients with GERD and alarm features. (Choice D) Helicobacter pylori causes peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and associated iron deficiency anemia. However, PUD presents with dyspepsia (eg, epigastric pain, bloating, early satiety) rather than acid reflux (substernal pain, regurgitation, cough, hoarseness). H pylori testing is not typically indicated in patients with GERD; however, endoscopic testing for H pylori may be done if findings suggestive of infection (eg, PUD) are present on endoscopy. (Choice E) Patients with severe GERD (ie, frequent symptoms) who lack alarm features can be treated with a proton pump inhibitor (eg, lansoprazole) and observation. However, this patient has microcytic anemia warranting urgent endoscopic evaluation to identify the source of bleeding. Medical therapy and observation alone are inappropriate. Educational objective: Iron deficiency anemia in the setting of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) raises concern for gastrointestinal bleeding. Etiologies may include GERD-related complications (eg, erosive esophagitis, esophageal cancer) or another cause of gastrointestinal bleeding (eg, gastric or colon cancer). Endoscopic evaluation is needed to identify the source of bleeding.

questions.explanation: Scabies Pathogenesis Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation Spread by direct person-to-person contact Clinical features Extremely pruritic, small, erythematous papules Distribution: interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, extensor elbows, axillae, feet, umbilicus & genitalia Burrows (thin serpiginous lines) may not be visible but pathognomonic if present Diagnosis Clinical Skin scraping with microscopy is confirmatory Treatment Topical 5% permethrin OR oral ivermectin Treat household members & close personal contacts Environmental measures (eg, launder clothing/bedding) This infant has a diffuse, pruritic rash consisting of papules, pustules, and vesicles with involvement of the soles and scalp. Given the child's mother also has erythematous papules on the wrists and elbows, these findings are suggestive of scabies, or skin infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei mite. Scabies is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, mite eggs, and mite feces that presents 3-6 weeks after initial epidermal infection. Examination often reveals erythematous papules, but vesicles and pustules may be present, as in this case. The lesions are intensely pruritic (particularly overnight) and, in infants, irritability may be the only manifestation of pruritus. The classic distribution of scabies in older children and adults includes the wrist and elbows (as seen in this child's mother) along with finger webs, genitalia, and axillae; however, infants frequently have diffuse skin involvement, including the scalp and trunk. The hands and feet are also significantly affected in young children. First-line treatment for scabies is topical permethrin. Because transmission occurs via direct person-to-person contact and there is a lengthy incubation period (eg, weeks), all close contacts (eg, household members, sexual partners) should be treated. In this case, the entire family, including those who are symptomatic (the patient and the mother) and asymptomatic (the father and the sibling), should be treated because they may have active infection but have not yet developed the rash (Choices A, C, D, and E). Management also includes laundering of recently used bedding and clothing because fomite transmission can occur. (Choice B) Chickenpox, or primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV), can cause a diffuse, pruritic vesicular rash. Symptomatic patients at risk for complications (eg, adults) warrant antiviral therapy, and nonimmune, exposed contacts typically require postexposure prophylaxis or routine varicella vaccination. In contrast to this case, however, chickenpox presents with a prodrome of fever and malaise, and lesions typically crust over and resolve within 1-2 weeks. Educational objective: Scabies classically presents with pruritic, erythematous papules on the extremities (eg, web spaces, wrists, elbows), genitalia, and axillae; however, infants often have diffuse involvement (including scalp and trunk). Treatment is topical permethrin, which should also be given to all close contacts (even if asymptomatic) due to the prolonged incubation period and mode of transmission (person-to-person contact).

questions.stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the office due to a worsening rash. The mother first noted a few red spots on the child's feet 2 weeks ago, but the rash has since spread diffusely. The patient has been more irritable than normal, particularly overnight. There has been no fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or cough. The mother recently developed a few erythematous papules along the wrists and elbows for which she has applied an over-the-counter topical lotion. The 5-year-old brother and the father are asymptomatic. Both the patient and the brother are unvaccinated. Examination shows a fussy but consolable infant. There are diffuse, 3- to 4-mm, erythematous papules, pustules, and vesicles on the trunk, extremities, fingers, soles, face, and scalp. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. The rash on the feet is shown below. The treatment plan for this patient's diagnosis is discussed. Medical intervention should be provided to which of the following people?

questions.explanation: Medication-induced dystonia Precipitating medications (dopamine antagonists) Antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol) Antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) Clinical features Onset minutes to 24 hours after starting medication Sudden, sustained contraction of muscles, most often impacting the neck, mouth, tongue, & extraocular muscles Painful, distressing, often with tachycardia &/or hypertension Preserved mental status ± Other extrapyramidal effects (eg, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) Treatment Cessation (or ↓ dose) of offending medication (if possible) Anticholinergics (eg, diphenhydramine, benztropine) This patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction manifested by torticollis and an oculogyric crisis (forced, sustained elevation of the eyes in an upward position). Acute dystonia is a type of extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) that develops within hours to days of starting or escalating the dose of antipsychotics and is due to dopamine imbalance. This patient's risk factors include young age, male sex, and use of a high-potency, first-generation antipsychotic (haloperidol). Other types of EPSs include akathisia (inner restlessness) and drug-induced parkinsonism (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked facies). The diagnosis is clinical. Very distressing, acute dystonic reactions are best treated with anticholinergic medication administered intravenously or intramuscularly. Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine with significant anticholinergic activity, or benztropine is commonly used. (Choices A and C) CT scan of the head can be used to assess for a stroke or intracranial hemorrhage; in some cases, lumbar puncture is obtained when subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected. These can cause neck stiffness and abnormal rigid posturing (eg, decerebrate). However, for a patient to have had a stroke causing abnormal posturing, mental status would be affected; nausea, vomiting, and headache would also be expected. (Choice B) Administration of haloperidol can acutely lower the seizure threshold; electroencephalography can detect seizure activity. However, seizures typically cause rhythmic contractions rather than rigidity; in addition, seizures that are widespread enough to lead to sustained upward eye movements would likely be accompanied by changes in mental status. (Choice E) Serum creatine kinases should be obtained in patients with suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but life-threatening condition that can develop following haloperidol administration. Although muscle rigidity occurs, it is typically generalized (vs focal in this patient), and patients also have mental status changes, high fever, and autonomic instability; it is unlikely in this patient who is awake and alert with relatively normal vital signs. Educational objective: Acute dystonic reaction is a type of extrapyramidal symptom that is highly disturbing to patients. It is most commonly seen with high-potency, first-generation antipsychotics and is treated with anticholinergics (eg, benztropine) or antihistamines (eg, diphenhydramine).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia is brought to the hospital by local police. He destroyed a television set at a local electronics store and then became extremely agitated and violent when employees attempted to intervene. The patient's speech is difficult to follow, and he is distracted, seemingly listening to voices that only he can hear. He is admitted to the psychiatric ward and given lorazepam and haloperidol, resolving the agitation. Later that evening, a nurse notes that the patient is restless and uncomfortable. He states that he has neck discomfort. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 145/84 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min. He is alert and awake. questions.explanation: Complications of nephrotic syndrome* Mechanism Hypercoagulability (↑ thromboembolism risk) Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (eg, antithrombin III) Hepatic synthesis of prothrombotic proteins (eg, fibrinogen) Hyperlipidemia (↑ atherosclerosis risk) Hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins Infection (particularly encapsulated bacteria) Urinary loss of immunoglobulins & opsonizing factors Protein malnutrition Negative nitrogen balance Intravascular volume depletion Low oncotic pressure *Nephrotic syndrome results from glomerular filtration barrier (eg, podocyte) injury that leads to heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia & peripheral edema. This patient's generalized edema and heavy proteinuria (4+ with frothy consistency) are manifestations of urinary albumin wasting seen in nephrotic syndrome. Kidney biopsy findings of diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening, IgG and C3 deposits, and subepithelial electron-dense deposits are consistent with membranous nephropathy, a common cause of adult nephrotic syndrome. In addition to the urinary losses of albumin that contribute to edema, nephrotic syndrome also causes urinary wasting of immunoglobulins and opsonizing factors. This wasting significantly impairs humoral (B-cell) immunity and increases susceptibility to infection, particularly by encapsulated bacteria (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae). Therefore, patients with nephrotic syndrome should receive pneumococcal vaccination to reduce the risk for recurrent pneumonia and sepsis. Other complications of nephrotic syndrome that benefit from intervention include hypercoagulability, which is mitigated with prophylactic anticoagulation (in select patients), and hyperlipidemia, which is treated with lipid-lowering therapy (eg, statins). Routine management of nephrotic syndrome also includes loop diuretics to reduce edema and renin-angiotensin system blockade (eg, ACE inhibitors) to minimize proteinuria. (Choice A) Heavy alcohol use (eg, >4 drinks/day) increases a patient's risk for infection, adversely affects lipid levels (eg, hypertriglyceridemia), and may increase the risk for thromboembolism. However, light to moderate alcohol consumption (eg, 1-2 drinks/day), as seen in this patient, is unlikely to cause these negative effects, so complete abstinence from alcohol is not necessary in patients with nephrotic syndrome. (Choice B) Although membranous nephropathy can be caused by solid tumors, it is typically associated with cancer involving the lung, prostate, breast, colon, or bladder. Cervical cancer is an exceedingly rare cause of membranous nephropathy, so routine Pap testing (typically every 3-5 years) is adequate. (Choices D and E) Cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity may be depressed in patients with nephrotic syndrome (possibly related to the urinary loss of vitamin D bound to vitamin D–binding protein). However, at the time of diagnosis, the risk for intracellular infection (eg, herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, Pneumocystis) is not significantly increased, making prophylactic acyclovir and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole unnecessary. In contrast, patients undergoing prolonged immunosuppression for treatment of nephrotic syndrome are at increased risk for these infections, and prophylaxis should be considered. This predisposition results from urinary wasting of immunoglobulins and opsonizing factors, which impairs humoral (B-cell) immunity. Pneumococcal vaccination can help reduce the risk of infection.

questions.explanation: Chickenpox (varicella) Epidemiology Primary infection with VZV Transmission via direct contact or airborne respiratory particles High risk: adolescents, adults, individuals who are immunocompromised, women who are pregnant, newborns Clinical features Prodrome (eg, fever, malaise) Pruritic macules, papules & vesicles in successive crops at different stages Complications: skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis VZV PCR in atypical cases Treatment Supportive (eg, antihistamines) Acyclovir for high-risk patients & complicated disease Prevention 2 doses of VZV vaccine (age 1 & 4) VZV = varicella-zoster virus. This patient has a diffuse, pruritic rash with lesions in different stages of progression (ie, papules, vesicles, pustules, crusting). This finding is characteristic of chickenpox, a primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV) that most commonly occurs in unvaccinated individuals, as seen here. A viral prodrome (eg, fever, pharyngitis) usually precedes the rash, which typically spreads over the course of a week before the lesions crust over. Although chickenpox is most commonly a benign, self-limited illness in young, healthy children, complications (eg, cellulitis, pneumonia, encephalitis) can develop, and unimmunized adolescents and adults as well as immunocompromised individuals are at highest risk. In this case, the patient's neurologic findings are concerning for VZV encephalitis, a rare complication of chickenpox. VZV encephalitis typically presents 1 week after the onset of fever and rash. It can cause altered mental status (eg, lethargy, confusion), headaches, seizures, and/or focal neurologic deficits (eg, decreased strength). The diagnosis is confirmed by PCR detection of VZV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid, and treatment is intravenous acyclovir. (Choice A) Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis presents with acute-onset fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits. A rash is often not present in conjunction with encephalitis, and typical HSV lesions include clusters of painful, monomorphic vesicles, not pruritic lesions in different stages of progression. (Choice B) Unimmunized patients are at increased risk for measles meningoencephalitis, but the prodrome typically includes cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis in addition to fever. Moreover, the measles rash is maculopapular, not vesicular, and it spreads cephalocaudally. (Choice C) Neisseria meningitidis infection can present with fever and sore throat, but patients have rapid deterioration within hours (not a week) to headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. In addition, the associated rash is petechial/purpuric, not vesicular. (Choice E) West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne illness that can present with fever, sore throat, and headache and progress to meningitis or encephalitis. An associated rash can occur, but in contrast to this case would be maculopapular, not vesicular/pustular. Educational objective: Chickenpox is characterized by fever and a pruritic rash with lesions in different stages (ie, papules, vesicles, pustules, crusting). Although chickenpox is typically mild and self-limited, unimmunized adolescents/adults and immunocompromised patients are at risk for complications such as varicella encephalitis, which presents a week after the rash with altered mental status and focal neurologic deficits.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents due to lethargy and confusion. A week ago, the patient had fever and sore throat. The next day, he developed an itchy rash on his back; the rash spread to his face, chest, and extremities. Yesterday he was more tired than usual and began complaining of headache, and today the patient is difficult to arouse and is speaking incoherently. He has not received any childhood vaccinations. Temperature is 38.3 C (101 F), blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 16/min. On examination, the patient is lethargic. Mucous membranes are moist, and the oropharynx is clear. The neck is supple. Heart and lung sounds are unremarkable. He has a diffuse rash with papules, pustules, and vesicles as well as some crusted lesions. Neurologic examination shows decreased strength throughout. This patient's condition is most likely caused by infection with which of the following?

choiceHtml: Advise exercise closer to bedtime to promote restorative sleep
choices: Advise exercise closer to bedtime to promote restorative sleep
questions.explanation: Normal aging is associated with hormonal changes (eg, decreased growth hormone) leading to natural changes in sleep, including: Decreased total sleep time (eg, 6-7 total sleep hours) Advancement in sleep phase (eg, going to bed and rising earlier) Decreased time spent in slow-wave sleep Increased sleep fragmentation with nocturnal awakenings Although this patient wakes earlier than desired, she functions well during the day (sleepiness after lunch is considered normal, and her fatigue is easily alleviated after a 20-min nap), indicating a sufficient total sleep time for her age. Her hypertension is well controlled and she has no other significant risk factors for sleep disorders (eg, normal BMI, no memory loss). Therefore, empathetic, patient-centered counseling and reassurance about normal sleep changes are most appropriate at this time. Reassurance can be useful in addressing the significant anxiety generated by strict sleep expectations (which can itself disrupt restful sleep). (Choice A) Moderating alcohol quantity and timing (eg, >2 hr before bedtime), rather than elimination, is usually sufficient to address sleep difficulties. This patient's occasional and moderate consumption is not likely contributing to her early morning awakening. (Choice B) Regular exercise improves sleep, but it should be done earlier in the day (eg, >4 hr before bedtime). Vigorous evening exercise can perpetuate sleep-onset insomnia (difficulty falling asleep), likely due to sympathetic activation. (Choice C) Strategic, short-term melatonin administration is appropriate for certain circadian rhythm disorders (eg, jet lag; delayed sleep-wake phase disorder). Its effectiveness and safety in addressing normal age-related sleep changes (especially in older adults) have not been established; reassurance is a more appropriate first step. (Choices E and F) A sleep diary or sleep actigraphy (using a wearable device that tracks sleep patterns) can generate concrete data about sleep efficiency (number of hours in bed spent asleep) and sleep quality. These tools are used to treat circadian rhythm disorders or chronic insomnia (persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sufficient sleep that disrupts daytime function). This patient's early morning awakening, without daytime impairment or insufficient sleep quantity, is more consistent with normal aging. Educational objective: Normal age-related changes in sleep patterns include decreased total sleep and advancement of sleep phase (eg, early-morning awakenings and/or earlier bedtimes). In the absence of concerning symptoms (eg, medical risk factors, disruption in daytime function), empathetic education is the most appropriate initial management.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the office due to concerns about lack of sleep that has been ongoing for the past 2 years. The patient goes to bed around 10:00 PM and is able to fall asleep quickly but wakes up at 4:30 AM every day. She is unable to fall back asleep; she reads a book in bed and rises at 7:00 AM. The patient feels sleepy after lunch and sometimes takes a nap for 20 minutes around 2:00 PM, after which she feels energetic. She does brisk walking for exercise 5 days a week around 4:30 PM. The patient lives with her husband and is retired; she participates regularly in volunteering activities with friends and enjoys playing with her 2 grandchildren several days a week. Medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, for which she takes lisinopril. She drinks 1 or 2 glasses of wine on weekends with dinner and does not smoke cigarettes. Vital signs are within normal limits. BMI is 21 kg/m2. Physical examination, including tests of recall and attention, are within normal limits. The patient is anxious that her health could be affected if she does not get more sleep. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: Eosinophilic esophagitis in children Pathogenesis & epidemiology Th2-mediated inflammatory response triggered by food antigen exposure Comorbid atopy (eg, asthma, eczema, food allergy, allergic rhinitis) common Presentation Toddler: feeding difficulties (eg, solid food refusal), weight loss School-aged: abdominal pain, vomiting Adolescent: dysphagia, heartburn, food impaction Diagnosis Endoscopy & esophageal biopsy (eosinophils: ≥15/hpf) Exclusion of alternate diagnoses (eg, achalasia, infection) Treatment Elimination diet Pharmacologic therapy (eg, PPI, topical glucocorticoid) Feeding therapy PPI = proton pump inhibitor; Th2 = T-helper cell type 2. This patient has postprandial abdominal pain, vomiting, and dysphagia, findings often due to gastroesophageal reflux disease. However, in a patient with symptoms refractory to empiric proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy, eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) should be investigated. A history of atopy, as in this child with eczema, supports the diagnosis and is seen in most patients with EoE. EoE is an immune-mediated inflammatory response to certain foods that classically presents with dysphagia (particularly to solid food) and/or the sensation of food stuck in the esophagus. Children often adapt by restricting their diets to soft food, which are better tolerated but may lead to poor weight gain. Other symptoms include heartburn, epigastric or chest pain, and vomiting. With chronic inflammation and progressive esophageal fibrosis, food impaction can occur. Evaluation of suspected EoE includes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; esophageal biopsy showing ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field is diagnostic. Treatment involves dietary elimination of trigger foods and topical (swallowed) glucocorticoid therapy. PPI therapy is helpful in some (but not all) patients with EoE due to its anti-inflammatory properties. (Choice A) CT scan can reveal an anterior mediastinal mass (eg, lymphoma) compressing the esophagus and causing dysphagia to solid food. However, a mass would also typically obstruct the respiratory tract and cause dyspnea, cough, and/or stridor, symptoms not seen in this patient. In addition, a mediastinal mass does not explain this patient's burning, postprandial abdominal pain. (Choice C) Esophageal manometry is used to diagnose achalasia, in which impaired peristalsis and incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter cause heartburn symptoms and difficulty swallowing. However, achalasia is uncommon in children, and associated dysphagia is typically to both solids and liquids. (Choice D) Modified barium swallow can assess for aspiration in a patient with choking or coughing while eating or for oropharyngeal dysfunction in a toddler who cannot advance past pureed foods. The priority in this patient with new-onset solid food refusal is to evaluate the esophagus with endoscopy. (Choice E) Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are present in myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder that can cause oropharyngeal muscle weakness that leads to dysphagia. However, abdominal pain is not typical, and other signs of muscle fatigue (eg, ptosis, proximal arm weakness) would be expected. Educational objective: Eosinophilic esophagitis classically presents with dysphagia and/or a sensation of food stuck in the esophagus. Other symptoms can include postprandial abdominal or chest pain and vomiting. Evaluation involves upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and esophageal biopsy, which shows ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his father for follow-up evaluation of chest and abdominal discomfort. He has also vomited on several occasions after eating solid food, so he restricts his diet mainly to soft food such as yogurt and mashed potatoes. Physical examination is normal apart from eczematous patches on bilateral antecubital fossae and behind both knees. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient has newly diagnosed lung cancer with a high likelihood of cure with aggressive treatment. Regardless of disease stage, burden of symptoms, or probability of cure, palliative care services are always appropriate for patients facing serious illness, such as cancer or chronic medical conditions (eg, heart failure, dementia, HIV). Palliative care emphasizes quality of life by focusing on symptom control, social and emotional support, and advanced care planning. These missions support and often enhance the goals of curative or disease-modifying treatments. As the underlying illness progresses or remits, the balance between palliative and disease-modifying care changes over time. This patient can benefit from palliation of his current respiratory symptoms (eg, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis) and any anticipated adverse effects of oncologic treatment (eg, postsurgical pain, chemotherapy toxicities). Palliative services can also be beneficial for patients who are minimally symptomatic: additional priorities include helping patients cope with anxiety as well as supporting their families and caregivers. For these reasons, palliative care services and curative treatment should be offered together for this patient who is facing a serious illness, experiencing worry and insomnia related to his condition, and reporting ongoing symptoms related to lung cancer and underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice B). (Choices C and D) Palliative services may become increasingly urgent if the patient develops progressive symptoms or metastatic disease. However, early proactive engagement is preferred because this patient has active issues (eg, anxiety, dyspnea) that require dedicated attention. In several conditions (eg, lung cancer), early involvement of palliative care is associated with improved survival. Therefore, although disease stage and symptom severity tend to correlate with prognosis, they are not the sole considerations when offering palliative care services. (Choice E) Hospice care helps patients with limited life expectancy (≤6 months) to die comfortably and with dignity, preferably at home. For patients under hospice care, the philosophy of care shifts completely toward symptom control; life-prolonging or curative therapies are no longer pursued. Palliative symptom control is the central component of hospice care. However, palliative care can (and should) be initiated separately, and ideally well ahead of the decision to enter hospice care. Educational objective: Palliative care services are beneficial for any patient with a serious illness (especially chronic medical conditions and cancers) regardless of disease stage or symptom severity and can be offered in parallel with curative or life-prolonging treatment.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is seen in the oncology clinic for newly diagnosed non–small cell lung cancer. Medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with moderate airflow limitation. The patient developed vague chest discomfort, increased cough, and episodic hemoptysis 6 months ago. Staging evaluation revealed a primary mass in the left upper lobe, involvement of ipsilateral hilar nodes, but no metastatic lesions. Based on large registry data and center experience, he has an 80% chance of cure with surgical resection followed by chemotherapy. The patient is anxious about his diagnosis and has been lying awake at night while ruminating about his future. His respiratory symptoms are mostly stable, but he reports slightly worsened dyspnea over the past few weeks. The patient remains active with no trouble completing daily household tasks and continues to participate in social gatherings with his friends. The oncology clinic works closely with the palliative care department. Which of the following best represents the services that should be offered to the patient?

choiceHtml: Withdrawing life support if neurologic status has not improved in a defined period of time

questions.explanation: Care philosophies at the end of life No escalation of treatment Time-limited trial Withdrawal of life support Sets upper limits on treatment (eg, no invasive ventilation) Avoids futile interventions with greatest morbidity Provides intensive care for a predefined interval (eg, 2-3 days) May entail temporary escalation, even if futile Focuses completely on comfort measures only Withdrawing life support ≠ "withdrawing care" Creates time to process impending loss & eases transition to withdrawal of life support Active dying soon follows This patient had a catastrophic anoxic brain injury due to cardiac arrest. Given her lack of meaningful neurologic improvement after several days, her prognosis is extremely poor. Ongoing efforts to sustain life, including mechanical ventilation and hemodialysis, are likely to be futile. The patient's care preferences are unknown, and there is family indecision about the goals of care. Physicians must balance the aims of offering treatments that can alter the disease course, protecting patients from interventions that may be futile, and assisting families in accepting the prognosis of their loved one. A time-limited trial (TLT) of intensive care balances futility in the face of family indecision. Maximal care is provided for a predefined time period (typically 2-3 days after the discussion with the family); care may be escalated if additional organ failure occurs (eg, vasopressors added for shock), even when its likely futility is acknowledged (Choice C). The TLT gives families time to process the loss of their loved one and feel more prepared to accept a transition toward withdrawal of care if there is no meaningful improvement (eg, spontaneous eye opening). TLTs improve family experiences while reducing futile interventions at the end of life. TLTs can also be introduced at initial presentation of acute illness (eg, patient with advanced cancer who is newly admitted with evolving sepsis), when great clinical uncertainty often exists surrounding prognosis and futility. TLTs offer a "test of time" for the prognosis to declare itself, allowing physicians and families to converge on shared goals of care. (Choice B) Neurologic recovery is very unlikely in this patient, and withdrawal of life support is indeed appropriate. However, the family remains internally conflicted about her preferences and goals of care. Immediately withdrawing life support is likely to exacerbate the family conflict, especially in this scenario of unexpected illness. (Choice D) Although it is always ideal for conflicted families to reach unanimity, full agreement on goals of care may not be realistic. Futile treatments should not be continued indefinitely in an open-ended manner while waiting for the entire family to arrive at an agreement. (Choice E) Goals of care should be defined cohesively (ie, TLT vs comfort only), rather than selectively continuing some life-sustaining treatments but not others. For example, withdrawing hemodialysis is likely to result in volume overload (due to anuria), resulting in pulmonary edema necessitating increased ventilator support. This action harms the patient and prolongs futile treatments. Educational objective: A time-limited trial (eg, 2-3 days) of intensive care places an endpoint on medically futile care while creating a timeframe for families to process the impending death of their loved one.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit for unwitnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. She required 30 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation before spontaneous circulation was restored. The patient was endotracheally intubated prior to transport to the hospital and has been comatose for the past 7 days, despite being weaned off sedation. Hemodialysis was initiated 2 days ago due to anuria, believed to be a result of ischemic tubular necrosis. On examination, the patient is unresponsive to any stimulus. Pupils are not reactive to light. Brain imaging reveals diffuse cerebral edema. During the family meeting to discuss her poor prognosis and goals of care, the patient's children express uncertainty and disagreement regarding their mother's wishes regarding end-of-life care. The patient has no advance directive for health care on file. Which of the following recommendations from the physician is most appropriate at this time?

questions.explanation: This patient with recent abdominal surgery has progressively increasing abdominal discomfort and distension without vomiting or obstipation (eg, inability to pass gas). Abdominal examination is relatively benign (eg, soft, mild tenderness only with no peritoneal signs), and x-ray shows a large volume of stool (eg, soft tissue opacities with internal air mottling) throughout the colon with no dilated loops of small bowel or air-fluid levels. This presentation is most consistent with postoperative constipation, a condition commonly caused by decreased bowel motility following intestinal manipulation, decreased physical activity in the recovery period (physical activity accelerates gut transit), and adverse effects of medications (eg, opioids, amlodipine). Treatment is supportive and includes laxatives and enemas (eg, tap water enemas). Recurrent small bowel obstruction (SBO) (eg, from recurrent intraabdominal adhesions) should also be considered as a potential cause of this patient's symptoms. However, in contrast to this patient, those with SBO typically have acute, colicky abdominal pain and vomiting and, often, obstipation; x-ray usually demonstrates dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. If SBO were suspected, an abdominal CT scan with contrast would usually be obtained to provide more detailed information (eg, transition point); fluoroscopic small bowel follow-through study could also confirm SBO but is rarely used compared to CT scan (Choices A and B). Conservative management of SBO would include nasogastric tube placement and bowel rest (Choice C). (Choice E) Urgent exploratory laparotomy may be indicated for acute conditions such as bowel ischemia or intraabdominal infection, which can occur following abdominal surgery. In contrast to this patient, those with acute intestinal ischemia typically have sudden, severe abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting; patients with intraabdominal infection usually have severe abdominal tenderness, often with fever or signs of peritonitis (eg, rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding). Educational objective: Constipation is common following abdominal surgery due to bowel manipulation, physical inactivity, and postoperative medications (eg, opioids). Symptoms typically include increasing abdominal discomfort and distension without vomiting or obstipation. Abdominal x-ray usually shows large amounts of stool without dilated loops of small bowel or air-fluid levels. Treament includes laxatives and enemas.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to gradually worsening abdominal pain. The patient underwent laparotomy and lysis of intraabdominal adhesions to treat small bowel obstruction 3 weeks ago. The surgery and immediate postoperative course were uncomplicated, and she was discharged after she began tolerating a diet. Over the past several days, the patient has had increasing diffuse abdominal discomfort without fever, nausea, or vomiting. She is able to eat and pass gas. Medical history includes hypertension and hysterectomy for uterine leiomyomas. Home medications are amlodipine and hydrocodone as needed. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg, and pulse is 66/min. Physical examination shows a well-healed surgical incision. questions.explanation: Adult hip osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) Clinical presentation Chronic/progressive groin, thigh, buttock pain Decreased ROM: abduction, internal rotation Pathogenesis Macro- or microvascular occlusion, bone necrosis Trabecular thinning & collapse of femoral head Risk factors Femoral head fracture (arterial disruption) Glucocorticoids Excessive alcohol use Sickle cell disease Systemic lupus erythematosus Diagnosis X-ray (low sensitivity): subchondral sclerosis, loss of sphericity MRI: serpiginous low-intensity lines (T1 images); bone marrow edema ROM = range of motion. This patient's right hip pain is most likely due to avascular necrosis (ie, osteonecrosis), a common sequela of femoral neck fracture (~10%-45% of cases). The dominant blood supply to the femoral head and neck is from the medial femoral circumflex artery and its branches (eg, retinacular arteries). These vessels can be injured by fracture (particularly with displacement) of the femoral neck, leading to impaired perfusion and osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Affected patients typically develop symptoms 6 months to 2 years following injury and have gradual-onset hip pain that is worse with weight bearing. Pain is most commonly located in the anterior hip or groin but can occur in the buttock or greater trochanter. Passive range of motion (ROM) is usually painful and, with progression of the disease, may become restricted. Early in the disease, plain x-rays are often normal; therefore, MRI is the study of choice to diagnose the condition. (Choice B) Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome occurs due to abnormal contact between the femoral head-neck junction and the acetabular rim during functional hip ROM. It can present with gradual-onset groin pain; however, symptoms are classically exacerbated with prolonged hip flexion during sitting (vs weight bearing), and patients with FAI are usually adolescents or young adults (eg, age <40). (Choice C) Greater trochanteric pain syndrome typically presents with chronic lateral (vs anterior) hip pain that is exacerbated by hip flexion (eg, climbing stairs, getting out of the car) or lying on the affected side. Pain is typically elicited by palpating over the greater trochanter. (Choice D) Piriformis muscle injury or hypertrophy can compress the sciatic nerve and cause hip and leg pain (known as piriformis syndrome); however, pain is typically located posteriorly (eg, buttock, posterior thigh), not in the groin or anterior thigh. (Choice E) Septic arthritis causes hip pain that is exacerbated with weight bearing; however, the pain is typically severe and limits range of motion. In addition, symptoms usually occur acutely (over 1-2 days vs 2 weeks), and other systemic symptoms (eg, fever, myalgia) are often present. Educational objective: Femoral neck fracture causes significant risk for osteonecrosis of the femoral head due to disruption of the dominant blood supply. Symptoms of osteonecrosis typically occur 6 months to 2 years following the injury and include the gradual onset of anterior hip or groin pain exacerbated by weight bearing.

questions.explanation: This patient with giant cell arteritis (GCA) was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids; he initially developed difficulty sleeping due to GCA pain but now has persistently impaired sleep despite resolution of the pain. Insomnia is a common adverse effect of glucocorticoid use. Because the patient's repeat inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR], C-reactive protein [CRP]) and his scalp and jaw pain have now normalized, tapering corticosteroids is the most appropriate next step and will likely improve his sleep. In addition to glucocorticoids, other medications and substances implicated in insomnia include the following: Central stimulants (eg, caffeine, methylphenidate) Decongestants (eg, pseudoephedrine) Respiratory stimulants (eg, theophylline) Appetite suppressants (eg, phentermine) Antidepressants (eg, fluoxetine, monoamine oxidase inhibitors) Beta blockers (eg, metoprolol) Management may involve switching to an alternate medication (eg, steroid-sparing agent for GCA), tapering the dose, or taking the medication earlier in the day. (Choice A) This patient's sleep difficulties and anxiety about sleep started after taking glucocorticoids; he has no other obvious manifestations of depression or generalized anxiety. Rather than initiating an antidepressant, corticosteroid tapering should be attempted first to address the underlying cause of his presentation. (Choices B and C) MR angiography is sometimes used in the work-up of GCA (eg, when the diagnosis is unclear), and GCA relapse can cause headaches. However, this patient's ESR and CRP are normal, and he has no further scalp or jaw pain, suggesting adequate treatment. questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up of giant cell arteritis. He was diagnosed 2 weeks ago after he began experiencing severe headaches, scalp pain, jaw tenderness, and difficulty sleeping due to pain; laboratory studies were notable for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 95 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein level of 15 mg/L. The patient was started on 60 mg of prednisone daily. He notes complete resolution of his scalp and jaw pain but still has difficulties with sleep. The patient cannot fall asleep until midnight or 1:00 AM despite going to bed at 9:00 PM and wakes at 5:00 AM. He had not had sleep difficulties in the past and feels anxious about them; he notes a mild, dull headache that wraps "like a band around his head." ESR and C-reactive protein are repeated and are within normal limits. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient's presentation?

questions.explanation: This relatively young woman has vague chest discomfort, dyspnea, and myocardial necrosis (elevated serum troponin I). An elevated troponin level can be due to ischemic and nonischemic processes. However, in a patient at risk for accelerated coronary artery disease (eg, mediastinal radiation, collagen vascular disorder), a high index of suspicion for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) should be maintained. When present, regional ST-segment elevation on ECG can help localize the infarct and associated coronary artery. However, ECG has poor sensitivity (~60%) for ischemia. During the evolution of acute myocardial infarction, ECG changes can be subtle and/or dynamic (eg, ST-segment depression transitioning to elevation). Therefore, a normal ECG does not exclude ACS. In particular, lateral and posterolateral infarcts tend to be electrically silent because the far lateral wall (eg, distal left circumflex artery territory) is not well covered by standard ECG leads. In patients with normal initial ECGs and borderline troponin levels, serial ECGs and troponin measurements are often indicated to rule in (or rule out) myocardial infarction. This patient's serum troponin level is already significantly elevated 4 hours after symptom onset, consistent with ongoing infarction. Bedside echocardiography can often reveal regional wall motion abnormalities, corroborating the diagnosis of ACS. (Choices B and D) Constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy are rare, late complications of mediastinal radiation. They both present with progressive and chronic (ie, months to years) manifestations of heart failure (eg, peripheral edema, jugulovenous distension with paradoxic inspiratory rise [ie, Kussmaul sign]). Neither condition involves myocardial necrosis; therefore, troponin is not expected to be elevated. Additional features (eg, pericardial knock or calcifications with constrictive pericarditis, decreased ECG voltages with restrictive cardiomyopathy) may be present. (Choice C) Submassive pulmonary embolism can cause troponin elevation from right ventricular demand ischemia. However, patients almost always have hypoxemia and some ECG abnormalities (eg, sinus tachycardia, evidence of right ventricular strain). (Choice E) Type A aortic dissection can produce acute myocardial infarction via retrograde extension into a main coronary artery. Accordingly, large vascular territories are involved (eg, right coronary artery dissection typically produces inferior wall infarction with ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF). Chest pain tends to have an excruciating, tearing quality and be maximal at onset (vs evolving over 30 min, as in this patient). Educational objective: A normal ECG does not exclude acute coronary syndrome, especially in patients with evidence of myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin) and high pretest probability for coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department in the winter for evaluation of dyspnea and chest discomfort. She describes breathlessness associated with a tight sensation. The symptoms began 4 hours ago soon after she woke up and intensified over the next 30 minutes. Medical history is significant for Hodgkin lymphoma 15 years ago that was treated successfully with chemotherapy and mediastinal radiation. Temperature is 36.5 C (97.7 F), blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 20/min. Pulse oximetry shows 97% on room air. On examination, the patient appears anxious and mildly diaphoretic. Cardiac auscultation is normal. Jugulovenous distension and peripheral edema are absent. The lungs are clear throughout. ECG demonstrates normal sinus rhythm with no acute ST-T segment changes. Serum troponin I is 1.12 ng/mL (normal: <0.04). Chest x-ray shows no acute abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Common prescribing cascades Initial drug prescribed → Adverse drug event → Subsequent drug prescribed Calcium channel blocker Peripheral edema Diuretic Diuretic or cholinesterase inhibitor Urinary incontinence Anticholinergic (eg, oxybutynin) Anticholinergic Agitation Antipsychotic Antipsychotic Extrapyramidal symptoms Levodopa NSAID Hypertension Antihypertensive Beta blocker Erectile dysfunction Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. This older patient has new-onset urge urinary incontinence with no immediately apparent cause (eg, negative urinalysis, stable physical/neurologic examination). This should raise the possibility of an adverse drug event (ADE), particularly given this patient's recent initiation of donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor often used for Alzheimer-related cognitive difficulties. Urinary incontinence is an increasingly recognized ADE of cholinergic medications (ie, the reverse of urinary retention from anticholinergics). In fact, due to increased risk (eg, age-related pharmacokinetic changes), older patients should have any new symptom investigated as a possible ADE. When ADEs are identified, the risk-benefit ratio of drug discontinuation vs continuation (usually with adverse effect mitigation) should be considered. This patient has shown little benefit in "forgetfulness" from donepezil and is now at risk for persistent urinary incontinence, which impacts her quality of life and has its own inherent risks (eg, increased falls). Therefore, her cholinesterase inhibitor should be discontinued, with monitoring for incontinence improvement. Often, ADEs are unrecognized and misdiagnosed as new conditions; this can precipitate a prescribing cascade that occurs when new medications are added to treat an ADE that is misinterpreted as a new disorder. Adding oxybutynin therapy to treat this patient's incontinence is an example of an avoidable prescribing cascade (Choice D); this would also place her at risk for further cascade (eg, she may experience anticholinergic-induced agitation, prompting antipsychotic therapy). (Choice A) Urinary incontinence is typically a consequence of severe dementia, for which memantine (an NMDA receptor antagonist) is sometimes used, often in combination with cholinesterase inhibitors. However, this patient has mild dementia, which does not classically cause urinary incontinence and for which memantine has shown inconclusive benefit. Drug-induced incontinence should first be excluded. (Choice B) Pelvic floor exercises are an important treatment for most forms of urinary incontinence. Given that this patient's incontinence is likely due to donepezil and is chronologically consistent with an ADE, drug discontinuation with monitoring is appropriate. (Choice E) Intermittent catheterization can help when overflow incontinence results from chronic urinary retention (eg, spinal cord injury). However, this patient's symptoms suggest urge incontinence; her lack of overflow symptoms (eg, dribbling, continuous leakage) and evidence for an ADE warrant stopping donepezil. Educational objective: Because of increased risk, older adults should have any new symptom investigated as a possible adverse drug event (ADE). Vigilance is important because misdiagnosis of an ADE as a new medical condition can lead to a prescribing cascade.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the office by her daughter due to urinary urgency and frequent episodes of urinary incontinence over the past month. There is no report of urinary leakage with coughing or exertion, and the patient has had no fever, chills, abdominal pain, or dysuria. Three months ago, she was prescribed donepezil, which she takes at the maximal dose, for mild Alzheimer dementia. Her daughter reports that the patient's forgetfulness is about the same, with no behavioral symptoms. The patient lives with her daughter and there have been no safety concerns. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 133/80 mm Hg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination shows no abdominal or costovertebral angle tenderness. The patient is oriented only to person and place and recalls 1 of 3 objects after 5 minutes. The remainder of the neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Blood cell counts, serum chemistry studies, and urinalysis are within normal limits. Her daughter takes oxybutynin for overactive bladder and requests that her mother be prescribed the same medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's urinary symptoms?

questions.explanation: This patient has acute liver injury (eg, right upper quadrant tenderness, elevated liver enzyme levels) after repeated excessive intake of acetaminophen over several days. Her presentation is consistent with acetaminophen toxicity from repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI), and treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should be initiated immediately to limit further hepatoxicity. Acute acetaminophen toxicity can occur after either a single large ingestion (usually >7.5 g in adults) or repeated ingestion of higher-than-recommended doses (RSTI). In cases of single ingestion, the decision to administer NAC is made by plotting the serum acetaminophen level against the time since ingestion on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; NAC treatment is indicated if the intersection point is above the treatment line. In cases of RSTI, the nomogram is not reliable to guide treatment. By the time patients with RSTI come to the emergency department for care, their acetaminophen level may be normal or only mildly elevated, despite ongoing hepatoxicity. NAC should be administered immediately if any evidence of liver injury is present, such as liver tenderness or elevated liver function tests >50 U/L. Although NAC is most effective when given within 8 hours of acetaminophen ingestion, it reduces mortality even after liver injury has begun. (Choice A) Activated charcoal decreases the enteric absorption of acetaminophen when administered within 4 hours after toxic ingestion. This patient took multiple doses over several days, and her last ingestion was >12 hours ago; charcoal would not be beneficial at this point. (Choice B) Although hemodialysis clears acetaminophen from the serum, it is invasive and not routinely used in the standard management of acetaminophen overdose. NAC is the mainstay of treatment, and prompt administration can help prevent further liver injury. (Choice C) Liver ultrasonography may be considered in the work-up of undifferentiated acute liver injury (eg, to assess for choledocholithiasis). However, this patient has a clear etiology for her liver injury, and the best next step is to treat it with NAC. (Choice D) Delaying treatment for 4 hours while awaiting a repeat acetaminophen level would be inappropriate. This patient with RSTI has signs of liver injury and warrants immediate treatment with NAC regardless of the acetaminophen level. Educational objective: Acetaminophen toxicity can occur after repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI), and acetaminophen levels measured at the time of presentation may not correlate with the degree of hepatoxicity. N-acetylcysteine should be initiated immediately in any patient with RSTI and evidence of acute liver injury.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to nausea and vomiting. She has a history of migraines and started having a severe headache 3 days ago. Since the onset of the headache, the patient has taken at least 50 caplets of combination 50 mg butalbital–300 mg acetaminophen–40 mg caffeine and multiple doses of her husband's acetaminophen with codeine. The headache has improved, but now she has developed nausea and 5 episodes of vomiting. The patient has taken no medications since the vomiting began 12 hours ago. Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 118/79, and pulse is 97/min. Pulse oximetry shows 97% on room air. She appears fatigued. The abdomen is soft but moderately tender in the right upper quadrant. Aspartate aminotransferases and alanine aminotransferases are 3,600 U/L and 3,900 U/L, respectively. Serum acetaminophen level is 19 mcg/mL (therapeutic range: 10-20). Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

questions.explanation: This patient has a headache that worsens with increased pressure (eg, bending forward), is associated with minor epistaxis, and began after a trip involving scuba diving. This presentation is most consistent with sinus barotrauma, which frequently affects divers. The gas-filled sinuses are lined with mucosa. The sinus ostia (openings) allow fluid to drain into the nasal cavity and allow pressure to equalize between the sinus cavities and outside atmosphere. Rapid changes in pressure (eg, diving, air travel) can lead to mucosal edema, which can acutely block the sinus ostia, preventing pressure from equilibrating and leading to acutely increased pain and pressure in the sinuses. This is usually temporary (<2 hr) but can sometimes be persistent, as in this patient. Treatment includes oral and nasal decongestants (eg, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline). Antibiotics should be used only if there is suspicion for superimposed bacterial infection (eg, fevers, purulent drainage), which can sometimes occur due to inspissated mucus in the sinuses. (Choice A) The environmental reservoir for Naegleria fowleri, the causative agent of amebic meningoencephalitis, is warm fresh water (vs salt water). In addition to headache, patients have a much more severe presentation usually including fever, confusion, vomiting, and seizures. (Choice C) Cluster headaches typically present with acute, unilateral retro-orbital pain accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic manifestations (eg, ptosis, miosis); episodes usually last about 90 minutes. This patient's persistent headache accompanied by sinus tenderness after diving is more consistent with barotrauma. (Choice D) Tension headaches can also present with primarily bifrontal symptoms. However, they are usually accompanied by temporal muscle tenderness (vs sinus tenderness) and occur after a period of increased stress. (Choice E) Vasomotor rhinitis, a type of nonallergic rhinitis, presents with nasal symptoms (eg, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion)—not seen in this patient—without an allergic etiology. Triggers often include temperature changes, strong odors, and eating spicy foods; headache is uncommon, and symptoms are typically chronic (>1 year). (Choice F) Exposure to large crowds can increase exposure to viruses that can lead to viral sinusitis, which can present with headache and sinus tenderness. However, additional upper respiratory symptoms (eg, congestion, malaise, fevers) would be expected, and the nasal mucosa would likely appear inflamed on examination. Educational objective: Barotrauma affecting the paranasal sinuses is common in divers and occurs because changes in barometric pressure generate mucosal edema, which causes obstruction of the sinus outflow tracts and an inability to equalize pressure. It presents with headache and sinus pressure/pain; sinuses are often tender to palpation.
