questions.explanation: Anorectal abscesses Etiology Obstruction of anal crypt gland → bacterial overgrowth Risk factors Constipation, anoreceptive intercourse Inflammatory bowel disease Diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression (eg, corticosteroids, HIV/AIDS) Clinical presentation Pruritus, pain with defecation → severe, constant pain ± fever Superficial: visible erythematous area with tenderness, induration, ± fluctuance Deep: palpable area of induration or fluctuance on DRE Management Imaging (eg, CT scan) if concern for deep infection Prompt incision & drainage Systemic antibiotic therapy* if cellulitis, fever, or ↑ risk for severe infection (eg, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression) present *Consider in all patients; may ↓ risk for fistula formation. DRE = digital rectal examination. This patient with severe anal pain and a well-defined, fluctuant, perianal mass likely has a perianal abscess, a type of anorectal abscess. Anorectal abscesses arise when anal crypt glands become blocked, leading to bacterial overgrowth. They vary in presentation based on their anatomic location: Simple perianal abscesses are located within the dermis and subcutaneous tissue surrounding the anal orifice; they are usually superficial and obvious on inspection as well-circumscribed, erythematous, hot, tender perianal masses. Perirectal abscesses are located within the intersphincteric, supralevator, and/or ischiorectal spaces. Because of their deeper location, they frequently have no associated perianal skin changes but instead cause signs of systemic infection (eg, fever, tachycardia) and tenderness, fluctuance, and/or induration on digital rectal examination. Both perianal and perirectal abscesses require prompt surgical incision and drainage (I&D). Because of their superficial location, perianal abscesses can often undergo I&D at the bedside, whereas perirectal abscesses usually require surgical drainage in the operating room. Following I&D, antibiotics are recommended for patients with extensive cellulitis, fever, or increased risk for severe infection (eg, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression). In these patients, antibiotic therapy decreases abscess recurrence (Choice D). In addition, antibiotic therapy may decrease the odds of anorectal fistula formation, a common (up to 50%) complication of anorectal abscess. (Choices A and B) Because of the deeper location of the abscess, treatment of perirectal (vs superficial perianal) abscesses typically includes admission to the hospital and IV antibiotics with prompt surgical I&D in the operating room. Waiting 48 hours to reevaluate before performing I&D is inappropriate and risks abscess expansion and worsening infection. Colonoscopy has no established role in evaluating or managing perirectal or perianal abscesses because it does not provide visualization or access to the deep perirectal spaces. (Choice C) Oral antibiotics and 48-hour follow-up are inadequate treatments for an anorectal abscess because antibiotics usually have limited penetration into encapsulated abscess cavities. Prompt I&D is primary in the treatment of abscesses. Educational objective: Perianal abscesses commonly present with severe anal pain and a tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass in the superficial perianal skin. Definitive treatment involves prompt incision and drainage, often performed at the bedside. Adjunctive antibiotic therapy should be given to patients with extensive cellulitis, fever, or increased risk for severe infection (eg, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression).

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to severe pain in her left buttock near the anus. The pain is particularly worse when passing stool. questions.explanation: Pharmacologic management of IBS Abdominal pain First line: antispasmodic therapy (eg, hyoscyamine) as needed Second line: tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline)* Diarrhea First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), loperamide Second line: bile acid sequestrants (eg, cholestyramine), serotonin-3 receptor antagonists (eg, alosetron) Constipation First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), osmotic laxatives (eg, PEG) Second line: lubiprostone, guanylate cyclase agonists (eg, linaclotide), sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor (eg, tenapanor) *Preferred for IBS with diarrhea; avoid with constipation. IBS = irritable bowel syndrome; PEG = polyethylene glycol. This patient with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) has chronic abdominal pain that is inadequately relieved with dietary changes and first-line antispasmodic therapy (eg, hyoscyamine). The most appropriate next step is the addition of a daily tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) (eg, amitriptyline, nortriptyline). TCAs have demonstrated analgesic properties and are useful for neuropathic pain as well as for pain associated with IBS. Furthermore, due to their anticholinergic effects (eg, slowing intestinal transit time), they can benefit patients whose IBS symptoms predominantly involve diarrhea but should be avoided in patients who have constipation. (Choice A) Lubiprostone is an enteric chloride channel activator that is used to treat functional constipation and constipation-predominant IBS; it acts by increasing intestinal fluid secretion and motility. It is likely to worsen this patient's symptoms of diarrhea and is not appropriate for treating his abdominal pain. (Choice B) Gabapentinoids (eg, gabapentin) inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing neuronal transmission of pain signals. Although they are useful primarily for neuropathic pain, their use in IBS has not been established, and TCAs are preferred. (Choice C) Opioid analgesics may slow intestinal transit, but long-term use is associated with several adverse effects (eg, dependency). TCAs are a safer and more appropriate option to treat this patient's frequent abdominal pain. (Choice D) Although nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs have pain-relieving properties, frequent or prolonged use is associated with adverse gastrointestinal effects (eg, bleeding, heartburn) and would not be appropriate for this patient with abdominal discomfort. Educational objective: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) may be used in patients with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome who have persistent abdominal pain despite antispasmodic therapy (eg, hyoscyamine). TCAs have analgesic effects independent of effects on mood and exert anticholinergic effects, which slow intestinal transit and improve diarrheal symptoms.

questions.explanation: Hypoparathyroidism Etiology Postsurgical: thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy Genetic disorder (eg, DiGeorge syndrome) Radiation Autoimmune disease Symptoms Asymptomatic Perioral or peripheral numbness/tingling, muscle cramps Carpal spasm (Trousseau sign) & facial twitch (Chvostek sign) Prolonged QT interval, tetany, seizure Diagnostic findings Hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia Low or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone level Elevated 24-hr urinary calcium excretion Management Mild hypocalcemia (corrected calcium >7.5 mg/dL): Oral calcium & calcitriol Severe hypocalcemia (corrected calcium ≤7.5 mg/dL): Intravenous calcium gluconate This patient has affective symptoms (eg, irritability, depressed mood) and features of neuromuscular excitability (eg, paresthesia, diffuse hyperreflexia). In the acute postsurgical phase following neck surgery, this presentation suggests iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism. Hypoparathyroidism can occur after anterior neck procedures (eg, thyroidectomy, lymph node dissection) due to direct injury, inadvertent removal, or devascularization to the parathyroid glands. Initial symptoms may be vague and nonspecific, but more severe manifestations may include tetany (eg, carpal spasm, Trousseau sign), QT interval prolongation, and/or seizure. Laboratory findings in hypoparathyroidism include hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and a low (or inappropriately normal) parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. The 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (reflecting total body stores) is generally normal, whereas 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (which requires PTH-mediated activation by 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidneys) may be low. Patients with mild hypocalcemia (eg, corrected serum calcium >7.5 mg/dL, mild symptoms) can generally be managed with oral calcium and vitamin D (calcitriol), but patients with severe hypocalcemia (serum calcium ≤7.5 mg/dL, seizures, significant QT interval prolongation) require intravenous calcium gluconate. (Choice A) Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, fluoxetine, citalopram) are appropriate for many affective and anxiety disorders. However, this patient's hyperreflexia, tingling, and recent neck surgery require that hypoparathyroidism be ruled out before attributing his symptoms to a mood disorder. (Choice B) Vitamin B12 deficiency can develop gradually (eg, years) following gastric or intestinal surgery and may cause neurocognitive deficits and paresthesia (as well as ataxia and loss of vibration sense). However, vitamin B12 deficiency would not be seen acutely following neck surgery, and this patient's hyperreflexia is more consistent with hypocalcemia. (Choice C) Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain has high sensitivity for brain metastases, which can cause neurocognitive symptoms. However, brain metastases often cause focal neurologic findings (eg, hemiparesis, pupillary changes) and may be associated with increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, nausea, vomiting). Given his recent neck surgery, the patient's serum calcium should be checked first. (Choice E) Hypothyroidism can cause neurocognitive and affective symptoms; however, reflexes are delayed rather than increased. In addition, thyroxine has a very long half-life (several days), so iatrogenic hypothyroidism is unlikely to be symptomatic so soon after surgery. Educational objective: Hypoparathyroidism can be caused by direct parathyroid injury or devascularization during surgical procedures in the anterior neck. Initial neurocognitive or affective symptoms may be nonspecific, but acute hypocalcemia may also cause paresthesia, hyperreflexia, tetany, or seizure. Laboratory findings include hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and a low parathyroid hormone level.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with an extensive history of tobacco use comes to the office for follow-up 10 days after undergoing total laryngectomy and unilateral modified radical neck dissection for advanced laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma with erosion completely through the thyroid cartilage. The patient has not yet received chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or radiation therapy. Today the patient is able to communicate well with an electrolarynx. He reports fatigue, irritability, memory difficulties, muscle aches, and tingling in both hands and feet. He says he has also been sleeping more than usual and feels depressed. Appetite is normal, and he has no suicidal ideation. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, the patient appears anxious but fully oriented. The surgical site is healing well with no erythema or discharge; the stoma is clean and open with no crusting. Lung and heart sounds are normal. Neurologic examination shows normal recall and attention. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in all 4 extremities with normal muscle tone and strength. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation is normal throughout. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: Hypoparathyroidism Etiology Postsurgical: thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy Genetic disorder (eg, DiGeorge syndrome) Radiation Autoimmune disease Symptoms Asymptomatic Perioral or peripheral numbness/tingling, muscle cramps Carpal spasm (Trousseau sign) & facial twitch (Chvostek sign) Prolonged QT interval, tetany, seizure Diagnostic findings Hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia Low or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone level Elevated 24-hr urinary calcium excretion Management Mild hypocalcemia (corrected calcium >7.5 mg/dL): Oral calcium & calcitriol Severe hypocalcemia (corrected calcium ≤7.5 mg/dL): Intravenous calcium gluconate Hypoparathyroidism is characterized by hypocalcemia and a low parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. Early manifestations of hypoparathyroidism can be nonspecific in young children (eg, fatigue, perioral paresthesia, irritability); more significant hypocalcemia can lead to tetany, seizures, and QT interval prolongation. In adults, acquired hypoparathyroidism is most often iatrogenic (eg, injury to parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery); in children, most cases are due to autoimmune disease, including polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type 1 (also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy). This patient's nail dystrophy and hyperpigmentation (ie, ectodermal dystrophy), chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and possible primary adrenal insufficiency (poor growth) strongly suggest this diagnosis. In addition, some patients may have congenital forms of hypoparathyroidism, also presenting in childhood. Management of hypoparathyroidism requires both calcium replacement (with intravenous replacement in patients with significant symptoms, such as this one) and vitamin D replacement. Because activity of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, is dependent on PTH, patients with hypoparathyroidism typically have normal levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (reflecting total body vitamin D stores) but can have low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (active form) levels. Therefore, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is preferred for vitamin D replacement. (Choices A and E) Bisphosphonates reduce bone resorption. They are used long term (eg, alendronate) for postmenopausal osteoporosis and in short courses (eg, zoledronic acid) for severe malignancy-related hypercalcemia; their use in children is limited due to potential suppression of bone remodeling during growth. Calcitonin is often given intranasally for reduction of pain due to acute osteoporotic fracture and is occasionally given subcutaneously or intramuscularly for hypercalcemia. These agents are contraindicated in hypoparathyroidism because they can worsen hypocalcemia. (Choice C) Hypomagnesemia (eg, due to diuretic use, gastrointestinal losses) can impair PTH secretion, leading to hypocalcemia; in such cases, correcting the hypocalcemia may be difficult unless the magnesium is replaced concurrently. However, this patient's low PTH level is likely due to autoimmune hypoparathyroidism rather than hypomagnesemia, and replacing magnesium is unnecessary. (Choice D) PTH increases renal phosphorus excretion. Patients with hypoparathyroidism often have hyperphosphatemia, and administration of phosphorus is contraindicated. Educational objective: Hypoparathyroidism presents with hypocalcemia and a low parathyroid hormone level. Acquired causes are usually iatrogenic (adults) or autoimmune (children). Management requires calcium and vitamin D supplementation; calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is preferred because it does not require PTH-mediated renal conversion to the active form.

  • Severe hypocalcemia (corrected calcium ≤7.5 mg/dL):
    • Intravenous calcium gluconate

Hypoparathyroidism is characterized by hypocalcemia and a low parathyroid hormone (PTH) level.  Early manifestations of hypoparathyroidism can be nonspecific in young children (eg, fatigue, perioral paresthesia, irritability); more significant hypocalcemia can lead to tetany, seizures, and QT interval prolongation.

In adults, acquired hypoparathyroidism is most often iatrogenic (eg, injury to parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery); in children, most cases are due to autoimmune disease, including polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type 1 (also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy).  This patient's nail dystrophy and hyperpigmentation (ie, ectodermal dystrophy), chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and possible primary adrenal insufficiency (poor growth) strongly suggest this diagnosis.  In addition, some patients may have congenital forms of hypoparathyroidism, also presenting in childhood.

Management of hypoparathyroidism requires both calcium replacement (with intravenous replacement in patients with significant symptoms, such as this one) and vitamin D replacement.  Because activity of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, is dependent on PTH, patients with hypoparathyroidism typically have normal levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (reflecting total body vitamin D stores) but can have low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (active form) levels.  Therefore, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is preferred for vitamin D replacement.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choices A and E)  Bisphosphonates reduce bone resorption.  They are used long term (eg, alendronate) for postmenopausal osteoporosis and in short courses (eg, zoledronic acid) for severe malignancy-related hypercalcemia; their use in children is limited due to potential suppression of bone remodeling during growth.  Calcitonin is often given intranasally for reduction of pain due to acute osteoporotic fracture and is occasionally given subcutaneously or intramuscularly for hypercalcemia.  These agents are contraindicated in hypoparathyroidism because they can worsen hypocalcemia.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Hypomagnesemia (eg, due to diuretic use, gastrointestinal losses) can impair PTH secretion, leading to hypocalcemia; in such cases, correcting the hypocalcemia may be difficult unless the magnesium is replaced concurrently.  However, this patient's low PTH level is likely due to autoimmune hypoparathyroidism rather than hypomagnesemia, and replacing magnesium is unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  PTH increases renal phosphorus excretion.  Patients with hypoparathyroidism often have hyperphosphatemia, and administration of phosphorus is contraindicated.

questions.explanation: Twin gestations are risk-stratified by chorionicity (number of placentas) and amnionicity (number of amniotic sacs). Monochorionic twins (one shared placenta) at risk for twin-twin transfusion syndrome because blood supply to one (donor) can be shunted to the other (recipient) via aberrant arteriovenous anastomoses, resulting in heart failure and possible fetal demise in both twins. Monoamniotic twins (one shared amniotic sac) are at risk for umbilical cord entanglement because the fetuses move around each other in utero. This movement can abruptly occlude the umbilical vessels, leading to hypoxia and fetal demise. Cord entanglement is spontaneous and unpredictable, and labor increases the risk due to constant agitation from uterine contractions. Therefore, monochorionic, monoamniotic twins require close antenatal fetal surveillance and planned cesarean delivery prior to the onset of labor (eg, at 32-34 weeks gestation). This patient at 29 weeks gestation is in spontaneous labor with monochorionic, monoamniotic twins. Due to the risk of cord entanglement and fetal demise during labor, emergent cesarean delivery is indicated (Choice B). (Choice C) Presentation refers to the fetal part closest to the cervix (eg, vertex, breech) whereas position refers to the relationship between the fetal head and the pelvic outlet (eg, occiput posterior). Occiput posterior position can prolong the second stage of labor because a larger diameter must pass through the pelvic outlet, but it is not an independent indication for cesarean delivery. (Choice D) Pregnant patients with chronic hypertension (defined in pregnancy as ≥140/≥90 mm Hg) and severe hypertension (≥160/≥110 mm Hg) first require antihypertensive treatment and evaluation for superimposed preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome (eg, platelet count, transaminases). Immediate cesarean delivery is not indicated unless the evaluation is abnormal, fetal status becomes nonreassuring (eg, late decelerations, minimal heart rate variability), or blood pressure cannot be controlled with antihypertensives. (Choice E) Some causes of vaginal bleeding, such as placenta previa or large placental abruption, may require cesarean delivery. In contrast, this patient's bloody vaginal discharge is consistent with "bloody show" of normal labor caused by the cervix dilating and stretching rapidly. Placenta previa and placental abruption are unlikely because the placenta is fundal and the fetal heart rate tracings are category I. Educational objective: Because monochorionic, monoamniotic twins share one amniotic sac, they are at risk for cord entanglement. This risk increases during labor and vaginal delivery; therefore, cesarean delivery is recommended.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, at 29 weeks gestation with a monochorionic, monoamniotic twin pregnancy presents with contractions. The contractions began this morning and are painful, occurring every 3 to 4 minutes. She has had no leakage of fluid. Her past medical history includes chronic hypertension. The patient has had only intermittent prenatal care, but her prior 2 pregnancies ended with spontaneous vaginal deliveries at term. External fetal monitoring shows category I tracing for both fetuses. Tocodynamometer shows contractions every 3 minutes. Blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 18/min. On physical examination, the cervix is 5 cm dilated and there is mucous-like vaginal discharge that is lightly blood tinged. Ultrasound shows that the presenting twin is in vertex, occiput anterior position. The second twin has a vertex presentation, and the placenta is located at the fundus. Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. A cesarean delivery is recommended. Which of the following is the indication for cesarean delivery in this patient?

questions.explanation: System-based strategies that increase the use of technology (eg, computerized provider order entry) can improve medication safety by reducing the potential for human error, including misinterpretation errors associated with illegible handwriting. When technology is unavailable (eg, planned maintenance, system outage), prescribers must use safe prescribing practices, including: Avoiding high-risk abbreviations, symbols, and dose designations that can be misinterpreted (whether orders are verbal, electronic, or written), writing out the word in entirety instead. For example, "U" can be mistakenly interpreted as "0" instead of "units"; "IU" can be misinterpreted as "10" or "IV" instead of "international units"; "SC" can be misinterpreted as "SL" (ie, sublingually) instead of "subcutaneously." Avoiding trailing zeros (decimal point followed by a zero) because the decimal point can be overlooked, leading to a 10-fold dosing error (eg, 10.0 units mistaken as 100 units) (Choice A). Using tall man lettering when writing prescriptions for look-alike drug names; in this technique, uppercase lettering is used to distinguish identifying characters of drugs with similar names (eg, vinCRIStine/vinBLAStine; DoBUTamine/DOPamine). (Choice B) Weight-based doses (eg, 1 mg/kg) are frequently used in pediatric dosing of intravenous or oral medications. Specifying a weight-based dose is not necessary or indicated for subcutaneous long-acting insulin in an adult. (Choice D) Clarifying details on the timing of administration can sometimes be useful for certain medications that are given multiple times a day (eg, every 8 hours) or that require a specific time interval for efficacy (eg, 30 minutes before a meal). Timing of administration is not necessary for an order for long-acting subcutaneous insulin (which is administered every 24 hours), nor is it likely to improve safety compared to writing out abbreviations. (Choice E) Using generic rather than brand names is recommended to optimize the safety of prescriptions for most drugs because brand names can vary (eg, across countries) and may be less familiar to providers compared to generic ingredients. When prescribing look-alike medications, specifying both brand and generic names can prevent confusion (eg, Paxil [paroxetine], which can be confused with Plavix [clopidogrel]). In contrast, glargine is not a look-alike medication, and specifying its brand name is unlikely to improve safety. Educational objective: Safe prescribing practices include avoiding high-risk abbreviations (eg, using "units" instead of "U" and "subcutaneously" instead of "SC"), avoiding trailing zeros (eg, using "1" instead of "1.0"), and using tall man (uppercase) lettering to distinguish identifying components of look-alike medications (eg, vinCRIStine/vinBLAStine).

questions.explanation: This patient has erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the scalp and retroauricular areas, findings consistent with plaque psoriasis. Psoriasis typically affects the extensor surfaces of the knees and elbows but can also occur on the scalp, hands, and gluteal cleft. Lesions can be asymptomatic or mildly pruritic and are typically symmetric in distribution. The diagnosis is made clinically, but biopsy may be indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain. Complications of psoriasis include psoriatic arthritis, nail changes (eg, pitting, onycholysis), and ocular inflammation (eg, conjunctivitis uveitis), which may manifest as the disease progresses. Factors that can lead to worsening symptoms include local skin trauma (Koebner phenomenon), infections (eg, HIV, streptococcal pharyngitis), and medications (eg, systemic glucocorticoid withdrawal, antimalarials, lithium, beta blockers). (Choice A) Chronic allergic or irritant contact dermatitis of the scalp typically results from hair products (eg, hair dye) and is characterized by lichenification and pruritus. The patient has no history of irritant exposure isolated to the lesion-affected areas, and the presence of thick, silvery scales in the absence of pruritus is atypical for contact dermatitis. (Choice B) Crusted scabies commonly presents in the hands, although it can affect the scalp and manifests with highly pruritic, rapidly progressing erythematous papules with burrows (eg, in interdigital spaces). Patients usually have an underlying risk factor (eg, immunocompromise). In contrast, this patient's lesions have followed an indolent course, lack burrows, and are not pruritic. (Choice D) Impetigo (due to staphyloccocal or streptococcal infection) can cause plaques and occasionally affect the retroauricular areas; however, it classically begins with papules and pustules that may be painful or pruritic and subsequently rupture and harden into a characteristic golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusting. (Choice E) Tinea capitis most commonly affects children and typically manifests with pruritic scaly patches with alopecia, black dots representing broken hairs, and a kerion (tender, boggy mass), none of which are observed in this patient. Regional lymphadenopathy can be present as well. Educational objective: Plaque psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition that typically presents with discrete erythematous plaques with silvery scales; common locations include extensor surfaces of the extremities (eg, elbows, knees), scalp, and retroauricular areas. The diagnosis is made clinically.

questions.explanation: This patient has monochorionic diamniotic twins (1 placenta, 2 amniotic sacs) based on an ultrasound revealing 2 embryos, a single placenta, and a thin intertwin membrane that meets the placenta at a 90-degree angle ("T sign"). This shape distinguishes monochorionic diamniotic gestations from fused dichorionic diamniotic gestations that typically have the "lambda sign" due to chorionic tissue (placenta) between the membranes. Because monochorionic diamniotic twins share a placenta, they are at risk for a complication called twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). In TTTS, unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses are found between the vessels supplying the umbilical cord of each twin. Due to the anastomoses, blood from the placental arteries (high resistance/pressure) of one twin (donor) is shunted into the placental veins (low resistance/pressure) of the other twin (recipient). Therefore, the donor twin is at risk for developing anemia, renal failure, oligohydramnios, low-output heart failure, and fetal growth restriction. In contrast, the recipient twin can develop polycythemia, which can lead to discordant fetal growth, polyhydramnios, cardiomegaly, high-output heart failure, and hydrops fetalis. Both twins are at risk for intrauterine and neonatal death. (Choice B) Fetal dysmaturity (eg, wrinkled, peeling skin; small for gestational age) can be seen in postterm pregnancies (ie, ≥42 weeks gestation) due to deteriorating placental function as the placenta ages. Twins are more likely to be delivered preterm (ie, <37 weeks gestation), and therefore unlikely to develop fetal dysmaturity. (Choices C and E) Placenta accreta is the abnormal placentation onto the myometrium, usually in areas of uterine scarring, and uterine rupture typically occurs in laboring patients with a weakened myometrium due to prior uterine scarring. The most common risk factor for both these conditions is a history of uterine surgery (eg, cesarean delivery, myomectomy). Twin gestations do not typically distend the uterus enough to cause spontaneous uterine rupture in the absence of prior scarring. (Choice D) Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum, which are more common in twin pregnancies, can lead to poor maternal weight gain. However, this patient can tolerate meals, and twin gestations typically lead to greater maternal weight gain compared to singleton gestations, making poor weight gain unlikely. Educational objective: Monochorionic diamniotic twins are distinguished from dichorionic diamniotic twins on ultrasound by an intertwin membrane that meets the placenta at a 90-degree angle (ie, "T sign"). Because monochorionic diamniotic twins share a placenta, they are at risk for twin-twin transfusion syndrome and discordant fetal growth.

questions.explanation: This patient has seborrheic keratosis (SK), which typically presents as an asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, well-demarcated plaque with a waxy or papillated (verrucous) surface. The raised surface, abrupt border, and distinct tan, brown, or black pigmentation of SK are common features that give it a stuck-on appearance. It is most often seen in middle-aged or older patients (eg, age ≥50); individuals typically develop numerous lesions over time, although an explosive onset of multiple pruritic SKs is occasionally associated with internal malignancy (ie, Leser-Trélat sign). In most cases, the diagnosis of SK is obvious based on clinical appearance; no further evaluation is generally needed. If desired, a magnified view (with a hand lens or dermatoscopy) may show whitish milia, irregular fissures and crypts, keratin plugs, and linear or fingerprint-like pigmentation. (Choices A and B) Excisional biopsy removes the entirety of a lesion and is appropriate when skin cancer is suspected. Narrow margins (eg, <3 mm from the edge of the visible lesion) are appropriate when low-risk malignancy is suspected (eg, small basal cell carcinoma), whereas wide margins (eg, >5-10 mm) are usually used for high-risk lesions (eg, suspected melanoma). The clinical features of this patient's lesion are adequate for diagnosis; biopsy is not necessary. (Choice C) Incisional and punch biopsy techniques sample only a portion of a lesion and are typically performed for large, inflammatory lesions, for which removal of the entire lesion is impractical (eg, bullous dermatoses) and if there is a low suspicion for malignancy. (Choice E) Shave biopsy can be performed to remove SKs for cosmetic reasons or for tissue confirmation in atypical lesions. Histopathology may reveal clustered, benign keratinocytes and keratin-filled cysts. However, tissue confirmation is rarely needed for diagnosis. Educational objective: Seborrheic keratosis presents as a well-demarcated, pigmented plaque with a waxy or papillated (verrucous) surface and characteristic stuck-on appearance. Onset is at age ≥50, and patients commonly develop numerous lesions over time. The diagnosis is usually apparent based on clinical appearance, and no further evaluation is needed.

explanationPanel.html:
Educational objective:
Seborrheic keratosis presents as a well-demarcated, pigmented plaque with a waxy or papillated (verrucous) surface and characteristic stuck-on appearance.  Onset is at age ≥50, and patients commonly develop numerous lesions over time.  The diagnosis is usually apparent based on clinical appearance, and no further evaluation is needed.
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
This patient has seborrheic keratosis (SK), which typically presents as an asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, well-demarcated plaque with a waxy or papillated (verrucous) surface.  The raised surface, abrupt border, and distinct tan, brown, or black pigmentation of SK are common features that give it a stuck-on appearance.  It is most often seen in middle-aged or older patients (eg, age ≥50); individuals typically develop numerous lesions over time, although an explosive onset of multiple pruritic SKs is occasionally associated with internal malignancy (ie, Leser-Trélat sign).

In most cases, the diagnosis of SK is obvious based on clinical appearance; no further evaluation is generally needed.  If desired, a magnified view (with a hand lens or dermatoscopy) may show whitish milia, irregular fissures and crypts, keratin plugs, and linear or fingerprint-like pigmentation.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choices A and B)  Excisional biopsy removes the entirety of a lesion and is appropriate when skin cancer is suspected.  Narrow margins (eg, <3 mm from the edge of the visible lesion) are appropriate when low-risk malignancy is suspected (eg, small basal cell carcinoma), whereas wide margins (eg, >5-10 mm) are usually used for high-risk lesions (eg, suspected melanoma).  The clinical features of this patient's lesion are adequate for diagnosis; biopsy is not necessary.
wrongAnswers.B: See the shared discussion for choice A.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  Incisional and punch biopsy techniques sample only a portion of a lesion and are typically performed for large, inflammatory lesions, for which removal of the entire lesion is impractical (eg, bullous dermatoses) and if there is a low suspicion for malignancy.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Shave biopsy can be performed to remove SKs for cosmetic reasons or for tissue confirmation in atypical lesions.  Histopathology may reveal clustered, benign keratinocytes and keratin-filled cysts.  However, tissue confirmation is rarely needed for diagnosis.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old woman is brought to the office by her daughter due to a skin lesion. The patient has Alzheimer disease with progressive dementia and moved into her daughter's house 6 months ago for closer care. The daughter noticed the lesion on the patient's back during bathing and has become concerned due to its slow enlargement. She reports no itching or pain at the lesion. Skin examination findings are shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis of the patient?

questions.explanation: Childhood obesity Definition BMI ≥95th percentile or ≥30 kg/m2 Dietary recommendations Minimize sugary drinks (eg, fruit juice) & fast food Scheduled, balanced meals & snacks Controlled portion sizes Activity recommendations Limited screen time (eg, <2 hr/day for adolescents) Daily physical activity (≥1 hr) Adequate sleep (8-12 hr depending on age) Comorbidity screening Hyperlipidemia: fasting lipid panel Type 2 diabetes mellitus*: HbA1c or fasting glucose Fatty liver disease: ALT Hypertension: blood pressure monitoring Sleep apnea: polysomnogram (for habitual snoring) *Screening indicated for children who are overweight/obese with an additional risk factor (eg, family history of diabetes mellitus, signs of insulin resistance [eg, acanthosis nigricans]). ALT = alanine aminotransferase. This patient has a BMI ≥95th percentile, which is consistent with obesity. Annual well-child visits are an opportunity to monitor growth and identify excessive weight gain, which is associated with comorbidities, such as elevated blood pressure and cholesterol, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Due to an increased risk for early-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD), children with obesity are screened regularly (every 1-3 years) for dyslipidemia with a fasting lipid panel starting at age 2. Additional tests include alanine aminotransferase (ALT) to evaluate for NAFLD as well as hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose if other risk factors for diabetes mellitus (eg, positive family history, acanthosis nigricans) are present. Initial treatment for dyslipidemia (eg, total cholesterol ≥200, LDL ≥130, HDL <40) is lifestyle changes, including daily exercise and a diet low in saturated fats. Pharmacotherapy with a statin can be considered for patients age ≥10 with persistent dyslipidemia after 6 months of lifestyle changes. (Choice A) Universal dyslipidemia screening is recommended in all children once at age 9-11 and again at age 17-21. Although no further testing is required in a 14-year-old child with a normal BMI and no other CVD risk factors (eg, family history, diabetes mellitus, hypertension), this patient's BMI is elevated, so screening tests are indicated. (Choice C) Urinalysis detects microscopic hematuria and proteinuria and may be performed in patients with findings concerning for renal disease (eg, hypertension, edema). This patient's blood pressure is normal (ie, <120/80 mm Hg), and urinalysis is not routinely performed in otherwise asymptomatic children with obesity. (Choice D) Obesity increases the risk for obstructive sleep apnea, and a sleep study is indicated if snoring occurs on a habitual basis (eg, ≥3 nights/week). In contrast, this patient snores only intermittently with illnesses. (Choice E) A screening ECG is performed prior to sports participation in adolescents with concerning findings on history (eg, exertional chest pain, dyspnea, syncope) or examination (eg, hypertension, murmur). It should also be performed in those with a family history of cardiomyopathy, arrythmia, or heart disease (eg, myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death) at age <50. None of these findings are present in this case, and an ECG is not indicated in adolescents with obesity alone. Educational objective: Childhood obesity (ie, BMI ≥95th percentile) is a risk factor for dyslipidemia, and periodic screening with a fasting lipid panel is performed in all children with obesity starting at age 2. Additional testing includes alanine aminotransferase (fatty liver disease) and hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose if other diabetes mellitus risk factors are present.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the office by his father for an annual well-child visit. He states that the patient eats 3 well-balanced meals a day and snacks frequently. He sleeps 9 hours per night and snores on occasion with illnesses. The patient has no chronic medical conditions and is up to date on vaccinations. The boy's father has hypertension, and his grandfather passed away from a myocardial infarction in his 70s. BMI is at the 97th percentile. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 118/71 mm Hg, pulse is 60/min, and respirations are 18/min. The oropharynx is clear with 2+ tonsils. Heart and lung sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. Extremities are nonedematous, and peripheral pulses are strong. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome Risk factors Advanced cirrhosis with portal hypertension Acute liver failure, severe alcoholic hepatitis Pathophysiology Splanchnic vasodilation* → renal hypoperfusion → RAAS activation → overwhelming renal vasoconstriction → AKI Precipitants: gastrointestinal bleed, infection (eg, SBP) Diagnosis Bland urinalysis Very low urine Na+ (<10 mEq/L) Exclusion of other causes of AKI No improvement with trial of volume expansion Treatment Albumin + splanchnic vasoconstrictors** (temporizing) Liver transplantation (curative) *Due to excess local release of vasodilators (eg, nitric oxide). **Terlipressin, norepinephrine, or midodrine plus octreotide. AKI = acute kidney injury; RAAS = renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; SBP = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. This patient with cirrhosis had a gastrointestinal bleed and now has acute kidney injury (AKI). AKI in patients with cirrhosis can be due to various etiologies, most concerningly hepatorenal syndrome (HRS). HRS, a unique form of prerenal AKI, is characterized by a potentially devastating neurohormonal cascade: Portal hypertension reduces portal blood flow, leading to the release of local vasodilators (eg, nitric oxide) that cause splanchnic vasodilation. Splanchnic vasodilation decreases effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion, thereby causing neurohormonal hyperactivity (ie, sympathetic nervous system, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system). Neurohormonal hyperactivity leads to renal vasoconstriction and profound renal sodium retention. Renal vasoconstriction eventually can become overwhelming—either spontaneously or following a specific hemodynamic insult (eg, gastrointestinal bleeding)—resulting in rapidly deteriorating AKI. The diagnosis of HRS is typically made by a combination of a bland urinalysis (ie, no protein, cells, or casts), a very low urine sodium (<10 mEq/L, reflecting sodium retention), and a lack of response to volume expansion (because it reflects disrupted blood flow rather than volume depletion). Treatment involves the administration of vasoconstrictors (eg, terlipressin, norepinephrine), which, in HRS, cause splanchnic more than systemic vasoconstriction. This shunts blood into the systemic circulation, thereby removing the stimulus for renal vasoconstriction and improving renal perfusion. Given the vasoconstrictive effects of these medications, increased mean arterial pressure is used as a parameter for dosage titration. (Choice A) Anemia in cirrhosis can be due to multiple factors (eg, hypersplenism, chronic inflammation). However, in the absence of active bleeding or hemoglobin level <7 g/dL, increasing the hemoglobin level (eg, blood transfusion) is not indicated. Higher target levels of hemoglobin can increase portal pressure, which can worsen ascites and increase the risk for variceal bleeding. (Choices C and D) Nonselective beta blockers (eg, nadolol) reduce cardiac contractility (ie, decreased cardiac output) and portal venous pressure (ie, alterations in portal blood flow). They are used as prophylaxis against esophageal variceal bleeding. In patients with HRS or decompensated cirrhosis (who have impaired hemodynamics), beta blockers are typically avoided due to worsened outcomes. (Choice E) Corticosteroids can be used to reduce renal interstitial inflammation in patients with AKI caused by acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). However, this patient's absence of pyuria and proteinuria makes AIN unlikely. Educational objective: Hepatorenal syndrome is a cause of acute kidney injury in cirrhosis that results from splanchnic vasodilation, which leads to neurohormonal hyperactivity with subsequently overwhelming renal vasoconstriction. Administration of vasoconstrictors (titrated based on an increase in mean arterial pressure) reduces splanchnic vasodilation, thereby alleviating renal vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old hospitalized man is evaluated for worsening renal dysfunction. The patient has a history of cirrhosis due to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. He was admitted 4 days ago with coffee-ground emesis and melena. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed bleeding gastric antral vascular ectasia that was treated endoscopically. The patient has had no further bleeding, and hemoglobin has remained stable. However, serum creatinine has increased to 2.6 mg/dL from 1.3 mg/dL. The patient's home furosemide and spironolactone were stopped at admission, and his current medications are pantoprazole, lactulose, and prophylactic ceftriaxone. Urine output over the last 24 hours has been 800 mL. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 90/62 mm Hg, and pulse is 78/min. Physical examination shows clear lungs, normal heart sounds, and normal jugular venous pressure. Abdominal examination shows moderate ascites without tenderness. There are scattered spider angiomas but no other rashes. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. The most recent laboratory studies are as follows: Complete blood count Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL Platelets 120,000/mm3 Leukocytes 4,200/mm3 Serum chemistry Sodium 132 mEq/L Potassium 4.8 mEq/L Chloride 103 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen 64 mg/dL Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL Urinalysis No protein, cells, or casts Urine sodium is 5 mEq/L. Renal ultrasonography reveals no abnormalities. Treatment for this patient's kidney dysfunction is aimed primarily at which of the following parameters?

questions.explanation: Alopecia areata Pathogenesis Autoimmune attack on hair bulb cells Associated with other autoimmune disorders (eg, hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism, vitiligo) Clinical presentation Diagnosis made by visual inspection (eg, with dermatoscope) Painless, patchy, nonscarring hair loss affecting scalp, face, or body Exclamation point hairs (small hairs with proximal tapering) may be seen Management Mild/moderate hair loss: intralesional or topical corticosteroid therapy Extensive hair loss: oral Janus kinase inhibitor (eg, baricitinib) or topical immunotherapy (eg, diphenylcyclopropenone) Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease (serum TSH) Prognosis Regrowth is common in mild cases Recurrence is common This patient has a relatively rapid onset (eg, over weeks) of patchy hair loss with normal underlying skin. This presentation is most consistent with alopecia areata (AA), an autoimmune disorder involving the hair bulb cells in any area (eg, eyebrows, beard, scalp). Typically, hair loss occurs rapidly in discrete patches without associated pruritus or pain. Patches may coalesce, sometimes resulting in total-scalp or total-body hair loss in severe cases. AA affects both children and adults. The diagnosis of AA is usually based on visual inspection, and additional laboratory testing or biopsy is not routinely required. Close inspection (eg, using a dermatoscope) may show 3- to 4-mm hairs with narrowing of hair shafts close to the skin surface (exclamation point hairs), which are reflective of shaft weakening caused by bulb inflammation. The hair pull test is often positive as well (a cluster of ~50 hair fibers is pulled firmly; extraction of >5 or 6 strands is abnormal). Biopsy may be performed in rare cases when the diagnosis is uncertain, from the periphery of the patch (to assess for contrast with the normal hair border) rather than from the center of the lesion (Choice A). (Choice C) Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, which can have cutaneous manifestations (eg, discoid lesions) in the scalp with hair loss and associated inflammation, scarring, and hypopigmentation, not seen in this patient. Moreover, although AA is associated with other autoimmune illnesses (eg, thyroid disorders), routine screening with ANAs is not recommended for asymptomatic patients. Rather, patients should be monitored regularly, and targeted testing offered based on the emergence of concerning symptoms. (Choices D) Iron deficiency causes diffuse (not patchy) hair loss and frequently manifests with associated symptoms (eg, fatigue). This patient's patchy hair loss affecting only the beard is more consistent with AA. (Choice E) Skin scraping for potassium hydroxide analysis is useful to diagnose tinea barbae, which presents with scaly, erythematous annular patches in the bearded area accompanied by pruritus and hair loss. Fungal folliculitis, presenting as follicular erythematous papules or pustules, can also be seen in tinea barbae. This patient has normal underlying skin and lacks findings of fungal infection. Educational objective: Alopecia areata presents as patchy hair loss with normal underlying skin. The diagnosis is largely made based on visual inspection.

questions.explanation: Hand osteoarthritis Clinical presentation Age >40 Chronic, progressive hand pain & stiffness DIP & PIP joints; 1st carpometacarpal joint Diagnosis Examination: bony enlargement (Heberden & Bouchard nodes), crepitus with range of motion X-ray: joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, periarticular osteophytes Initial management Stretching & strengthening exercises Topical or oral NSAIDs DIP = distal interphalangeal; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; PIP = proximal interphalangeal. This patient has insidious hand pain with involvement of multiple hand joints, primarily in the right hand. Several conditions can cause arthritis involving the hand. This patient's history of skin psoriasis increases her risk for developing psoriatic arthritis (PsA), an inflammatory type of arthritis. However, many of her current symptoms are more consistent with osteoarthritis (OA), particularly given the lack of inflammatory features. Lack of inflammation is suggested by: activity-provoked pain that is relieved by rest; limited morning stiffness (<30 mins vs ≥30 mins with inflammatory arthritis); and absence of synovitis (joint swelling, redness) or dactylitis (ie, severe, "sausage finger" swelling) (Choice D). Distinguishing between OA and other types of arthritis is important in guiding appropriate treatment (eg, physical therapy for OA versus systemic immunotherapy for PsA). The following features help increase suspicion for OA: OA typically becomes symptomatic at age >40 and is associated with prior joint trauma or overuse (in contrast, PsA can occur at any age but typically is preceded by several years of skin involvement). Hand OA classically affects the first carpometacarpal and distal interphalangeal joint and may be unilateral (eg, dominant hand) or bilateral (in contrast, PsA can also involve distal hand joints and is typically bilateral). Examination findings in OA include bony enlargement at the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (ie, Heberden and Bouchard nodes), are commonly associated with OA (in contrast, findings of dactylitis and nail changes such as onycholysis, pitting, and oil spots suggest PsA). Hand OA is typically a clinical diagnosis; however, x-rays are useful when the diagnosis is uncertain. (Choice A) Enthesitis is inflammation of the insertion site of ligaments and tendons onto the bone; it frequently occurs in inflammatory arthritides, including PsA and ankylosing spondylitis. This patient lacks historical and clinical features (eg, prolonged morning stiffness, swelling) seen in inflammatory arthritis. (Choice B) Acute gouty arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis that presents with severe pain, swelling, and erythema, typically involving the first metatarsal phalangeal joint or knee. Involvement of the fingers and absence of joint inflammation on examination make acute gouty arthritis highly unlikely. (Choice E) Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis that presents with joint pain, swelling, and prolonged morning stiffness. When it involves the hands, rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. These features are absent in this patient. Educational objective: Hand osteoarthritis typically involves the distal interphalangeal and first carpometacarpal joints in patients age >40. Pain is provoked by activity and relieved by rest. In a patient with skin psoriasis, pain that involves these joints and is unaccompanied by prolonged morning stiffness, synovitis, and nail psoriasis suggests osteoarthritis.

  • Chronic, progressive hand pain & stiffness
  • DIP & PIP joints; 1st carpometacarpal joint
Diagnosis
  • Examination: bony enlargement (Heberden & Bouchard nodes), crepitus with range of motion
  • X-ray: joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, periarticular osteophytes
Initial management
  • Stretching & strengthening exercises
  • Topical or oral NSAIDs
DIP = distal interphalangeal; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; PIP = proximal interphalangeal.

This patient has insidious hand pain with involvement of multiple hand joints, primarily in the right hand.  Several conditions can cause arthritis involving the hand.  This patient's history of skin psoriasis increases her risk for developing psoriatic arthritis (PsA), an inflammatory type of arthritis.  However, many of her current symptoms are more consistent with osteoarthritis (OA), particularly given the lack of inflammatory features.

Distinguishing between OA and other types of arthritis is important in guiding appropriate treatment (eg, physical therapy for OA versus systemic immunotherapy for PsA).  The following features help increase suspicion for OA:

  • OA typically becomes symptomatic at age >40 and is associated with prior joint trauma or overuse (in contrast, PsA can occur at any age but typically is preceded by several years of skin involvement).
  • Hand OA classically affects the first carpometacarpal and distal interphalangeal joint and may be unilateral (eg, dominant hand) or bilateral (in contrast, PsA can also involve distal hand joints and is typically bilateral).
  • Examination findings in OA include bony enlargement at the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (ie, Heberden and Bouchard nodes), are commonly associated with OA (in contrast, findings of dactylitis and nail changes such as onycholysis, pitting, and oil spots suggest PsA).

Hand OA is typically a clinical diagnosis; however, x-rays are useful when the diagnosis is uncertain.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Enthesitis is inflammation of the insertion site of ligaments and tendons onto the bone; it frequently occurs in inflammatory arthritides, including PsA and ankylosing spondylitis.  This patient lacks historical and clinical features (eg, prolonged morning stiffness, swelling) seen in inflammatory arthritis.
wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Acute gouty arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis that presents with severe pain, swelling, and erythema, typically involving the first metatarsal phalangeal joint or knee.  Involvement of the fingers and absence of joint inflammation on examination make acute gouty arthritis highly unlikely.
wrongAnswers.D: Lack of inflammation is suggested by: activity-provoked pain that is relieved by rest; limited morning stiffness (<30 mins vs ≥30 mins with inflammatory arthritis); and absence of synovitis (joint swelling, redness) or dactylitis (ie, severe, "sausage finger" swelling) (Choice D).
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis that presents with joint pain, swelling, and prolonged morning stiffness.  When it involves the hands, rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.  These features are absent in this patient.

questions.explanation: Groin hernias Epidemiology Inguinal: more common in male patients Femoral: more common in female patients; more likely to become incarcerated/strangulated (~40%) Clinical features Uncomplicated (reducible): ↑ groin bulge with ↑ abdominal pressure (eg, cough) ± discomfort Incarcerated (nonreducible): moderate to severe groin pain & swelling Strangulated (nonreducible & ischemic): severe groin pain & swelling, vomiting, fever ± peritonitis Diagnosis Clinical diagnosis; confirmatory testing typically not required If diagnosis unclear: ultrasonography (preferred), CT scan, or MRI of the groin Management Watchful waiting considered for male patients with asymptomatic inguinal hernias Elective surgical repair: symptomatic groin hernias; femoral hernias Urgent or immediate surgical repair: incarcerated or strangulated hernias This patient with an acutely painful groin bulge and clinical features of bowel compromise (eg, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, diffuse abdominal tenderness) most likely has a strangulated hernia. Groin hernias result from protrusion of abdominal (eg, small bowel) or pelvic (eg, bladder) contents through the abdominal wall. Although hernias most commonly present as an easily reducible, intermittent groin bulge (ie, uncomplicated), hernia contents occasionally become trapped (ie, incarcerated). This leads to inflammation and edema that, when prolonged (eg, 8 hr), can result in compromised venous outflow, reduced arterial inflow, and eventual necrosis of hernia contents (ie, strangulation). Strangulated hernia is typically a clinical diagnosis that does not require confirmatory imaging. Diagnosis should prompt emergency surgical consultation while intravenous fluids and antibiotics are initiated. The hernia should not be reduced due to the risk of introducing necrotic bowel and leaked enteric contents into the abdominal cavity. If concerning clinical findings associated with the compromised bowel remain localized to the groin (eg, scrotal edema, erythema, tenderness), then urgent operative intervention (eg, within 4-6 hr of presentation) is usually sufficient to prevent serious complications. However, if the abdomen is also involved (eg, diffuse abdominal tenderness), as in this patient, then immediate operative intervention is required. (Choices A and E) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (which may show signs of small bowel obstruction or ischemia) and scrotal ultrasonography (which can show herniated contents) can confirm the diagnosis of strangulated hernia in unclear cases. However, these studies are unnecessary in this patient with a clear clinical diagnosis and would delay operative intervention, which should be performed immediately given his likely peritonitis. (Choice C) A nasogastric tube may be appropriate in this patient with vomiting due to bowel obstruction (the incarcerated bowel segment is the transition point). However, observation is inappropriate when signs of bowel compromise are present. (Choice D) Attempting reduction of herniated abdominal contents is appropriate for some incarcerated hernias (eg, short duration of incarceration). This patient has fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and diffuse abdominal tenderness highly concerning for strangulation; hernia reduction should not be attempted. Educational objective: An acutely painful groin bulge accompanied by clinical features of bowel compromise (eg, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, diffuse abdominal tenderness) is consistent with strangulated hernia. The diagnosis can typically be made clinically, without confirmatory imaging, and requires prompt operative intervention.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to right groin pain. The pain started suddenly 8 hours ago and has been accompanied by several episodes of vomiting. The patient says he noticed a bulge in his right groin a few months ago and that it "comes and goes," but now it is larger and painful. Medical history is significant for hypertension. Temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F), blood pressure is 125/75 mm Hg, pulse is 115/min, and respirations are 16/min. On examination, the patient appears uncomfortable. The abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation. The right scrotum is edematous and tender. Intravenous fluids and pain medications are administered. Laboratory results show a white blood cell count of 18,000/mm³. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

questions.explanation: This patient has a classic presentation of ischemic rest pain caused by peripheral artery disease. Risk factors for peripheral artery disease are similar to those for coronary artery disease and include age >50, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and smoking; chronic kidney disease also likely accelerates atherosclerotic disease. Many patients with peripheral artery disease present with intermittent claudication, which results from partial atherosclerotic occlusion that limits distal blood flow during exertion and typically manifests as foot or lower extremity (eg, calf, thigh) muscle pain brought on by exercise and relieved by rest; these patients can be initially managed conservatively (eg, exercise program, smoking cessation). Ischemic rest pain results from substantial atherosclerotic obstruction, with inadequate blood delivery to meet baseline metabolic demands. It classically manifests as pain in the forefoot or toes (eg, metatarsal joints) that is worse with elevation and relieved by standing or hanging the legs over the side of the bed (likely due to a gravitational increase in perfusion). In the setting of consistent symptoms, absent pulses (eg, dorsalis pedis) and an abnormal ankle-brachial index (ABI) ≤0.9 are diagnostic of ischemic rest pain. It is an indication for invasive revascularization (eg, stent placement, bypass surgery) to prevent limb loss. (Choice A) Metatarsal corticosteroid injections can be helpful for gout or an inflammatory flare of osteoarthritis. However, this patient has no redness, swelling, or tenderness of the foot to suggest an inflammatory state that would benefit from corticosteroids. (Choices B and E) Strict glycemic control and medications such as duloxetine or gabapentin can help reduce diabetic neuropathy pain. However, this patient's diabetes mellitus is relatively well controlled (ie, hemoglobin A1c <8.0%) and diabetic neuropathy symptoms are typically bilateral. This patient's symptoms are fully explained by ischemic rest pain (confirmed by absent pulses and abnormal ABI); loss of sensation and diminished reflexes are common with foot ischemia. (Choice C) Orthotic footwear may be helpful for plantar fasciitis, but plantar fasciitis involves heel pain that typically worsens with the first steps in the morning and with prolonged standing, and focal tenderness is commonly present on examination. Educational objective: Ischemic rest pain results from substantial progression of peripheral artery disease and classically presents with pain in the forefoot or toes that is worse with elevation and relieved by gravitational dependence. It is confirmed by absent pulses and an abnormal ankle-brachial index ≤0.9; it is an indication for prompt invasive revascularization to prevent limb loss.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the office due to left foot pain at night for the past 2 months. The patient describes a gnawing pain across the base of the metatarsal heads that begins shortly after he goes to bed. The pain is often relieved after he gets up and walks around the room or sits at the edge of the bed for a few minutes. Medical history includes diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. The patient is a former smoker with a 20-pack-year history. Blood pressure is 132/70 mm Hg and pulse is 68/min. Physical examination shows normal jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, and normal heart sounds. The left foot appears normal with no redness, swelling, or focal tenderness. The foot joints are normal with a normal foot arch. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses are not palpable. Neurologic examination demonstrates absent ankle reflex bilaterally. There is diminished sensation at the tip of the toes bilaterally on monofilament testing. The ankle-brachial index is <0.4 on the left and 0.6 on the right. The most recent hemoglobin A1c was 7.8%. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient's foot pain?

questions.explanation: Common ocular complications of diabetes mellitus Refractive changes Hyperglycemia, blurred vision Acute myopia & ↓ acuity; no other examination findings Cataract Blurred vision, ↓ acuity, ↑ glare Lens opacity, ↓ red reflex, ↓ fundus detail Glaucoma Open-angle: painless peripheral vision loss; ↑ IOP Angle-closure: conjunctival redness, corneal edema, middilated pupil, ↑ IOP Diabetic retinopathy & complications Nonproliferative: cotton-wool spot, retinal hemorrhage, microaneurysm Proliferative: neovascularization arising from the disc or retinal vessels Macular edema: thickening/edema of macular retina Vitreous hemorrhage: vitreous blood obscuring fundus Tractional retinal detachment: detachment with fibrovascular bands & no tears IOP = intraocular pressure. Patients with diabetes mellitus are susceptible to several disease-related eye complications, so any vision change requires urgent evaluation. This patient experienced an acute vision change without other eye symptoms during a period of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and symptomatic hyperglycemia (ie, increased thirst and urination). Given her relatively short time with type 1 diabetes mellitus and her recent normal ophthalmologic examination 3 months ago, the patient's current eye examination findings (normal fundus and intraocular pressure) are reassuring that she does not have a complication of long-term microvascular change (eg, diabetic retinopathy, diabetic macular edema) or an acute ophthalmologic emergency (eg, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment). Therefore, her vision change is likely due to osmotic changes in the lens. Hyperglycemia (eg, due to missed insulin doses when working overnight shifts) results in a hyperosmolar state that can cause lens edema and change the thickness, curvature, and/or refractive index of the lens (eg, blurry vision, myopia). Patients can experience acute or subacute changes in vision and sometimes seek medical attention after multiple changes to their glasses or contact lens prescriptions in a short time (ie, weeks to months). Other symptoms of hyperglycemia (eg, polyuria, polydipsia) can support the diagnosis. Improving glycemic control usually restores vision to baseline; it also helps decrease the risk of diabetic microvascular disease. (Choice A) Anterior chamber angle measurement can be helpful in the evaluation of suspected glaucoma. If glaucoma is chronic, it presents with painless loss of peripheral vision. If acute, it presents with corneal edema (which can affect vision); a fixed, middilated pupil; and conjunctival erythema, which are not present in this patient. (Choices B and E) Neovascularization of the retina occurs with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) in response to progressive retinal ischemia from diabetes mellitus. Neovascularization is often treated with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor injections into the vitreous humor and/or laser photocoagulation therapy. However, this patient has had diabetes mellitus for only 2 years, which is not usually long enough for PDR to develop. Furthermore, normal findings from her current funduscopic examination and ophthalmology follow-up 3 months ago make PDR and neovascularization extremely unlikely. (Choice C) Corneal examination with fluorescein staining is most commonly used to detect corneal abrasions and other injuries, which can lead to acute changes in vision. However, most corneal abrasions are painful and cause increased tearing. Educational objective: Hyperglycemia can cause osmotic changes in the lens that result in vision changes. Patients typically experience acute or subacute changes in vision and other symptoms of hyperglycemia (eg, polyuria, polydipsia) but have normal ocular examination findings. Improving glycemic control usually improves vision.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office due to blurry vision in both eyes for the past week. The patient works as a nurse and first noticed the vision change when she had difficulty reading telemetry monitors. She has had no eye pain, redness, or discharge. The patient also reports increased thirst and urination. Medical history includes type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 years ago and currently managed with a basal-bolus insulin regimen. The patient states she recently started overnight shifts and has not been able to take insulin as prescribed. Blood glucose level as measured at home ranges from 200 to 300 mg/dL. The patient's most recent ophthalmology evaluation was 3 months ago and was unremarkable, with visual acuity measured as 20/20. Vital signs are normal. On physical examination, extraocular movements and pupillary responses are normal. There is no conjunctival edema or erythema. Visual acuity using a Snellen chart is 20/50. The fundus appears grossly normal on ophthalmoscopic examination, and tonometry readings are normal. Point-of-care hemoglobin A1c is 9.0%. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient's vision change?

questions.explanation: Thoracic aortic aneurysm Risk factors Advanced age (>60), smoking, HTN Connective tissue disease (eg, Marfan syndrome) Family history, bicuspid aortic valve Clinical presentation Usually asymptomatic & discovered incidentally Subacute symptoms due to expansion: Vague chest/back pain Compression of structures (eg, hoarseness, dysphagia) Symptoms indicate imminent risk of dissection/rupture Imaging CXR may show widened mediastinum, enlarged aortic knob Chest CT or MR angiography for diagnostic confirmation CXR = chest x-ray; HTN = hypertension. This patient's new-onset, persistent, and worsening chest pain in the setting of underlying bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) should raise suspicion for an expanding thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA). Patients with BAV are at increased risk for ascending aortic aneurysm at a relatively young age and are recommended to undergo routine surveillance. TAA is usually asymptomatic, but an expanding TAA can cause chest pain due to encroachment on surrounding tissues (eg, mediastinal or neck tissues), as well as other symptoms due to compression of nearby structures (eg, dysphagia due to esophageal compression, hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression, cough due to tracheobronchial compression). Other potential complications include heart failure due to aortic root dilation causing aortic valve regurgitation and ischemic chest pain due to coronary artery compression. Chest x-ray may be unremarkable or reveal nonspecific abnormalities (eg, mediastinal widening); therefore, chest CT aortography (or MR aortography) is indicated to fully visualize the thoracic aorta. An expanding TAA causing symptoms is at imminent risk for dissection and rupture and requires prompt surgical repair. (Choice A) Contrast esophagography can be used to diagnose esophageal perforation (ie, Boerhaave syndrome). However, nontraumatic esophageal perforation typically occurs following an episode of severe retching and presents with sudden-onset and severe, rather than gradually worsening, retrosternal pain. (Choices C and E) Pharmacologic stress radionuclide imaging and treadmill stress testing can be used to evaluate for ischemic chest pain due to underlying coronary artery disease (CAD). However, substantial CAD is unlikely in this relatively young patient, especially since the pain does not worsen with exertion and his ECG demonstrates no findings to suggest myocardial ischemia. His history of BAV with a lapse in routine surveillance should raise suspicion for an expanding TAA. (Choice D) Pulmonary function testing is useful in the diagnosis of obstructive lung disease (eg, asthma). Asthma may sometimes present with chest tightness, but chest pain radiating to the neck would be highly unusual. In addition, the chest tightness would typically be accompanied by cough and/or shortness of breath. Educational objective: Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve are at increased risk for developing ascending aortic aneurysm. An expanding thoracic aortic aneurysm causing symptoms (eg, chest pain radiating to the neck) is at imminent risk for dissection and rupture. Chest CT aortography (or MR aortography) is indicated for diagnostic confirmation, and prompt surgical repair is needed.

Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve are at increased risk for developing ascending aortic aneurysm.  An expanding thoracic aortic aneurysm causing symptoms (eg, chest pain radiating to the neck) is at imminent risk for dissection and rupture.  Chest CT aortography (or MR aortography) is indicated for diagnostic confirmation, and prompt surgical repair is needed.

Thoracic aortic aneurysm
Risk factors
  • Advanced age (>60), smoking, HTN
  • Connective tissue disease (eg, Marfan syndrome)
  • Family history, bicuspid aortic valve
Clinical
presentation
  • Usually asymptomatic & discovered incidentally
  • Subacute symptoms due to expansion:
    • Vague chest/back pain
    • Compression of structures (eg, hoarseness, dysphagia)
  • Symptoms indicate imminent risk of dissection/rupture

  • CXR may show widened mediastinum, enlarged aortic knob
  • Chest CT or MR angiography for diagnostic confirmation
CXR = chest x-ray; HTN = hypertension.

This patient's new-onset, persistent, and worsening chest pain in the setting of underlying bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) should raise suspicion for an expanding thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA).  Patients with BAV are at increased risk for ascending aortic aneurysm at a relatively young age and are recommended to undergo routine surveillance.

TAA is usually asymptomatic, but an expanding TAA can cause chest pain due to encroachment on surrounding tissues (eg, mediastinal or neck tissues), as well as other symptoms due to compression of nearby structures (eg, dysphagia due to esophageal compression, hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression, cough due to tracheobronchial compression).  Other potential complications include heart failure due to aortic root dilation causing aortic valve regurgitation and ischemic chest pain due to coronary artery compression.  Chest x-ray may be unremarkable or reveal nonspecific abnormalities (eg, mediastinal widening); therefore, chest CT aortography (or MR aortography) is indicated to fully visualize the thoracic aorta.  An expanding TAA causing symptoms is at imminent risk for dissection and rupture and requires prompt surgical repair.

wrongAnswers.A: (Choice A)  Contrast esophagography can be used to diagnose esophageal perforation (ie, Boerhaave syndrome).  However, nontraumatic esophageal perforation typically occurs following an episode of severe retching and presents with sudden-onset and severe, rather than gradually worsening, retrosternal pain.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choices C and E)  Pharmacologic stress radionuclide imaging and treadmill stress testing can be used to evaluate for ischemic chest pain due to underlying coronary artery disease (CAD).  However, substantial CAD is unlikely in this relatively young patient, especially since the pain does not worsen with exertion and his ECG demonstrates no findings to suggest myocardial ischemia.  His history of BAV with a lapse in routine surveillance should raise suspicion for an expanding TAA.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Pulmonary function testing is useful in the diagnosis of obstructive lung disease (eg, asthma).  Asthma may sometimes present with chest tightness, but chest pain radiating to the neck would be highly unusual.  In addition, the chest tightness would typically be accompanied by cough and/or shortness of breath.
wrongAnswers.E: See the shared discussion for choice C.

questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism Etiology Parathyroid adenoma (most common), hyperplasia, carcinoma Increased risk in MEN types 1 & 2A Symptoms Asymptomatic (most common) Mild, nonspecific symptoms (eg, fatigue, constipation) Abdominal pain, renal stones, bone pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms May be unmasked by thiazide diuretics Diagnostic findings Hypercalcemia Elevated or inappropriately normal PTH Elevated 24-hour urinary calcium excretion MEN = multiple endocrine neoplasia; PTH = parathyroid hormone. This patient with hypercalcemia most likely has primary hyperparathyroidism. This condition is most commonly caused by autonomously functioning parathyroid tissue (eg, adenoma), which escapes the normal inhibitory feedback effect of rising extracellular calcium levels on parathyroid hormone (PTH) production, resulting in hypercalcemia with elevated PTH levels. Patients with uncomplicated hyperparathyroidism often remain undiagnosed because calcium levels are typically only modestly elevated and associated symptoms may be mild or absent. However, as seen in this patient, the diagnosis can be unmasked by the addition of thiazide diuretics (eg, chlorthalidone), which increase calcium reabsorption in the distal renal tubule. Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism can develop significant hypercalcemia and associated symptoms (eg, fatigue, constipation) after taking these drugs. In contrast, otherwise healthy patients are unlikely to develop significant hypercalcemia with thiazide use because rising calcium levels suppress PTH secretion. (Choice A) Medications that promote osmotic diuresis (eg, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) can sometimes result in significant plasma volume contraction, which concentrates the remaining albumin and other proteins. Because circulating calcium is largely albumin-bound, the proportional increase in calcium binding to albumin can lead to pseudohypercalcemia, characterized by an increase in measured serum calcium (ie, total serum calcium, uncorrected for albumin) without an increase in ionized calcium. However, this patient's albumin concentration is normal, making significant volume depletion and pseudohypercalcemia unlikely (ie, both his measured and corrected serum calcium levels are elevated). (Choices B and C) Malignancy is a common cause of symptomatic hypercalcemia, either due to bone metastasis with release of calcium from bone, or as a paraneoplastic syndrome due to production of parathyroid hormone-related protein (eg, lung cancer). In such cases, PTH is suppressed. (Choice E) Granulomatous diseases (eg, sarcoidosis) can cause hypercalcemia due to increased production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (active form of vitamin D), which induces intestinal calcium absorption. However, PTH is suppressed. Educational objective: Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism (eg, autonomously functioning parathyroid tissue) have hypercalcemia in the setting of elevated parathyroid hormone. The disorder is typically mild and can remain undiagnosed; however, the addition of thiazide diuretics, which decrease urinary calcium excretion, can precipitate significant hypercalcemia and unmask the diagnosis.
