questions.explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion Risk factors Atherosclerotic risk factors (eg, hypertension, diabetes mellitus) Embolic sources (eg, carotid stenosis, valvular heart disease) Giant cell arteritis Clinical features Acute monocular vision loss ("dark curtain over one eye") Painless Isolated (ie, often no other associated symptoms) Examination findings Severe-profound monocular vision loss Otherwise normal neurologic examination Funduscopy: pale retina with a macular cherry-red spot Treatment Revascularization (eg, tPA) Corticosteroids (in patients with suspected giant cell arteritis) Management of underlying etiology (eg, carotid ultrasound, antiplatelet therapy) tPA = tissue plasminogen activator. This patient has acute, painless, profound, monocular vision loss. He also has a left afferent pupillary defect (APD), indicating a damaged left optic nerve or retina. APD is characterized by sluggish or absent bilateral pupillary constriction when shining a light into the affected eye but normal bilateral pupillary constriction when shining a light into the unaffected eye (because signals from this eye bypass the damaged optic nerve). Given the patient's known atherosclerotic risk factors (hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus), this presentation is very concerning for central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), an ophthalmologic emergency due to vascular occlusion causing optic nerve/retinal ischemia. By analogy with stroke, CRAO can be due to embolism (eg, carotid artery atherosclerosis) or—less commonly—vasculitis (eg, giant cell arteritis). The most important next step to diagnose this condition is a dilated funduscopic examination, which often reveals a pale retina (due to ischemia that makes it more opaque) with a macular cherry-red spot (the fovea is thinnest here, so the red choroid is visible underneath). (Choice B) Fluorescein angiography (evaluating retinal vasculature) can be used as a confirmatory test for CRAO, but it is often not needed given a classic history and funduscopic examination. (Choice C) Ocular tonometry can be used to diagnose glaucoma, which can present acutely with vision loss and pupillary defects. However, patients with acute glaucoma usually have pain (eye pain and headache), corneal edema/cloudiness, and conjunctival erythema. The vision loss from acute glaucoma is also usually less profound than in CRAO and is classically described as halos around lights. (Choice D) MRI of the brain should be obtained in patients with concern for stroke. Although CRAO is a vascular occlusive complication, total monocular vision loss in the absence of other associated neurologic symptoms localizes only to the central retinal artery. MRI of the brain often does not reveal the occlusion in the retinal artery, and the diagnosis can usually be made more quickly with funduscopy. (Choice E) Visual field testing can be helpful if a patient with acute vision loss retains some visual perception. However, funduscopy is usually performed first. Moreover, in this patient who cannot even distinguish fingers, visual field testing is unlikely to be helpful. Educational objective: Central retinal artery occlusion presents with acute, painless, profound, monocular vision loss without other associated neurologic findings. Diagnosis is usually clinical with history and funduscopic examination that classically shows a pale retina with a macular cherry-red spot.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to loss of vision in his left eye. He says that he was playing catch with his grandchildren 2 hours ago when the vision in his left eye "just went away." He did not experience any noticeable trauma and has had no pain. The right eye is unaffected. Medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, both of which have been reasonably well controlled with medication. On examination, extraocular movements are intact, and there is no conjunctival erythema or edema. There is an afferent pupillary defect of the left eye. He has light perception in both eyes, but he cannot distinguish fingers with the left eye. Right eye visual acuity is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Obesity & pregnancy-related complications Pregnancy & delivery Infertility Miscarriage Gestational diabetes mellitus Hypertensive disorders Shoulder dystocia Cesarean delivery Postpartum Hemorrhage Infection Venous thromboembolism Fetal Preterm birth Congenital malformations Macrosomia & large for gestational age Stillbirth The preconception visit (ie, health maintenance visit prior to conception) is an ideal time for counseling and planned intervention to address medical comorbidities and other health maintenance concerns prior to pregnancy to reduce both maternal and neonatal morbidity. Optimization of comorbid conditions: in this patient, this includes discussion of asthma and obesity. Poorly controlled asthma in pregnancy is associated with both maternal (eg, respiratory distress) and fetal (eg, growth restriction) complications. This patient's asthma is controlled with her current regimen of inhaled glucocorticoids and long-acting beta agonists, which are both safe in pregnancy and should be continued to minimize complications (Choices B and C). Obesity is associated with various antenatal (eg, gestational diabetes mellitus), fetal (eg, stillbirth, macrosomia), and delivery (eg, shoulder dystocia, hemorrhage) complications. Therefore, in this patient, weight reduction prior to pregnancy is the most important recommendation. Although normalization of BMI is ideal, even modest prepregnancy weight loss is associated with improved pregnancy outcomes. However, weight loss during pregnancy is not recommended due to an increased risk of neonates who are small for gestational age. Prenatal vitamins: Pregnancy increases the daily requirements for micronutrients and other minerals (eg, iron, calcium, folic acid) that are often not adequately consumed; therefore, initiation of a daily prenatal vitamin is recommended. Folic acid is especially important prior to conception to prevent neural tube defects (NTD). The standard daily recommended intake (0.4 mg) is found in prenatal vitamins. Although obesity is associated with a slight increased risk of NTDs, additional folic acid is not effective at reducing this risk. Therefore, this patient does not need additional folic acid beyond her prenatal vitamin (Choice A). Vaccination review: Vaccines help prevent congenital infections (eg, rubella, varicella) and their sequelae, and administration of live virus vaccinations (eg, varicella; measles, mumps, and rubella) is recommended at least 1 month prior to conception. Tetanus–reduced diphtheria–acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccination is recommended during each pregnancy between 27 and 36 weeks gestation to provide passive neonatal immunity through the transplacental transfer of maternal antibodies. Vaccination prior to pregnancy is ineffective at providing neonatal immunity (Choice E). Educational objective: Obesity during pregnancy is associated with antenatal, delivery, postpartum, and fetal complications. The preconception visit is an ideal time to encourage prepregnancy weight loss to optimize pregnancy outcomes.

questions.explanation: A panic attack can present similarly to acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Although this patient has a history of panic disorder and much of her presentation could be explained by a panic attack (eg, chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia, tachypnea), a panic attack would not explain even a mild degree of hypoxemia (PaO2 <75 mm Hg). In addition, oral contraceptives induce hypercoagulability and increase the risk for venous thromboembolism. Using the modified Wells criteria, hypoxemia with clear lungs on chest x-ray is best explained by PE (+3 points), and combined with tachycardia (+1.5 points) gives this patient likely probability of PE (score >4). CT pulmonary angiography is the test of choice for the initial diagnostic evaluation of patients with likely probability of PE. Acute respiratory alkalosis is the expected acid-base finding in a panic attack (due to anxiety-driven hyperventilation), but it is also the expected finding in acute PE because the ventilation/perfusion mismatch created by PE stimulates hyperventilation. (Choice B) Inhaled albuterol and ipratropium can be helpful during an exacerbation of obstructive lung disease (eg, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), but this patient has no wheezing on physical examination and no evidence of airtrapping on chest x-ray to suggest obstructive lung disease. (Choice C) An intravenous benzodiazepine (eg, lorazepam) would be appropriate in the management of a panic attack. However, this patient's hypoxemia is not explained by a panic attack. Benzodiazepines should be avoided in suspected PE because they cause respiratory depression and could worsen hypoxemia. (Choice D) Rebreathing into a paper bag can increase blood CO2 levels and may sometimes help calm a panic attack, but it can worsen hypoxemia and is not appropriate in patients with suspected respiratory pathology. (Choice E) Serial serum troponin measurements are appropriate for patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS). ACS can present with chest pain and shortness of breath, but it is unlikely in this young woman with no risk factors for coronary artery disease. It also would not explain hypoxemia in the setting of clear lungs (pulmonary edema is the expected cause of hypoxemia in ACS). Educational objective: A panic attack can present similarly to acute pulmonary embolism, but a panic attack does not explain even a mild degree of hypoxemia. CT pulmonary angiography is the test of choice for the initial diagnostic evaluation of patients with likely probability of pulmonary embolism.

A panic attack can present similarly to acute pulmonary embolism (PE).  Although this patient has a history of panic disorder and much of her presentation could be explained by a panic attack (eg, chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia, tachypnea), a panic attack would not explain even a mild degree of hypoxemia (PaO2 <75 mm Hg).  In addition, oral contraceptives induce hypercoagulability and increase the risk for venous thromboembolism.

Using the modified Wells criteria, hypoxemia with clear lungs on chest x-ray is best explained by PE (+3 points), and combined with tachycardia (+1.5 points) gives this patient likely probability of PE (score >4).  CT pulmonary angiography is the test of choice for the initial diagnostic evaluation of patients with likely probability of PE.

Acute respiratory alkalosis is the expected acid-base finding in a panic attack (due to anxiety-driven hyperventilation), but it is also the expected finding in acute PE because the ventilation/perfusion mismatch created by PE stimulates hyperventilation.

wrongAnswers.B: (Choice B)  Inhaled albuterol and ipratropium can be helpful during an exacerbation of obstructive lung disease (eg, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), but this patient has no wheezing on physical examination and no evidence of airtrapping on chest x-ray to suggest obstructive lung disease.
wrongAnswers.C: (Choice C)  An intravenous benzodiazepine (eg, lorazepam) would be appropriate in the management of a panic attack.  However, this patient's hypoxemia is not explained by a panic attack.  Benzodiazepines should be avoided in suspected PE because they cause respiratory depression and could worsen hypoxemia.
wrongAnswers.D: (Choice D)  Rebreathing into a paper bag can increase blood CO2 levels and may sometimes help calm a panic attack, but it can worsen hypoxemia and is not appropriate in patients with suspected respiratory pathology.
wrongAnswers.E: (Choice E)  Serial serum troponin measurements are appropriate for patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS).  ACS can present with chest pain and shortness of breath, but it is unlikely in this young woman with no risk factors for coronary artery disease.  It also would not explain hypoxemia in the setting of clear lungs (pulmonary edema is the expected cause of hypoxemia in ACS).
